title: From shocking cruelty to the reason Claudia hid in a bush: 10 things you need to know about The Celebrity Traitors | Television | The Guardian
description: Meltdowns, more contestants, Ross Kemp being ‘the daddy’: read on for our guide to the return of TV’s best reality gameshow
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Meltdowns, more contestants, Ross Kemp being ‘the daddy’: read on for our guide to the return of TV’s best reality gameshow
Content: Ross Kemp, James Blunt, Myha’la, Rob Beckett, Prof Hannah Fry, Richard E Grant, Sharon Rooney, Bella Ramsey, Romesh Ranganathan, Jerry Hall, Claudia Winkleman, Amol Rajan, Miranda Hart, Maya Jama, James Acaster, Sebastian Croft, Michael Sheen, Joe Lycett, Julie Hesmondhalgh, Joanne McNally, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and King Kenny.Photograph: Cody Burridge/BBC/Studio Lambert/BBC CreativeView image in fullscreenRoss Kemp, James Blunt, Myha’la, Rob Beckett, Prof Hannah Fry, Richard E Grant, Sharon Rooney, Bella Ramsey, Romesh Ranganathan, Jerry Hall, Claudia Winkleman, Amol Rajan, Miranda Hart, Maya Jama, James Acaster, Sebastian Croft, Michael Sheen, Joe Lycett, Julie Hesmondhalgh, Joanne McNally, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and King Kenny.Photograph: Cody Burridge/BBC/Studio Lambert/BBC CreativeTelevisionFrom shocking cruelty to the reason Claudia hid in a bush: 10 things you need to know about The Celebrity TraitorsMeltdowns, more contestants, Ross Kemp being ‘the daddy’: read on for our guide to the return of TV’s best reality gameshowMichael HoganFri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrepare to become obsessed with famous people backstabbing and betraying one another in a Scottish castle. Yes, autumn is upon us, meaning the return of last year’s TV sensation, TheCelebrityTraitors.The inaugural VIP version of the BBC’s reality gameshow proved a runaway hit and broke ratings records asAlan Carrchaotically schemed and sobbed his way to victory. The second series promises to be bigger, better and more murderous with extra episodes, shock twists and an even starrier lineup.The cloaks are freshly laundered. Poisoned chalices have been polished.Claudia Winklemanhas fluffed her pet owl’s feathers. With less than a week to go, here’s everything you need to know …1. The famous facesThis year’s contest has an expanded field of 21, up from 19, and has attracted what has been hailed as “one of the most high-profile casts ever assembled for a reality show”. Filming took place from late May to early June in the now-familiar surroundings of Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands. The cast stayed 30 miles away at Inverness Airport’s Courtyard by Marriott hotel.The headline names – “Big Dogs”, in Traitors parlance – are the actorsRichard E Grantand Michael Sheen, the supermodel Jerry Hall and the comedian Miranda Hart, making a welcome TV comeback after years out of the spotlight due to chronic illness. They’re joined by the singers James Blunt and Leigh-Anne Pinnock, formerly of girlband Little Mix, alongside soap royalty Ross Kemp (AKA EastEnders’ Grant Mitchell) and Julie Hesmondhalgh (AKA Coronation Street’s Hayley Cropper).There are boffins in the mathematician Prof Hannah Fry and University Challenge quizmaster Amol Rajan, plus half a dozen relative youngsters: the actorsBella Ramsey, Myha’la, Sebastian Croft and Sharon Rooney, plus the Love Island presenter Maya Jama and the content creator King Kenny. The cast is rounded out by slightly too many comedians: Joanne McNally, Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan, Joe Lycett and James Acaster.View image in fullscreenFringe benefits … Claudia Winkleman is back in the chair.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge2. The haute hostShe might have bowed out ofStrictly Come Dancingbut fear not, Winkleman still presides over this contest, sporting her trademark fringe and talking-point wardrobe. “It goes a little Artful Dodger for this series,” she admits. The presenter also confessed to corpsing regularly, adding: “Rob Beckett said something that made me hide in a bush until I composed myself.”3. The long-awaited airdateRichard Osman caused a kerfuffle three weeks ago by letting slip the embargoed launch date. During a live edition of The Rest Is Entertainment podcast, he let slip that the series would start on 23 September. Cue sighs of relief at Traitors HQ because Osman was wrong.The mind games actually begin on Thursday 1 October at 8pm onBBCOne, kicking off with an extended 75-minute opener. There’s also a one-off bonus show, Traitor or Faithful? Claudia Decides, exclusive to BBC iPlayer and revealing how La Winkle chooses her cloaked conspirators.View image in fullscreenBookies’ favourite … Bella Ramsey.Photograph: Cody Burridge/BBC/Studio Lambert/BBC Creative4. The series scheduleThe series will air two nights each week, on Thursday and Friday. Last year’s run had nine episodes but the BBC has realised it’s on to a winner and added one to make 10. Each will be directly followed by spin-off show Celebrity Traitors: Uncloaked, the “vizpod” (visualised podcast) helmed by comedian Ed Gamble.5. The bookies’ favouritesMcNally and Ramsey are bookies’ favourites to win, followed by Blunt and Sheen. Ramsey is predicted to be a strategic player, after revealing they have been playing a similar board game for the past 12 years.Jama and Acaster are also hotly tipped. King Kenny is the rank outsider, with Rajan just behind. Your starter for 10: will he be first out?6. The trailer cluesTwo trailers have been released so far and fans have been scrutinising them for clues. Ramsey is shown suppressing a devilish smirk, suggesting they might be a Traitor. Thespy elders Sheen and Grant look as if they’re relishing the action. Blunt and Jama appear equally thrilled.Rajan gives an annoying wink at the Round Table, which could be pride before a fall. There’s also eager anticipation of how Myha’la’s name might be misspelt on the slates. Hart seems endearingly excited but hard man Kemp looks terrified. Perhaps he’s seen the ghost of Paloma Faith.7. The buzz from filmingThe “toxically competitive” Fry says she used statistical analysis and Alan Turing’s codebreaking strategies to give her an edge. Action man Kemp apparently emerges as “the Daddy” in the early stages, leading the group on their first mission.Grant admits to being surprised by the game’s “cruelty”. On a more lavatorial note, Lycett confessed that he spent his entire castle stint “trying not to fart”.8. The record ratingsThe debut series was a smash hit, dominating the pop cultural conversation for weeks. It averaged 14.9 million viewers, peaking at 15.4 million for the final. This made it the year’s most-watched show and the top-rated entertainment programme since 2016. Can the follow-up hit the same heights?9. The juicy gossipAn intriguing rumour is that a third of the contestants, ie seven, end up as Traitors, presumably meaning plenty of recruitment to the turret. Gamble promises a “wildly different game”, while Ed Havard, the BBC’s director of entertainment, says: “Things happen that you didn’t think could happen on Traitors and have never seen before.”View image in fullscreenRob Beckett was not a fan of his headshot.Photograph: Cody Burridge/BBC/Studio Lambert/BBC CreativeThe Guardian’s own Marina Hyde has promised “some real meltdowns – mainly from the men”. Osman added that it’s “intense”, while tabloids have teased “an epic sequel”, full of “plot twists and paranoia”.Celebrities have also been complaining about their official headshots. Beckett wrote on Instagram: “I think there’s a Traitor in the Photoshop department. What the fuck has happened to my face?” Jama was quick to reply, adding: “They did us all dirty tbh.”10. The fan theoriesThere’s been speculation that showrunners want the Faithful to win. After all, Traitors have triumphed in the last two UK series – Carr in the celebrity spin-off,Stephen Libbyand Rachel Duffy in this year’s civilian edition. Does this mean producers will tip the game to favour the Faithful?This year’s extensive cohort of comedians have grumbled that the “Alan Carr factor” means they will automatically be mistrusted, making it harder for them to win. Some have taken this to mean none of Hart, McNally, Beckett, Lycett, Acaster nor Ranganathan survive until the later stages.However, McNally let slip on her podcast that she knows who wins. Only players who get close to the endgame know this, hinting that McNally is among them.The Celebrity Traitors is on BBC One on1OctoberThis article was amended on 25 September 2026 to use the correct pronouns for Bella Ramsey.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionStrictly Come DancingBBCEntertainment TVReality TVCelebrityClaudia WinklemanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: NAZA - official trailer | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Watch the official trailer for NAZA, an award-winning documentary produced by the Guardian that details the systems behind Israel’s mass killings in Gaza. The critically acclaimed film, produced with the team behind the Zone of Interest and directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, includes testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders, shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv. Abraham and Szor are the two Israeli directors of the four behind No Other Land, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025. It will be released in cinemas in more than 50 countries in the coming weeks, and then will stream on the Guardian’s website, for free, from late November

title: ‘We will get stuff done’: Burnham seeks to banish ghosts of Starmerism at Labour conference | Labour conference | The Guardian
description: The PM returns to Liverpool, where he was mocked last year, with a promise that no one will be left wondering what he’s trying to do
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: The PM returns to Liverpool, where he was mocked last year, with a promise that no one will be left wondering what he’s trying to do
Content: Burnham will emphasise again that he intends to deliver the biggest change to Britain in 40 years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnham will emphasise again that he intends to deliver the biggest change to Britain in 40 years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesLabour conference‘We will get stuff done’: Burnham seeks to banish ghosts of Starmerism at Labour conferenceThe PM returns to Liverpool, where he was mocked last year, with a promise that no one will be left wondering what he’s trying to doUK politics live – latest updatesJessica ElgotDeputy political editorFri 25 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham was not even in the audience for the prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference this time last year. As Keir Starmer made the case for continuity to his restive party, Burnham was spotted slipping out over the bridge towards Liverpool’s Albert Dock.The then Greater Manchester mayor had been vying for the spotlight throughout the party’s annual gathering, presenting the argument for change. But even he could not have envisaged the schism that would take place in the ensuing 12 months and would put him on the main stage as prime minister at this year’s conference, beginning in Merseyside on Sunday.At the time, Starmer retained a tentative grip on the party, while Burnham was mocked for leaving Liverpool with his tail between his legs, awkward and abashed, especially over his controversial comments about the government being too “in hock” to the bond markets.But below the surface, disquiet was starting to take shape in the party. Several cabinet ministers confided privately in Liverpool last year that they believed Burnham would ultimately be seen as the party’s Cassandra: comically ham-fisted, but nonetheless telling hard truths about the party’s problems.After hesucceeded Starmer in the top job in July, Burnham has made “Hope again” his conference slogan, with No 10 strategists pitching this year’s event as a definitive break with the past.Burnham has been promising to defy the political and economic consensus of the last 40 years sincehe was elected as MP for Makerfieldin a byelection that proved to be the final domino for Starmer’s faltering leadership, and he will use this conference to set out how he aims to do this.View image in fullscreenBurnham at last year’s Labour conference.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesIt will also attempt to break old habits in theLabourparty’s way of doing business, which has often been hindered by pessimism, fear and factionalism. Cynics in the party will wonder if this effort can withstand current economic pressures, given soaring borrowing costs.Hayden Munro, Burnham’s new political director, has told cabinet ministers and special advisers they must defy such cynics, and every message they send must be about how there is renewed faith in Britain.Munro, a former strategist for Jacinda Ardern, who colleagues say is the “in-house hype man”, told them the theme of conference would be how help was coming for ordinary working people.Burnham’s government would put care of people as the first consideration, he told them, restoring “the right values” – a nod to the widespread fears in Labour about the rise of overt racism across the political sphere.Ministers have been tasked with announcing policies that deliver immediate breathing room for families, but also long-term plans and investment to make everyday life easier and more affordable, with a particular focus on public control of essential services. Burnham will emphasise again that he intends to deliver the biggest change to Britain in 40 years.But the other theme of the conference will be courage, that this will finally be a government that will fix problems long been thought to be intractable: rough sleeping, social care, and youth inactivity.“‘It’s too hard’ will no longer be used as a justification for not acting,” Munro wrote in his note to advisers. “We will get stuff done.”Addressing theLabour conferencein Liverpool is a kind of homecoming for Burnham, even though he is most closely associated with Manchester. He was born in its suburbs, it is where he had his formative political awakening on the Hillsborough injustice, and the area where he returned just a fortnight ago in tragic circumstances, after his father’s death from Alzheimer’s.Burnham writes all of his own speeches and has spent the last few weeks, in between meetings and travelling by train between London and Manchester, working through his ideas. He told reporters at the UN general assembly in New York this week that his conference speech would be his own political philosophy spelled out in primary colours.“I keep saying: ‘Nobody won’t know what I’m trying to do.’ People will know, you can make your judgment on whether it’s right or wrong. But people are going to know the direction I want to take this country in,” he said.This approach marks a definitive break with Starmerism. One Labour strategist said: “If we achieve one thing at this conference, it will be that no one will ever say about Andy Burnham what they said about Keir Starmer. You can never say ‘we don’t know what he stands for’.”Burnham is the beneficiary of a gentler political landscape than Starmer was a year ago, when Reform and the rapid rise of far-right demonstrations had dominated the summer. Labour had been sinking in the polls even before the scandal-fuelled resignations of Angela Rayner and Peter Mandelson just weeks before the event.Going into conference now, Labour is in the lead with all pollsters for the first time since October 2024, partly thanks to Burnham’s own bounce but also as a result of declining trust in Reform after a series of scandals.There is very little appetite for rebellion among the Labour rank and file who have often made it awkward for Labour leaders with votes on the conference floor. “It is going to be very boring,” one senior party figure said. “Everyone is desperate to make it work.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionActivists will be pushing for conference to commit to a commission on electoral reform, which Burnham has said he will put in Labour’s next manifesto but which strategists do not want to make a major topic of his first months in office. At least three dozen local parties have submitted motions on the subject, more than on any single policy issue since conference rules were tightened in 2023, making it likely it will be one of the priority topics for debate.The only other unwelcome surprise would be an emergency motion on Israel and Palestine. Ministers had hoped Ed Miliband’s announcement of sweeping sanctions against West Bank settlements would be an answer to calls for Labour to take a much more robust position on Israel.But party staff believe something more could come when emergency motions are tabled this weekend. “There is always another demand, and conference will always vote for almost anything put in front of it on this,” another senior figure said. “The unions have very left policy mandates.”Most of the exiled former cabinet ministers and Starmer loyalists are swerving conference this year – the exception being Darren Jones, the former chief secretary to the prime minister, who will take part in some keenly watched fringes. But few have his inclination. One ex-minister said he did not feel welcome.“No one wants a spectre at the feast,” he said. “Any appearance is going to attract some unwelcome attention. I do think more of us will start to speak out, whether on oil and gas, on the economy, maybe on Europe, but frankly doing that at conference is too unhelpful – even if it’s the kind of tactic that Andy himself has been doing for years.”Healey appoints Labour manifesto writer, adding to election speculationRead moreMany said they saw it as a chance for a break. One former minister close to Starmer compared himself to Arsenal’s Declan Rice, who played more minutes last season than any other English footballer but who will now sit out England’s matches over the international break. “I haven’t had a rest in about six years. I think it makes sense to miss the first Labour conference in about 15 years,” he said.There will be time for interventions – helpful or otherwise – in the coming months. Conference is the first of four phases that No 10 views as opportunities for Burnham to seize public attention and set direction. After that will be the budget, his 10-year plan expected later in the autumn, and then the spending review next year.But if conference gives Burnham another poll boost, it will add to the chatter in Westminster that he could decide to call a general election sooner rather than later.“Conference could be make-or-break for that decision,” one MP said. “If the left looks united, if the polls continue as they are – and if we then beat [the Greens’ Zack] Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras then there will never be a better time.”Most cabinet ministers are wary. “Why are we here if not to use this majority we have got to improve the country?” one said. “If we are saying we are here to get things done, then let’s do them now.”For now, Burnham seems to agree. Speaking to broadcasters before the conference, he said he was “not particularly” tempted to call an election. “I see all the speculation and it just races ahead,” he told BBC West’s political editor, Paul Barltrop.“The time has come: draw a line, get the country looking forward, pulling together, people feeling a bit of hope in their lives again. That’s what I’m trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period rather than putting people back into an election cycle.”Explore more on these topicsLabour conferenceAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Birdwatching is close to rapture’: Margaret Atwood on why she has given C$1m to avian research | Margaret Atwood | The Guardian
description: Award-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Award-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology
Content: Margaret Atwood‘Birdwatching is close to rapture’: Margaret Atwood on why she has given C$1m to avian researchAward-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biologyWords and photographs byLeyland Ceccoin Pelee IslandFri 25 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareView image in fullscreen‘They’re social, playful and just a very intelligent bird’… Margaret Atwood on ravens.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianIf she could be any bird,Margaret Atwoodwould transform into a raven. “They’re very smart. They’re social, playful and just a very successful bird,” she says while seated in a corner of a bird observatory in the Lake Erie Islands archipelago. “They’re quite an intelligent problem solver.”View image in fullscreenPelee Island sits at the nexus of two important migration routes, making it a destination for birds travelling thousands of kilometres each year.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianThe observatory, which she set up with her late partner, Graeme Gibson, is located on the west shore of Pelee Island – the southernmost community inCanada– and is so new that there are no lightbulbs in a handful of lamps.Pelee sits at the nexus of two important migration routes, making it a destination for birds travelling thousands of kilometres each year. Ravens are not among its regular visitors – only one was spotted in recent memory, in 2023 – butAtwood likes the old Inuit joke about them.A hunter arrives at a place he has never camped before, and asks a raven where to spend the night. “The raven says, ‘The base of that hill is a good place,’ and so he sets up his little tent there,” says Atwood.“In the middle of the night, a boulder rolls down the hill and crushes him. And the raven, as he’s enjoying the feast, says, ‘Works every time.’”View image in fullscreenThe bestselling author has blended the lines that separate humans and birds in her work.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianThe bestselling Canadian author, whose prophetic works of speculative fiction have won countless awards, has blurred the lines that separate humans and birds bothin her workand, at times, in her life.She and Gibson, also a novelist, once dressed up for a party as Odin’s ravens, Thought and Memory. They wore black gloves and fashioned beaks from black construction paper.Gibson died in 2019. In his final years, vascular dementia overtook his ability to journal about the birds. Still, he would watch them daily.View image in fullscreenPelee Island is accessible only by boat and plane and sits 20 miles off the Ontario mainland in Lake Erie.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The Guardian“Our back yard feeder and our birdbath were attracting only sparrows and robins and grackles and the occasional pigeon, but he didn’t care: every bird was worthy of attention,” Atwood wrote in a foreword to Gibson’s book, The Bedside Book ofBirds. “‘I no longer know their names,’ he told a friend of ours. ‘But then, they don’t know my name either.’”Now, Gibson’s legacy is about to help expand humanity’s understanding of birds. On Friday Western University, in London, Ontario, announced that Atwood had donated C$1m (£540,000) to celebrate her late partner’s love of birds.The gift will create the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology, with the goal of better understanding the fundamental processes that shape how birds move, adapt and behave in an environment undergoing profound transformation.Atwood has championed many causes, including Indigenous education and human rights, but environmental protection is at the forefront of them.“I have what they call a platform,” she says. “And I also had what they call extra money.”View image in fullscreenPelee Island has intact Carolinian forests.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianBehind the deadpan is a longstanding belief in the power of science to answer deceptively simple questions about the natural world. How do birds navigate thousands of kilometres? How do they sense magnetic fields? How do they know where to go?“Look at navigation,” says Chris Guglielmo, the co-director of the advanced facility for avian research at Western University, which received Atwood’s gift.“We have a lot of descriptive understanding of what happens when we manipulate the magnetic fields, for example, the bird changes its orientation. We know they have these senses. But how they actually work is still a big mystery, and very exciting for people to try to study.”The university has emerged as a global leader in avian research, developing the world’s first hypobaric climatic wind tunnel for bird flight in order to better study how they move through different types of air.Guglielmo and his team have also made significant contributions to understanding how migratory birds fuel themselves, travel and survive long-distance journeys. But even the leading minds remain stumped by many of the mysteries that still surround the lives – and minds – of birds.View image in fullscreenVincent Moreau, a researcher with the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, helps ‘band’ birds that are caught each morning in fine mesh nets. Staff log details about the bird to help study their migratory patterns.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The Guardian“Our new graduate students sometimes struggle to come up with a scientific question,” Guglielmo says. “And we tell them, there’s a million questions we don’t know the answer to. I have a whiteboard covered with potential questions. I just don’t have enough funding, people and time to even begin answering them.”That’s why when he received the call about the gift, he was told to sit down first.“It made me feel so good that we’re not only reaching and having impact in the scientific community, but that more broadly in the public sphere,” he says, adding that the gift was a “validation” of work done by the university’s scientists.View image in fullscreenPelee Island is an important migration stopover for more than 200 species of birds.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianWeeks before the gift was announced, Atwood celebrated the opening of the Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre on Pelee Island. Resembling a towel hung loosely from a clothesline, Pelee Island is a rare enclave that blends Carolinian forest, dunes and marshes. Sitting at the intersection of the Atlantic and Mississippi migration routes, each spring it welcomes more than 200 species, not to mention thousands of serious birders.At the event, she was simultaneously treated as literary royalty – attenders queued nervously for a chance to speak to her and pose for photographs – and as Peggy, the no-nonsense islander who often spends months at her cottage there and is woven into the community of 235 full-time residents.The new building expands the footprint of the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, which the couple co-founded more than two decades ago to study the transcontinental movement of birds. It is also a refuge from Atwood’s nemesis: chiggers.“You don’t know about chiggers?” she says of the six-legged larval mites hiding in the grass around the building. “Once you learn about their bite – and the itching that never stops – you never forget.”While Atwood was exposed to birds – and chiggers – during a youth spent in the Ontario hinterlands with her forest entomologist father, Gibson became a bird lover later in life, with the zeal of a born-again religious convert.“At its heightened moments, birdwatching can encourage a state of being close to rapture,” he wrote in his book. “It is an ecstasy that is said to accompany the writing of poetry; sometimes it comes when we’re listening to music.”View image in fullscreenThe red-tailed hawk, the bird that sparked Graeme Gibson’s love of birdwatching.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesHis “spark bird” – the name birders give to the particular species that triggers a lifelong love of the pursuit–was the red-tailed hawk, which is spotted frequently on the island.Others, including the blackpoll warbler, are declining rapidly. The warbler breeds in the northern boreal forest, as far north as the Arctic, before embarking on a nonstop journey of almost 1,800 miles over open water to South America. Its population has dropped more than 80% in the last five decades, making it the fastest declining songbird.Canada and the US have lost nearly 3bn birds since 1970. While certain species, including ducks and birds of prey, have surged in number, birds that travel thousands of miles each year have dropped in population by nearly 30%.The declines, expected to increase further with the climate emergency, matter profoundly for a place such as Canada, where many bird species are migratory.Atwood says the four biggest threats to birds – windows, cats, toxic pollution and environmental destruction of their habitats – are all things humans can help stop.The first two are easier to address, but the latter are more challenging.“People think: we can cut down this forest, and we’ll just make another forest over there. It’s not going to be the same. Birds have specific habitats that they need, so it’s not like spreading butter on a piece of toast.”Atwood, who has spent much of her career imagining dystopian futures, is nonetheless optimistic about a future that has not yet been decided.“Let’s say hope is a built-in human characteristic. Unless you’re deeply depressed, you wake up every morning thinking, what will this day bring? Maybe it will be a chocolate bar. Maybe there’ll be some surprises. If our ancestors didn’t have that, we probably wouldn’t be here,” she says.View image in fullscreenMargaret Atwood with Graeme Gibson at a cocktail party at the Book Lovers Ball at the Royal York hotel in Toronto.Photograph: Steve Russell/Toronto Star/Getty Images“All of us trust this possibility that the doors are not locked. Yes, you may open door A and fall down a flight of stairs, but you may open door B and there will be a chocolate bar.”She points to how young people, especially children, appear hardwired to engage deeply with nature.“The passion is built in. They’re very interested in anything that moves, anything outside, and unless some grown-up teaches them to be afraid of such things, that interest will continue,” she says. “We are part of the natural world. It’s your choice of how to be in it.”More than 11 years ago,Atwood and others signed a letter of outrageafter the Oxford Junior Dictionary dropped a number of nature-themed words – including raven – in favour of a technology-heavy vernacular.The writer Robert Macfarlane and the children’s book illustrator Jackie Morrisreleased an elegy to youthful wonderin response to Oxford’s decision. But against the odds, birding is surging in interest among young people.“If there’s no young people interested in a thing, whatever that thing is, it will die out. The fact that it’s not dying out, but it’s going in the other direction, is quite hopeful,” says Atwood. “I was talking to some booksellers recently, and I said, ‘What are young people buying?’ They said, ‘They’re buying great big fat Victorian novels.’ Who would have thought that?”Birding can nevertheless appear to be a rather niche interest. To those who do not quite grasp the appeal: “I don’t think it’s a question of what birders are seeing that you’re not. It’s a question of what they’re feeling that you’re not,” she says.“So maybe you should take some magic mushrooms. Because it all comes down to passion. Most of what we do in our lives we think it’s reason; we think it’s something that you can put into an argument. But everything begins with emotion.”View image in fullscreen‘Utopia is impossible, but if you don’t believe in the ability to attain something better, you will inevitably end up in a dystopia. Because dystopia is quite possible,’ Atwood says.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianAtwood has spent much of her career examining the implications of societies that allow their freedoms and ecosystems to erode. But she is also a critic of those who neglect the relationship between humans and the natural world, cautioning that neglecting one can have dire consequences for the other.“It’s easy, for example, to raise money for kidneys. Because people think: ‘Everybody’s got kidneys. I’ve got kidneys. If anything happened to my kidneys, I would want there to be a kidney facility for me,” she says.“But people don’t make that immediate connection between their bodies and the natural world. There’s so much research that shows just how beneficial it is for our bodies to spend time in nature.”Indeed, Atwood’s writing has long contained a warning that societies can allow the systems that sustain them to erode, often recognising only too late what was lost.“Utopia is impossible, but if you don’t believe in the ability to attain something better, you will inevitably end up in a dystopia. Because dystopia is quite possible,” she says.“Or to put it another way, we’re much better at creating hell than we are at creating heaven. Although I also think heaven would be quite boring.”

title: ‘I’d strip for £100!’ Dominic West and Sienna Miller on nudity, narcissism and their juicy new show War | Drama | The Guardian
description: The stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revolting
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revolting
Content: ‘I decided to be narcissistic’ … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreen‘I decided to be narcissistic’ … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesDramaInterview‘I’d strip for £100!’ Dominic West and Sienna Miller on nudity, narcissism and their juicy new show WarEmine SanerThe stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revoltingFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a London hotel room, Dominic West is weighing up how much he would accept to strip to his socks. In the new series War, West plays a social media billionaire who is supposed to be fairly decent, though there’s one excruciating scene – goading someone to strip for money – that reveals he’s definitely also a bit of a git. “That, I suppose, is the kick billionaires must get: that people would do anything for money,” he says. He wonders what his price would be. His co-starSienna Millerlaughs and says he’d do it “for the lols”, and West grins and says: “No, I’d want three figures. A hundred quid.”War is a juicy eight-part legal drama, where Miller and West are a divorcing couple – she a narcissistic film star, he said billionaire – so just about all their scenes together are suppurating with contempt, which is fun, but also a bit of a shame because they have such good chemistry. They first worked together 21 years ago in the West End production of Shakespeare’sAs You Like It. “So we had a history, which was great,” says Miller. There have been many times she’s gone into jobs where “on the first day you’re married to someone and you don’t know them. It’s helpful to have some sort of rapport.”West was cast first – he had worked with the creator George Kay previously on the classy BBC drama The Hour, and Kay had written the role of Morgan Henderson, a tech entrepreneur, with him in mind. Miller plays Carla Duval, a Hollywood star who wants half of her philandering ex’s wealth – with the help of her formidable legal team. Neither Carla nor Morgan have much to recommend them. Miller struggled, she says with a laugh, to “find the more human aspects of her, until I realised it was really fun not to. I decided to have fun leaning into the unappealing qualities of Carla, which was quite uncomfortable for somebody who errs on the side of people-pleasing. To not be invested in other people’s reactions or responses. To be narcissistic, basically.”View image in fullscreenThrowing shade … Miller with James McArdle and Phoebe Fox in War.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/Sky/HBO/New PicturesFor West, it must have been just as tricky finding his way into playing a “benign billionaire”. Do they exist? The BBC podcast Good Bad Billionaire came in useful, he says. Only a handful of the billionaires covered could be considered “good”. “Basically they’re the ones who give away all the money … It was intriguing to me, the idea of a benign billionaire.” But Morgan obviously has a ruthless side – the hardball divorce negotiations, and that strip scene. “And you go, oh,nowwe see why he’s a billionaire. But other than that, I was doing what Sienna was avoiding, and I do all the time, which is desperately try to make people like me.”Was the high-profile divorce based on real-life cases? No, says Kay when we speak. Only one scene was inspired by real events – when the actor and director Olivia Wilde wasserved custody papersat a public event on behalf of Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis. “It was one of our most emotional days [on set],” says Kay, “because it’s such a horrible thing to do.”The show was inspired by a conversation Kay overheard in a queue in an airport lounge. “This woman screamed ‘Yes!’ into her phone. I turned around, because I’m quite nosy, and said: ‘Can I ask what has made you so happy?’” She told him her husband had finally signed the papers after a four-year divorce battle. The more Kay looked into high-stakes, high-end divorces, the more he realised it was filled with drama – the prenups, the affairs, the property – and ideal for the kind of glossy legal shows he’d grown up watching. “I’m a kid of the 90s,” he says. He loved the big law shows such asAlly McBeal, and laterThe Good Wife, andThe West Wingwas inspiration as a workplace-based drama. “I loved the humour. I wanted to do something with the sort of zip and repartee of those shows.” It’s the reason the cast of War is so comedian-heavy, includingMiles JuppandNick Mohammedas solicitors at rival firms. “People [who] are just super-sharp on the cues because if anyone slows down, it dies on its feet.” (Extra fun fact: Mohammed and Celia Imrie, who plays a barrister, were also filming The Celebrity Traitors at the same time. “They were so tight-lipped!” says Kay.)View image in fullscreenLaw and disorder … West with Nina Sosanya and Pip Torrens in War.Photograph: New Pictures/Sky/HBOHe had previously worked with writer Abi Morgan on her showThe Hour; Morgan’s seriesThe Splitalso features glossy divorce lawyers, but Kay says his were “all American references”. There’s already a second series with the rival law firms taking on a defamation case. Expect more juice.A public divorce brings wild scrutiny of the private lives of the people going through it, and when it’s a celebrity couple – as Morgan and Carla discover – it’s on a different scale altogether. Miller and West both have experience of this, though not in divorces. West had a brief period of what might politely be called “marital scrutiny” (in late 2020, photographers camped outside his house after photographs were published of him with hisThe Pursuit of Loveco-star Lily James) but Miller had years of intense hounding during her relationship with the actor Jude Law. A victim of phone hacking by the News of the World, she won damages in 2011, gave evidence to the Leveson inquiry, and settled with News Group Newspapers in 2021 over alleged hacking.“They [the paparazzi] were hounding you, weren’t they?” says West, remembering scenes outside the London theatre where they worked in 2005. Yes, says Miller, “but it feels like another life and another world. It’s now almost, from a kind of sociological perspective, interesting to look back on what the culture was like then.”What is curious, though, is why Miller seems so willing to put herself through it in her work: in War, as in Netflix’sAnatomy of a Scandal, she’s harassed by paps and dealing with an unfaithful husband. Having only got the later scripts after signing on, she didn’t know what Carla would be dealing with. She laughs and says maybe directors instantly think of her for “that kind of storyline, which is something I’ll now avoid”. But does it stir up difficult memories, or is there a catharsis in playing it? “Maybe that’s it. Maybe it is kind of reframing it for myself – to pretend at it, and to then remember how crazy that was as a way of living.” Separately, Kay says his stars’ personal experiences didn’t influence the casting or writing. “One of the things we did quite quickly was we resisted any of that meta-referencing, because they are incredibly good actors, and these parts are different from their own experiences.”West has had plenty of accolades, but Miller has always been underrated; she has said that the emphasis on her personal life probably derailed her career. She puts in a wonderful performance in War, as she has in other roles such as the weighty 2018 filmAmerican Woman. “I feel less like I have to prove something, and I’m not sure whether that’s because I don’t have anything to prove, or I just don’t care about proving myself any more,” she says.There are also a few better roles now for older women. “I remember speaking to actresses who were like: ‘You’re so lucky that you’re turning 40 now, because we were obsolete when that happened.’ But I still wish I’d played Juliet.” She remembers speaking to a theatre heavyweight not so long ago and asking if he thought she could still play Juliet. She laughs as she remembers: “He said, ‘I just think people will struggle to see you as a virgin.’” West adds with a laugh, “You just need an old Romeo.”Has this show put them off ever getting divorced? “Of course!” says West (married since 2010). “I think that’s the big takeaway. I was talking to a guy who was rich and getting a divorce, and he backed up everything in the show. The interesting thing, and George anatomises it so well, is how two people who loved each other can descend into warfare. That’s where the drama is: that knife edge between love and hate. You get it in any relationship, when you’re arguing or whatever, but this is in a wildly expensive public arena. Like a battle in any commercial situation, with big lawyers, your marriage becomes that.” A commodity, says Miller (she’s engaged to the actor Oli Green), “to be bartered with, and the more acrimonious, the more money [for the lawyers]”.The stress and vitriol unleashed by this divorce, arguing over numbers so big they’re almost meaningless, seems barely worth it. I’d have settled for a lot less to avoid it (I’d be a terrible divorce lawyer). “I imagine that kind of money to be incredibly corrosive,” says Miller. “I have been in proximity to people who have a huge amount of money, and I just don’t see them as happier. I mean, it’s a revolting amount of money.” West has given billionaires more thought recently than he’d probably like to. “If you’ve got several hundred billion, and you’re not solving the climate crisis, then really something’s deeply wrong.”War is on Sky Atlantic on Friday2 Octoberat 9pm.Explore more on these topicsDramaTelevisionSienna MillerDominic WestfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein | The Guardian
description: Israel and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is here
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Israel and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is here
Content: ‘The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already hereGranate Kim and Mohamed HusseinIsrael and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is hereFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTShareIn recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis HassabisjoinedDario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sandersteamed upwith Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’swarnings on Twitter/Xthat AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.The reality is, we don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing.Bill Gates’s nearly 6,000-wordessayin late August warning about AI and its potential harms to humanity doesn’t come as a surprise. One of us has been a Microsoft employee for nearly a decade, witnessing all the dangers unfold in real time. Together, we’ve spent the past two years organizing with other Microsoft employees and activists to uncoverthe company’s rolein the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. We havecollectively called onMicrosoft to cut ties with the Israeli military.But it’s not justMicrosoftthat is involved in AI-driven destruction.Watching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in Gaza | Mahmoud MushtahaRead moreIsrael’s genocidal war on Gaza wasa testing groundfor the use of AI in warfare and the results were deeply disturbing. Israel’s military used AI to identify people to kill, with12,000 targets generated and bombed in the first month alone. This was done with little to no meaningful human oversight, as documented in aninvestigationby Oscar-winning Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, whose latest filmNAZA, a Guardian-produced film, includes chilling testimonials by the soldiers involved.Earlier this year in Iran, the US military launched an AI-involved airstrike that hit Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing 156 children, teachers and other civilians. The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied onfaulty data.The horrors wrought by AI aren’t limited to people overseas – they’re already being felt by vulnerable communities in the US The Department of Homeland Security is using AI tools –includingMicrosoft’s Azure – tomonitor, arrest and deportimmigrants at a massive scale. Law enforcement agencies nationwide are deploying facial recognition technology despiteevidenceof algorithmic bias that has led to the wrongful arrest and incarceration of Latino and Black Americans. The NYPD alsopartneredwith Microsoft to build its Domain Awareness System, using Azure to connect to18,000 security cameras, according to the New York Daily News, creating a mass surveillance system that has expanded to Georgia and other parts of the world, including Brazil and Singapore. Datacenters that power AIare being builtin rural and low-income neighborhoods throughout the US where many are living under the poverty line and are now facing significant health threats from air pollution caused by these facilities.Though many of these harms have been documented over the years, rightwing government leaders are continuing to shut down dissent through dishonest and draconian measures. Donald Trump hascalledAI risks a “hoax” and said any attempts to limit the power of the technology were part of a “sick conspiracy”. House Republicans have dismissed the public’sconcernsabout AI,blamingChinese government disinformation for public opposition to datacenters. Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, hasthreatenedto revoke the citizenship of NAZA film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state”.One thing is clear: the dangerous future that Gates, Amodei, and others are warning us about is already here, and we must act now to prevent further harm. Those of us with families inGaza, Lebanon, Iran and US neighborhoods terrorized by ICE already know people living through the nightmare.The Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treason | EditorialRead moreIn the last few weeks, we’ve seen promising efforts from US policymakers attempting to curtail the potential harms of AI technology. The Houserecently proposedthe Frontier Act to embed third-party evaluators within tech companies to conduct safety assessments, and earlier this month, Sanders and the representative Greg Casarintroducedthe Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop tech leaders from building and developing technologies that humans cannot control.These bills are a good starting point. But they could take years to pass and don’t address the devastation already being caused. Frontier AI companies and governments must act now to ban the selling and use of AI technologies in military targeting, autonomous weapons systems, and mass surveillance. This is what employees fromAnthropic,OpenAIandGoogle DeepMindare calling for.We are living through a precious and fleeting moment when we can still confront the harms AI has already caused to the most vulnerable and course-correct before they become irreversible, spreading into more communities. We need to establish clear guardrails right now and shape the future of AI so that it protects everyone, not just a privileged few.Mohamed Hussein organizes withNo Azure for Apartheid, an employee-led movement calling on Microsoft to end its involvement with the Israeli military. He is also a leader in Palestinians and Allies at Microsoft, an internal employee group.Granate Kim works withNo Azure for Apartheidand is theCampaigns Director atMPower Change, an organization that mobilizes Muslim communities in defense of human rights.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionMicrosoftTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rules | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City face substantial sanctions from the Premier League after an independent panel found they had broken rules over financial fair play
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Manchester City face substantial sanctions from the Premier League after an independent panel found they had broken rules over financial fair play
Content: Manchester City celebrate with the Premier League trophy in 2018. Later that year the league began its investigation into the club.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester City celebrate with the Premier League trophy in 2018. Later that year the league began its investigation into the club.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesManchester CityManchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rulesCity face sanctions after more than 100 rule breachesClub insist on innocence and are expected to appealMatt Hughes,Paul MacInnesandWill UnwinFri 25 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of more than a hundred charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, throwing English football into turmoil.The serial champions now face the possibility of being relegated from thePremier League, or expelled from the competition altogether, after a verdict in the biggest disciplinary case in the history of the sport was finally delivered.Manchester City timeline: trophies, transfers and more than 100 chargesRead moreNeither party was willing to publicly confirm the outcome on Friday with an appeal process expected to be pursued imminently by City. Two years after the hearings first began, however, there is now some clarity as to the scale of City’s rule-breaking.The 134 charges made against City cover the seasons 2009-10 to 2022-23 and cover a number of areas, with the most serious relating to claims that the club failed to provide “accurate financial information” to the league during this time. From season 2009-10 to 2022-23 inclusive City won seven Premier League titles, a Champions League, three FA Cups and six League Cups.A City spokesperson said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”The Premier League did not comment, citing the confidential nature of the case. Club executives are understood to have learned about the outcome following a shareholders’ meeting in central London on Thursday and subsequently signed non-disclosure agreements.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Andy Burnham was asked about the news on Friday evening. The prime minister told ITV Granada Reports: “I’ve only just been made aware of it – I think these are reports at this stage. But if they’re confirmed, obviously I will want to look at the report of the independent commission.“People shouldn’t jump to those kind of conclusions. I know, this has been a long process between the club and the Premier League. I think quite a contested process. So I don’t think it’s as simple as jumping to conclusions. I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”The verdict was reached more than three and a half years after the 134 charges were first brought and more than two years since disciplinary hearings began. According to the Premier League rulebook, the appeal process has a stricter time frame, whereby any party who wishes to appeal a decision by a judicial panel must do so by email within 14 days of a decision being announced. Under rule W.86 any hearing should conclude no longer than 12 weeks after the first appeal is submitted. Any decision by the appeal board must also be published, alongside full written reasons, within 30 days of the conclusion of the hearing.Should City fail in their appeal, the judicial panel would then be expected to produce its verdict on the level of sanction applied to the club. Premier League rule W.64 describes the list of punishments available to a panel. Alongside levying a fine, any disciplinary committee could first suspend a club from competition, or levy a points deduction, or in the most extreme circumstances expel a club from competition altogether.Such is the scale of the charges brought against City that there is no direct comparison to be made with other disciplinary cases. The recent case involving Chelsea, who were found to have breached the FA’s rules on agents on 74 occasions, resulted only in a cash fine of £10m but Chelsea were adjudged not to have gained significant sporting advantage from their actions and were praised for self-reporting the misdemeanours, which had occurred under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. Neither of these factors would appear to apply in the City case, given the systemic claims of financial misreporting and the fact that a majority of the charges related to a failure to comply with league rules.The unprecedented catalogue of charges related to five distinct areas of alleged rule-breaking. More than 80 charges related to a club’s obligation to act in “the utmost good faith” when relaying information to the Premier League and to give complete disclosure of any information requested. These claims pointed towards the league’s belief that City had given an inaccurate picture of the club’s financial situation and withheld documents that might have cast greater light on it.The rest of the charges related to alleged breaches of profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) and the related Uefa financial fair play regulations. Finally, 20 charges related to the club’s obligation to provide “full details of … remuneration”, with breaches being claimed in the rules relating to the payment of players and managers.The extent of the charge sheet reflected a process that had been a decade in the making. Uefa found City in breach of FFP in 2014, a decision which resulted in City paying a €20m fine. The Football Leaks affair, in which millions of private documents relating to football clubs and players were hacked and made public in 2015, led to reporting on City’s affairs and a new investigation from Uefa. By 2020, Uefa had suspended City from the Champions League for “overstating its sponsorship revenue in its accounts”. This suspension was overturned by City on appeal to the court of arbitration for sport.In December 2018 the Premier League began its own investigation into City. A highly secretive inquiry, which required legal action by the Mail on Sunday to prove it was taking place, it is believed to have been inspired by the Football Leaks revelations and resulted, four years later, in City being charged.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancesFinancial fair playnewsShareReuse this content

title: No general election before 2029, Andy Burnham says | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Prime minister quashes speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could prompt early contest
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Prime minister quashes speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could prompt early contest
Content: Andy Burnham said: ‘All this speculation of an early election – I can knock that dead.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said: ‘All this speculation of an early election – I can knock that dead.’Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAAndy BurnhamNo general election before 2029, Andy Burnham saysPrime minister quashes speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could prompt early contestRowena MasonandHeather StewartFri 25 Sep 2026 13.06 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he will not call a general election before 2029, after days of speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could tempt him to call an early contest.The prime minister was repeatedly questioned on the prospect during a round of broadcast interviews to regional media on Friday.He initially said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea of an early election, but later became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and he was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job.Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election – I can knock that dead.“You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we’ve discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I’m not going to do that.”Talk of an early election had grown during the last week after polls showedLabourpulling into the lead with support in the low 20s, and the Conservatives and Reform neck-and-neck a few points behind them.Westminster sources said Downing Street advisers and MPs had been discussing the merits of an early poll but that even though the right was split, Labour would be at risk of losing its majority and having to form a coalition.The Guardian revealed on Friday that Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, was taking on a senior role as an adviser toJohn Healey, the chancellor, to strengthen his team before the budget. This fuelled further speculation that the party’s preparations for a campaign were gathering pace.Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, devised Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government.Healey poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell, a Blair-era cabinet minister.All the parties had begun increasing their preparations for a potential campaign since Burnham replaced Starmer in the summer, in case he decided to take advantage of the bounce in his popularity.However, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out, both before and after taking office. In his regional interviews, he stressed his attention was on the party’s autumn conference, saying a big focus of his speech would be on setting out more details of a new model for the water industry that increases public control.He told BBC South: “As we go into the Labour conference, we will set out more thinking about the change that we need to see in the running of water across the country. But it is clear to me that what we’ve had in the last 30 years is nowhere near good enough and is actually letting the public pay.”During the interviews, Burnham confirmed reports that he would not be giving any exclusive interviews or articles to the Sun. The policy of declining special interviews with the newspaper has arisen from solidarity with victims of the Hillsborough disaster over the media outlet’s coverage of the 1989 tragedy that falsely blamed Liverpool fans for the deaths of supporters – for which it has since apologised.Leading up to the conference in Liverpool, Labour members have been cheered by Burnham’s takeover, which has led to a modest recovery in the party’s popularity.An MRP poll of more than 8,000 voters reported by the Guardian this week showed asignificant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour. This encouraged those in the party who have been thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April. The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.It also showed progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting was widespread.Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamGeneral electionsLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Noah Woods died after leaving playground through gap in fence, inquest told  | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Three-year-old became separated from a relative in Suffolk and went in direction of pond where he was later found dead
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Three-year-old became separated from a relative in Suffolk and went in direction of pond where he was later found dead
Content: The inquest into the death of Noah Woods was opened and adjourned on Friday.Photograph: Family Handout/PAView image in fullscreenThe inquest into the death of Noah Woods was opened and adjourned on Friday.Photograph: Family Handout/PASuffolkNoah Woods died after leaving playground through gap in fence, inquest toldThree-year-old became separated from a relative in Suffolk and went in direction of pond where he was later found deadEmine Sinmazand the Press AssociationFri 25 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 06.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA three-year-old boy who was found dead in a pond after going missing from a playground had left the play area “through a gap in the fence”, an inquest heard.Noah Woods became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on the afternoon of 15 September, Suffolk police said.About 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism.Met police diversrecovered his bodyfrom what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk police said his death was not being treated as suspicious.After the inquest into his death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday, Noah’s family said they would like him to be remembered as “the happy little boy that he was”.In a statement, they said: “Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world.“Noah was being assessed for autism, although he had not received a diagnosis. He also had mild hearing loss and was speech delayed.“Despite the challenges he faced, he was learning every day. He was saying new words all the time and had only just started finding and using his little voice. One of the things we miss most is the special sound of his voice. It was unique, wonderful, and something we will carry with us forever.”Noah was “the most affectionate” boy who had an “incredibly special” bond with his brother, the statement said.DCI Matthew Connick told the inquest that on 15 September, Noah, of East Bergholt, Suffolk, was being “looked after by relatives and this was part of a normal routine for Noah”.He said they walked to an under-fives play area and CCTV footage in the park “showed Noah playing with his relative”. The first piece of footage was timed at 2.13pm and he was last seen playing at 2.37pm, said Connick, who added that the CCTV was motion-activated so did not provide continuous footage.He said the relative, who was not named at the hearing, had provided a statement to police. The officer said Noah “left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate”. He said Noah went in the direction of Decoy Pond and he was “being closely followed by his relative who was trying to keep up with him”.He said the relative “shouted after him” but after 200 metres Noah could not be seen. “Police were called and a large-scale search operation began,” Connick said.Noah was found by a Met police diver “approximately 5 metres from the bank and within submerged tree roots”. The depth was estimated at 1.8 metres at that point, he added.Noah’s death was confirmed at 4.31pm by paramedics and his identity was formally confirmed by his mother, Charlie Peck, at Ipswich hospital that evening. A postmortem examination at Addenbrooke’s hospital mortuary in Cambridge recorded his medical cause of death as pending further investigation, Connick said.The Suffolk assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said at the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by the boy’s family: “I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah’s family and friends and all those affected by Noah’s death.”She said at the end of the six-minute hearing: “The inquest is adjourned to a date to be fixed in due course.”Noah’s father, Rhys Woods, had paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.”Football players paid tribute to Noah duringEverton’s home match against Ipswich Townon Saturday by wearing black armbands.Explore more on these topicsSuffolkEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after alleged dinghy slashing in Channel | UK news | The Guardian
description: Far-right activist who was filmed appearing to slash boat with blade is refused bail as he denies charges
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Far-right activist who was filmed appearing to slash boat with blade is refused bail as he denies charges
Content: Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, appeared via video link at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday.Composite: Elizabeth Cook/PAView image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, appeared via video link at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday.Composite: Elizabeth Cook/PAUK newsDaniel Thomas pleads not guilty after alleged dinghy slashing in ChannelFar-right activist who was filmed appearing to slash boat with blade is refused bail as he denies chargesKevin RawlinsonFri 25 Sep 2026 09.28 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to causing criminal damage after he was filmed apparently slashing a boat in the Channel with a blade while an emergency responder was onboard.Thomas, 37, appeared at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday morning. He also pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose to police the pin number of his phone, under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.The prosecutor Kevin Lucie, outlining the basis of the criminal damage charge, alleged Thomas slashed an adrift boat with a knife.He told the court: “On 22 September, around 4.30pm, the defendant on his social platform livestreamed himself from a boat on the English Channel. He broadcast to a significant number of people a boat of migrants being supported by the RNLI in the English Channel. It was a single Rib [rigid inflatable boat] which was adrift.“He armed himself with a knife. He slashed the boat.”View image in fullscreenMedia, police officers and supporters outside Basingstoke magistrates court.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PALucie said Thomas was arrested at a BP service station and taken into custody, where his mobile phone was seized but he allegedly refused to provide the pin code.When asked about the boat, Lucie confirmed he was unsure if the damage was worth more or less than £5,000, and said: “Unfortunately, it is the case that it did go back to France. We have asked for the cost of the damage.”Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, was refused bail. The father of four, described as a professional roofer, was seen dabbing his eyes with a tissue at one point during the hearing.He appeared for the hearing via video link, wearing a black top and grey coat, and spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth. He was supported in court by his teenage son, as well as fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson. Other supporters were placed in a separate room to watch a live stream from the court, a routine measure when interest in a case outstrips the space available in a courtroom.There was a visible police presence, with an officer in the public gallery of the courtroom, another at the courtroom door and third in the seated waiting area outside the courtroom.On Thursday evening, several hundred people, many wearing black, gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke, apparently in the belief Thomas was inside. Dozens of police officers could be seen monitoring the group as the protest continued for several hours.Thomas has said he would like a crown court trial. A hearing will take place in Portsmouth crown court on Tuesday 29 September.His lawyer, Simon Pentol KC, said: “This defendant is not charged with an offence of political activism, whether you agree with it or not, that is not the issue. He has elected crown court trial over criminal damage simpliciter and nothing more, and for not acquiescing to a notice requiring him to provide a pin number.”He added: “I invite this court to bear in mind it’s dealing with a 37-year-old man who lives with his long-standing partner and their four children, all aged between 18 and three, his partner is pregnant once again, four months. She is a full-time mother, he is the full-time provider, or breadwinner, as they used to say.“He is a professional roofer by trade. He is, therefore, having to look after his family who, through his political activism, have been under huge threat and due to publication of his mother’s home address, she has had to move home.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Society needs children’: Alan Johnson calls for better-paid UK paternity leave | Alan Johnson | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Former Labour minister says working-class fathers are being shortchanged and budget should correct it
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Exclusive: Former Labour minister says working-class fathers are being shortchanged and budget should correct it
Content: Alan Johnson said action was needed to encourage take-up of paternity leave among the lower-paid.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenAlan Johnson said action was needed to encourage take-up of paternity leave among the lower-paid.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverAlan Johnson‘Society needs children’: Alan Johnson calls for better-paid UK paternity leaveExclusive:Former Labour minister says working-class fathers are being shortchanged and budget should correct itAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParliament was in recess when Tony Blair calledAlan Johnsonup to his flat above No 11. The former prime minister was relaxed, padding around in his socks, while his son Leo played with his toys. Johnson, then the education secretary, spoke about his own son from his second marriage, who was a similar age.“Tony said: ‘Oh you’re a father?’” recalled Johnson. “I said: ‘Tony, I had three kids by the age of 20!’ He looked at me and said: ‘So you really are working-class …’”It may be almost a quarter of a century since Johnson introduced paid paternity leave during his time as the trade and industry secretary, but working-class fathers are still being shortchanged, the former minister has told the Guardian.Johnson has added his name to agrowing number of current and former MPs and senior Labour figurescalling for six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers, who are currently the only parents with no entitlement to paid leave.The author married his first wife, Judith, when he was 18, adopting her daughter and going on to have two more children by the time he was 20. His fourth child, with his second wife, was born when he was a minister in the New Labour government in his 50s.Johnson recalls that when his second child was born, he came home from work on a night shift in the postal service to find a note from his wife telling him she had gone to hospital to have a baby. He slept for a few hours and went back to work.“Men were meant to go down the pub, buy everyone a drink, smoke a cigar, and leave all the kind of hard work to their partners,” he said. “By the time my fourth child was born, it was practically compulsory to be at the birth – things move on and the law has to move with it.”Working-class fathers are still far less likely to take up the current paternity leave of £187.18 a week for two weeks, among the least generous offerings in Europe. According to analysis of HMRC data by the campaign group the Dad Shift, 90% of paternity leave in 2024-25 was claimed by fathers in the UK’s top half of earners – those who generally make more than £37,800 a year – and 95% of claims for shared parental leave were made by fathers or partners in the top 50% bracket.Many fathers and partners would still be in the position of having to go back to work the day after the birth of a child, just like he did, added Johnson.“The statistics about who is actually accessing paternity leave is just stunning. It shows that it’s a class issue,” he said. “It’s great that more prosperous dads are taking paternity leave, but we’ve got to do something to increase the take-up among the lower paid.”The Joseph Rowntree Foundation estimates that introducing the new policy of six weeks at 90% of pay in the forthcoming budget would cost the government an additional £1bn, but increased tax receipts from women going back to work could reduce that cost to £220m.Asked if the government should introduce the change in the next budget, despite the strong economic headwinds faced by the chancellor,John Healey, Johnson was in no doubt. “Absolutely. In government terms, the cost is money down the back of the sofa,” he said. “And actually if the finances are preventing couples from having children, ultimately that is bad for society. Society needs children, mankind needs to procreate. So encouraging childbirth is good for society, full stop.”The policy would be popular, and unlikely to be opposed, he added. “If it was, in pure political terms, it’s a good dividing line for Andy Burnham and the Labour party to take,” he said. “It’s an excellent dividing line.”Explore more on these topicsAlan JohnsonMaternity & paternity rightsParents and parentingJohn HealeyFamilyUK cost of living crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jeffrey Donaldson could face more than 10 years in jail for child sexual abuse, court told | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Age difference between former Democratic Unionist party leader and his victims an aggravating factor, say prosecutors
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Age difference between former Democratic Unionist party leader and his victims an aggravating factor, say prosecutors
Content: Court artist drawing of Jeffrey Donaldson appearing at Newry court on 25 September 2026.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAView image in fullscreenCourt artist drawing of Jeffrey Donaldson appearing at Newry court on 25 September 2026.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PANorthern IrelandJeffrey Donaldson could face more than 10 years in jail for child sexual abuse, court toldAge difference between former Democratic Unionist party leader and his victims an aggravating factor, say prosecutorsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11
