EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party inNorthern Ireland, could be sent to prison for more than 10 years over the sexual assault of two women when they were children, a court heard on Friday.The disgraced politician, who headed the DUP between 2021 and 2024, was found guilty of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape against the women in June.Recounting the case, Rosemary Walsh KC reminded Judge Ramsey how the distress felt by Complainant B while giving evidence was “palpable” in the court room.Referring to a victim statement already with the judge, she told how Complainant B had described the trial as “a terrible experience” and how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” of her life.Sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”, Walsh said, adding that as a result of the abuse she “does not know what love and trust really is”.The other victim, Complainant A, wrote in her victim impact statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger.Her sleep and sense of wellbeing were affected to this day and sometimes she felt burnt out from the emotional stress.Walsh spoke of various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years, but others which carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historical tariffs for crimes, she told the court.She said historical legislation did not differentiate between a child and an adult victim in all the counts, so the disparity in age between Donaldson and his victims should be considered an “aggravating” factor in sentencing.She said Complainant B was “nine or 10” during some of the offending by Donaldson when he was 25 or 26 years old. She had described how she felt “sick” when he abused her and “wanted to scream out” but thought it was her fault.Complainant B suffered other types of sexual assault by Donaldson when she was as young as “seven or eight”.Donaldson, 63, who is planning to appeal, sat stony-faced throughout the 70-minute pre-sentencing hearing in Newry courthouse.Kieran Vaughan KC urged the judge to take into account several “mitigating” factors including Donaldson’s current age and that he was a man of “previous good character”.He also told the court “there was no offending of this type” in the past 18 years and during this time Donaldson had significant achievements which were “obliterated” by the conviction.Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has already lodged an appeal against the court’s finding that she had committed acts alleged in relation to five of the charges he had faced.She was found unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did or did not commit the acts of which she was accused.She cannot be sent to jail but is appealing to have the court conclusions overturned.Donaldson is expected to be sentenced next month.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandNorthern Irish politicsDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)CrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were false | Jay-Z | The Guardian
description: Unnamed woman who filed and later dropped lawsuit against rap superstar states that she never met him, contrary to initial allegation of 2000 assault
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Unnamed woman who filed and later dropped lawsuit against rap superstar states that she never met him, contrary to initial allegation of 2000 assault
Content: Jay-Z performing in Paris, 10 September.Photograph: Edmond Sadaka/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJay-Z performing in Paris, 10 September.Photograph: Edmond Sadaka/SIPA/ShutterstockJay-ZWoman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were falseUnnamed woman who filed and later dropped lawsuit against rap superstar states that she never met him, contrary to initial allegation of 2000 assaultBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 25 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman whoaccused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 years oldhas formally withdrawn her allegation, saying that she has never met the rap superstar.The unnamed woman had originally made the allegation in a lawsuit filed in 2024, claiming thatJay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, had drugged and raped her with Sean Combs, known as P Diddy. The incident was alleged to have happened at a party after an MTV awards ceremony in 2000.Jay-Z denied the allegations, describing them as a blackmail attempt, and Combs also denied them. Jay-Z’s lawyer maintained the events relied on an “impossible timeline”.The woman dropped the lawsuit in 2025, and Jay-Zfiled a counter suit.As that lawsuit progresses, the woman has now said her claims were false. “Shawn ‘Jay-Z’ Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr Carter. Mr Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever,” she said ina declaration obtained by Rolling Stone.She added that there was “no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter. I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone.”The woman has now been dropped from Jay-Z’s lawsuit, though the rapper is still pursuing her former lawyers, claiming they should have known the allegations were “contradicted by publicly available information, internally inconsistent, and unsupported by any credible story or investigation”. Earlier this month, as they made a motion to have the lawsuit dismissed, lawyer Tony Buzbee and his co-counsel described it as “a malicious prosecution”.Regarding the woman’s new statement, Buzbee told Rolling Stone: “If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that’s new information.”The woman’s current lawyer, James Blair Newman Jr, said: “Our client maintains that she was a victim of sexual assault, but she was entirely mistaken in her allegations identifying Mr Carter.”Continuing her statement, the woman said memories of sexual assault were triggered by seeing an advertisement calling for victims of Combs to come forward. Combs was being investigated for a number of alleged sexual assaults, and – unrelated to the unnamed woman’s case – was eventually found guilty on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution,receiving a four year and two month sentencein October 2025.The woman said that after making the allegations, she was unaware of the lawsuit being filed on her behalf and, after she expressed doubts about her claims, the lawsuit was dropped.Jay-Z has previously spoken about the impact the allegations had on his life. When the case was dropped, he said: “The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed,” and speaking to GQ in March he said: “I haven’t been that angry in a long time, uncontrollable anger. You don’t put that on someone – that’s a thing that you better be super sure [about].”He said he had refused to settle the lawsuit out of court: “I can’t take a settlement – it ain’t in my DNA … I would die.”Explore more on these topicsJay-ZRapHip-hopRape and sexual assaultnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We skate on the rooftops of damaged buildings’: a day in the life of a skateboarder in Gaza | Global development | The Guardian
description: Rajab al-Reefi teaches children to skate to ‘bring some joy’, but finding boards and safe spaces is a daily challenge
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: Rajab al-Reefi teaches children to skate to ‘bring some joy’, but finding boards and safe spaces is a daily challenge
Content: Rajab. Montage by Guardian DesignGaza: a week in the lifeGlobal development‘We skate on the rooftops of damaged buildings’: a day in the life of a skateboarder in GazaAs the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardianfollows five ordinary Palestiniansas they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Rajab al-Reefi teaches children to skate to ‘bring some joy’, but finding boards and safe spaces is a daily challengeSupported byAbout this contentSeham Tanteshin Gaza andTess McClureFri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTShareRajab al-Reefi remembers the day the club’s last skateboard broke. Those pastry-thin layers of maple, carefully pressed into a curve, had carried child after child up and down the homemade ramps of the skatepark. Having endured years beyond their typical lifespan, the board’s layers buckled, cracked and finally snapped.At 30, Rajab is a leader of the Gaza skate club, a group that has spent the past decade teaching girls and boys to skate. But Israel’s siege of Gaza blocks avast arrayof ordinary household goods from entering the territory, with the Israelis claiming they could be used by Hamas. One of the banned items is a skateboard.Rajab is a skater inGaza, a place with almost no boards left. This is what a day in his life looks like.Rajab repairs the few boards they have left in GazaDaybreakdouble quotation markI wake up early in the morning, and the first thing I do is go to get water for the house and bring drinking water.Water trucks stopped reaching our area because drivers are afraid to come this close, due to the risks. We have been living about 30 metres away from the yellow line[a border line controlled by Israel]. As a result, I have to travel to other areas – water for daily use is even harder to obtain, as it arrives only once a week and at a specific time.After I get the water, my wife prepares breakfastand we have it together. I take my children to kindergarten, thenreturn home, get dressed, prepare my equipmentand head to work. Before the war, all of my work revolved around skateboarding and working with children. But now, with skateboarding activities mostly suspended, Iwork as a photographer whenever opportunities arise, so that I cansupport my family. I also spend timeposting on social mediato bring attention to our cause.Rajab walks with his son to skate at the YMCAMiddaydouble quotation markAfter I finish work, I go home andprepare myself to go to skateboard practice with the kids, so we can do the things we dream about.Getting the boards we have now was extraordinarily difficult.When the war began, I had to leave all our skateboards with some of the children I train, because I couldn’t take them with me. Our area is near the[yellow line]border, and I was afraid that something might happen to the houses we had left there, and that I would lose whatever equipment remained.In the end we lost them – some of the houses were bombed with the boards inside. Only a very small amount remained.In Gaza, we always try to repair and reuse whatever we can. We have even managed to produce fuel from old car tyres. So of course we tried every possible way to repair our skateboards and keep going. But eventually we reached a point where repairs were no longer possible because of heavy wear and the lack of spare parts.When the last board broke a few months ago, honestly, we felt hopeless. But we started contacting the children who we’d left skate equipment with during the war, asking if it was still in their destroyed homes. Some said yes – so we searched under the rubble to retrieve these boards. Honestly, while we were digging, we were working with our bare hands. We knew we might encounter unexploded ordnance. We were in great danger, but wefound some equipment there, and now we have a few repaired boards.Skateboards had to be salvaged, at great risk, from the rubble of bombed homesAfternoonIn the sun outside the YMCA, a group of about 40 children have gathered. They stand in an orderly line against the fences and watch two small girls wearing matching pink trousers, white T-shirts and long ponytails run a few steps, drop the boards and jump on. They bounce over the uneven ground, attempting a body aerial – where you jump 180 degrees and land back on the board. Neither quite lands it, but when they turn at the edge of the court, both are grinning.double quotation markIn the afternoon, it is time for skateboarding. I walk with my son past streets full of rubble, go to the YMCA and we practise skating until sunset and the call to prayer.There used to be awhole skate park that we built herewith the help of friends overseas, but it has all been demolished to make way for tents. For training spaces now we can use the courtyard of the YMCA, the remaining open areas along the seaport, or even the rooftops of damaged buildings. We do tricks in the rubble – sometimes on empty missile casings – and post them online.Rajab performs a skate trick on an empty missile cylinderToday, we try to skate using simple moves, just to bring some joy to the children. Let them do simple moves, just so they feel that skateboarding still exists in Gaza.Trying out simple moves in the YMCA courtyardLosing childrenwhom we had trained was one of the hardest tragedies we experienced. We also lost the places– like our homes and the skate park– we had dreamed of for years and worked tirelessly to build. As soon as those dreams became reality, the war came and destroyed everything.When we had no boards, the absence of skateboarding completely changed my life. I have become more irritable and less able to cope with what is happening around me. Still, I continue reaching out to many people in the hope of finding a solution.I find it astonishing that in 2026 no one is able to bring in a simple wooden skateboard – something that harms no one andcould bring happiness to hundreds of children.Eveningdouble quotation markAfter the skating is over, I make my way back home. In the evening, we often feel anxious because the bombing has not stopped.Back at home, Rajab spends the evening with his familySometimes we cannot fall asleep straight away, and we spend the whole night feeling anxious because of the sound of aircraft. Since I have children, I try to calm and reassure them. I tell them, “Don’t worry, the bombing is far away. We are safe, and nothing will happen to us.”I do not do anything in the evening apart from spendtime with my children and my wife.My main goal is to help children release the negative emotions caused by everything they have witnessed and endured during the war, while also ensuring that skateboarding continuesto exist in Gaza.CreditsVideo: Tantesh Media ServicesArt direction: Harry Fischer, Anaïs Mims, Barry Ainslie and Alessia AmitrianoVideo editor/producer: Joshua JacobVideo executive producers: Temujin Doran and Augusta AnthonyAdditional reporting and research: Aseel Mousa and Harriet Barber

title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
Content: People in Iran’s capital, Tehran, walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople in Iran’s capital, Tehran, walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranAnalysisTrump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midtermsPatrick Wintourin New YorkIran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTShareIran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricateDonald Trumpfrom a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah inLebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six daysRead moreIran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says the new deal contains the elements of June’s memorandum of understanding.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesIn the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.Republican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fearsRead moreIran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US.In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible.It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.View image in fullscreenIs Trump prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterm elections?Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersTrump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzIranTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS foreign policyUS politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Why Ed Miliband has embraced his ‘awkward dad’ image in viral TikTok video | Ed Miliband | The Guardian
description: About 1.5 million people have watched footage of foreign secretary that capitalises on social media’s love of a cringe moment
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: About 1.5 million people have watched footage of foreign secretary that capitalises on social media’s love of a cringe moment
Content: Ed Miliband speaking to the TikTok creator Feroz Khan on the streets of New York.Composite: Instagram/@khann_journeyView image in fullscreenEd Miliband speaking to the TikTok creator Feroz Khan on the streets of New York.Composite: Instagram/@khann_journeyEd MilibandWhy Ed Miliband has embraced his ‘awkward dad’ image in viral TikTok videoAbout 1.5 million people have watched footage of foreign secretary that capitalises on social media’s love of a cringe momentAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sparked delight among the diehard Milifans and a begrudging smile from those less keen on the foreign secretary, but a viral video ofEd Milibandhas – possibly – confirmed his status as the internet’s awkward dad.About 1.5 million people have viewed an interaction between Miliband and the TikTok personality Feroz Khan on the streets of New York, during which the digital content creator asks Miliband a series of questions including his name, job and his top piece of advice.Following the same formula employed by Khan in every video, Miliband is stopped in a seemingly – though of course not at all – impromptu manner by the influencer who says: “You’re very well dressed, what do you do for a living?”When Miliband, in New York for the UN general assembly, explains that he is the foreign secretary (adding that he is the UK equivalent of Marco Rubio when Khan claims not to know what that is), the influencer asks: “What makes your work so special?” Miliband gushes that he is “trying to make the world a better place”.So far, so soft serve. But it is when Miliband is asked about any challenges he has faced and, with the charm of an ingenue, replies – “Oh wow! I ran to be prime minister of Britain. It didn’t go so well … but I kept going!” – that it is clear his media team have fully capitalised on social media’s love of the cringe moment.View image in fullscreenMiliband is asked a series of questions including his name, job and his top piece of advice.Photograph: khann_journey/InstagramMiliband has been on a journey since May 2014, when the then Labour leader was photographed ineptly eating a bacon rollduring a campaign visit in New Malden. It was an image that launched a thousand memes and, occasionally, if daftly, was pointed to as a reason that Labour lost the 2015 general election.Freed of the shackles of leadership – and embraced by a generation that frames mortifying incidents as unifying moments – Miliband is now free to take pleasure in the delights of a vegan fruity flapjack, safe in the knowledge that the video of him doing so will probably bolster his particular internet aura rather than damage it.While Reform UK’s Lee Anderson wrote thunderously of the video, “Our Foreign Secretary! Putin will be quaking in his boots!”, his team were perhaps notching up the hits and watching Miliband’s expanding online presence.The PR consultant Mark Borkowski said: “Ed Miliband has finally worked out that the awkward dad thing isn’t a reputational defect. It’s his brand. In an age of politicians desperately trying to manufacture authenticity, the slight cringe actually makes him feel human. He’s not trying to be cool, he’s letting the socials enjoy the fact that he isn’t.”While the video nods to content consumers being in on the joke, some observers have pointed out that it is clearly staged rather than spontaneous, because Miliband’s aides do not stop when the foreign secretary starts speaking with a “stranger” and his answers seem rehearsed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA government source agreed that it may well indeed have been a remarkable coincidence if Miliband had just bumped into an internet celebrity who also just happens to bump into famous people including Jennifer Lopez, Sydney Sweeney and Bradley Cooper.“This isn’t Ed trying to hoodwink anyone. This is how these videos work – it’s really exciting working with content creators, but you have to outsource editorial control,” they said. “The vast majority of people who watch a video like this understand that the tone is native to the format.”With the clock of views ticking up, the video had clearly reached a lot of people who may have been unfamiliar with Miliband’s early oeuvre. But Borkowski said there was potential for the knowing nod about Miliband’s maladroit moments to backfire.“The danger comes when the choreography becomes visible,” he said. “Awkwardness works because it feels accidental. Once people think the ‘dad dancing’ has been Blackfriars Road focus-grouped, the joke shrivels.”Explore more on these topicsEd MilibandLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Game, set … match? Can a dating coach help you win at love? | Dating | The Guardian
description: Would you pay thousands to meet the love of your life? In an age of app fatigue, many singles are hiring coaches to help them find partners. But are they chancers preying on the lovelorn, or do they hold the key to true romance?
Author: Louis Staples
Headline: Would you pay thousands to meet the love of your life? In an age of app fatigue, many singles are hiring coaches to help them find partners. But are they chancers preying on the lovelorn, or do they hold the key to true romance?
Content: Illustration: Jason Ford/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jason Ford/The GuardianDatingGame, set … match? Can a dating coach help you win at love?Would you pay thousands to meet the love of your life? In an age of app fatigue, many singles are hiring coaches to help them find partners. But are they chancers preying on the lovelorn, or do they hold the key to true romance?Louis StaplesFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleModern dating is a hellscape. Just ask any single person, who will probably regale you with stories of endless swiping, ghosting, cringe Hinge dates and unfulfilling “situationships”. But what if there was a way to escape all this and put yourself on a fast track to finding The One?That very aim is driving the rise of dating coaches – people who make money from helping their clients to find a partner. According to theNew York Times, now is a better time than ever to be a relationship coach, with the widespread dissatisfaction with dating apps and a growing sense of “heteropessimism” fuelling their popularity. In 2023, Shirley Williams, a then 37‑year‑old from New York, went viral when sheposted a videosharing that she spent $10,000 on a dating coach, and got engaged within a year. Her post sparked intense debate between people who thought it was a ridiculous expense, and others who wondered why this was so much more controversial than, say, investing in education, travel and work.Dating coaches shouldn’t be confused with matchmakers, who aim to fast-track things by setting their clients up with people. Instead, most coaches follow a programme of self-care and confidence exercises, alongside elements ofmanifestation– the very unscientific practice of visualising your life goals. My instinctive reaction was to assume that they’re simply the latest way for my generation of millennials to outsource our problems. And after speaking to coaches and their clients, I’m still sceptical that they’re the key to finding love, but I’ve learned that there’s much more to it. In fact, if you want to form a better relationship with dating, or figure out where you’ve been going wrong, then a dating coach may be just what you need.My introduction to dating coaches happened at a party, when I got talking to Izzy, who excitedly told me how hiring one had changed her life. At 30, Izzy had never been in a relationship. “At one point, I was the only one in a female friendship group of 15 who was single, so I found that really alienating,” she says. “It makes you feel like you’ve done something wrong – like there’s a missing piece in the puzzle.” It got so bad that Izzy had begun to internalise the belief that she was uniquely unworthy of love. But that started to change when her brother introduced her to dating coachLucy Yarrow. A year after completing the 12-week Love With Lucy programme, Izzy is nine months into her first serious relationship – and she couldn’t be happier.double quotation markMy goal was to find a partner, but really I needed to feel happy, confident and good at being singleHow did the coaching actually work? Yarrow’s programme was based around identifying Izzy’s “limiting beliefs” about herself – for example, that she was “going to be single for ever” – and challenging the ways they were holding her back from finding love. The first step was delving into her romantic past, all the way back to her first kiss, to find the origin of her insecurities. “Through that, so many things surfaced – some of the terrible, awful horror stories I hadn’t really shared or picked up on, even from being a teenager,” Izzy remembers. “Obviously, that shapes who we are now. So we did a full retrospective.”Once they had identified the core issues, Izzy was given “empowering beliefs” to counter negative thoughts about herself. (Including slides featuring daily tasks, with written affirmations to read out loud.) Yarrow also set her homework, like asking herself a specific set of questions after a date, such as, “What side of me did they bring out?” and “Did I feel valued and attractive in their company?”In fact, one of the biggest hurdles Izzy had to overcome was learning to focus on her own experience. She realised she was so preoccupied by wondering what men were thinking on dates that she forgot to even consider whethershewas enjoying herself. “I’d always go to these negative spaces like, ‘What if he doesn’t want another date? What if he ghosts me?’” she explains. “I think that’s a pattern a lot of women probably fall into, because we’re conditioned to be that way. But Lucy would say: ‘Izzy, you also have autonomy and power here. What is it thatyouwant?’”It’s important to note that, while many dating coaches have some life coaching qualifications, they don’t have to undergo any official training. Unlike professionally regulated titles, such as psychiatrist, anybody can call themselves a coach (or a therapist, because many therapist titles aren’t protected either). Ian MacRae, a psychologist and member of theBritish Psychological Society’s research board, says dating coaches are essentially left to self-regulate and are not bound by the same rules as his peers, such as patient confidentiality. This is what allows so many life and dating coaches to double as content creators on Instagram and TikTok (or appear as “experts” on reality shows such as Married at First Sight).Even so, MacRae says this doesn’t mean they’re all bad: “Most people who do it are probably well meaning, but a subsection of them are actually good at it, so it’s about doing the research to figure out who is both well-meaningandgood at it.”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Jason Ford/The GuardianMany coaches have completed some form of training. Yarrow, who coached Izzy, studied at The Clique Academy (now known asShe Leads) – an online programme that specialises in training women to be life coaches. She tells me that the vast majority of her clients are heterosexual women in their 30s, and that the most crucial part of the process is zoning in on what they actually want. “A lot of people want a partner, but it’s about really homing in on what those top priorities are. I want to be in a relationship and feel ‘X, Y, Z’ with someone who is ‘X, Y, Z’.”How much does all of this cost? As with therapists, the prices of dating coaches can vary immensely. Some have huge social followings and charge thousands for their guidance. Yarrow costs about £85 a session, depending on the length, with clients usually requiring between eight and 12 weekly meetings to cover her programme.The rise of dating coaches, plus the fact that they seem to be largely a heterosexual phenomenon, points to a growing dissonance in straight dating culture. In her 2025 book,Love in Exile,the writerShon Fayedescribes this as a “crisis of expectation”. In previous generations, the primary goal was for men to be a provider, but today women want someone who can be a best friend, a therapist, a soulmate, with whom they share emotional intelligence and a physical connection – a list that most straight men aren’t yet being socialised to fulfil.Laurence Houde, who is based in New York City, has been working as a men’s dating coach for two and a half years. She realised that, although we’re used to hearing about the so-called “dating crisis” from women, men are equally unhappy with the romantic experiences they’re having. She usually starts with a 90-minute session, priced at $397. This features a “love life audit” of previous partners, and includes a week of follow-up support, including messages and voice notes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIf you’re thinking about hiring a dating coach, it’s advisable to be sceptical of anyone demanding thousands for their servicesHoude splits her clients into two categories. The first are men who are “a little bit more emotionally prepared to invest in a relationship” and have already done some of the “groundwork” on their own, often with the help of a therapist. The second category don’t quite understand what’s not working yet and wonder what they’re doing wrong. These men, she says, can be prime targets formanosphere influencers, who cynically use their insecurities as a gateway to extreme, misogynistic content online. Instead, she takes the opposite approach. “Usually, I find that expressing their emotions doesn’t come as easily for them,” she says. “Often, it’s a fear of being seen, so we look at that fear and dig into why it’s there, and then I give them exercises to overcome it.”Perhaps the most interesting thing about the rise of dating coaches is how they normalise the idea of changing yourself to find love. When millennials like me were growing up, romcoms promoted the fantasy of being loved for being totally yourself, flaws and all. (At the end ofBridget Jones’s Diary, Mark Darcy tells the clumsy, expletive-loving, cigarette-puffing heroine:“I like you very much just as you are.”) This summer, The Project – the debut novel by British Vogue dating columnistAnnie Lord– suggested that the dating zeitgeist has shifted. In the book, Daisy and her best friend, Maya, essentially act as coaches (in all but name) to James – a friend from university who they think has so much potential if he could learn to open up about his emotions and dress a little better. When romantic feelings start to develop between James and Daisy, she realises it’s not just James who needs to change, because she’s got a lot of deep-rooted patterns that are holding her back, too.Single men: tell us about your dating experiencesRead moreLord tells me that when she was writing the book she started therapy and began to unpack some of the reasons why she has been single for so long. (These included being attracted to men who weren’t interested in her, and suspicious of those who were.) “I poured a lot of that into Daisy’s character, which is why she probably goes through a bigger change than James by the end,” she says. “And change can be good. Right now, we’re treating people so disposably that we don’t allow the space for them to change. We’re not patient enough.”If you’re thinking about hiring a dating coach, it’s advisable to be sceptical of anyone demanding thousands for their services – particularly those who make unrealistic promises about finding Happily Ever After, or suggest you can “manifest” your way to love by carrying crystals, lighting candles and chanting. “My advice,” MacRae says, “whether you’re seeing a psychologist, a psychiatrist, a therapist or a dating coach, is taking everything with a grain of salt.”But if you can find the right coach, with a reasonably priced programme that works for you? Then there is potential for personal growth – and, yes, love. “My goal was to find a partner, but it wasn’t really about that,” Izzy says. “I needed to feel happy, confident and good at being single and exploring romance. I needed to do the work to be in a better place myself.”Explore more on these topicsDatingRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rights | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Despite the club’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: Despite the club’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed
Content: ‘Is City’s guilty verdict itself unjust? Some fans will say yes – but some of us believe we’re bang to rights.’Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Is City’s guilty verdict itself unjust? Some fans will say yes – but some of us believe we’re bang to rights.’Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesManchester CityWe Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rightsSimon HattenstoneDespite attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failedFri 25 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt couldn’t have been more prophetic. In 2008, 15 years before Manchester City were charged with financial fraud, fans started singing “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” to the tune of Yellow Submarine. This was because the former Thailand president Thaksin Shinawatra’s 15-month ownership of Cityhad come to an abrupt endwhenmore than £1bn of his assets were frozen. And although Sheikh Mansour of the UAE had stepped in to save City, we were sinking fast.Despite the UAE’s untold riches, by December we were in the relegation zone. It’s called Cityitis – shorthand for our tendency to self-destruct when things appear to be going well. In fact we won trophy after trophy. But we continued to sing the song about going down with a billion in the bank. When the financial fair play investigation was launched in 2018, the chant got louder. Then in 2023 we learnedthere were more than 100 charges. The chant became even louder and more cavalier. And now that our grubby, griftin’, cheatin’ chicken hascome home to roost, you can bank on one thing (if banks still deal with us) – the chanting will be louder and more cavalier than ever.Manchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rulesRead moreAfter all, this is a club that believes schadenfreude starts at home. We brag about our failings. Other songs we sing include “Empty seats at home” (to the tune of the Beautiful South’s Rotterdam) because we can’t sell out our tickets and “Is This the Etihad?” (to La donna è mobile from Verdi’s Rigoletto, natch) at deathly quiet away grounds.It’s not about tempting fate. Nor is it hubristic irony – we can’t sell out despite winning all these trophies. It’s simply an acceptance that one way or another we’ll always be City, always suffer from Cityitis, and come the day, despite our endless UAE riches, we’ll do a City.And that day has come. We don’t know what our fate, or sentence, is yet. When Iinterviewed Wayne Rooneyrecently he suggested we would have 60 points docked, making it virtually impossible for us to avoid relegation.It could be worse, of course. We could lose all eight trophies we won in the period (2009-10 to 2017-18) we flouted fair play, including three Premier League titles and our record-breaking centurions season whenwe won with 100 pointsin 2017-18. To me, that would be disproportionate and would in effect mean the Premier League eating itself.But is the verdict itself unjust? City will say yes because they don’t want anything as petty as fair-play rules thwarting their bid for global domination. The lawyers will say yes because they’re paid to do so. Many fans will say yes because they’re fans. But some of us believe we’re bang to rights.Everton and Nottingham Forest have been docked points for lesser offences, so it would be embarrassing if City had got away with it; an undeniable case of one rule for the rich. Despite City’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed. Although it appears this is not the end because City intend to appeal.View image in fullscreenThe 2017-18 Premier League title may be one of eight trophies that Manchester City fear losing.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesOur behaviour has been pretty outrageous at Dodge City. Failing to provide accurate and up-to-date financial reports, concealing salary details and bonuses, inflating sponsorship revenues and failing to cooperate or supply requested documents during the investigation all feature on the charge sheet. We used lawyers to royally take the piss. And when it comes down to it, that is not very City. After all, this is a club founded in 1880 as St Mark’s (West Gorton) by members of St Mark’s Church of England for humanitarian and social rescue purposes to serve the deprived area of east Manchester, where Shameless was filmed a century later.So what happens next? We may lose trophies. We will almost certainly get relegated. We almost certainly lose our best players and sayha det brato Erling Haaland, the great Nordic God of goalscoring (having said that he may stay just to see how many he could get in a Championship season). And we start building again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf the very worst happens, and we lose all those trophies, at least we still have ouranni mirabileswhen we did the unprecedented domestic quadruple (2018-19), and treble including the Champions League (2022-23). There was barely a whiff of scandal in these years. We were simply obscenely wealthy, brilliantly run and managed by the world’s numero uno Pep Guardiola.And plenty of positives will come out of our disgrace. The biggest being that justice is done. But there is so much more. City may get to play in the Championship where we enjoyed some of our finest moments (“We’ve got Kevin Keegan 100 goals a season,” sung to the tune of Let’s All Do the Conga a mere 24 years ago). League One? Halcyon days. For City fans of a certain age and disposition, beating Gillingham in the playoff is our top footballing memory. League Two? Thrill of the unknown. The only way is up, as the song goes.Ticket prices come down, allowing regular civilians back into the Etihad. Prices become so low that we fill the ground. Fans begin to realise Wembley visits and winning trophies are to be treasured. Pep has already gone so there’s no danger of losing him. We learn some humility and stop coming over all sullen because we’ve only won the League Cup and FA Cup in one season.Perhaps the biggest positive is that rather than simply pulling out the chequebook and signing the world’s best, we learn to think imaginatively. I noticed the God of Bermudan goalscoring Shaun Goater this year left his job coaching Aston Villa Women. He’s only 56, never relied entirely on pace, and I bet he’s a free agent.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFinancial fair playcommentShareReuse this content

title: English National Ballet: Rhythm Riot review – this triple whammy brings zing, grit and chills | Dance | The Guardian
description: A trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanship
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: A trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanship
Content: Peppy energy … Daniel McCormick and Swanice Luong in Symphony in Three Movements from Rhythm Riot.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeppy energy … Daniel McCormick and Swanice Luong in Symphony in Three Movements from Rhythm Riot.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewEnglish National Ballet: Rhythm Riot review – this triple whammy brings zing, grit and chillsSadler’s Wells, LondonA trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanshipLyndsey WinshipFri 25 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDamn, there was some amazing dance going on in mid-20th century New York. You had George Balanchine forging a new American ballet, all slick speed and striking angles, and in Harlem there was the Cotton Club and the Savoy, swinging dancefloors and entertainers like the legendaryNicholas Brothers, of whom Balanchine was a fan. There’s a taste of this world in English National Ballet’s latest triple bill, with a distinctly American flavour and a focus on propulsive rhythm.Balanchine’s Symphony in Three Movements was made in 1972 as a memorial to Stravinsky, although the eponymous music is from 1945. Balanchine and Stravinsky were an absolute dream team, architects of multiple masterpieces. Here the clarity of line and stripped-back nature of the design crossed with the depth and crunchy complexity of Stravinsky’s score is a perfect balance. There’s palpable power from the pit, with theEnglish National BalletPhilharmonic relishing the music under the baton of Maria Seletskaja.The choreography has peppy energy as Swanice Luong arrives with a zing in a bubblegum pink leotard, bouncing into a jazzy tuck jump like a Gap advert. She, Emma Hawes and Ksenia Ovsyanick are like a trio of mean girls competing to be queen bee. Sharp of gesture and brilliant of smile, Ovsyanick is particularly aloof. It’s such a specific technique and ENB aren’t a Balanchine company, but they do it justice.View image in fullscreenImmensely enjoyable … Micaela Taylor’s Bow Out.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe spirit of the Nicholas Brothers arrives in a new piece, Bow Out, by American choreographer Micaela Taylor, inspired by the showstopping tap duo’s acrobatics in the 1943 film Stormy Weather. It’s an exuberant blend of classical, jazz, hip-hop, tap and Lindy hop, in soft shoes and black tailcoats, to a soundtrack of jazz, clattering tap beats, and new music by Philip Patrick Harper Bucknor, AKA Tru. Taylor bounces off the syncopation, hooking tightly into the rhythm or squeezing out the juice between the beats while the dancers snatch movements from the air. There’s precision, virtuosity and showmanship, but also something more ominous: disillusionment, farewell, a grittier texture, and showbusiness itself almost becomes its own character. An immensely enjoyable and intriguing debut from Taylor.View image in fullscreenVibes piece … Ksenia Ovsyanick and Daniel McCormick in Auguries of Innocence by Jae Man Joo.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAnother premiere comes from a choreographer who’s been working in New York for 30 years but hails from Korea, Jae Man Joo. It’s thoroughly of the now in the sense that this is a vibes piece that harnesses lots of ritualistic mass-unison movement and creates an intense, immersive world through atmospheric visuals and score. The soundtrack is two works by Latvian composer Pēteris Vasks (plus some Korean beopgogongyang drumming), outwardly emotive, strung-out strings that signify angst and melodrama, but the whole piece is so committed to its aesthetic that somehow it works.Everything is black – costumes and artfully distressed backdrop – and Sangeun Lee is like a goth Miss Havisham in bedraggled black ballgown, a ghostly figure haunting the stage. Joo’s piece is named after theWilliam Blakepoem Auguries of Innocence, a meditation on the moral failures of man and our destruction of nature. The intricacies of Joo’s interpretation are mostly lost to a first-time viewer, but there’s plenty to get to grips with in this finale to a wildly eclectic triple bill.AtSadler’s Wells, London, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceEnglish National BalletSadler's WellsBalletGeorge BalanchineIgor StravinskyWilliam BlakereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s luxury that wants to be seen’: aristocrats and eccentrics inspire Demna’s vision for Gucci in Milan | Milan fashion week | The Guardian
description: Collection by the designer, brought in to return the ailing fashion house to profit, is on the money
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Collection by the designer, brought in to return the ailing fashion house to profit, is on the money
Content: A model on the runway at Gucci’s Milan fashion week show on 25 September 2026.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model on the runway at Gucci’s Milan fashion week show on 25 September 2026.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesMilan fashion week‘It’s luxury that wants to be seen’: aristocrats and eccentrics inspire Demna’s vision for Gucci in MilanCollection by the designer, brought in to return the ailing fashion house to profit, is on the moneyChloe Mac DonnellFri 25 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe’s the mononymic designer who has been charged with rescuingGuccifrom plummeting sales. So where better for Demna to stage his third catwalk show than at the forefront of commerce – a purpose-built Gucci shop.DuringMilan fashion weekon Friday, the designer transformed a convention centre into a sprawling retail space that mirrored the design for the brand’s new boutiques.Amid giant stone columns and slabs of Paonazzo marble (in the show’s case, fake), guests including Romeo Beckham, Bianca Jagger, Cardi B and Edward Norton sat on plush couches surrounded by shelves displaying pieces from Demna’s previous collections. Sales assistants hovered close by, available to answer any questions but, to the disappointment of some VICs (very important clients) hoping to indulge in retail therapy, unable to carry out any actual sales.View image in fullscreenOversized tailoring featured in Gucci’s menswear, while rugby shirts were for both sexes.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesDemna, who joined the house last July, said he had spent the first year “dedicated to understanding and formulating what Gucci stands for”. He described the show as “his complete personal vision for the brand”, explaining that his research has taught him that Gucci “is about luxury that wants to be seen”.Until 2022, Gucci, which is owned by Kering and accounts for roughly half of its sales, was thriving. However, when Sabato de Sarno did a sharp U-turn from his predecessor Alessandro Michele’s theatrical romantic vision to minimalism, the brand plummeted. Over three years, revenue almost halved.Demna, who during his 10 years at Balenciaga transformed it into a luxury powerhouse, has now been tasked with making Gucci relevant again.‘Going places with panache’: Max Mara channels audacious women for Milan showRead moreThere are hints that he is on the right path. In July,Kering reported a return to growthwith the company crediting Demna’s new collections. But the pressure is mounting to accelerate a turnaround. Kering’s chief executive, Luca de Meo, who joined from Renault last year, has said it is important Gucci is “immediately recognisable and culturally pertinent”. Get that right and Gucci’s hope is queues will return to its shops.Setting out his new vision on Friday, Demna divided the collection into three character-driven archetypes: “the rebellious aristocrat, the snob and the eccentric”, with a cast of models that captured its cross-generational appeal.In menswear, oversized tailoring, loafers and tasselled slippers replaced the muscle tees and skinny jeans from February’s catwalk. Jeans hung low on the hips while the brand’s signature triple horse-bit belts hung even lower. Blazers featured exaggerated peaked shoulders and despite previously saying he wouldn’t do hoodies at Gucci (his signature design at Balenciaga), they did make an appearance.View image in fullscreenThe model Alex Consani channels ‘nocturnal glamour’ on the runway at Gucci.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesFor women, a “study of posh dress codes” led to both rugby tops and neat little skirt suits. Nods to the brand’s equestrian heritage came Rivals-coded with spiky-heeled, stirrup-motif riding boots and clingy white jodhpurs. There were plenty of references to bourgeois Italian ladies, now rebranded as “nonnamaxxing” by the TikTok generation, with fuzzy coats and shawls worn with wiggly pencil skirts. London’s Sloane Rangers were also acknowledged with pleated A-line skirts in Scottish tartans and Oxford shirting. Demna mentioned he liked the idea of bringing Gucci back to its roots, the Savoy hotel, where the brand’s founder, Guccio Gucci, worked as a porter during the 1890s.There were also plenty of references to Gucci’s provocative and powerful 90s Tom Ford era. Demna described it as “nocturnal glamour” with bottom-grazing hemlines and metal-heeled stilettos. The model Alex Consani wore a long black dress with a slit from toe to bust, fastened with a bedazzled G logo at the hip, while a slinky and backless dress was loosely secured with a teardrop weight.Explore more on these topicsMilan fashion weekGucciFashion industrynewsShareReuse this content
