title: The makers of the 7 Up series set out to prove a point about class. What they achieved is far more profound | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human life, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human life, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Symon (standing, fifth from right) surrounded by family in ITV’s 70 Up documentary.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSymon (standing, fifth from right) surrounded by family in ITV’s 70 Up documentary.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockOpinionTelevisionThe makers of the 7 Up series set out to prove a point about class. What they achieved is far more profoundJonathan FreedlandThe epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human lifeFri 25 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareFor an hour or two this week, I’ve been in the company of people whose lives I’ve seen unfold, almost from the beginning, almost to the end. They are people whom, with one exception, I’ve never met. And yet I’ve shared in their triumphs and disappointments for decades.They are the group who, in 1964, when they were seven years old, were the subjects of what was initially a single, 40-minute ITV documentary, but which flowered into a work that isquite magical. Returning to those same boys and girls every seven years, watching as they turned first into shy and awkward teenagers, then into husbands and wives, then into parents and grandparents, the 7 Up series has become a document of our times – but also something larger and far more revealing. This week the broadcaster aired what it says will bethe final chapter: the seven-year-olds are now 70.The original aim of the show, made under the World in Action banner, was sociological and transparently political. It wanted to expose the entrenched nature of the British class system. And so it watched a trio of pre-prep school boys singing verses in Latin, contrasting them with the cheeky East End kids living just a few miles and a world away. While the posh trio could name, even then, the specific Oxbridge colleges their parents had in mind for them, Paul, raised in a children’s home, asked: “What does university mean?”Sure enough, we have seen how those born into money keep it, while those with less have less – though what the programme missed was the huge and expanding group in between. By focusing either on foxhunting John at one end or cabbie Tony at the other, it largely left out what would turn out to be the story of these decades, namely the sprawling growth of the middle class.View image in fullscreenThe subjects of ITV’s 70 Up documentary.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockIndeed, it’s the programme’s early assumptions that often turn out to illuminate most sharply how much society has changed. In 1964, the researchers only thought to include one child who wasn’t white: Symon. In a later episode, we hear the director, thelate Michael Apted, ask him about being “illegitimate”, until Symon gently sets him straight: “We’re living in different times.” Apted is also admonished for his sexism: why, says Jackie, does he always ask the women about marrying and settling down, but not the men?We get glimpses of the politics of these years. Lynn was a devoted children’s librarian, until successive rounds of budget cuts hacked away at the service to which she had given much of her life. We hear Tony complain about immigrants enjoying easy access to benefits, including housing – except that footage is from the 1970s, a reminder that the current debates are anything but new. We see that Bruce, who as a seven-year-old aspired to be a missionary in Africa in order to help the neediest, is now a lifeboat volunteer for the RNLI. Aware ofthe recent assaultson that organisation, we suspect he’s still doing God’s work.Perhaps most striking is the shifting view of mental illness. When 28 Up aired in 1984, much of the nation was shocked by the fate of Neil, who as a wide-eyed seven-year-old had dreamed of being an astronaut, and who was now found lonely, wandering and homeless. There is vague talk of a “nervous complaint” and Apted asks him, “Can you lick it?”, as if a stiff upper lip and cold shower might do the trick. Now, Neil speaks directly of a lifelong battle with depression, naming it at last.It’s not wrong to speak of “much of the nation”, by the way. 7 Up came of age in the era of terrestrial, limited-choice TV when the audiences were enormous and major programmes were collective experiences. The medium had weight and a kind of patience, so that a six-decades-long project like this one was at least conceivable. In the age of YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, there won’t be another. (Though before we romanticise the olden days too much, 70 Up self-critically notes that the children’s parents never gave anything that we would recognise as consent.)View image in fullscreenThe participants of the series in 1978, aged 21.Photograph: ITVStill, it’s not here – in the charting of shifts in society or broadcasting – that the magic lies. If the original ambition was to examine class in modern Britain, the series very soon transcended that to becomebigger, to become, like the best works of art, both timeless and universal. As Peter, now retired from teaching, says, “It’s a film about living a human life.”We see the compromises that real people in real situations have to make. Bruce was once “the only socialist in the village” who, on principle, taught maths at an inner London school to kids who had none of the privileges he had known as a boy. At 49, we found him in a master’s gown at a public school, facing accusations from old friends that he had sold out. But life, we realise, is not political theory. Sometimes it just takes a different course. There are events you cannot plan for, including, of course, the lottery of health and the random intrusions of mortality. You know it’s coming, but it stops you all the same: two of the seven-year-olds of 1964 are dead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose who remain are very clear on what matters. One after another, they say they now understand the centrality of family. At 70 and a retired lawyer, Andrew offers an age-old lament when he wonders if, perhaps, he should have forsaken those extra hours in the office that seemed so important at the time, and gone instead to his children’s school play or sports day. Apted overlooked this dimension, too, often asking his subjects about their career disappointments or the apparent modesty of their achievements, failing to see what he eventually recognised as the “power” of the families they had built.We hardly need to be told that, because we see it for ourselves. We see again and again how these people were shaped, yes, by class but also by the family situations they were born into, and especially by what was missing. So many of them devoted themselves to avoiding the mistakes of their parents, to ensuring their own children enjoyed the stability they had lacked.Perhaps the most vivid example is Symon. At seven he was in care; now aged 70, it still gnaws at him that he never knew his father. In the 1964 film, the kids visited an adventure playground: Symon and Paul, both raised in the same children’s home, immediately set about moving planks and bricks. They were trying to build a house. In the latest film, we learn that Symon and his wife became foster parents, not just once or twice but, over the decades, to a staggering 130 children. As Symon said of his own children when he was 28, “They’ve got everything. They’ve got a father.” The animating premise of each of the Up films was the old Jesuit saying: “Give me a child until he is seven, and I will give you the man.” There turns out to be great truth in that, a truth far more profound than the political point the film-makers first set out to prove.As Nick, a boy who dreamed of exploring the moon and went on to become a nuclear physicist, says, we are moved when we see time-lapse photography of a single flower, watching it “blossom and then fade away”. How breathtaking then to see the full span of a human life, several of them at once – the quiet, ordinary mystery of it. How breathtaking and how beautiful.70 Up is available on ITVXJonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionOpinionITVDocumentaryClass issuescommentShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it  | Will Hutton and Andy Haldane | The Guardian
description: Nationalisation is not the ultimate answer for companies like Thames Water – but they could be run for the public benefit, say journalist and economist Will Hutton and former chief economist of the Bank of England Andy Haldane
Author: Andy Haldane
Headline: Nationalisation is not the ultimate answer for companies like Thames Water – but they could be run for the public benefit, say journalist and economist Will Hutton and former chief economist of the Bank of England Andy Haldane
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionUtilitiesAndy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through itNationalisation is not the ultimate answer for companies like Thames Water – but they could be run for the public benefitWill Hutton is a journalist and political economist. Andy Haldane is a former chief economist of the Bank of EnglandWill HuttonandAndy HaldaneFri 25 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.47 EDTShareView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham came to power promising greater “public control” over the UK’sutilities, such as water and energy. His reasons for doing so were to cut what is described as the “privatisation premium” paid for public services by consumers, and to improve their quality. The plight of thestricken Thames Waterexemplifies the scale of those problems.Yet two months on, the government has failed to provide any real clarification of whatit means by “public control”, beyond stating that this may not necessarily mean public ownership of these companies. One option under discussion is tobuild a network of regional political bodiesto hold water companies to account. But such a step would not, by itself, confer the control needed to meet the prime minister’s objectives. Meanwhile, in a febrile environment for borrowers, uncertainty about “public control” is imposing real costs, both on those companies affected and the UK government.As a result of this uncertainty, bond issues by utility companies that would have financed investment are being deferred and their costs are rising.Thames Water is in a state of suspended animation, in part because no one knows what its ultimate proposed ownership and regulatory structure will be. With public ownership not having been ruled out, its potentially significant cost is another factor adding to pressures in UK government debt markets.In the face of these mounting costs, there is a strong case for the government to quickly clarify its intentions. Whatshouldit mean by public control of utilities, in order to secure the best possible services at a reasonable cost?Good governance typically involves seeking an appropriate balance between incentives and expertise. For public services, this means a set of incentives well aligned with the interests of customers – namely, the general public – while having the expertise to deliver services effectively.This underlines the perils of the privatised model. For example,Thames Wateris owned by a consortium of investors, including highly leveraged hedge funds. This governance structure has no shortage of high-quality financial expertise. Unfortunately, this highly “innovative” (and leveraged) financing structure is singularly ill-suited to a low-risk public utility; investor incentives are horribly misaligned with the public good.Full nationalisation faces the opposite problems. In this scenario, the company’s incentives would be aligned, by statute, with the public good. But without commercial discipline and expertise, there are fewer reasons to expect it to be run expertly and efficiently. Past experience – from British Rail to British Steel to British Leyland – demonstrates this risk.For public utilities, then, “public control” should mean seeking governance structures with aims that are aligned with those of the general public. This should not be mistaken to mean that the public sector itself should necessarily play a central role in owning or operating the company. This erroneous belief is costing the UK (and the utilities) dear, and needs dismissing once and for all.View image in fullscreenProtesters ask for Thames Water to be nationalised outside the high court in London, February 2025.Photograph: Victoria Jones/REX/ShutterstockHaving done so, what alternative governance structures strike a better balance than the extremes of nationalisation or privatisation? Aligning the incentives of utilities with those of the public could be done most easily and effectively by turning them into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim.This has the advantage that it could be introduced within the current ownership and licensing regime. While not without potential legal challenge, in principle it would not require expensive compensation to shareholders who have already considered a level of regulatory risk when making their investment. The government itself could take a special or “golden share” at a nominal cost of £1, of the type used to maintain BAE Systems and Rolls-Royce (and latterly Royal Mail) in domestic ownership.Importantly, the utility companies would go beyond “benefit” or B Corps (obliged to display high standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability), and instead would have more demanding governance requirements, tailored to their needs and standards. These could be taken off the shelf – for example, Ofgem already requires energy companies to comply with certain international environmental standards – or alternatively, stakeholders could work together to develop industry-specific standards.With this core structure, there are various ways the governance regime could be enhanced. For example, utilities could be required to have a minimum fraction of their shares publicly listed and traded, which would help transparency and market discipline. Publicly quoted utilities have tended to outperform the alternatives across all metrics.To strengthen further public incentives, executive pay could be linked to public-benefit outcomes. This could also be achieved by requiring each utility to create an independent customer group and incorporating its views in all dimensions of the companies’ decision-making. There is good evidence across the utilities of customer involvement improving outcomes.Lastly, this would imply a paradigm shift in the culture and architecture of regulation, currently alternating between regulatory capture and mutual distrust, which has palpably failed. Public-benefit utilities would be constitutionally obliged to want the same outcomes as public-interest regulators. Open-book accounting would be routine as regulator and regulated both prioritised the delivery of high-quality public services.There is an urgent need for the government to clarify its intention around public control before uncertainty imposes further costs on fragile utilities and public finances alike. A public-benefit structure would, we believe, achieve a much better balance between public-good incentives and operational expertise at a much lower cost for consumers, investors and the government. It would be measured in single pounds rather than hundreds of millions. Burnham won power by daring to be different. Daring to be different – within practical bounds – should also inform his approach to public control of utilities.Will Hutton is a journalist and political economist and host of the We Society podcast. Andy Haldane is president of the British Chambers of Commerce anda former chief economist of the Bank of England

title: What are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politics | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: Ed Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out for, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: Ed Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out for, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: The Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, serves up fish and chips at Brighton’s Palace Pier ahead of his party’s conference, 19 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenThe Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, serves up fish and chips at Brighton’s Palace Pier ahead of his party’s conference, 19 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionLiberal DemocratsWhat are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politicsSimon JenkinsEd Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out forFri 25 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTShareSeptember is the cruellest month for political commentators because it is when something has to be said about the Liberal Democrats. They are a play without a plot, a chorus line of seemingly endless “don’t knows”. Their leader, Ed Davey,recently warnedthat “we’re in the fight of our lives” to defend the values of liberty and equality. Really? How can this be when Davey is becoming about as relevant as Count Binface?The Lib Dems’ central predicament has remained unchanged for a century, ever since the decline of David Lloyd George and the rise of the Labour party. There is simply no space in Britain for a centrist party when so little divides the big parties and they broadly stick to the prevailing ecomomic orthodoxy.But there is now a ray of hope. One of the newer developments in British politics is the rise of single-issue parties. In Scotland and Wales, the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru demand independence from the UK, while in England the Reform party has dedicated itself to curbing immigration.A lack of a clarifying message could partly explain why the Lib Dems have sufferedheavy defeats at recent byelections, and slipped to fourth or fifth place in many national opinion polls, regularly trailing the Greens and Reform.In order to improve their electoral fortunes, the Lib Dems need an equally straightforward cause, one that should have broad appeal and identify an area neglected by the other parties. That cause is now glaring: the devolution of government authority.Time and again in national league tables, England ranks as having one of themost concentrated central governments in Europe, and by some measures in the world. English citizens’ ability to participate in local democracy is extremely weak compared to other countries such as France, Germany and those in Scandinavia.Welfare comparisons showthe UK’s local services fare poorly and inequitably compared with those, for instance, in localised Scandinavia. The authority of Britain’s central executive over local government is overbearing, with ever more disappointing outcomes for citizens.Localism is the issue and one that has featured prominently in political debate for decades. New Labour even proposed a“new localism”. The result was just 12 elected mayors in England and Wales between 2001 and 2005.In 2010, David Cameron pledged a“radical shift in power from central government to neighbourhoods”. He then did the opposite through enforced housing targets and a fierce programme of austerity. Similarly, in 2024 Keir Starmer promised to “deepen democracy by … devolving power to communities”. Yet one of his first moves was to overrule local discretion in planning approvals, describing councils as “blockers and nimbys”.Over the years, the phrase “shifting power locally” became an almost ritualistic election chant, clearly based on polling data. No government really meant it. Ever since Margaret Thatcher, the centre has taken ever more control of local taxation, education, housing, care services and planning. The job of a British local council today is in effect to do what the centre tells it. It has not much money nor power for anything else. It is therefore no wonder that local democracy is subject to ridicule: see, for instance, therecent “independence” votein the Oxfordshire village of Piddington.Unquestionably the most headline-grabbing of Westminster’s pseudo-localists isAndy Burnham. Does he mean it? His innovation of a cohort of metro mayors – introduced under the Conservatives – inserts a new level of regional bureaucracy between central and local government. Their role will primarily be to enforce national targets of housebuilding and energy investment, and presumably to override decisions of local councils beneath them.Burnham’s announcement that mayors in England will be able to keep a share of income tax andbusiness rateswas cited as proof of his commitment to his so-called devolution agenda. But the extent to which mayors will be able to wield these powers remains to be seen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prime minister’s moving ofparts of the No 10 operation to Manchesterhardly reduces the power of the centre. It merely relocates it, temporarily. Here, surely, is a Liberal Democrat cause.Significantly, the one area in which the Lib Dems have flourished is local government. At last May’s local elections,the party took their control of councils up to 76, establishing them as a major political force across local government. This was a major achievement. There are now more Liberal Democrat council leaders in Britain than the 71 Lib Dem MPs. As such, their impact on the actual government of the country is substantial.This cries out for revolution and the Lib Dems have every reason to be its champions. The party should go flat out for democratic, truly local self-government. Models of appropriate tiers and functions can be found across Europe. The cause is now aided by mountainous evidence that Britain’s centrist model – the famous“Rolls-Royce” of Whitehall– is now a clapped out jalopy. Every week the headlines cry that nothing seems to work.This is the all-consuming challenge for the Lib Dems to make their own. Propose a major constitutional reform. The party’s 76 local councils can list the powers they want restored to them. It is these council leaders who must stand on stage at their conference, not Westminster’s indolent parliamentarians.Liberal Democratsshould become the party of local Britain and restore the government of the people to the people.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsOpinionLocal politicsLocal governmentDevolutionAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: I love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern football | Marva Kreel | The Guardian
description: Focusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeper, says broadcaster Marva Kreel
Author: Marva Kreel
Headline: Focusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeper, says broadcaster Marva Kreel
Content: England fans at the Frankfurt Arena, Germany, on 20 June 2024.Photograph: Stefan Matzke/sampics/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEngland fans at the Frankfurt Arena, Germany, on 20 June 2024.Photograph: Stefan Matzke/sampics/Corbis/Getty ImagesOpinionSoccerI love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern footballMarva KreelFocusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeperFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTShareAndy Burnham is right that football fans have historically been treated differently from other sports fans. But if we’re going to talk about discrimination in football, the ban on drinking at your seat feels like a strange place to start.The rule may have its roots in a very different era of football, but for many fans today, being able to take a pint to your seat may not be top of their list of changes they’d like to see in the game. Especially at a time when discrimination is very much present elsewhere in football.The legislation, introduced under Margaret Thatcherin the 1980sas part of a crackdown on football hooliganism, was rooted in the idea that football fans needed to be treated differently from the supposedly better-behaved crowds at rugby and cricket – which smacks of classism and the stereotyping of working-class fans. But football has changed since then, and so has drinking culture. Fans have adapted to the restrictions and built a matchday ritual around them. A good fan concourse pint is up there with an airport pint or a beer-garden pint on the first day of summer.Fans have got used to this routine, and one of the biggest concerns of lifting this ban now seems to be the Boxpark-ification of football: the dreadedperformative beer throwwhen anything good happens.Even when it’s not performative, it does raise a problem of logistics. With no cup holders, when a 95th-minute winner goes in and you’re suddenly off your seat with your limbs in the air, a pint is unlikely to remain where you left it. There will be people walking back and forth from the concourse during the game for another pint or the toilet, too. It used to happen before, of course, but it would still be a new irritation that fans would have to adapt to. And, most importantly, it isn’t a change many fans seem to have been asking for.As a fan of both men’s and women’s football, I’ve experienced theWomen’s Super League’s successful trialof beer at your seats, as well as drinking at non-league games, and it was a nice change. It has even become a distinct part of the matchday experience in leagues where the atmosphere is different and the crowds are smaller. But the women’s game is not simply the men’s game with fewer people in the stands. The matchday experience is different – and that’s important when we talk about what works.Watching Everton Women with a beer in hand can be lovely. So can spending a long day at the cricket with a pint. But I was also at the game in whichChloe Kelly scored the winner for England against Germanyat Euro 2022, and was immediately swallowed up in the chaos of the celebrations, being thrown around by the people around me. Having a pint in my hand in that moment would have been less than ideal. Beer and football can clearly coexist, but what works at one level of the game, or in one kind of crowd, doesn’t necessarily translate neatly to another.View image in fullscreenChloe Kelly pokes home the winning goal for England against Germany in the final of the Women’s Euros on 31 July 2022.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBut this is where Burnham’s argument starts to feel out of step with the reality of football now. At a time when working-class fans are beingpriced out of their season tickets, racist, sexist, homophobiconline abuseis ever-present, and figures at the very top of the game –such as Jim Ratcliffe– use their platform to push deeply divisive politics, it feels out of touch to make the right to drink a pint in your seat a headline example of football discrimination.And that’s not to deny discrimination of working-class fans, but this is a problem that runs much deeper in the game. And if the old assumption is that football fans are uniquely likely to cause trouble when alcohol is involved, lifting the ban doesn’t automatically remove that belief. It’s possible these biases will show up in how games are policed, with a heavy pre-emptive police and security presence.If the ban is lifted, there’ll be teething problems, there will be beer showers, complaints and no doubt a bunch of stories in the press making an example of any issues of violence held up as evidence that football fans can’t be trusted with a pint. Eventually, though, fans will adapt, security will relax and, for the most part, it will probably become normal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut that’s precisely why Burnham’s argument feels like such an odd intervention. There are serious questions about class and access in football that deserve to be scrutinised as discrimination. If Burnham wants to tackle the ways football fans are treated unfairly, there are plenty of other places to start.Football fans have every right to drink their beer wherever the rules allow. But sometimes a pint is just a pint – and football has bigger battles to fight.Marva Kreel is a broadcaster and football content creatorExplore more on these topicsFootballOpinionAlcoholAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: I had Nigella down as tradwife burlesque but her Bake Off debut won me over | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Plus, Prince Harry spreads his love of Marmite to his kids, and Dolly Parton’s nephew turns out to be fairly unusual
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Plus, Prince Harry spreads his love of Marmite to his kids, and Dolly Parton’s nephew turns out to be fairly unusual
Content: Nigella Lawson gets to grips with Paul Hollywood and The Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Channel 4/PAView image in fullscreenNigella Lawson gets to grips with Paul Hollywood and The Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Channel 4/PADigested weekNigella LawsonDigested week: I had Nigella down as tradwife burlesque but her Bake Off debut won me overEmma BrockesPlus, Prince Harry spreads his love of Marmite to his kids, and Dolly Parton’s nephew turns out to be fairly unusualFri 25 Sep 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.22 EDTShareMondayIt was a big week at the UN, Buckingham Palace and the White House, but for all sentient people of Britain, the top story this week was thatBake Off is backand we need to talk about Nigella. (“Isn’t that the thing you use on cold sores?” said my gen Alpha child, as yet uninitiated into the lifestyle icons of our age. “That’s Bonjela,” I said.) I went into the opener of the show’s 17th season crankily resenting the departure of Prue Leith, who I love, and who offers, apart from anything else, a corrective to all the women on TV at the moment lecturing us about how to age from behind Maga-style glow-ups. (Youth on HBO anyone? No thanks!)And in the first half of the show, Nigella did indeed seem to struggle. She was quiet, watchful and seemingly unsure of herself in the face of the wide array of personality types on the show, who were also struggling to adapt to new surroundings. This isn’t working at all, I thought, and then halfway through the show she clicked, or possibly I did.I should say that going back I was never a big Nigella person. I bought her first cookery book a million years ago and loved the excess of all that butter and cheese. But over the years, as her brand grew and refined, I just assumed she was part of the large cohort of women who aren’t really for me – broadly speaking, who commit themselves to a kind of tradwife burlesque that, even at ironic remove, seethes with the conventionality of the thing it’s critiquing.Anyway so much for that. As Bake Off unfolded, I crumbled like a flapjack in biscuit week (don’t email; per UK tax law, a flapjack is, indeed, a biscuit). It is so rare to watch someone of Nigella’s star power comport themselves on telly in such pensive style, so that even when she’s trying to be saucy, it seems to me, her natural state is one of anxious enthusiasm and a depth of feeling that comes out in odd places. “May I just say, I love salt,” she said, with the mad emphasis of someone correcting a widely held but incorrect assumption about themselves and instantly, of course, I loved her.TuesdayWhile the rest of the House of Windsor wrestled with the fallout from Tuesday’s publication of Charles Spencer’s book, Prince Harry – surely closer to his uncle in thought and style than anyone else in the family – gave us somebenign royal newsin the form of an update on his children’s eating habits.Since moving from the US to the UK last month, the prince said his two children were enjoying Marmite for the first time – and I’m going to have to run the quotes in full here, for their jolliness and mild strangeness. “Is that a British thing?” said Harry to Hello! magazine at the WellChild awards this week, referring to Marmite. “Because it’s always been in my life, and now the kids are eating Marmite on crumpets, which is big for me.” I mean, what’s that about? Of course he knows it’s British; perhaps he feels in brand competition with the iconic British spread. Anyway, on he went: “They used to diss me for having Marmite in the house, and now they’re in the UK it’s like that’s kind of like water under the bridge, so it’s good.”That’s nice; I mean it. I was happy when one of my two accepted that Marmite was the only way, although I’ve never had much success with any of the other British staples and nor has Harry, who said his attempt to put his kids on to beans on toast “hadn’t gone down very well”. I’d watch a full series on this, in which Harry puts toad in the hole, yorkshire pudding and the full English (“is that a British thing?”) in front of his kids – but no one tell Brooklyn Beckham or he’ll be round with his cookbook.WednesdayDisappointing news from the Dolly Parton estate, where that very nice-seeming nephew of hers who broke the news of her death in a video statement last month has turned out,judging by court papers filed by the Parton estate in Tennessee this week, to be – how to put this? – fairly unusual.Bryan Seaver, who Parton employed for more than two decades as her head of security, is alleged to have sent Danny Nozell, Parton’s manager who runs the late singer’s estate, a series of communications, including the lines, “I’m a killer” and, “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” Meanwhile, in trying to explain himself to TMZ this week, Seaver apparently made things worse with the explanation: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.” So that’s OK.To be fair to Seaver, “all I do is warfare” is a great line I will be trying to work into my own conversations from now on. One wonders what this scene was like while Parton was alive. Famously, the singer employed large numbers of her family at Dollywood and elsewhere, and one has to assume kept any awkward characters in check. Now the queen is dead, can the centre hold?ThursdayNews of the one-in-a-thousand-year El Niño coming down the pike is so grim, let’s cling to the odd bit of cheer from the climate frontline. This week in West Bengal,newsof a baby elephant calf, separated from its mother and drowning in flood water, was rescued by two heroic fishers who spotted its trunk, waving out of the water like a periscope, and after following it for 3 miles into shallow water, managed to fish it out of the murk.The calf, which was a few days old, had lost its mum and the rest of the herd at the Teesta River and, improbably, after wrestling it on to the boat, the fishers managed to find the herd and reunite it with its mum, who got in such a frenzy at the sight of her missing baby that onlookers fleetingly worried she’d kill it. Instead, she wrapped her trunk around its body, splashed its head with water and flapped her ears with abandon, making witnesses on the bank hold themselves in at the beauty of it all.FridayWeek two of trying to change mobile phone providers comes to a close without success and what have I learned? That the phrase “I know it’s not your fault” followed by a giant rage spiral doesn’t achieve the desired outcome. That the phrases “why are you like this?” and “what is wrong with your company?” equally have little to no effect. And that inserting “literally” into the sentence “we’re talking about a £10-a-month contract, literally what’s wrong with you?” doesn’t provide the needle-moving emphasis I’d hoped. Time for a lie down and a rethink.The week in picturesView image in fullscreen‘The problem with this country is all the people taking money for pretending to do jobs they don’t do.’ Kemi Badenoch and Helen Whately visit Cleanology in London.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Me! Me, me, me, me, me!’ Charles Spencer talks about his new book.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreen‘And then he was like “your country’s so special!” and I was like, “oh, thank you, Mr President, I love you, too.”’ Andy Burnham chats to Ireland’s PM, Micheal Martin.Photograph: Oli Scraff/Pool AFP/APExplore more on these topicsNigella LawsonDigested weekThe Great British Bake OffTelevisionFood TVPrince HarryDolly PartoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Plans are under way to finally help Britain’s unemployed young people – will Labour pull it off? | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Alan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it through, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Alan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it through, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: People at the London Job Show in Westfield shopping centre, London, 15 May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople at the London Job Show in Westfield shopping centre, London, 15 May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianOpinionLabourPlans are under way to finally help Britain’s unemployed young people – will Labour pull it off?Polly ToynbeeAlan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it throughFri 25 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTShareAs certainly as the moon pulls on the tides, Labour governments improve the lives of the poorest children. Just as surely, Conservative governments pull back and reverse the good done. Here we go again: despite the social devastation caused by George Osborne’s cuts last time, Kemi Badenoch announces that she wants to imposecuts to universal creditfor the poorest if she gets the chance.She doesn’t do subtle, none of Iain Duncan Smith’s cruel-to-be-kind routine, but goes straight for populist rabble-rousing, stirring up fact-free contempt for anyone on benefits, with aproposed banon buying cigarettes and alcohol, or gambling, with benefit money. Welfare, she says, must not be “a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered”. As with all crude rightwing populism, the harm she does spreads hatred of the weak. In this most unequal country, it encourages bullies to kick downwards, stifling more generous human instincts.Here’s how the pendulum swings: NewLabourlifted nearly a million children out of poverty and set up 3,500 Sure Start centres, which supported families from birth. David Cameron and Osborne swept all that away with billions of pounds in benefit cuts directed at families, tipping more children into food-bank poverty.Naturally, this Labour government has swung the pendulum back, taking 450,000 children from destitution by removing the Tory two-child benefit cap – albeit with too much delay. For the first time ever, the universal credit standard allowance will permanentlyrise above inflation, with free breakfast clubs for all primary schoolchildren in England, half a million more children eligible for free school meals in England, cheaper school uniforms and Best Start family hubs opening.But Labour has been bequeathed the worst fallout from 14 Tory years. The nearly 1 million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – are a legacy of Tory rule. Labour has made turning the tide on thoseaged 18 to 24its flagship goal, hoping that numbers fall fast by the next election. Can it be done?The man who says it can is most in demand at meetings around the Labour conference next week. Alan Milburn’sencyclopaedic reporton the problem revealed the myriad reasons why so many of the young get left in limbo.Next month, before the budget, he will publish the plan for what’s to be done. I hear intense negotiations are in progress, down to the wire because this is in effect a white paper, not a report to gather dust but one ready to be implemented at once, with costings pre-agreed with PM, chancellor and relevant ministers. Milburn knows the system, and he is determined to short-circuit any blockers.Here’s the problem. His diagnosis points to everything from inequality and profound deprivation to mental illness, failures of the education system, refusal of employers to offer first breaks, falling apprenticeships, lack of early support in areas where many families are in trouble, and declining youth services. Neets are the fallout from deep social dysfunction, accelerated by the cuts.Which will be the first priorities? It has been good to see Lucy Powell, the education secretary, start right away on new vocational GCSEs, which Milburn thinks will keep pupils engaged instead of dropping out. Copying the Dutch system of intensive one-to-one personal support will getNeets into training or work. That needs upfront investment from the new chancellor, John Healey, who is said to agree, even though he knows the results take time. The quid pro quo expected from Neets is a “duty to engage”, so they must take part in the help offered, as all benefits are always conditional, with penalties as a backstop. Milburn’s research defies Badenoch’s kneejerk nastiness, as he finds84% of Neetswant urgent help into work.Success will be judged by falling numbers of Neets, but there is the “stock and flow” question: preventing more from joining tomorrow’s list starts at the very earliest years. Children who are not school-ready at ages four to five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet at ages 16 to 17, as Milburn said in the report. That’s not certain destiny, but it is a high risk.The good news is that Milburn will reset the nursery system that currently discriminates against the poorest. He tells me he is shocked that only68% of childrenare school-ready, even after they have had a year in reception at primary school. He tells me he will be announcing a new target of 90% to reach that level by five years old: all research shows how investment at the earliest age yields most.What would that take? The nursery system inherited from the Tories deliberately holds back the most deprived children by denying funded nursery hours in England to most children with a non-working parent. Here was Tory thinking: both parents must work to stop lazy mothers idling in nail bars while the state acts as childminder. But deprived children with non-working parents need nursery education to close the growing gap between them and the rest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere’s how it works: a child with working parents can get 30 hours of free nursery care from the age of nine months up to primary school. Only some disadvantaged two-year-olds can qualify for 15 hours a week, but that entitlement now reaches“fewer than 30% of two-year-olds”,says theInstitute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).This means that children of the best-off are eight times more likely to benefit from state-funded nursery than the most disadvantaged children,says the New Economics Foundation. As the IFS says, the system “almost by definition excludes the poorest families”. No wonder primary headteachers I have spoken to say they can immediately tell which children have had full nursery education, which have had a little, and which have had none.Sarah Ronan, the director of the Early Education and Childcare Coalition, tells me pithily: “Imagine denying the poorest children access to primary education. We just wouldn’t stand for it. Yet we allow that to happen in the early years while we wring our hands about school-readiness and scratch our heads about Neets.”The head-scratching may be over when Milburn’s report lands. Meanwhile, Badenoch has little to say about Neets, but her wider plans for the jobless see no investment in training or extra support into work. Reform UK dared to sayshe didn’t go far enough. There it is: the age-old divide, psychological and emotional as well as political, between the left’s practical social policy to lift people up and the right’s punitive desire to give every underdog a kick.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionYoung peopleUnemploymentcommentShareReuse this content

title: Meryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues? | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators
Author: Ben Child
Headline: The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators
Content: Aslan in The Lion the Witch and the WardrobePhotograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenAslan in The Lion the Witch and the WardrobePhotograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarWeek in geekMoviesMeryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues?Ben ChildThe Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentatorsFri 25 Sep 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTShareIt is a confusing time to be alive, given how often these days Hollywood indulges in revisionism. Who knew that the Wicked Witch of the West wasthe heroineafter all, thatCruella de Vil simply had a difficult childhood, or thatMufasa was adopted? Now it turns out that Aslan, CS Lewis’s messiah with a mane, is a lioness – or at least, may sound like one in Greta Gerwig’s upcoming adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, because Meryl Streep is providing the voice.News that the Oscar-winner might be portraying Narnia’s Christ-like big catfirst surfaced in April last year, prompting a flurry of complaints from conservative Christians. This week, the naysayers were back afterEmpire published a first look at the film, along with an interview with Gerwig in which the director confirmed the casting and explained her choice of actor. Streep, it turns out, was hired not because the Barbie director desperately fancied stoking the flames of controversy, but because she needed someone over 70 who could convey both wisdom and childlike wonder.“I wanted someone who was profound but not pretentious, who had gravitas but not morose self-seriousness,” Gerwig said. She also explained she wanted one of the finest actors working today, adding: “That list is not a long one.”View image in fullscreenThe Magician’s Nephew director Greta Gerwig.Photograph: Presley Ann/Getty Images for Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtSome American evangelical commentators have already made up their minds that this new version of Narnia comes from from the seventh circle of hell. Radio host Jenna Ellis accused Gerwig of “profaning Christ with the divine feminine”, while Texas preacher David Fairchild called the casting “creative vandalism”.The Daily Wire’s Isabel Brown saidthe decision to cast Streep was offensive because “CS Lewis literally intended Aslan to be the incarnation of Christ inside the world of Narnia”. She pointed to the end of Lewis’s novel The Voyage of the Dawn Treader, in which Aslan tells Lucy and Edmund they will come to know him by another name in their own world. For Brown, casting Streep was a “deliberate mockery of Christianity”.There has been no confirmation from Gerwig that this new Aslan is in fact female. And not everyone agrees that casting Streep is a problem: Christian writer Mary Pezzulohas pointed out the ironythat some evangelicals think it’s perfectly all right for Jesus to be portrayed as an animal yet draw the line when he’s given a woman’s voice. “Very Online conservative Christians really think that portraying Christ as a lion, a carnivorous beast with notoriously smelly urine who sleeps 23 hours a day and steals meat from hyaenas, is beautiful sacred art,” she wrote. “But having Christ portrayed by a woman is sacrilege.”However you view this one, it’s weird that a film adaptation of one of the least known books in the Narnia series now feels like the subject of an emergency reconvening ofthe Council of Nicaea. Also, Gerwig has said she plans to reimagine the fantasy world through a rock opera prism: the great lion king’s eyes have been coloured like David Bowie’s mismatched peepers in publicity shots, and the creation of Narnia is apparently designed to look and sound as if Genesis is being staged by the Spiders from Mars. Daniel Craig is playing the deeply suspect sorcerer of the title, while Emma Mackey steps into Tilda Swinton’s shoes as the White Witch, Jadis. But all anyone can think about is that Aslan now sounds remarkably similar to Miranda Priestly, Julia Child and Mrs Thatcher.View image in fullscreenMeryl StreepPhotograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesThat’s actually a shame, because The Magician’s Nephew has enough going on that it shouldn’t require a culture war to make a splash. Its story sees two children discover a wood full of pools leading to other worlds; one takes them to a dead city beneath a dying sun, where they wake the queen who exterminated its entire population and accidentally bring her back to London. The book has a sense of madcap wonder about it that occasionally makes all the waiting for Aslan to turn up in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, only for him to immediately sacrifice himself, feel like a glacially paced, religiously didactic slog by way of comparison.Remember whenBarbiewent from a potentially cheesy movie about an anatomically unlikely child’s doll to the most talked about film of the year? Something similar could happen here. And then again, Streep might just be playing a lion in a children’s film. Either way, it seems remarkable that an actor whose voice nobody has yet heard in the movie has apparently displaced the White Witch herself – or perhaps even some of her famously addictive turkish delight – as Narnia’s most devious and malign influence.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekGreta GerwigMeryl StreepCS LewisFilm adaptationsChristianityReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: People have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real life
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: People have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real life
Content: ‘You hardly notice how, over time, the world outside has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world.’Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘You hardly notice how, over time, the world outside has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world.’Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial mediaOur lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insaneBrigid DelaneyPeople have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real lifeFri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 20.17 EDTShareThink of your online life as a garden. At first it’s just a few seeds here or there – a Facebook profile where you created entire albums from a night at the pub, or maybe a Tumblr or a Myspace page listing your favourite bands. It is fun – something just for you and your friends to enjoy.Then the garden grows. You get an Instagram account and document moments from each day on Stories, use LinkedIn for networking and sharing career triumphs, and check your X/Twitter hyper-vigilantly in case you wrote something that just got you cancelled.Your online garden grows more sprawling and complex; now it’s no longer just a fun project for yourself on weekends and weeknights. As it grows, you start to view it through the eyes of others.How will this garden be seen? Will people like it? What can I plant in this garden that will make more people like it?A few more years pass. And now, instead of working on the garden here and there, you’re in there all the time. You have discovered if your garden is really enticing, you can make money off it. You want – then need – big numbers coming in there. You look at other people’s gardens all the time and you get jealous. They have better gardens.We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism? | Brigid DelaneyRead moreWhen you’re not in your garden, you’re still somehow tending to it – looking at the number of people coming in, and comparing them with what it used to be, and being worried that maybe you didn’t plant the right things. But people will tell you if you’re doing it wrong. They’ll spray paint all over the garden walls how much your garden sucks, how you’re a loser, how ugly it all is.And with all this activity going on you hardly notice how, over time, the world outside your garden has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world. The garden is your home now.When this current moment ends and a more enlightened time kicks in, descendants looking back will see that millions (or is it billions?) of us have spent the last 10 years or more migrating our lives and identities, and our political, communal and social selves, to a digital realm that has sent many of us insane.The (digital) signal that we are living a better life has been imbued with more energy and importance than living a better life itself.Those descendants will see what we can’t really see now – a massive serf culture has emerged, where people have become servants to these gardens.They’ll see how truly unfree so many of us are – allowing the rich, real, tactile world to recede, while the digital gardens have sprawled to take up all our time and energy (the average userspends about 2 hours and 39 minutes a dayon social media.)And it will become apparent that the real elite won’t be the people with the most popular digital gardens. They’ll be the people who never had gardens. Or people who had small private gardens, where they only let a few friends in.Brand strategists and trend forecasters are saying that, in 2026, the true measure of status is privacy and a low or no digital footprint.This is a different way of living off-grid.You experience a rich and interesting life in the real world and don’t feel the need to post about it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYour sense of self worth is not linked to how many people see that you’ve been somewhere, hung out with someone or worn something.Your income, status and financial security is not dependent on your social media account.Your attention span has not been corrupted or shortened by chronic social media consumption and AI use – and this gives you almost superhuman powers such as the ability to read long, difficult novels, think critically, and retain information in your head.Your emotional stability is not dependent on how your content is performing.You have not internalised the digital panopticon where everything you do is with an eye to how it is perceived.You have a healthy social life in the real world, meaning you have less time or inclination to post.Brand strategistEugene Healeyin his Substack wrote a recent series on “post-luxury status symbols” and said “the greatest privilege is to be chronically offline” and “in this culture of overexposure – it’s only natural that it becomes desirable to opt out”.The ultimate flex is not needing social media, walking away from your digital garden and back into your real life.Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the SageExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionPsychologycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations
Content: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on 25 September 2026. ‘Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Xi Jinping on 25 September 2026. ‘Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOpinionDonald TrumpThe Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensionsEditorialThe Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relationsFri 25 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTShareWithin days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly,around $1m a yearper pair.Americans’ viewsof China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.It is telling that the announcement was one of themain takeawaysof Mr Xi’svisit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.In a sense that is not surprising. Mr Trump admires and envies authoritarians with untrammelled powers. Chinese state media were welcome at the White House, unlike CNN, MS Now and Politico. Since he rarely pays even lip service to human rights, the treatment of Uyghurs or jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong –facing another lengthy sentencefor his international advocacy – were never likely to figure large, whatever the hopesof protesters outside.Mr Trump told Mr Xi that any Chinese help for Iran is unacceptable; Mr Xi said that the US should adhere to the “correct position” of opposing Taiwanese independence. Beijing wants Washington to shift from the long-held stance of “not supporting” it. That would be a grave mistake, but Mr Trump has given worryingly mixed messages onTaiwan.It is striking how little of consequence has emerged from the summit given that this is arguably the most consequential diplomatic relationship in the world. A two-month extension of the trade war truce was announced as Mr Xi arrived in the US. China’s curb of rare earth exports has checked Mr Trump’s appetite for an economic offensive; Beijing is anxious about itsstrugglingeconomy. But if they are more wary of the fallout, they are also more fearful of the other side gaining ground. AI is central to this battle. Mr Trump has resisted all calls to restrain development because“Whoever wins AI, wins.” Mr Xi said it had to be managed responsibly, but Beijing has attacked “threat narratives”, fearing that the US wants to prevent it catching up.CNN last week highlighted the dangers: the US militaryreportedly prepared to intercepta Chinese ship in the Middle East after an intelligence report said it was carrying nuclear weapons components – only for officials to realise that the partially AI-generated analysis had misidentified the cargo. Controls on development are desperately needed, but neither side is willing to accept them. Even the limited AI dialogue and “notification hotline” for AI safety proposed by Scott Bessent, treasury secretary, seem to be ratherless than meets the eye. This summit should be viewed with alarm not because it saw substantive developments – but because it illustrates the dangers of drift.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the 2026 Booker shortlist: what it takes to be a man | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: All the contenders for this year’s prize are a reflection of the crisis in masculinity
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: All the contenders for this year’s prize are a reflection of the crisis in masculinity
Content: The 2026 Booker prize judging panel: Jarvis Cocker, Rebecca Liu, Mary Beard, Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/GettyView image in fullscreenThe 2026 Booker prize judging panel: Jarvis Cocker, Rebecca Liu, Mary Beard, Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/GettyOpinionBooker prizeThe Guardian view on the 2026 Booker shortlist: what it takes to be a manEditorialAll the contenders for this year’s prize are a reflection of the crisis in masculinityFri 25 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTShareJarvis Cocker, one of the judges for this year’s Booker prize, hasexpressedsurprise that theshortlist, announced this week, contains four male authors and only two female writers, because, “generally speaking, the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”.The Pulp frontman might be on to something. Over the past 10 years, however, seven Booker winners have been men; the number of women boosted to four by the controversial joint win between Bernardine Evaristo and Margaret Atwood in 2019. The2024 Booker shortlistwas the first to have five female authors in the prize’s history. Last year’s winnerFlesh, by British-Hungarian author David Szalay, stripped what being a man means down to its bones.This year’s contenders all approach the same question through wildly different forms: historical, domestic, dystopian and comic fiction. The novels by female authors both have male protagonists: a reluctant medieval monarch in Rebecca Perry’sMay We Feed the Kingand a 57-year-old history teacher in contemporary Massachusetts inThe Things We Never Sayby Elizabeth Strout.The Disappearersby Marlon James andJohn of Johnby Douglas Stuart, both previous Booker winners, show young men confronting their sexuality in the repressive climates of late 20th-century Jamaica and the Outer Hebrides, respectively. InThe End of Everythingfrom science-fiction giant M John Harrison, the central character is trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic Britain under invasion from ambiguous entities (AI is never explicitly mentioned). InBlack Bag, by Luke Kennard, an out-of-work actor lands a job in which he has to wear a black bag all the time, based ona 1967 social psychology experimentin which a student was asked to wear a big black bag for a whole semester. “It’s a statement about being a man,” one character says of the eponymous bag. “There’s a whole contingent of men who are lost and dissatisfied.”All the male characters in these novels are walking around in metaphorical black bags, flailing awkwardly in the dark, unknowable to those closest to them. Whether set in medieval times, Donald Trump’s America or a nightmarish near future, the 2026 shortlist is a reflection of current anxieties about masculinity.Publishing is just catching up. Thanks to the so-calledSally Rooney phenomenon, the book world (if not the Booker) has been dominated by novels written by and about young women, a long overdue pushback against generations of swaggering fiction by men. The male gaze has finally shifted. As Szalay hassaid, “you can’t write like Martin Amis or Norman Mailer or Philip Roth now”. Notable exceptions such as Szalay and Ben Lerner, whose novelTranscriptionwas a surprise omission from the longlist, have been steadily chronicling 21st-century manhood. But somefearedthat male writers and stories were being overlooked altogether. Last year, the independent publisher,Conduit Books, was set up exclusively for male authors.The shortlist shows a renewed confidence in narratives about men. Here are fathers and sons, husbands and lovers, kings and losers, none of whom conform to male stereotypes. All of the novels are about a longing for purpose and connection. In a world where the strongman myth is mighty, the characters show vulnerability and uncertainty. As the lyrics of a1998 Pulp songhave it, they make us “start to wonder what it takes to be a man”.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How Labour can reform Britain’s pensions triple lock | State pensions | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers offer solutions to the thorny problem facing the government, in response to an article by Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers offer solutions to the thorny problem facing the government, in response to an article by Gaby Hinsliff
Content: ‘We do need a new deal to achieve generational fairness, but breaking the lock will leave millions facing poverty.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘We do need a new deal to achieve generational fairness, but breaking the lock will leave millions facing poverty.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoState pensionsLettersHow Labour can reform Britain’s pensions triple lockReaders offer solutions to the thorny problem facing the government, in response to an article by Gaby HinsliffFri 25 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareGaby Hinsliff(Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?, 22 September) is right that public policy should not subsidise wealth without limit, but breaking the triple lock is a poor way to target affluent pensioners. Most pensioners are not affluent. Indeed, a quarter of pensionersrequire benefitsin addition to the state pension just to survive and keep a roof over their heads.If the aim is to stop subsidising wealth, a more direct target is the generous tax treatment of private pension savings. A taxpayer contributing £100 to a pension can receive £40 or £45 in tax relief if they pay higher- or additional-rate tax, compared with £20 for the basic rate. Tax and national insurance contributions relief on private pensions costs the government a staggering£84bn a year.Most of this money (almost three-quarters) goes to the wealthiest 20% taxpayers because they can afford to save the most and receive the highest rate of relief. Instead, a flat 20% rate of tax relief on private pensions would preserve the incentive for basic-rate taxpayers while reducing the additional subsidy concentrated among higher earners. It’s also fair because when pensions are drawn down, much less tax is recovered by the Treasury, making the net cost of this relief over £50bn a year.This could raise billions more than breaking the triple lock. Thetriple lock’s 2.5% floorwas only significant during the period when both earnings growth and inflation were close to zero. When inflation and earnings growth are above 2%, as they are now and are expected to be over the coming years, the difference between the triple lock and a conventional uprating mechanism becomes irrelevant.The policy challenge therefore is to avoid the economically irrelevant, politically damaging and socially divisive red herring that is breaking the triple lock and instead reform the far more regressive support given to large private pension pots.Stephen RichardsonGrange-over-Sands, CumbriaGaby Hinsliff makes the point that retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers. But it is precisely this that justifies maintaining the triple lock as a bulwark against poverty. Young and middle‑aged workers do indeed face the prospect of an impoverished old age. As highlighted in thePensions Commission interim report, according to 2025 figures, 43% of working-age people are undersaving for retirement, with just 25% of Bangladeshis and Pakistanis of working age participating in a pension scheme.The pensions crisis is likely to grow, given the rise in the numbers of self-employed people – the group least likely to be saving for a pension. Millions of workers in their 40s and 50s face the prospect of poverty in retirement, given the rise of precarious working and continuing age discrimination in employment.We do need a new deal to achieve generational fairness, but breaking the lock will leave millions facing poverty. The alternative must be keeping the lock, but tackling the reasons that justify its existence – low incomes, insecure employment and the high cost of housing.Chris PhillipsonEmeritus professor of sociology and social gerontology, University of ManchesterThere is a simple tweak that would improve the affordability of the triple lock. The goal of the triple lock is to ensure that the value of the pension keeps up with both price inflation and wage inflation. But the way it has been implemented allows pensioners to do much better than this.Between 2011 and 2026, prices rose by 60% and earnings rose by 66%, butpensions rose by 89%. This happens because in some years prices rise more than wages, but in other years wages rise more. So the pension does better than both of them.The fix is to smooth out the earnings link. Instead of looking at wages growth over the last year, we should look at growth over the past five years, for example. Pensioners would still be protected against price rises, and would maintain their current position in the wages league table. But they would no longer rise up it.Bob VickersTwickenham, LondonGaby Hinsliff claims that “Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock.” The problem is that everybody might think they know this, but that does not mean it is right.If we do need to find money, it is within the government’s power to create it. And if it refuses to use that power, it can look elsewhere within the pension system for funds. For example, the pension tax relief given to the highest-earning people in this country, at rates above the basic level of income tax, costs at least£15bn a year– vastly more than costs attributed to the triple lock.We have a cost of living crisis and a pension poverty crisis. So why is everyone looking at punishing some of the most vulnerable people in our society when the rich continue to have their ever-increasing wealth subsidised by the state at a cost of many billions of pounds a year?Richard MurphyEmeritus professor of accounting practice, Sheffield UniversityAlong with my state pension, I receive two small pensions from the Ministry of Defence and the NHS. If my husband should die before me, I don’t know how I would survive financially. We have a small cottage and downsizing wouldn’t result in a significant profit.My “inheritance” from my parents disappeared when my mother had to go into care with Alzheimer’s; her house had to be sold to pay for her care.In a week when the billionaire tax avoider Jim Ratcliffe badmouths the country, Gaby Hinsliff makes no reference to the tax system and how the very rich can get away with paying very little.She also makes no reference to why the UK is doing so badly financially or why young people are struggling – my son can’t afford a house – after a decade of Tory misrule, a decade of Brexit wilderness and the legacy of Thatcherism. Removing the triple lock won’t solve the now endemic financial challenges the UK is facing.Ingrid MarshNewton Abbot, DevonGaby Hinsliff is right about the triple lock: it has done its work in raising the ratio between the state retirement pension and average earnings from 18% in 2010 to about 30% now. Two problems remain: what should replace it and how to stop an opportunist opposition from playing politics with the issue?There is no need to decide this matter now. Far better to announce the end of the triple lock in the forthcoming budget and refer the question of a replacement to a time-limited, cross-party commission. The state pension should not become a political football or part of a short-term fiscal fix.David PurdyCausewayhead, StirlingHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Arts Council England doesn’t need ‘swagger’, it needs reform | Arts Council England | The Guardian
description: Letters: Reader Chris Hodgkins proposes a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Reader Chris Hodgkins proposes a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music
Content: The organisation’s new chair, Dawn Airey, visited ACE-funded projects in Barrow in Furness, including pupils taking part in sessions led by musicians and conductors from the Liverpool Philharmonic at the Barrow Youth Hub, 15 September.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe organisation’s new chair, Dawn Airey, visited ACE-funded projects in Barrow in Furness, including pupils taking part in sessions led by musicians and conductors from the Liverpool Philharmonic at the Barrow Youth Hub, 15 September.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianArts Council EnglandLettersArts Council England doesn’t need ‘swagger’, it needs reformReaderChris Hodgkinsproposes a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and musicFri 25 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareThe interview with the new chair of Arts Council England (ACE), who says she wants the organisation to “get its swagger back”, misdiagnoses the crisis facing England’s cultural system(‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with culture, 18 September). Swagger is not what is missing. What is required is contrition, honesty and structural reform.Eighty years after its creation, Arts Council England remains built on a 1946 architecture that privileges opera and classical institutions while systematically marginalising jazz, folk, world, brass, choral and grassroots arts and music. This is not a matter of confidence or energy; it is a matter of structural imbalance.The Review of Jazz in England(2025),Margaret Hodge’s review(2025), and ACE/Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s 2026 responses all identify bureaucracy, mistrust and inconsistent decision‑making – yet none confront the deeper failures: lottery funding misuse,national portfolio organisationdominance, regional inequity, governance opacity, and the collapse of grassroots infrastructure. These problems are not recent. Every major review confirms the same pattern: ACE’s centralised model reproduces historical privilege and suppresses contemporary cultural practice.International evidence shows that modern cultural systems – in Scandinavia, Ireland and Australia – are built on devolved delivery, direct investment in artists, touring infrastructure, and integrated cultural‑education policy.Englandhas none of these. ACE’s legacy architecture cannot deliver the government’s growth agenda, cannot support regional cultural economies, and cannot unlock the high‑growth potential of grassroots arts and music.What is needed now is not swagger but a new organisation.I proposea dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music, with transparent allocation formulas, restored lottery funding, art form‑specific policy and a national touring infrastructure. Swagger will not fix England’s cultural system. Structural reform will.Chris HodgkinsEaling, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
