title: New map projections don’t make the Mercator wrong | Maps | The Guardian
description: Letters: The transverse Mercator projection was created for European sailors – and it worked for their world, writes Paul Harwood
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The transverse Mercator projection was created for European sailors – and it worked for their world, writes Paul Harwood
Content: Map showing Africa using the Mercator projection, left, and one from the Equal Earth campaign.Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMap showing Africa using the Mercator projection, left, and one from the Equal Earth campaign.Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty ImagesMapsLettersNew map projections don’t make the Mercator wrongThe transverse Mercator projection was created for European sailors – and it worked for their world, writesPaul HarwoodFri 25 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareThe subject of projections is incredibly complicated and you did a good job of navigating the discussion (‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias, 18 September).However, suggesting that transverse Mercator is inherently biased is not fair (if it is possible to be unfair to an equation) to both the projection and the cartographers.Mercator et al just did the job of creating maps that were useful for the European sailors they were working for. The fact that everyone carried on using it was our laziness and not their bias.The Equal Earth projection is a much better representation for what we use maps for now, but that does not make the Mercator wrong.You say “A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented.” But I can think of almost no maps that have London at the centre. The international coordinate system (ie latitude-longitude, which is unchanged by this resolution) is based for arbitrary historical reasons on a meridian drawn through Greenwich.However, the “centre” of this coordinate system is not London but a point in the sea off west Africa. No map or representation has to use this as the centre and the current best practice – called UTM – has 60 different zones (thus 60 centres) to represent all parts of the globe.Even the UKOrdnance Surveymapping system is not “centred” on London. As far as you can say it has a centre, it would be somewhere in Lancashire.Paul HarwoodLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The dark art of maths and the AI revolution | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letter: Bev Littlewood reminds us that mathematics has been the prime driver of the rise in AI, in response to an editorial
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Bev Littlewood reminds us that mathematics has been the prime driver of the rise in AI, in response to an editorial
Content: A painting of Saint Augustine: ‘The good Christian should beware the mathematician.’Photograph: Los Angeles County Museum of ArtView image in fullscreenA painting of Saint Augustine: ‘The good Christian should beware the mathematician.’Photograph: Los Angeles County Museum of ArtAI (artificial intelligence)LettersThe dark art of maths and the AI revolutionBev Littlewoodreminds us that mathematics has been the prime driver of the rise in AI, in response to an editorialFri 25 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareYou report in your leader that some mathematicians feel discomfiture at the AI solution to a Navier-Stokes problem (The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that, 20 September). I fear that they have been hoist by their own petard: mathematics, after all, has been the prime mover of the AI revolution.As a somewhat lowly mathematician, let me remind others of the famous quote of Augustine: “The good Christian should beware the mathematician and all those who make empty promises. The danger already exists that the mathematicians have made a covenant with the devil to darken the spirit and to confine man in the bonds of hell.”While the accuracy of the quote, and Augustine’s meaning, are in some dispute, its appropriateness here is too good to waste.Bev LittlewoodEmeritus professor of software engineering, City St George’s, University of LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted now | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Friday’s verdict against Manchester City changes everything we understood about their era and Premier League title triumphs
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Friday’s verdict against Manchester City changes everything we understood about their era and Premier League title triumphs
Content: ‘There could yet be a dramatic reversal of the verdict against Manchester City but for now this is a good day for football.’Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘There could yet be a dramatic reversal of the verdict against Manchester City but for now this is a good day for football.’Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesManchester CityThe age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted nowBarney RonayFriday’s verdict against Manchester City will change everything we understood about their Premier League title triumphsFri 25 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWelcome, then, to the age of asterisk. Whatever punishmentManchester Cityand their owners receive at the end of this process, the fact remains, everything is tainted now.Overturn the tables, scatter the gold coins. Throw your medals in the bin. You cheated to win them. Whatever that thing was, it’s done. Stolen glory, stolen income, stolen joy. Every chant, every “we won the lot”, every awkward documentary scene about the deep, throbbing heart of this empire of love. It all looks odd, sinister, cold, sloppy, but also, and this is always the best response, utterly absurd.We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rightsRead moreThis is not over of course. We still work on the principle of innocent until repeatedly proven guilty, pending mega-bucks final appeals. There could yet be a dramatic reversal at the next stage. And if so, fair enough. Trust the process. So for now we must also asterisk the asterisk. It should also be pointed out that City still deny all allegations, even when proven at the first instance. They have also, in fairness, not been found guilty of all of those 100-plus charges. Maybe the club can spin this, take the positives, a vital away charge to take into the appeal.But for now this is a good day for football. And also a good day for, of all things, the world. ThePremier Leaguemay seem an unlikely revolutionary. But in the age of despotism, of endless chatter about the decline of the rules-based international order, any tribunal that finds a fund back by the one of the United Arab Emirates’ ruling families guilty of breaches of minor but still vital sporting regulations deserves its own statue outside the Royal Courts of Justice. People in wigs: not always slaves to power, or indeed the enemies of the people.View image in fullscreenSergio Agüero scores his title-winning goal in added time against Queens Park Rangers in May 2012.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersMainly this is a great day for the Premier League, which must be commended above all for its refusal to bend. There has been frustration at the time it has taken to reach this verdict. Technically it is a full eight years since Der Spiegel published the first allegations of industrial-scale cheating. And spare a thought here too for Rui Pinto, the original whistleblower, currently in witness protection after being found guilty of information-related offences. This verdict suggest football’s greatest vigilante was also right, or right enough. Raise a glass, José Bloggs of Oporto, or whatever you go by these days.That extreme delay is simply another consequence of taking on an entity that is willing to spend so aggressively on the world’s most energetic lawyers, to threaten to bankrupt the organisation it signed up to serve and nourish. It always seemed worrying that an accusation of not cooperating with financial reporting, a charge that on the face of it could be cleared up in half a day, should take three years to reach a verdict.But this is testimony to the lawfare-level response. In this context, and pending a proper sanction, the entire case speaks to the basic sanctity of the rule of law, of applying the same rules to all irrespective of status, a small but high-profile rejection of the idea wealth and political heft can steamroller regulation and process.And that punishment really is key. Because everything is on the cards here, not least the much‑trailed potential destruction of the brand. There has always been a whispered suggestion the league is taking a hammer to its own knees in this process. That thing we sold you all those years? Well, it’s not straight. The product you paid for and believed in wasn’t real.Arguably everyone who bought a Sky Sports subscription in that period now has a legal claim against City. I signed up for sport. This was an exhibition event. But the Premier League has been rigid in the right way. What is that legacy actually worth, how much more damaged will it be, if its owners shy away from their own rules and allow the serial champions to shortcut their way to plastic success? The answer is: very little. At that point we may as well all turn off the lights and abandon the stage to the world of scripted product.It is important in all this to spare a thought for City fans, who are innocent of anything other than wanting their team to win and believing the evidence presented to their eyes. There will be some who see conspiracy, because they want to, who choose to fight on, or pretend not to understand. We live in an age when even billionaire inherited rulers get to style themselves as victims of oppressive power structures.View image in fullscreenManchester City players celebrate the first of Pep Guardiola’s Premier League titles on the Etihad Stadium’s pitch in May 2018.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesBut the fact is the rules do matter, even if you think they shouldn’t exist. They matter because other teams were abiding by them. Other teams didn’t buy players, lost bidding wars, lost games and league titles by fine margins during a period when one team was saying, well, thanks but no thanks. This is why cheating matters. You can disagree with the offside law and try to get it changed. But if you just ignore it and keep on hammering the ball into the net, you’ve destroyed your own sport.City’s fans deserve sympathy generally. They don’t run the club, they simply support it. They have been loyal to their owners, even while those owners, on the basis of this decision, were turning the club into a toxic entity, a parasite on its host and on the basic idea of sport. What is the right response to this? Some will simply feel sad at the tarnishing of memories.But there is also a legitimate suggestion it is time for those owners to sell up and move on. This has been a disgraceful episode in so many ways: the casual cheating, the refusal to mitigate or compromise, the assault on English football, the attempt to bleed the rest of the field dry.The fact is anyone with an interest in justice, equality and abiding by universal rules, should be pleased with this result, including City fans. Although there is of course still a huge opportunity for the process to hole itself below the waterline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuilt followed by a minor slap on the wrist. This would asterisk the asterisk, would provide a complete reversal of all that goodwill. What would be the point of going through this only to blink at the sanctions stage? And yes, this is the job of an independent tribunal, but the league will have agency in how this is interpreted, through its submission and its evidence.View image in fullscreenMohamed Salah celebrates putting Liverpool 2-1 up against Wolves on the last day of the 2022-23 season. Manchester City took the title by one point.Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesAnd there is very little mitigation here. Not reporting financial information might sound trivial in another sphere. But in football, where success is defined by expenditure, this is deliberate and highly effective deceit. City have continued to spend freely, to win things under this shadow, in a space where more than simply results and titles are at stake. Football is a zero-sum game. When you cheat, you’re taking money and opportunities out of the pockets of others.Not to mention glory, happiness, life chances, things people work and bleed for all their lives. In their place you’re introducing failure, doubt, career regression, moving home, moving jobs, cutting ties, losing connections, all based on skewed results on a sports field, all based on cheating.The list of teams that might have won league titles in those years reads: Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal. Perhaps these clubs will even consider suing City for compensation. The Premier League could pre-empt this by stripping titles and reallocating glory. That still feels like an overload of asterisks. But this is what happens when you cheat. You degrade the experience for everyone.Everything you need to know about Manchester City’s hearing and chargesRead moreThere are two final things worth saying. Last month Bloomberg reported that the UAE had been in touch with the UK government expressing concerns about the Premier League process, and potentially, it was implied, damaging the prospect of that wider relationship.If true, and it is simply a suggestion, this would demonstrate yet another profound misunderstanding of the culture you’re buying into. The law is not supposed to bend to power and influence. Does anyone actually want to live in a world where this is the case?But then, it is also worth remembering that skimping on some financial rules is hardly the worst thing the UAE has been accused of in those years. There are accusations of supporting the bloodshed in Sudan, as well as numerous human rights abuses, the curtailment of dissent and massive social inequality.Whatever its ultimate outcome the entire process stands as a warning for every sport with it eyes in a spin at the offer of transformative financial investment. Look very hard at who you get into bed with. Jam today, pain tomorrow. And it never, ever comes for free.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFootball politicsPremier LeaguecommentShareReuse this content

title: Thomas Tuchel warns Cole Palmer about ‘missing way too many’ England camps | England | The Guardian
description: The head coach said before England host Spain in the Nations League that Cole Palmer’s latest withdrawal with a minor injury was a ‘missed opportunity’
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: The head coach said before England host Spain in the Nations League that Cole Palmer’s latest withdrawal with a minor injury was a ‘missed opportunity’
Content: Thomas Tuchel said he is ‘not ready to focus on players who are not here’ when questioned on Cole Palmer’s absence.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said he is ‘not ready to focus on players who are not here’ when questioned on Cole Palmer’s absence.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandThomas Tuchel warns Cole Palmer about ‘missing way too many’ England campsHead coach said latest withdrawal is ‘missed opportunity’England host Spain in Nations League on SaturdayJacob SteinbergFri 25 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel has thrown Cole Palmer’s England future into major doubt by questioning whether the Chelsea attacker wants to be part of his squad.England’s head coach did not hold back onPalmer’s latest withdrawalfrom international duty, warning that the 24-year-old has missed too many opportunities to play for his country. Palmer has only 14 caps and his decision not to join up with the squad this week, because of a minor muscular injury, caused disappointment given he wasleft out of Tuchel’s World Cup squadafter struggling with form and fitness last season.De la Fuente brings insatiable Spain to England knowing World Cup is not enoughRead moreTuchel has put a lot of store in team spirit and is clear about wanting commitment. The German has rarely been able to work with Palmer, who had earned a high-profile recall after making a strong start to the campaign, and did not go down the diplomatic route when it was suggested the former Manchester City player does not seem desperate to play forEngland. “Hard to argue against what you’re saying,” Tuchel said.The line came with a warning for Palmer. “He misses too many camps,” Tuchel said. “That’s the overall headline. We have a lot of invitations and he couldn’t make this one. It is what it is. I am not ready to focus on players who are not here. The players that are here have my full attention.“It is a missed opportunity. He [Palmer] misses too many opportunities. I don’t blame him for it. It is just a fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries, and I only want to rely on what I witness within my team, and for that you have to be in camp.”The idea of asking Palmer to join the squad to build connections did not cross Tuchel’s mind. “To bring someone and take away capacity from our physios, it’s not helpful,” he said. “This is about the guys who are here and this is where the energy goes.”England open their Nations League campaign by hosting Spain at Wembley on Saturday evening and Tuchel is not short of alternatives to Palmer. Morgan Gibbs-White was called up as Palmer’s replacement from a holiday in Dubai.View image in fullscreenCole Palmer played in all four of Chelsea’s Premier League matches before pulling out of the England squad with a minor injury.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA“It leaves us with Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze,” Tuchel said. “All in camp. All desperate to be here. All available. And all ready to go, ready to stop a holiday after one day in Dubai.”Palmer, who has played in all of Chelsea’s Premier League games this season, was not the only player to withdraw. However Tuchel has no issue with Tino Livramento, who missed Newcastle’s win over Hull last weekend. Concerns over the withdrawals of Manchester United’s Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford were also brushed aside. Declan Rice, also unavailable, was given a pass. The Arsenal midfielder played through pain at the World Cup and has had a draining workload.“Every case is individual and if Declan calls me and explains to me and I actually see him play v Brighton, I see straight away on TV that something is off,” Tuchel said. “He just confirmed that impression. Every case is different and I knew from Marcus, I knew from Kobbie that they play with discomfort.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland go into their game against the world champions hoping to make a statement after the disappointment of theirWorld Cup semi-final defeatby Argentina. There has been a lot of focus on English football’s DNA but Rogers argued that Tuchel’s side are capable of keeping the ball if they go 1-0 up against Spain. The pain of losing to Argentina lingers.“We’re definitely good enough to do it,” the Chelsea attacker said. “But there’s not many teams in the world who can do that, especially in a World Cup semi-final in that moment. I was on the pitch, I felt it, we’re doing everything we can not to let them score and sometimes that can be a negative thought.“It is about keeping that calmness and composure. As heartbreaking as it was, I’m hoping that experience will put me and the group in massive stead going forward, that in those situations we can remember how it felt when the whistle went in that game, of how the last half-hour [against Argentina] felt. It just felt a bit sour, the way it ended.”Rogers accepted that other forwards needed to lower the side’s reliance on Harry Kane and Bellingham for goals. “They’re not going to be here for ever,” he said. “They might not be here for a camp or whatever, and other people need to step up. Starting now, the World Cup is done.”Tuchel has a call to make at right-back, with Jarell Quansah competing with Trent Alexander-Arnold. The uncapped Alex Scott hopes to get the nod over Myles Lewis-Skelly and James Garner in midfield.Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Irwin holds nerve to sink Leeds and send Warrington to Grand Final | Super League | The Guardian
description: A late penalty from Ewan Irwin gave Warrington a 14-12 win at Leeds and a place in the Super League Grand Final
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: A late penalty from Ewan Irwin gave Warrington a 14-12 win at Leeds and a place in the Super League Grand Final
Content: Ewan Irwin’s reliable boot was crucial for Warrington.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenEwan Irwin’s reliable boot was crucial for Warrington.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PASuper LeagueIrwin holds nerve to sink Leeds and send Warrington to Grand FinalLeeds 12-14 WarringtonLate penalty clinches Old Trafford tripAaron Bowerat AMT HeadingleyFri 25 Sep 2026 17.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRugby league’s most noteworthy drought is tantalisingly within reach of coming to an end once again. We have been here before – several times, in fact – but Warrington Wolves are within one victory of a first league title not just in the Super League era, but since all the way back in 1955.It was a night not without drama: and perhaps even a shade of controversy. But as 4,000Warringtonsupporters burst into raptures under the Headingley lights as Jake Connor’s last-ditch attempt to send this engrossing semi-final into extra time fell short, it was worth a brief pause to reflect on how far this club have come in a short space of time.Toulouse lit up Super League but French fans miss out on TV coverageRead moreThis was not the most glamorous, dazzling display from a Warrington side you will see. It is abundantly clear they will have to be better in key areas next week at Old Trafford. But these games, at this time of the year, are really about one thing and one thing only: victory.Not even the most optimistic Warrington supporter could have predicted this would be their fate in 2026 after they limped to an eighth-placed finish last season. Failure to even make the playoffs meant the knives were sharpening for Sam Burgess, and questions arising about whether he could be the man to finally deliver a league title to the town.But with this playoff on a knife-edge, it is difficult to escape the fact it was ultimately decided in controversial fashion.The semi-final was all-square at 12-12 as it entered the final quarter before the most significant moment of both teams’ season. James McDonnell was penalised for a bodycheck on George Williams, affording Ewan Irwin a simple penalty to kick the Wolves ahead.It was soft, and certainly controversial given the stage in both the game and the season, and the prize at stake. But Warrington deserve credit for how they navigated the period after that penalty to book their place at Old Trafford for the first time since 2018: they will face Wigan Warriors or Wakefield Trinity next Saturday in the Grand Final.“We want to enjoy this week and make the most of it,” Burgess said. “And get our best performance on to the field. We want to do everything that will help that. I was nervous, and I wanted us to experience this as a group together, getting to the final week of the season.” He should enjoy this moment more than most after a difficult 2025 campaign: he has proven he is an exceptional head coach throughout this year.View image in fullscreenJames Bentley scores Warrington’s first try.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAIn a game of few genuine scoring moments, the two sides could not be separated at half-time. Warrington took an early lead with James Bentley’s try before the Rhinos hit back with excellent tries for Ryan Hall and Connor, who once again dragged Leeds around the field when it mattered most.But the Wolves’ response through Luke Yates on the stroke of half-time levelled it up at 12-12, the least their effort deserved. However, the tension would only rise after the break as both teams spurned opportunities to go back in front. The prospect of extra time felt inevitable, even with a quarter of the game remaining.That was before the most decisive moment of them all. Leeds were penalised in front of their own posts, they failed to overturn it through a captain’s challenge and Irwin did the rest. It left the Rhinos’ coach, Brad Arthur, bitterly disappointed post-match. “I don’t know what more we could have done,” he said.“It would have been nice if the game had been decided by the teams with a piece of skill and we’re talking about someone nailing a big moment instead of a soft penalty to decide such a big game. It’s a soft penalty. One of our guys got escorted off the ball four or five times and I wasn’t expecting penalties – but that is a soft penalty.”There was even late drama beyond that. Leeds were awarded a penalty just inside their own half as the full-time hooter sounded; instead of kicking deep to try to score a try from the last play, Connor attempted a remarkable goal from 60 metres out. But as he fell short, so too did Leeds’ dreams – and Warrington’s wait for that elusive league title is now once again desperately close.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueRugby leagueLeeds RhinosWarringtonmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Moment of magic from Santi Carreras helps Bath overpower Harlequins | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: The 2024-25 Prem champions Bath kicked off their new campaign with a convincing bonus-point win against Harlequins at Twickenham Stoop
Author: Michael Aylwin
Headline: The 2024-25 Prem champions Bath kicked off their new campaign with a convincing bonus-point win against Harlequins at Twickenham Stoop
Content: Santi Carreras runs in the third try for Bath after skilfully intercepting a pass with his foot.Photograph: Bob Bradford/CameraSport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSanti Carreras runs in the third try for Bath after skilfully intercepting a pass with his foot.Photograph: Bob Bradford/CameraSport/Getty ImagesPrem RugbyMoment of magic from Santi Carreras helps Bath overpower HarlequinsHarlequins 17-33 BathArgentinian full-back scores stunning try on counterMichael Aylwinat Twickenham StoopFri 25 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast season’s top two kicked off the season in opposition to last season’s bottom two. Bath duly completed the expected, joining Northampton with a bonus-point win to open their account. The team the Saints succeeded as champions last season travelled to the Stoop to remindHarlequinshow much more they have to work on if they are to return to the sort of form that made them champions not so long ago.The home team took to the field with a host of absentees, it is true. No Marcus Smith; no Alex Dombrandt; no George Furbank, a new signing with a shiny champion’s gong around his neck. They were bright as they always are, but the substance of their visitors was too much in the end, leavened by a flash of genius by the Argentinian Santi Carreras that will long stay with all who witnessed it. To boast that sort of muscle, to boast that sort of genius,Bathwill take some beating again this season.Freeman and Pater inspire Northampton to opening win against NewcastleRead moreThey had the bonus point by half-time, which felt a bit harsh on a Quins team that had enjoyed plenty of bright moments. Their challenge, it seems again, will be to find the composure to fill in the stretches of time between them with something substantial. As it is, they flare up from time to time with a flash of brilliance. Bath have more in the way of relentless intensity. And they have Carreras. And Finn Russell, of course. But of the two geniuses it has been Carreras turning heads of late, apparently playing in training as if he were, to quote his coach, the best player in the world.The cruellest turning point of the match was courtesy of a moment that might as well have been in training it was so casually, instinctively of another planet, might as well have been conjured by Maradona or Messi. The ledger read two tries apiece on the half-hour when Quins had just worked another of their sparks.Tyrone Green was homing in on Carreras, the last man, with Oscar Beard outside him. Nothing wrong with the pass. But a dilemma for the last man in those circumstances is always whether to stick out a hand for the interception and risk a penalty try if it knocks on? Carreras supplied the answer. Use your foot. Green’s pass fizzed across him and he flicked up his boot to volley the ball sweetly into the air, coolly ran on and reached one hand over the touchline to regather it from the air. And on he ran to the tryline some 75 yards away. Did we mention he is also seriously quick?“In my view that is going to be try of the season for us in round one,” said the Bath head coach, Johann van Graan. “What a player, what a moment.” That meant it was to be Bath, not Quins, who would be the first to score a third try. Suddenly it was 21-10 to the visitors. More punishing still they scored that fourth try on the stroke of half-time from a penalty to the corner, Dan Frost at the back of an advancing maul, much as Dan du Preez had earlier opened the scoring on his Bath debut.Joe Cokanasiga hit a hard line for Bath’s second, while Harlequins had kept in the match with two of those flashes, first by Will Porter, who went through or round three defenders off loose lineout ball, then when Chandler Cunningham-South ran home after Beard’s brilliant turn.More of the same had Quins their third on the resumption. This time Cadan Murley was away doing his thing down the left. His run established the position; Pedro Delgado’s rumble round the fringes finished the job. Quins seemed happier all of a sudden, but their case was not helped by the yellow card shown to Sam Riley a few minutes later for an illegal tackle on Beno Obano.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBath hardly made it tell. They meandered a little themselves in the third quarter, but when you have set-piece weaponry it is only a matter of time before you get a chance to use it. And so they did, putting the game beyond their hosts in the last 10 minutes, scoring from a driven lineout for the third time, when Ewan Richards finished from another penalty to the corner.One cloud on the horizon for Bath and England might be Sam Underhill’s departure early in the second half. Van Graan is concerned he might have suffered a biceps injury, which would mean months on the sidelines. Otherwise, though, the usual suspects are flexing their muscles into the new campaign.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyHarlequinsBathRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League: Kylian Mbappé injured after scoring France winner in Turkey | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Victory in Zinedine Zidane’s first game in charge was marred by Mbappé’s injury, while Belgium spoiled Roberto Mancini’s Italy return
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Victory in Zinedine Zidane’s first game in charge was marred by Mbappé’s injury, while Belgium spoiled Roberto Mancini’s Italy return
Content: Kylian Mbappé goes down holding his left knee shortly after scoring for France in Izmit.Photograph: Ali Atmaca/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKylian Mbappé goes down holding his left knee shortly after scoring for France in Izmit.Photograph: Ali Atmaca/Anadolu/Getty ImagesNations LeagueNations League: Kylian Mbappé injured after scoring France winner in TurkeyFrance beat 10-man Turkey 1-0 to start Zidane eraItaly 0-2 Belgium, Georgia 0-1 Northern IrelandPress Association, AFP and APFri 25 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKylian Mbappé limped off with an apparent knee injury, moments after scoring France’s winner against Turkey in theNations Leagueon Friday.The Real Madrid striker rifled in a low shot in the 55th minute after he was set up by Michael Olise. Soon after his record-extending 67thFrancegoal, Mbappé sat on the ground and grimaced as he rubbed the area around his left knee.Turkey 0-1 France, Italy 0-2 Belgium, Georgia 0-1 Northern Ireland: Nations League – as it happenedRead moreThe new France head coach, Zinedine Zidane, replaced Mbappé with Désiré Doué. In an encouraging sight, he was able to walk off the field of his own accord – but Zidane said afterwards that he expects his captain to return to Real Madrid for treatment.“It’s not great. Unfortunately I think he [Mbappé] is going to have to go home. We don’t want to take any risks,” Zidane told French broadcaster TF1. “He overextended his knee while shooting. It’s not very encouraging.”Jules Koundé hit the post for France before Turkey were reduced to 10 men, goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir sent off for handling the ball outside his area after Bradley Barcola had been played through on goal.Elsewhere in Group A2, Roberto Mancini’s second debut as theItalyhead coach ended with a barrage of boos as the Azzurri were beaten 2-0 at home byBelgium.Mika Godts marked his first competitive cap with a fine individual goal after 20 minutes at the Stadio Olimpico. Dodi Lukebakio’s powerful strike in the 69th minute put the visitors out of sight in a chastening first game for Mancini, who accepted the home fans’ frustration.“It will be even better in the end, when you reach the top,” he said afterwards. “This is quite normal, you lose and the fans are disappointed and angry, that is part of the game.”It was an encouraging start, though, for new Belgium coach Mark van Bommel, who said after the game: “I’m 100% happy and satisfied, but I understand there’s always room for improvement.” Belgium host France in their next match on Monday, while Italy travel to Turkey.View image in fullscreenDodi Lukebakio celebrates with the Belgium substitutes after scoring against Italy in Rome.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesEarlier, Shea Charles scored a last-gasp winner after his brother Pierce saved Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s penalty asNorthern Irelandbegan their Nations League campaign with a dramatic 1-0 win overGeorgiain Tbilisi.Pierce Charles guessed right to keep out a poor penalty from Kvaratskhelia in the 65th minute, having already made an excellent save to keep out Georges Mikautadze’s close-range shot earlier in the second half of their Group B2 game.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt the other end, Shea Charles had spurned the visitors’ best chances to score but, in the ninth minute of time added on, he scrambled home from Trai Hume’s cross, securing a first ever away win for Northern Ireland in the Nations League.There was a nervous VAR check for offside but eventually Shea Charles could celebrate just his second international goal. Although Northern Ireland left the pitch celebrating, there was a major blow in stoppage time as defender Dan Ballard pulled up clutching his hamstring.View image in fullscreenShea and Pierce Charles embrace after both played a key role in Northern Ireland’s win.Photograph: Tamuna Kulumbegashvili/APMichael O’Neill had been frustrated with several decisions from the referee, Orel Grinfeeld – not least the penalty, which came after Ballard and Luka Locoshvili tussled in the box and Grinfeeld was sent to the VAR monitor. Northern Ireland’s next opponents,Hungary, lost 1-0 toUkrainein Budapest thanks to Danylo Sikan’s goal.In Group B4,Swedensecured a 2-1 home win overRomaniawith Alexander Isak and Viktor Gyökeres both on target for Graham Potter’s side. In the group’s other game,Polandwere held to a goalless draw byBosnia and Herzegovinain Warsaw.In the third-tier Group C2, Milution Osmajic’s 86th-minute goal helpedMontenegrofight back to beatCyprusin Podgorica. The visitors led through Marcus Edwards’ goal on his international debut, but Nikola Krstovic levelled before Osmajic’s late winner.Armeniatop the group after beatingLatvia2-0 at home earlier on Friday.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueFranceBelgiumNorthern IrelandSwedennewsShareReuse this content

title: Carlos Alcaraz leads by example as Europe take early lead in Laver Cup | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Team Europe led Team World 3-1 after the first day of the Laver Cup, with Carlos Alcaraz featuring in the doubles with Jakub Mensik
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Team Europe led Team World 3-1 after the first day of the Laver Cup, with Carlos Alcaraz featuring in the doubles with Jakub Mensik
Content: Carlos Alcaraz and Jakub Mensik celebrate after winning their doubles match against Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz and Jakub Mensik celebrate after winning their doubles match against Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersTennisCarlos Alcaraz leads by example as Europe take early lead in Laver CupEurope lead Team World 3-1 after opening dayAlcaraz wins doubles match with Jakub MensikTumaini Carayolat the O2Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time Casper Ruud had completed his typically tenacious comeback to capture victory in the opening scuffle of this year’s Laver Cup,Carlos Alcarazwas on the floor. The Spaniard had worked harder than any other player on the sidelines as he repeatedly cheered, animated the crowd and offered a steady stream of thoughtful tactical advice to his teammate. He reacted to Ruud’s triumphant final smash with a jubilant scream, his legs dramatically giving way as he slid down his seat on to the ground.Alcaraz is well aware of his status as the leading star of this year’s event, and in his third Laver Cup outing, the seven-time grand slam champion at times practically took on the role of Europe’s third coach behind Yannick Noah and Tim Henman. This provided a number of insightful glimpses into the way he sees the sport. During one exchange with Ruud, Alcaraz suggested that the Norwegian should attempt more down-the-line backhands and drop shots to draw Francisco Cerundolo, his opponent, into uncomfortable positions on the court. Whether Ruud possesses the skillset to follow Alcaraz’s tactics is another question, but the reasoning he gave for those suggestions was particularly interesting: The ultimate goal, Alcaraz said, should be to “make [Cerundolo] think a little bit more.”Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worthRead moreOn the opening day of the Laver Cup Team Europe established an early 3-1 lead over Team World and the focus of this weekend at the O2 Arena is on the two teams rather than any one player. However, in some ways this week carries greater individual significance for Alcaraz than anyone else. While the other players are moving towards the final stretch of a long, gruelling season that has taken them around the world, Alcaraz is still just finding his way back. With the season nearing its conclusion, Alcaraz has minimal time to rediscover his top form.Alcaraz and Jakub Mensik’s 6-4, 6-4 win over Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz marked just the second competitive appearance of Alcaraz’s comeback after being sidelined for four and a half months, from April till August, due to a right wrist injury. His first tournament at the US Open two weeks ago, ended in remarkable fashion: Alcaraz beaming in the corridor after losing a fifth set tiebreak against Ben Shelton at 3.33am, so happy he was to be healthy, tussling with top players in front of passionate fans and feeling like himself on the court again.Coming back from lengthy injury layoffs is challenging for all players and it can take time for many to find their form and rhythm. However, his time away also presents a rare opportunity. The indoor swing at the end of the year remains the one stretch of the season that Alcaraz, the youngest man to ever achieve the career grand slam, is yet to conquer. The faster indoor conditions have sometimes exposed Alcaraz more temperamental serve in the past, but his diminished form at this stage of the season has often been a consequence of his physical and mental fatigue.For once, he is fresh. Alcaraz returns to the Laver Cup attempting to take a step towards finding his form after such a disruptive injury and finish the season as triumphantly as it began: “I know that I have really important tournaments ahead of me, tournaments that I really want to win at least once, and if we see the record for me, the last part of the season it’s never been my good point,” he said. “But hopefully, right now that I’m just fresh mentally, physically, I’m feeling great. So hopefully, I’m gonna do great tournaments and try to find my good tennis again soon.”View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz (second left) celebrates with Rafael Jodar, Flavio Cobolli and Alexander after Casper Ruud’s victory.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersAfter Ruud’s tight 6-7 (4), 6-4, 10-8 win over Cerundolo and Team World Brandon Nakashima’s 6-1, 3-6, 10-7 win over Mensik, the evening session was defined by one statement performance, a reminder that despite the fact that although Alcaraz is still just 23 years old, an even younger Spanish talent has arrived. On a day that Jannik Sinner announced his withdrawal from the upcoming Beijing Open on Friday, extending his injury layoff to three months, and during an overall depressing ATP season ravaged by so many injuries, the ascension of the 19-year-old Rafael Jodar has been one of the brightest developments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJodar marked his O2 Arena debut with a near flawless performance, picking apart Bublik’s game with his spotless, destructive shotmaking off both wings, and he wreaked havoc on one of the biggest serves on the tour as he led 6-2, 4-0 before closing out a 6-2, 6-3 win. Jodar’s stratospheric level of play was best reflected in the raised eyebrows and shocked facial expressions from the groups of players spread across both team benches. Back in the warm-up room, as he prepared for his upcoming doubles match, the Spaniard’s performance surely provoked a few more vigorous fist pumps from his elder countryman, who by comparison is now an old veteran.Explore more on these topicsTennisCarlos AlcaraznewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli hits wall as George Russell takes F1 Azerbaijan GP pole | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kimi Antonelli crashed out in Q1 while his Mercedes teammate George Russell was in brilliant form, taking pole in Baku by 0.837 from Charles Leclerc
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Kimi Antonelli crashed out in Q1 while his Mercedes teammate George Russell was in brilliant form, taking pole in Baku by 0.837 from Charles Leclerc
Content: George Russell with his pole position award after qualifying for the F1 Azerbaijan GP.Photograph: Bryn Lennon/Formula 1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell with his pole position award after qualifying for the F1 Azerbaijan GP.Photograph: Bryn Lennon/Formula 1/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli hits wall as George Russell takes F1 Azerbaijan GP poleChampionship leader Antonelli crashes out in Q1Mercedes teammate takes pole by 0.837 from LeclercGiles RichardsFri 25 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor all his youth, such has been Kimi Antonelli’s consummate control this season he has barely put a foot wrong. In qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, however, he was given a salutary reminder that the full-on commitment that makes him so engrossing to watch can still bite.The F1 championship leader was disconsolate at being eliminated after hitting the wall in the first session but with his Mercedes teammateGeorge Russellon pole it has set up a potentially fascinating showdown for Saturday’s race.George Russell on pole for Azerbaijan GP after F1 leader Antonelli crashes out – live updatesRead moreAntonelli’s error was uncharacteristic and, he conceded, unnecessary. He knows his lead in the championship – 81 points over Russell – is such that he need take no chances, especially at a track where Mercedes enjoy such a huge advantage over their rivals. Russell’s pole, an immense lap of the street circuit in Baku, was eight-tenths clear of Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc in second, the largest margin to pole of the season.Antonelli has been a revelation in only his second season in F1 with eight victories so far but on Friday in Baku he was sat disconsolately trackside after only 11 minutes of running. A little too eager into the 90-degree left-handed turn one, he clipped the barrier.He took damage to the track rod and a puncture and while he attempted to bring the car home, he was told to park up by a race engineer Pete Bonnington. “We can’t fix this, mate,” Bonnington said. The 20-year-old’s time was enough to see him through to Q2, in which he took no part. Finishing in 16th and angry with himself he held his hands up to the error, caught out as the grip ramped up.“I turned in and suddenly I had a lot more front end than the lap before and touched the wall,” he said. “Mistake from my side, very unnecessary. I’m very mad about it and we’ll try to do better tomorrow. We’ll try our best to recover as many places as possible.”The mistake is Antonelli’s only serious error this year since he crashed in final practice at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix and he was understandably crestfallen, aware a fractional misjudgment had been enormously costly.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli’s broken front left is clearly visible as he tries in vain to get back to the pits.Photograph: Michael Potts/LAT ImagesRussell in is every position to take advantage and to try to claw back some of the points he desperately needs to keep the title fight alive but Antonelli knows that the race is far from a write-off.At Monza hecame back from 19th to take victoryand Baku, with its long straights, has similarly generous opportunities for overtaking. But he cannot afford to be caught in incidents in the midfield.“Race smart in the early stages tomorrow and I am sure he has the pace to climb his way back up the field,” said the Mercedes deputy team principal, Bradley Lord.Quick GuideAzerbaijan F1 qualifying timesShow1George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes1:42.5362Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari1:43.3633Oscar Piastri🇦🇺McLaren1:43.3644Isack Hadjar🇫🇷Red Bull1:43.5005Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:43.6726Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari1:43.8587Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine1:44.0478Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull1:44.0819Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams1:44.56610Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine1:44.963Q2 eliminations11Oliver Bearman🇬🇧Haas1:44.77512Liam Lawson🇳🇿Racing Bulls1:44.86013Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams1:45.00114Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas1:45.01615Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls1:45.10616Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes1:45.504Q1 eliminations17Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi1:45.79918Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi1:45.920*19Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin1:46.59320Sergio Pérez🇲🇽Cadillac1:46.658*21Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin1:47.33722Valtteri Bottas🇫🇮Cadillac1:48.920Alonso and Stroll will start 21st and 22nd because of power-unit penalties.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.In Monza, when Antonelli took a new engine and accrued grid penalties – an imposition still to come for Russell at some point – Mercedes had been hopeful he might come back as high as fifth and he bettered that with a win. Such is the pace of the Mercedes in Baku it is not inconceivable that he could go as high as second, if beating his teammate on this form may be a bridge too far.Indeed, Russell did everything that was required of him with a confidence and touch that he has lacked at points this season. He has been quick all weekend in Azerbaijan, outpacing his teammate, and qualifying proved one of his best performances.The pre-season favourite, the British driver has been on the back foot due to problems around the car’s energy deployment which left him frustrated and examining his own driving style. However, having said he intended to drive more instinctively, he came into the weekend confident and backed it up with an inch-perfect run in qualifying. If he can convert it on Saturday he will have at least kept his slender title hopes alive.View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell (centre), Charles Leclerc (left) and Oscar Piastri – first, second and third – pose after qualifying.Photograph: Ali Haider/EPARussell was initially pushed hard by the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri but with the track evolving and grip at its peak his last hot lap was a belter. Enormously quick in the first sector, he continued to improve and finished in 1min 42.526sec. Norris locked up on his final lap at turn three and could manage only fifth. Piastri was third and Isack Hadjar fourth, with his Red Bull teammate, Max Verstappen, in eighth and Lewis Hamilton in sixth.Russell will take heart from his fifth pole this year, his first in Baku and his first since the Austrian GP but the serious business remains on Saturday. On both sides of the Mercedes garage.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026George RussellKimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You learn more from the losses and the draws’: Red Roses relishing clash with revitalised Black Ferns | England women's rugby union team | The Guardian
description: A week after Canada ended their winning run, England’s World Cup winners face a New Zealand team aiming to inflict more pain at Twickenham
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: A week after Canada ended their winning run, England’s World Cup winners face a New Zealand team aiming to inflict more pain at Twickenham
Content: The England scrum-half Lucy Packer leads the Red Roses in preparations for Saturday’s clash with New Zealand.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe England scrum-half Lucy Packer leads the Red Roses in preparations for Saturday’s clash with New Zealand.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesEngland women's rugby union team‘You learn more from the losses and the draws’: Red Roses relishing clash with revitalised Black FernsA week after Canada ended their winning run, England’s World Cup winners face a New Zealand team aiming to inflict more pain at TwickenhamSarah RendellFri 25 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAwounded animal is the most dangerous. The Red Roses might not have lost to Canada last Saturday but they did not win either, for the first time since 2022. England’s 40-game unbeaten streak continues with a blemish and when things do not go to plan they usually respond with a dominant swing.Despite adding defence specialist Shaun Edwards as a coaching consultant earlier this week, the Tests do not get easier. This Saturday they face the team who last made them taste defeat in the World Cup final four years ago, the Black Ferns.Shaun Edwards inspired by mum’s memory as he beds in with Red RosesRead moreIn recent years England have had their number, winning the three Tests they have played against each other in the past three years. But the nations have not played one another in two years and the Black Ferns are revitalised under the new head coach, Whitney Hansen, who has not yet lost since taking over the job in December of last year.Panic buttons will not be grasped for by the hosts; the match against Canada was a thrilling and close Test which deservedly came out as a draw. On-field battles like that can help the Red Roses get better, according to the England back-row Abi Burton.“I am not scared of losing any more, I am scared that we will become stagnant,” Burton said. “I don’t think we are at that point because we constantly look to get better in training and push each other from a selection point of view. But ultimately you don’t know what you don’t know and if we are at the point of we don’t feel like we are potentially progressing … you do need that ‘they are actually here now, they are on our tails, we were fighting before but we need to fight even more now’. You learn more from the losses and the draws than you do the wins.”The discourse has been about their non-win but the biggest news out of the England camp this week is Edwards’s arrival. The head coach, John Mitchell, has said the 59-year-old is already forming good relationships with the players and Burton echoes that sentiment, saying they bonded over their rugby league backgrounds. Burton comes from a rugby league family with her father, Danny, playing for clubs such as Bradford Bulls.“We got to have that moment of connection to have a chat about that, it felt really cool and special to share that with such a legend of the game,” she said. “It helps you connect and learn about each other.”View image in fullscreenAbby Dow looks to offload as she is chased by Katelyn Vaha’akolo when England last played New Zealand, in October 2024Photograph: Rich Lam/World Rugby/Getty ImagesThe general consensus from camp is that Edwards has slotted in seamlessly and has given the players defensive areas to work on this Saturday. Burton added the coach has an aura about him and has brought a new energy.“That is something we haven’t had in a while,” she said. “Obviously Scaz [Emily Scarratt] went into her coaching role but she has been a constant. I think that aura is so powerful and it makes us want to step up because it is like this man is legendary. You don’t want to let him down, you want to step up. You don’t realise you have another gear to give until you get put in that situation. I think it is super exciting that he has joined us and he will be a real asset to the squad.”The game will be played in front of almost 60,000 at Allianz Stadium almost a year to the day since the Rugby World Cup final, a game the Red Roses won after beating Canada. Prior to the tournament many had believed the showpiece in 2025 would have been between England and New Zealand. The Black Ferns did play on that final day but won the bronze medal after Canada beat them in the semi-final.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe New Zealand lock, Maiakawanakaulani Roos, says downing the Red Roses is their target and having several players compete in England’s PWR last season has aided their preparation. Roos herself played for Trailfinders, as did the captain Georgia Ponsonby with others like Liana Mikaele-Tu’u competing for Harlequins.“We haven’t played them in two years and our game has grown so much and they have just gone from strength to strength,” Roos said. “I am really excited to see how we go and turn up for the challenge that is the Red Roses.“I think we have seen how each other trains, seen the habits that we hold and it is so competitive. I really cannot wait to play them just because we know how they train now and how they do things. I think that is a bit of a point of difference that the girls who have played in the PWR have been able to help our team understand.”England’s goal this weekend will be to start a new winning streak, while New Zealand’s will be to make sure the Red Roses head to Canada in October with their world record firmly in the rear view.Explore more on these topicsEngland women's rugby union teamNew Zealand women's rugby union teamRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AI | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Xi’s state visit to the US emphasized personal rapport with the US president, rather than substantial agreements to pause their respective countries’ AI arms race
Author: David Smith
Headline: Xi’s state visit to the US emphasized personal rapport with the US president, rather than substantial agreements to pause their respective countries’ AI arms race
Content: Donald Trump shakes hands with Chinese president Xi Jinping as they depart the National Archives Museum following a tour on 25 September.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump shakes hands with Chinese president Xi Jinping as they depart the National Archives Museum following a tour on 25 September.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AIXi’s state visit to the US emphasized personal rapport with the US president, rather than substantial agreements to pause their respective countries’ AI arms raceDavid Smithin WashingtonFri 25 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped uptheir Washington summiton Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race.The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce.But despite the presence of top tech executives ata White House state dinneron Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in WashingtonRead more“It was such a layup,” saidRo Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead.“I believeXi Jinpingwould have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups. But he [Trump] didn’t want to; he has no interest in doing that.”It wasthe first visit to the White Houseby a Chinese president in more than a decade and Xi’s second state visit to the US. Three days of pomp and circumstance culminated on Friday with Trump and Xi drinking tea. Trump said ⁠the summit ⁠had produced great strides and that “our ​farmers are going to be happy,” but did not provide details.The pair thenwent to the National Archives, where Trump and Xi looked at the original Declaration of Independence, the constitution and Bill of Rights. Trump told reporters they were comparing China’s documents to America’s founding documents. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of. Theirs goes 6,000 years. So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250. But we’re very proud of our 250.”On Thursday, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always ​under human control”. China aims to have next-generation smart terminals and AI agentsreach more than 90% penetrationby 2030.But Trump – who has repeatedly said the US must forge ahead to maintain its lead overChina– appeared more focused on his push to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, later claiming on social media that Xi “seems to like” the term without divulging the substance of their discussions.Later Trump hosteda black-tie state dinnerattended by titans of the tech industry. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator of Vermont,used social mediato label a photo of Trump and Xi’s table with guests’ net worth: Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla ($928bn), Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ($3.5bn), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ($186bn) and Tim Cook of Apple ($3.1bn). Sanders commented: “A government of, by and for the billionaire class.”But their counterparts in the Chinese tech industry were not present and there was little sign of either country making even a symbolic gesture to apply the brakes.Khanna commented: “Trump didn’t have to have some groundbreaking treaty like Reagan and Gorbachev did [on nuclear weapons]. He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.”Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said.“Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.”The state visit underlinedthe contrast between Trump’s treatmentof democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden ismockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said.But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May,when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference.Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.”Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI.Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate,said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.”Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December theGroup of 20 summitwill be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Donald TrumpXi JinpingUS foreign policyChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Group calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on court
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Group calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on court
Content: South Africa's foreign minister, Ronald Lamola, addresses the UN general assembly in New York on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APView image in fullscreenSouth Africa's foreign minister, Ronald Lamola, addresses the UN general assembly in New York on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APUnited NationsAlarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal courtGroup calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on courtPatrick Wintourin New YorkFri 25 Sep 2026 14.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US threat to impose sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) as an institution, not just its leading judges, could fundamentally disrupt its operation and needed to be resisted, a coalition of countries to defend international law heard at theUnited Nationson Friday.Ronald Lamola,South Africa’s foreign minister, issued the warning at an event during the UN general assembly called to protect the system of international law from a growing array of threats, including open flouting of its tenets and rulings byIsrael.The meeting was organised by the Hague Group, of which Lamola is co-chair, and which was set up in 2025 to protect international law and to call for the proper enforcement of the rulings of its two primary bodies: the ICC and the international court of justice (ICJ).Leaders join push to create UN body to tackle ‘awful reality’ of inequalityRead moreLamola told the gathering that the US had already sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, but was now planning sanctions against the ICC itself.“If imposed, such measures could fundamentally disrupt its operations,” he said. “An independent court remains independent only if judges and officials cannot be punished for carrying out their mandates.”The head of the ICC, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, was sanctioned by the US in August, along with senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, for engaging in the ICC’s efforts to “prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. The attack on Akane was condemned this week by the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.The US has admitted it seeks to dismantle the Hague-based ICC. In his address to the UN general assembly this week,Donald Trumponce again criticised the “out of control” court, which he smeared as an “evil group of people” and urged other nations to reject.The US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, has accused the court of being “a corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty.”The next step by the US is likely to be to impose secondary sanctions on anyone who cooperates with the court, as opposed to sanctioning its senior judiciary. A designation of the whole institution would reach every European bank, insurer and technology supplier serving the court, which sits in theNetherlands.The Dutch government, as the host of the ICC, is taking the lead in trying to warn the US away from the effective immobilisation of the court. The Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, told the UN general assembly: “International law either works for everyone or for no one. This court was established to protect us against impunity and it was built on the foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials. And now, with the ICC under attack, the writing is truly on the wall.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After all, how can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? And I believe there can be only one response: to say, hands off the ICC and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.”William Schabas, a specialist in international law, noted to the meeting the irony that the resort to international law and courts was increasing dramatically even as the institutions were under attack. He said nations needed to strengthen the ICC, including by ensuring positions are not traded and only the highest calibre judges are elected.Diana Buttu, the prominent Palestinian lawyer, was among many to complain of western powers’ partial resort to international law. “The greatest threat to international law is not the state that openly defies it,” she said. “The greatest threat is our selectivity – the quiet decision that is made in capitals and rooms that the rules don’t bind everybody, they only bind some. It is the belief that we can excuse some because they are our allies, our partners and our friends.”Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsInternational criminal courtInternational court of justiceTrump administrationDonald TrumpMarco RubioIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Overcrowding and racism at Manston asylum centre linked to government decisions, inquiry hears | Manston asylum centre | The Guardian
description: Kent facility became dangerously overburdened after ministers halted transfers to hotels
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Kent facility became dangerously overburdened after ministers halted transfers to hotels
Content: The Manston arrivals and processing centre at a former military base near Ramsgate.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Manston arrivals and processing centre at a former military base near Ramsgate.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesManston asylum centreOvercrowding and racism at Manston asylum centre linked to government decisions, inquiry hearsKent facility became dangerously overburdened after ministers halted transfers to hotelsDiane TaylorFri 25 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA catalogue of failures including racism, use of force and chronic overcrowding at a Home Office processing site for people who arrive on small boat were linked to decisions made at the highest level of government, an independent inquiry has heard.The government commissioned the Manston independent inquiry to look at problems under the Conservative government between 1 June and 22 November 2022 at the facility in Kent.Almost 200 asylum seekers detained at Manston are participating in the inquiry along with the former home secretariesSuella Bravermanand Priti Patel, several government departments including the Home Office, Treasury, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence, and HM Inspectorate of Prisons and the UK Health Security Agency.The problems began when the site became vastly overcrowded. Manston was designed to hold a maximum of 1,600 new arrivals for no more than 24 hours as there are no proper sleeping or other facilities there. But after decisions by ministers to pause transfers of many of the asylum seekers to other accommodation such as hotels the site became dangerously overcrowded.Up to 4,000 people were accommodated there unlawfully for several weeks at the peak of the crisis, most of them sleeping on the floor in profoundly insanitary conditions.There were outbreaks of infectious conditions including scabies and diphtheria, the latter of which can be fatal in approximately 30% of cases in unvaccinated populations. There were also reports of assaults and drug use by guards, racist abuse from guards, and the death of a man after contracting diphtheria.The inquiry, chaired by Sophie Cartwright KC, heard that two former prime ministers,Boris Johnsonand Rishi Sunak, who were both in post at different points in 2022, were involved in decision-making about the Manston site.Laura Dubinsky KC, representing some of the participants, told the inquiry that the decision to pause sending many asylum seekers on to hotels was in line with the thinking at No 10.“No 10 clearly did play a decision-making role,” she said. Patel has provided evidence to the inquiry that funding was deemed inadequate to address the small boats issue, including funding for Manston and onward accommodation.The inquiry heard that events in Manston “raise very serious questions for ministers”.Clair Dobbin KC, counsel to the inquiry, said it was taking place in a “crucible of hostility” at a time when the arrival of small boats remains a significant issue.She added that “to put it bluntly” the inquiry would look at whether at certain points “the entire operation at Manston was outside the law”.One senior Home Office official wrote a report saying: “To be frank, I’m struggling for words,” after observing what he said were “the worst conditions I have observed working in this environment”.Hussein Haseeb Ahmed, 31, was taken to Manston after arriving in a small boat. Hedied in hospital after becoming ill with diphtheria. He was belatedly admitted for care and was kept in handcuffs as he lay dying. The handcuffs were only removed two and a half hours before he died. According to the inquiry, evidence about his death suggests “a succession of missed opportunities”.The inquiry also heard that “very racist language was used towards detainees by some staff”.Sixty families were crammed into 11 rooms in a barracks building with no hot water, showers or clean clothes for nine days with one toilet for 81 people, and no soap or sanitiser available.Some used toothpaste to soothe bites and one used a croissant wrapper to dress wounds.Questions were raised about whether some unvetted staff were working legally at Manston.Shu Shin Luh, one of the lawyers representing participants in the inquiry, said: “Why were people treated as less than human?”Stephanie Harrison KC, also representing some of the participants in the inquiry, accused the Home Office of presiding over “an institutional culture defined by impunity with widespread illegality and non-compliance with the law”.Future dates for inquiry hearings have not yet been confirmed.Explore more on these topicsManston asylum centreMigrationBoris JohnsonRishi SunakPriti PatelSuella BravermanEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Turning Point USA knew of security concerns yet insisted Charlie Kirk speak outdoors, report says | Charlie Kirk shooting | The Guardian
description: According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot
Content: Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah on 10 September 2025.Photograph: Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/ReutersView image in fullscreenCharlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah on 10 September 2025.Photograph: Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/ReutersCharlie Kirk shootingTurning Point USA knew of security concerns yet insisted Charlie Kirk speak outdoors, report saysAccording to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shotMaya YangFri 25 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 17.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political group’s leaderCharlie Kirkspeak outdoors at Utah Valley University – where he was ultimately assassinated – despite security concerns raised with his team by the school’s leaders and its police chief.The independentreportwith those findings was commissioned by UVU and released on Friday. The report examined security procedures leading up to the 31-year-old’s fatal shooting on 10 September 2025 during a talk at the university’s campus in Orem, Utah.According to the 158-page report, school staff recommended Turning Point USA (TPUSA) move its event to a more secure location weeks before Kirk’s slaying. However, TPUSA “insisted upon” an outdoor location which “created significant protective operations considerations”, the report said.It added that a face-to-face, pre-event briefing and walkthrough with UVU police chief Jeff Long and the TPUSA protection detail – including the organization’s security supervisor Dan Flood – “should also have occurred” on UVU’s campus hours prior to the event.“Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway at 11[am], however, this face-to-face meeting did not occur,” the report said.Kirk was shot and killed by a sniper that day in the early afternoon.According to the report, the university also asked TPUSA for an estimated attendance figure. But the organization never provided one, despite saying it would control ticketing for the event, Utah’s Salt Lake Tribune newspaperreported.“Based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” the report said.However, it also noted UVU’s having deferred to TPUSA on various event logistics. “Several key event security decisions were deferred to the TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor fountain courtyard area and using TPUSA’s ticketing process,” the university’s report said.“Those decisions placed the event in an area that was more difficult to control and limited UVU’s ability to obtain reliable, real-time information regarding anticipated attendance and crowd size.”The report added: “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control and other conditions necessary to support campus safety.”In response to the report, Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said: “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement.“Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.”Meanwhile, a statement from Jon Anderson, UVU’s president, said the university had a responsibility to “learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations”.“This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn,” Anderson’s statement also said.Anderson, who became the university’s president in August, also said in his statement that UVU had made “meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year”.Kirk’s family is planning to sue the university.
