His family alleged in a 16 Septemberlegal noticepresaging wrongful death litigation that UVU had placed “a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event … surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms” – and that the setup was like “walking him into a fishbowl”.UVU said it was aware of the notice and said it “addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes”, according to the Tribune.Utah resident Tyler Robinson has been charged with aggravated murder in connection with Kirk’s killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and no trial date had been set for him as of Friday.The Associated Presscontributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCharlie Kirk shootingUS crimeUtahUS universitiesFar right (US)US gun controlnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why a supercharged El Niño is putting Hawaii in the bullseye of more storms  | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: Hurricane Nolo is the latest storm to menace the islands as sees warming ocean temperatures fuel more severe weather
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Hurricane Nolo is the latest storm to menace the islands as sees warming ocean temperatures fuel more severe weather
Content: ‘An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare.’Photograph: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/APView image in fullscreen‘An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare.’Photograph: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/APEl Niño southern oscillationWhy a supercharged El Niño is putting Hawaii in the bullseye of more stormsHurricane Nolo is the latest storm to menace the islands as sees warming ocean temperatures fuel more severe weatherGabrielle CanonFri 25 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith Hurricane Nolo, the islands ofHawaiiare grappling with the third major tropical storm in recent months.Hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September flooded homes and roads, downed trees and toppled electricity lines across the islands. Nolo, which strengthened to a hurricane on Thursday night, is expected to batter the islands with rain and high surf.Despite its location, stretching across roughly 1,500 miles in the central north Pacific Ocean, Hawaii typically avoids the worst effects from hurricanes. In fact, the island chain so often dodges direct hits from the violent storms thatit’s been quipped they have a force field around them.But the islands have seen an unusual amount of severe storms this year. Already, more than 500 homes have been damaged or destroyed as Nolo threatens to unleash downpours that could measure in feet instead of inches.“An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center,saidduring a broadcast discussion as Lowell swirled closer last month, adding that Hawaii has not had a direct hurricane landfall since Iniki in 1992. That violent stormunleashed 145 mile-per-hour windsas it tore through Kauai, destroying or damaging roughly 70% of the island’s homes and businesses.It’s not luck (or a force field) that typically protected the islands, but location, according to Dr Nicholas Grondin, assistant professor of environmental science at the University of Tampa. Among the most isolated chains of islands on Earth, Hawaii is simply a small target in the vast open ocean, Grondin explained in an editorial published by the Conversation.Most approaching storms also must pass over cooler water temperatures to the east of the islands, which helps calm them. “Without warm oceans to provide fuel, hurricanes tend to weaken and fizzle out as they approach the islands,” Grondin said.Sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific are, however, exceptionally warm this year due toEl Niño. The climate phenomenon typically limits hurricane activity in the Atlantic and enhances the development and strength of storms in the Pacific. El Niño has already developed, but is expected to strengthen through the coming months, and forecasters have warned there is a high probability it will reach a historic intensity.El Niño has caused hurricanes to form further to the south and west this year, according to Matthew Rosencrans, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s lead forecaster for the seasonal hurricane outlook, which “puts them in a place where they could make that westward run towards the Hawaiian islands”.It also makes for a lagging storm season. Hurricane risks typically extend from July to the end of November but fall off into the later months. September and October are far busier in El Niño years.The climate crisis has also played a part in strengthening the storms. The effects of El Niño are layered on top of the warming trends.“The oceans are absorbing 92% of the excess heat to the climate system from the addition of heat-trapping pollutants to the atmosphere,” Union of Concerned Scientists climate scientist Dr Marc Alessisaidin a thread shared on Bluesky. According to Alessi, the energy added to oceans over just the last year is on par with roughly 12 Hiroshima bombs of heat released every second.“For the next year, we can expect to see precipitation and other weather extremes unlike anything we’ve seen before,” he said.For Pacific storms, Rosencrans said, it means they may carry more moisture and produce stronger winds.As efforts begin to clear debris and repair roads and infrastructure damaged during Lowell, emergency management officials must continue keeping close watch on the waters for the next big storm.“They just need to reset and regard any potential upcoming impacts,” Rosencrans said. “The season is not over – there is still a long bit to go.”Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationHawaiiUS weatherExtreme weatherHurricanesClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We don’t have time for more promises’: the Croatian town that took on an illegal waste dump | Waste | The Guardian
description: After years of illegal mass flytipping in Gospić, fed-up residents decided to take matters into their own hands
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: After years of illegal mass flytipping in Gospić, fed-up residents decided to take matters into their own hands
Content: A woman at a national protest against toxic waste dumping in Zagreb earlier this month.Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPAView image in fullscreenA woman at a national protest against toxic waste dumping in Zagreb earlier this month.Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPAWaste‘We don’t have time for more promises’: the Croatian town that took on an illegal waste dumpAfter years of illegal mass flytipping in Gospić, fed-up residents decided to take matters into their own handsPippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Gospić is our home,” Željka Šikić shouted to a crowd of 40,000 people outside the Croatian parliament earlier this month. The slogan is the name of a campaign she helped to set up to protest against the illegal dumping of waste in Gospić, a town in the mountainous Lika region of centralCroatia.Between 2022 and 2024, waste was illegally abandoned at several sites in the town. At one of the biggest, just 50 metres from Šikić’s home, an estimated 35,000 tonnes of waste, some of it hazardous, was dumped and buried.In the dead of night, lorries heaving with waste would pass her front door and enter a nearby industrial site. This activity went largely unnoticed by the local authorities and police. But residents in Gospić were well aware and started taking it in turns to stay up to photograph the vehicles coming in and out of the site.“I don’t think it should be our job to stay awake all night to see what’s going on,” Šikić says.View image in fullscreenAn illegal waste site in Gospić in August.Photograph: Pixsell/AlamyThe waste became a blight on the community and a recentreport from the Croatian Institute of Public HealthrevealedPfas“forever chemicals” had been detected in groundwater samples nearby. Elevated concentrations of copper and lead were also detected in the soil.Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that have beenlinked to serious health conditions, including several types of cancer. They are known as “forever chemicals” because of how long they persist in the environment.Despite assurances that their drinking water is safe, a lack of trust means many residents have resorted to buying bottled water.“I’m really scared,” Šikić says. “I would like to move house but I don’t know who would pay for the house on the first road next to the waste. I feel betrayed.”View image in fullscreenResidents took to filming lorries going in and out of one of the dumping sites on the outskirts of Gospić, seen here last month.Photograph: Pixsell/AlamyIn February 2025, years after the activity began, police and law enforcement officers arrested 13 people on suspicion of being part of the environmental criminal network involved in dumping the waste.The main suspects, two Croatian nationals, were considered high-value targets byEuropoland were believed to have orchestrated the illegal import of hazardous waste from Italy, Slovenia and Germany. It is thought the criminals generated upwards of €4m (£3.4m) in profit from this activity.Waste crime is big business. Criminal networks often take advantage of the high costs associated with treating and disposing of waste properly. By falsifying documents to declare the waste as destined for recycling, they can save on the costs and pocket the difference.Residents in Gospić had hoped the arrests would finally mean the site was shut down and cleaned up. But 18 months later, it is still there.Frustrated by the lack of action, Šikić and 16 other residents joined together to form the “Gospić is our home” movement.Ivana Rukavina Sarić, another member of the campaign group, says: “We called people from different professional backgrounds because we knew from the beginning that this would be highly complicated and would need a multi-disciplinary approach.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving shared information about their struggles online and with Croatian media, Sarić says the campaign turned national, with the group now getting calls daily from other affected communities.“There are so many waste hotspots in the whole of Croatia and so many people facing similar problems. The problem we have in Gospić is the drop of liquid that overflows the glass,” she says. “It’s become a national, even global problem.”Similar dumping has been reported inseveral otherCroatian towns, but the issue extends far beyond national borders. The United Nations estimates that 15% to 30% of EU waste shipments are illegal, and arecent investigationby the Guardian uncovered irrigation canals contaminated with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste exports.View image in fullscreenWhat began as a small local campaign has grown into a national movement, with thousands attending a demonstration about the issue in Zagreb this month.Photograph: Ronald Gorsic/Cropix/SIPA/ShutterstockAnger at the scale of the problem prompted tens of thousands of people from across Croatia to descend on the capital on 5 September. It is thought there were upwards of 40,000 people marching through Zagreb. “The capital was full,” Sarić says.The group is demanding a comprehensive remediation of the site and the urgent removal of the buried waste. It also wants all known waste hotspots in Croatia to be included in a national waste strategy.The government has opened two public procurement procedures for the removal, disposal or recovery of the waste. But with the waste still there four years since the illegal activity began, and concerns mounting over potential health and environmental impacts, the group plans to head to Brussels where it will protest at the European parliament.“We’ve lost so much time, we don’t have time for more promises,” Sarić says. “We want clear information, clear deadlines and clear action.”The Croatian government did not respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsWastePfasCroatiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We can’t ride this storm’: the English farmers facing uncertainty after sustainability funding runs dry | Farming | The Guardian
description: After the available money ran out after just six hours, some fear they will have to reverse efforts to boost nature
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: After the available money ran out after just six hours, some fear they will have to reverse efforts to boost nature
Content: Peter Hatley has spent years slowly diversifying his farm and creating space for nature.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeter Hatley has spent years slowly diversifying his farm and creating space for nature.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianFarming‘We can’t ride this storm’: the English farmers facing uncertainty after sustainability funding runs dryAfter the available money ran out after just six hours, some fear they will have to reverse efforts to boost naturePippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 25 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 04.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Tuesday morning, farmer Peter Hatley logged on to his computer at 10am. England’s 2026 sustainable farming incentive (SFI) was opening for applicants and, after three bad harvests, the money would be a lifeline.But Hatley, who runs a 240-hectare family farm inCambridgeshire, was faced with repeated error messages. He called the government’s helpline, which he says acknowledged there were problems with the scheme, but says by the time the problem was fixed, the money had gone.“We tried our utmost. We were fully prepared; everything was checked and triple-checked and through no fault of our own we were denied this opportunity. I’m shell-shocked,” he says.View image in fullscreenThe wild bird feed mix field alongside a corn field on Peter Hatley’s farm in Landbeach, Cambridgeshire.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianBy 4pm on Tuesday, just six hours after it launched, the SFI hadrun outof money after a rush somecompared with “the scramble for Oasis tickets”.SFI is part of a package of payments that replaced the EU’s common agricultural policy, paying farmers to look after nature, soil and other public goods, rather than simply for farming and owning land. Figures suggest that up to 10,000 farmers with funding agreements that will expire in March 2027 either chose not to apply or could not apply.‘Worse than the scramble for Oasis tickets’: England’s sustainable farming funds run out in just six hoursRead moreHistorically, Hatley says his farm could weather a level of uncertainty with confidence that, if he had one bad harvest, the next would probably be good. But in the face of the rapidly changing climate, this is no longer a given.“In 2024 we had extreme rain, in 2025 a lack of rain caused depressed yields and then this year, I mean, it’s 25C at the end of September. We’re at breaking point. We can’t ride this storm,” he says.Farmers across the country are reporting a devastating outlook, with crop-destroying heat and drought, and soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran piling pressure on what has already been a challenging few years.View image in fullscreenHatley says not receiving funding will undo 20 years of hard work to create diversity.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianHatley has spent years slowly diversifying his farm and creating space for nature but says without the SFI funding he has no choice but to reverse this.“I will undo all the hard work over the last 20 years and move to a mono crop with maize. It’s not a threat, it’s what I will do for my family. It will break our hearts but my children come first. I’m just thankful my father is not here to see it,” he says.“The skylarks, the lapwings, they’ll go. I’ll have to put more cows on my grass so the bugs and the dragonflies will suffer. If I said this to anybody else, it would sound like blackmail, but it’s not; it’s a business fact. How do I explain to the bank manager that I can’t afford to pay my mortgage this month because I put wood pigeons and birds of prey first?”Martin Lines, chief executive of the Nature FriendlyFarmingNetwork, said the speed at which the funding ran out showed the “desperation” many farmers were experiencing.Mat Cole, an uplands farmer in the south of England, could not log in to the scheme as it launched because he was busy at market day. But as soon as he could, he rushed home and by noon was ready to apply. After spending a few hours preparing his application, he submitted it at 3.50pm, only to be greeted by an error message.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I then understood they had run out of money,” he said. “I thought I probably had a week or so to apply.”View image in fullscreenHatley grows kale as part of a wild bird feed mix on his farm.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianLike Peter, he has been left in an uncertain situation, not knowing if he can continue with the environmental improvements he has been making on his farm.“We’ve engaged with these schemes to try and improve our environment. We’ve used the money to improve hedgerows, grasslands and water quality. To have the drawbridges pulled up like that, it’s just shambolic,” he says.‘It’s really taking off’: hedge revival as farmers rediscover ancient toolsRead moreThe last few years have presented farmers with a number of financial challenges, on top of dealing with a changing climate. Brexit meant losing access to the basic payment scheme (BPS) through the common agricultural policy; the BPS is being phased out, however, and replaced by a complex system of funds for environmental management, which seem much more likely to run out or be unexpectedly wound up for the year. This comes as basic costs for fuel and inputs are also soaring, thanks to global conflict.The National Farmers’ Union is calling on the government to commit now to the 2027 SFI scheme.“For food-producing businesses already questioning whether they can survive the year ahead, this clarity is critical,” said Robyn Munt, the union’s vice-president.Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: “Farmers will receive almost a third of a billion pounds each year for three years under new SFI26 agreements. That’s nearly a billion pounds invested in resilient farming.“Previously a quarter of funding headed to just 4% of farms making claims. That’s why this government developed a fairer system to reach more farmers by capping applications at £100,000 and ensured small farms and those new to environmental land management schemes were prioritised. “I know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be deeply disappointed not to have secured an agreement during Window 2, particularly given the challenges the sector has faced this year. I have heard those concerns and am determined to work closely with farmers as we learn lessons from this year and shape SFI27, including exploring alternatives to a first-come, first-served application process.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingEnglandSustainable developmentCambridgeshireAgricultureRural affairsClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More sex offenders in England and Wales could be released amid court system crisis, police sources say | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Sources tell the Guardian they are braced for more offenders being bailed into the community ahead of October’s early prisoner release
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Sources tell the Guardian they are braced for more offenders being bailed into the community ahead of October’s early prisoner release
Content: The government’s early release policy is aimed at reducing pressure on oversubscribed jails.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe government’s early release policy is aimed at reducing pressure on oversubscribed jails.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrisons and probationMore sex offenders in England and Wales could be released amid court system crisis, police sources saySources tell the Guardian they are braced for more offenders being bailed into the community ahead of October’s early prisoner releaseVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore sexual predators inEnglandand Wales could be freed instead of jailed because of the pressure on courts and prisons, police sources have told the Guardian.The warning comes after the Metropolitan police commissioner, Mark Rowley, on Thursday condemned the release on bail of a man after he admitted taking pictures of children and women, and then using AI to sexualise them.Zafer Dogan was bailed to his flatoverlooking a children’s playground, from which he committed some of the offences he admitted, despite prosecutors and police saying he should be remanded in custody.One of his victims said they had to move after courts declined to send him to jail ahead of his sentencing on Thursday, where he was imprisoned for two years.Prisoners to ‘double up’ in one-person prefab cells, leaked documents showRead moreA senior police source said they feared more such cases across England andWales, where charged suspects are released rather than jailed: “We are bracing ourselves for more of this across the country, that is, offenders who should be remanded, instead being freed on bail, to the distress of their victims.“Some forces are better resourced to deal with this than others. It is going to be a nationwide issue.”The government’s early release policy, to ease pressure on prisons where places are on the verge of running out, is expected to start next Thursday.The police source added: “Probation is crumbling, policing is having to pick up extra offender management work which it has not had to do before. Something has got to give.“The work that will be created because of increases in crime and the management of offenders in the community will take away from regular frontline crime fighting.”Some in policing suspect courts are more reluctant than before to send suspects to prison.A senior Met source said they believed courts were increasingly reluctant to remand knife crime suspects in custody as cases progressed, because they suspected the final sentence would not be custodial. “On knife crime we are seeing less imprisonment, possibly the effects of a mindset of courts where they think if suspects are not going to custody at the end [when convicted], why remand them to prison,” they said.The Met released details on a new case to show the crisis the system faces.The force said a 17-year-old boy had been bailed five times between June and September, and when released breached conditions for his electronic tag twice and committed four further crimes, including two robberies and making and distributing indecent images of children.Officers worked 23-hour shifts hoping to see him remanded in custody, only for him to be bailed, the Met said.DS Wess Kalam, who led the investigation, said: “It is incredibly frustrating for those officers to see him repeatedly released on bail, only to be arrested again for further alleged offending or breaches.“We continually work to make decisions which prioritise victim safety, but when an individual we have arrested and remanded is released back into the community, it both limits the impact we can have and increases the risk to the public.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMinisters propose converting female prison estate into cells for menRead moreAssistant chief constable Jason Devonport, the National Police Chiefs’ Council’s (NPCC) lead for criminal justice reform, said: “We recognise that the criminal justice system is operating under severe stress and challenging circumstances. That is why we broadly support the aim of theSentencingAct to ease the current and long-term pressure on prison capacity.“However, public trust and confidence in the criminal justice system must not be lost through these reforms. The system must work as one to protect the public, prioritising prison spaces for dangerous and prolific criminals.“We will continue to play our part in arresting offenders and putting them before the courts, advocating for the toughest sentences possible where appropriate. We will also continue to work with the government to ensure we collectively have the officers and tools we need to keep communities safe.”Rowley has made several interventions about the justice system and its failings. A senior Met source added: “The criminal justice system is overloaded, we worry we will see more and more of these cases.”The NPCC estimates costs to policing in England and Wales of early release to be £480m and a rise in crime of up to 6%.The bill for the Met alone could be about £100m, at a time when it and other forces were already making cuts.Zafer Dogan was released on bail to his flat near a playground.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAThe London victims’ commissioner, Andrea Simon, said: “Dogan’s case is a stark illustration of what can happen when victims’ safety is not prioritised. It is unacceptable that, in this case, it was the victims and their families who felt forced to leave their home and move into temporary accommodation after Dogan was bailed to the address he had been offending from.“It raises serious questions about the justice system’s ability to manage the influx of offenders into the community following the early prisoner release scheme in October. Pressure to reduce the remand population cannot come at the expense of victims’ safety.”Simon said police themselves had also let down victims: “Parallels can be drawn with this case and the handling of serial sex offender and murderer Simon Levy,who was also shockingly bailedand allowed to continue his offending.“In Levy’s case I have called on government to commit to a multi-agency review to examine and learn from the significant cross-justice agency failings from the police, crown prosecutors and the courts around information sharing and understanding and responding to risk.”A government spokesperson, asked if they agreed with Rowley’s criticism, said: “These were awful crimes and our thoughts are with the victims and their loved ones.“The protection of victims, witnesses, and the public must always be considered when deciding whether or not an offender should be released on bail. While CPS have the right to challenge these, final decisions are made by the independent judiciary.“We’ve brought in tough new laws to ban AI tools designed to create child sexual abuse images, target websites that spread them and stop this vile material being created in the first place.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceCrimePoliceSentencingEnglandWalesShareReuse this content

title: Couple jailed for at least 21 years for murder of vulnerable man in their care | Crime | The Guardian
description: Kenneth Newton and Melanie James filmed themselves mocking and abusing Rubin Blount, 28, who weighed 40kg when he died
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Kenneth Newton and Melanie James filmed themselves mocking and abusing Rubin Blount, 28, who weighed 40kg when he died
Content: Kenneth Newton and Melanie James’s ‘cruel’ behaviour towards their victim was demonstrated in videos shown to the jury.Composite: Staffordshire police/PAView image in fullscreenKenneth Newton and Melanie James’s ‘cruel’ behaviour towards their victim was demonstrated in videos shown to the jury.Composite: Staffordshire police/PACrimeCouple jailed for at least 21 years for murder of vulnerable man in their careKenneth Newton and Melanie James filmed themselves mocking and abusing Rubin Blount, 28, who weighed 40kg when he diedCaroline Daviesand agencyFri 25 Sep 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA couple convicted of murder after inflicting “deliberate cruelty” on a vulnerable 28-year-old man in their care, who at the time of his death weighed just 40kg (6st 4lb), have been jailed for life.Rubin Blount was made to stand for long periods of time, left to lie in his own urine and forced to eat out of bins by his stepbrother Kenneth Newton and Newton’s partner, Melanie James, at a property in Tamworth,Staffordshire, Stafford crown court heard.Newton, 58, and James, 64, both from Birmingham, who had filmed themselves mocking and abusing the victim, were convicted by a jury in July of his murder.Jailing them each for a minimum of 21 years, Mrs Justice Jefford said they had been in a position of trust which they had abused and had shown an “abject failure to help him when he was in pain and suffering”.Blount was severely dehydrated and malnourished when he was taken to hospital after he became unwell, and he had a cardiac arrest upon arrival. He died three days later on 30 November 2022.Doctors found he had extensive pneumonia, severe infection, fractures to his ribs and spine, and burns, lesions and grazes. He had 50 rib fractures, 47 of which had been inflicted in the weeks leading up to his death.View image in fullscreenRubin Blount was described as ‘considerably mentally impaired’ and particularly vulnerable.Photograph: Staffordshire police/PAJennifer Josephs KC, prosecuting, told Friday’s sentencing hearing that Blount had been described as “considerably mentally impaired” and was particularly vulnerable, and that the defendants’ “cruel” behaviour towards him was demonstrated in videos shown to the jury.Josephs said Blount must have been in “extreme pain and suffering” before his death, and the couple had denied him access to medical care until he was “beyond help”.“Mr Blount’s death was the culmination of a prolonged course of conduct perpetrated against a man who was unable to speak for himself,” she said.Blount’s mother, Jeanette Blount, said in a victim impact statement that her son was vulnerable and deserved “compassion, dignity and a chance to live his life”.“We all believed they loved him and would take care of him. We had no reason to believe otherwise,” she said.The judge said a series of videos made by the defendants on 2 November 2022 “show Rubin emaciated, gaunt, stooped and broken, standing in the doorway”. Videos showed the pair mocking him and flinging abuse at him while he was “unable to defend himself or even walk away”.“The first 25 rib fractures were inflicted before or shortly after this recording was made,” she added.James sobbed as the court was told that the abuse and violence inflicted on Blount went on for months.Rebecca Wade KC, defending James, said: “No one could fail to be disgusted by Melanie James’s actions towards this vulnerable man. She is a woman who has had a difficult life of her own.“There is some evidence to show that at one point she did care for Rubin and did love him, and him her.” Something “shifted”, she said, due to James’s “ability to cope with the stresses and strains of life and that was much to Rubin’s detriment”.Mark Heywood KC, defending Newton, said Blount was, through no fault of his own, a “challenging” person to care for. The circumstances leading to his death “can’t be dealt with as simply as saying he was financially advantageous for them, or that he became a burden”, he said. The couple were “ill-equipped”.Speaking outside the court, DCI Ian Fitzgerald, of Staffordshire police, said: “The extent of the injuries Rubin suffered, the state that he was in and the arrogance [of the defendants] in the way they thought they could try and get away with it and blame him for his injuries was shocking and very, very distressing.”Explore more on these topicsCrimeStaffordshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS boss says staff suspected of snooping on patients’ records should be suspended immediately | NHS | The Guardian
description: Jim Mackey urges ‘zero tolerance approach’ in England amid growing concern over breaches of confidential data
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Jim Mackey urges ‘zero tolerance approach’ in England amid growing concern over breaches of confidential data
Content: The call follows reports that NHS staff accessed the medical records of victims of the Nottingham and Southport attacks without authorisation.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenThe call follows reports that NHS staff accessed the medical records of victims of the Nottingham and Southport attacks without authorisation.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PANHSNHS boss says staff suspected of snooping on patients’ records should be suspended immediatelyJim Mackey urges ‘zero tolerance approach’ in England amid growing concern over breaches of confidential dataDenis CampbellHealth policy editorFri 25 Sep 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS staff suspected of snooping on patients’ medical records should besuspended immediatelyand barred from using health service computers, the head of NHS England has said.Jim Mackey urged NHS England’s 205 health trusts to pursue a “zero tolerance” approach to staff who are suspected of inappropriately accessing records.He called for a “hardline” stance towards anyone found to have accessed patients’ notes or medical histories without a clinical justification.His intervention comes amid growing concern that staff sometimes use their position to view medical records but rarely face any meaningful penalty for doing so.Mackey said on Friday: “Patient records contain some of the most private information people will ever share. We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust and enough is enough.”He wrote to all trusts demanding that they routinely implement whatNHSEngland called a “crackdown” on breaching patients’ confidential data.The problem has gained attention after reports that NHS staff illicitly accessed medical records of victims of the attacks by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023 and stabbings by Axel Rudakubana in Southport in 2024, among other high-profile incidents.Mackey said: “If someone is suspected of snooping we cannot leave them in post with access to patients’ records while an investigation takes days or weeks. From now on we will expect them to be suspended and have their access to NHS systems cut off immediately, while the facts are established.”That should happen already, but rarely does so in practice.He added: “Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient’s record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record.”Since 2020, more than 200 NHS staff in England have been dismissed and 2,000 others sanctioned for snooping on patients’ records, an investigation by Sky News and theHealthService Journal found this month.One employee was sacked after viewing up to 179 people’s records, another had accessed their spouse’s details in a “potential domestic violence situation”, and others had shared information they had gathered in WhatsApp groups.Responses by 140 trusts to freedom of information requests by the media outlets showed that 214 staff were dismissed, three suspended and 540 given a final written warning over the last five years.The Liberal Democrat MP Layla Moran, who chairs the health and social care select committee, has warned that official numbers for staff accessing patients’ records illegally under the Data Protection Act were likely to be “canaries in the coal mine”.However, Paul Arnold, the chief executive of the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), the data watchdog,said in Junethat “inappropriate access is rare and does not represent the behaviour of the vast majority of healthcare staff who take their duty of confidentiality extremely seriously”.Bristol NHS foundation trust has apologisedto Paula and Tom McGowan for staff snooping on the medical records of their son Oliver, who died in 2016 aged 18. At least five members of staff, including three nurses and a doctor, accessed his records without permission.Gillian Merron, a health minister,disclosed in Julythat health service bodies reported 1,445 cases of inappropriate access to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.Explore more on these topicsNHSHealthData protectionHospitalsEnglandShareReuse this content

title: Mosques given £66m in emergency security funds after Southport disorder | Islamophobia | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Full government funding figures ‘tell sombre story about rise in hostility that British Muslims live with’, trust says
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Exclusive: Full government funding figures ‘tell sombre story about rise in hostility that British Muslims live with’, trust says
Content: Islam, who attends the Jami community centre in Birmingham, which has had windows smashed and racist graffiti daubed on its premises.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIslam, who attends the Jami community centre in Birmingham, which has had windows smashed and racist graffiti daubed on its premises.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianIslamophobiaMosques given £66m in emergency security funds after Southport disorderExclusive: Full government funding figures ‘tell sombre story about rise in hostility that British Muslims live with’, trust saysNeha GohilMidlands correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA record £66m of emergency security funding was issued by theHome Officefor mosques and related community sites in the UK when violent disorder spread in the aftermath of the Southport attacks in 2024.Exclusive figures obtained by the Guardian also reveal a record of about £41m in security funding was issued for mosques and related community sites for the year from April 2025-26 as part of the protective security scheme.The chief executive of the British Muslim Trust, the government’s partner for monitoring anti-Muslim hatred, said the figures “tell an incredibly sombre story about the rise in anti-Muslim hostility that British Muslims are living with”.“Security needs are increasing as a direct response to the increase in attacks that mosques are under,” Akeela Ahmed said. “If we want to bring down the costs for protecting British Muslims in the UK then we need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities.”The trust published data in July showing thatone mosque was attacked every five daysacross Britain in the past year.The government launched a security scheme for places of worship in 2016 forEnglandand Wales, and in 2023 it created a dedicated scheme worth £29.4m for mosques and faith schools in the UK to provide security to ensure the safety of Muslim communities.View image in fullscreenThe Jami centre, which is seeking funding but has had to introduce its own security measures, including gates and blackout boards.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianAccording to figures obtained via a freedom of information request, the security funding issued for mosques, Islamic faith schools and associated sites was £73,147 in 2016-17, before increasing to about £3m in 2022-23, £29m in 2024-25 and a record of about £41m in 2025-26.Graph of security funding for mosques and related community sitesThe Home Office introduced a separate emergency security scheme as a temporary measure for places of worship when violent disorder spread across cities after a knife attack in Southport in 2024 in which three girls at a dance class were murdered.Of the almost £69m granted to places of worship in the UK as part of this scheme, about £66m was issued to mosques and associated sites, the data revealed. At the time, mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers were targeted after false news had spread online claiming that the perpetrator of the attack was a Muslim asylum seeker.Shaista Gohir, the chief executive of Muslim Women’s Network UK, said the figures created “the impression that substantial action is being taken to tackle anti-Muslim hostility” but the government’s response remained “limited compared with the scale of the problem”.“There is little visible action to address the safety of Muslim women, and most of the funding doesn’t even appear to reach mosques or other community sites. One mosque leader I spoke to recently had to apply several times and still only received funding for some requested measures. Many others are still waiting for decisions,” Gohir said.Graph of security funding applicationsThe Jami community centre inBirminghamhas reported at least five incidents relating to hate crime and racially aggravated criminal damage between March and July this year, according to West Midlands police. The centre has introduced its own security measures, including gates and blackout boards, while it completes its application for security funding.Worshippers told the Guardian about the incidents – some of which had not been reported to police – including smashed windows and Islamophobic graffiti.View image in fullscreenKhalid, a volunteer at the Jami centre, alongside smashed windows. ‘The centre feels that they’re not being supported enough.’Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianKhalid, a volunteer at the centre, organised an emergency meeting with MPs, councillors and police. He criticised the lack of response from West Midlands police to the several incidents that have occurred.“We’ve had the Prevent team from the council coming here. We’ve had the imam being verbally abused. There’s people being verbally abused … What are we waiting for? Like a disaster to happen?” he said.He added: “The centre feels that they’re not being supported enough. More needs to be done. No one should ever feel unsafe coming to pray. It’s not safe. They feel insecure in their own home and in their own place of worship.”Islam, a 41-year-old private hire driver who attends the centre, reported one incident to the police earlier this year, when an individual shouted abuse at worshippers.He said the attacks had forced many women and children to attend another mosque nearby because of fears for their safety. “I don’t think any Muslim hijabi lady would walk to this centre on their own,” Islam said.Paulette Hamilton, the MP for Birmingham Erdington, said she was “deeply concerned” by the attacks on the centre. “It’s absolutely hateful. I think the people who are doing it are cowardly and there is no place for that sort of thing in the constituency.”West Midlands police said they remained in “close contact with leaders and worshippers” at the centre. “We take all forms of hate crime seriously, and every report of it made to us is investigated as we work to bring offenders to justice,” a spokesperson said.The Home Office said it was working to process all applications for security funding as soon as possible. “To help protect Muslim communities from the appalling levels of hate crime they face, the government has made £40m available through protective security schemes. This is part of a record £77.4m investment in security funding for faith communities in 2026-27,” a spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsIslamophobiaHome OfficeHate crimeBirminghamCommunitiesIslamReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Earth microbes survive simulated conditions of Saturn moon’s ocean | Saturn | The Guardian
description: Experiment suggests organisms could live in harsh environment under Enceladus’s icy crust, strengthening possibility moon could support life
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Experiment suggests organisms could live in harsh environment under Enceladus’s icy crust, strengthening possibility moon could support life
Content: Observations of Enceladus have revealed it emits massive plumes of water vapour into space, suggesting a saltwater ocean exists under its frozen crust.Photograph: Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenObservations of Enceladus have revealed it emits massive plumes of water vapour into space, suggesting a saltwater ocean exists under its frozen crust.Photograph: Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSaturnEarth microbes survive simulated conditions of Saturn moon’s oceanExperiment suggests organisms could live in harsh environment under Enceladus’s icy crust, strengthening possibility moon could support lifeIan SampleScience editorFri 25 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the moment scientists spotted plumes of water erupting from Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, it became the most tantalising place in the solar system to search for life beyond Earth.Now the case is even more compelling after researchers found that organisms that live in deep-sea waters off Japan can survive the harsh conditions expected in the briny ocean that lurks beneath Enceladus’s icy crust.The microbes, which thrive near hydrothermal vents on the seafloor by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, survived in a brine that mimicked the Saturnian moon’s ocean. The work suggests the distant world may be habitable, if not exactly hospitable, to at least some forms of life.“If we use the cellular definition of life that we understand on Earth today, the experiments tell us that if this organism, or something similar to it, was on Enceladus, there’s a good chance it could survive,” said William Orsi, a professor of geomicrobiology at Ludwig-Maximilian University in Munich.Saturn has more moons than any other planet in the solar system, with nearly 300 known to orbit the gas giant. For more than two centuries, Enceladus, a 300-mile-wide ice ball, did not seem particularly remarkable. But that changed with the arrival of robotic spacecraft.Since the 2000s, observations from Nasa’sCassini probeand, more recently, the James Webb space telescope have revealedgigantic plumes of water vapour and ice grainsspewing from Enceladus and evidence for ahuge saltwater oceanunder its frozen crust.View image in fullscreenAn illustration of water plumes on Enceladus, a 300-mile-wide ice moon of Saturn, as they vent into space.Illustration: Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library/Getty ImagesThe seafloor is thought to be dotted with hydrothermal vents that warm the water around them. Last year, scientists foundorganic substancesin samples collected by Cassini as it swooped through one of Enceladus’s spectacular plumes.Orsi and his colleagues wanted to see if they could concoct a miniature version of Enceladus’s ocean to study in the laboratory. By combining water with salts and carbonates and adding powdered rock, they recreated not only the extremely alkaline environment of the ocean but also crucial reactions that take place between the water and the rocky seafloor.The rock-water reactions were active enough to start churning out hydrogen, a process that seems to happen in the ocean on Enceladus. It led the researchers to wonder whether Earthly microbes called methanogens, which survive by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, could survive in the solution. “It was a long shot,” said Orsi.To find out, the scientists turned to microbes originally found near deep-sea hydrothermal vents in the Okinawa trough between Japan and Taiwan. Hydrothermal vents are hot springs on the seafloor that release hot, mineral-rich water.Surprisingly, the microbes grew in the simulated ocean despite its pH reaching 11, which is far more alkaline than the organisms’ known limit. The microbes even adapted their metabolism to cope with low concentrations of carbon dioxide in the water. Details are published inScience Advances.David Rothery, a professor of planetary geosciences at the Open University, said that by showing that methanogenesis – the process that sustains the microbes – was possible in the simulated Enceladus ocean, the work “removes another barrier to the viability of microbial life there”.View image in fullscreenA photo of Enceladus taken in visible light by Nasa’s Cassini spacecraft in 2016.Photograph: Nasa/ReutersOrsi stressed that if life ever evolved on Enceladus it could be radically different from that on Earth. Even if similar bugs did somehow arise, it is not clear if methane-making microbes would thrive in the moon’s ocean: his experiments lasted only days. “Could they survive for a year? Could they survive for a million years? We don’t know,” Orsi said.In asecond paperin the journal, some of the same researchers describe how ice grains in Enceladus’s plumes freeze and fragment in a way that separates the different constituents of the ocean. If ocean droplets contained bits of alien microbes, these might turn up in a small fraction of ice particles but be highly concentrated within them.That would be “great news” for the search for life, said Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary sciences at the Free University of Berlin, who said it would be relatively easy to identify signs of life with today’s technology.The tantalising science around Enceladus has fuelled interest in a return trip. The EuropeanSpaceAgency’s L4 mission aims to combine a Saturn orbiter with an Enceladus lander that would touch down at the moon’s south pole and hunt for biosignatures in the plumes erupting from its ocean. But scientists face a long wait: with a launch proposed for about 2042, it would not reach Saturn until the 2050s.Dr Rachael Hamp, also at the Open University, who has worked on Enceladus’s plumes, said: “It’s fantastic to see new research pushing our understanding further and providing additional evidence for the potential habitability of this little icy world. I think this makes the European Space Agency’s proposed mission to Enceladus even more exciting.”Explore more on these topicsSaturnAstronomySpaceNasaAlien lifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada
Content: A map labeling Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ is displayed as Donald Trump signs an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House on 27 August 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA map labeling Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ is displayed as Donald Trump signs an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House on 27 August 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesMichiganMichigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweatersJane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with CanadaLucy CampbellFri 25 Sep 2026 18.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CEO of aMichigancredit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to sayLake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sureCanadawill.”The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deletedaccording to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role inhostingthousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw,Michigan– said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smithtold the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said astatementfrom the organization shared on social media.After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive orderchangingLake Ontario’s name to Lake America.Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” hewroteon X.Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compelCanada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS politicsDonald TrumpCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: US senators propose legislation to limit ICE arrests and indefinite detention | US Senate | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Democrats Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California seek to prevent unlawful arrests
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Exclusive: Democrats Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California seek to prevent unlawful arrests
Content: A protest in New York City on 14 September.Photograph: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protest in New York City on 14 September.Photograph: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/ShutterstockUS SenateUS senators propose legislation to limit ICE arrests and indefinite detentionExclusive: Democrats Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California seek to prevent unlawful arrestsMaanvi SinghFri 25 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS senators have introduced legislation aimed at cutting down warrantless or specious ICE arrests, and curbing the agency’s ability to indefinitely detain immigrants who do not pose any danger to their communities.The new legislation, shared exclusively with the Guardian, would require immigration officers to obtain an administrative warrant from a supervisor outlining a probable cause for detaining someone. Such a warrant must also be presented to each person who is detained, the bill says, alongside notice of when the detainee must appear in immigration court.The bill would require a bond hearing within 24 hours of any warrantless arrests, and custody review of every noncitizen in immigration detention every 60 days by an immigration judge or US district judge – ideally ensuring that detainees are not held in ICE custody indefinitely without clear cause.The Democratic senators Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California – – said they are introducing the “Immigration Warrant Reform Act” to prevent unlawful arrests and detentions following reports that US citizens and immigrants with legal status were being apprehended. By clarifying how and when ICE can make arrests and detain individuals, the senators said,they also hope to stop the agency from racial profiling or detaining people for arbitrary reasoning.“This bill would establish stronger accountability and oversight,” Padilla said, referring to Americans and noncitizens alike.“The disturbing reality today is that many American citizens and immigrants with lawful status have been caught in the Trump administration’s indiscriminate and violent immigration enforcement dragnet across the country,” said Durbin. “[The legislation] is commonsense, and I encourage my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to support it.”With Republicans in the majority in both chambers of Congress, there isn’t an easy path for the the bill to become law. But Durbin said he was compelled to do something after seeing civil rights abuses during the Trump administration’sOperation Midway Blitz– the militarized immigration raid in Chicago last fall and winter.Immigration advocates and attorneys who reviewed the legislation were concerned that it still left several groups of immigrants vulnerable to arbitrary arrest and detention by granting ICE officers broad leeway in deciding when to conduct a warrantless arrest. The proposed law states, for example, that a warrant isn’t required when someone poses an “imminent danger to the community” – but doesn’t clarify what that means.“The framework neglects how the current administration routinely weaponizes unsubstantiated national security allegations to advance its anti-immigrant agenda,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit.Donald Trump and his administration have specifically claimed that Venezuelan asylum seekers without criminal records pose a national security threat, or arbitrarily proclaimed that families who have lived in the US with temporary legal status for years are dangerous criminals. It is also unclear, advocates said, how the bill would hold ICE accountable for violating these standards.Durbin’s office said the bill codifies constitutional safeguards, by requiring immigration agents to prove they have a probable cause to detain someone – and if not, release them within 24 hours. Requiring that detainees get a hearing every 60 days would also force the government to justify its reasoning for the continued detention. The bill would “help prevent these due process violations while ensuring noncitizens who present a threat to public safety are not released”, Durbin said.Al-Juburi said he was skeptical the bill meets the moment. And a bigger question raised by the bill is whether immigrants should be detained at all for civil violations such as entering the US without authorization, he added.. “My concern here is that this approach fails to reject the inhumane notion that people should face detention, and loss of liberty, for non-criminal matters,” said Al-Juburi. “Detaining people for civil immigration enforcement stands in direct conflict with what are ostensibly core constitutional protections.”Explore more on these topicsUS SenateICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)DemocratsUS politicsLaw (US)US immigrationUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton Day declared in various cities and states across the US on 9/25 | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Late Queen of Country and philanthropist celebrated with parades, karaoke and live music across the country
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Late Queen of Country and philanthropist celebrated with parades, karaoke and live music across the country
Content: Wendy Delehanty and Nancy Beaty of New Jersey on Dolly Parton Day 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenWendy Delehanty and Nancy Beaty of New Jersey on Dolly Parton Day 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee.Photograph: George Walker IV/APDolly PartonDolly Parton Day declared in various cities and states across the US on 9/25Late Queen of Country and philanthropist celebrated with parades, karaoke and live music across the countryMarina DunbarFri 25 Sep 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCities and states across the country are declaring 25 SeptemberDolly PartonDay, month after the Queen of Country died at age 80.The date, 9/25, is a tribute toParton’s popular single, 9 to 5.CaliforniaandOhiohave officially declared the date Dolly Parton Day, while communities nationwide are planning tributes from parades and pink lights to karaoke and live music performances.California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, signed legislation last weekestablishing25 September as Dolly Parton Day in the state every year. The bill was sponsored by state senators Shannon Grove and John Laird.“We could all afford to live a little more like Dolly,” Newsom said in a statement. “Be kind, be humble and have some fun … Be a diamond in a rhinestone world. With this bill, we are not just establishing a day to celebrate Dolly Parton, we are creating an annual reminder to us, every year, to live the way she did – joyfully, graciously and with a whole lot of heart.”View image in fullscreenChristy Oakes and Beth Sloan of Kentucky pose with a mural of Dolly Parton in Nashville.Photograph: George Walker IV/APTheLos Angelescounty library will be hosting a Dolly Parton Day event at several locations: Dolly Day: Smarty Pants Storytime, which will include songs, rhymes and movement along with teaching school-readiness skills. Parton was a big advocate for encouraging young people to read, and her juvenile literacy charity, the Imagination Library, provided millions of books for children around the world.‘She should have been queen of the world!’ Readers remember Dolly PartonRead moreIn Ohio, the governor, Mike DeWine, and the lieutenant governor, Jim Tressel, signed aproclamationearlier this month recognizing Dolly Parton Day. Unlike California’s law, Ohio’s proclamation applies only to 2026.New York andPennsylvanialawmakers are considering similar measures. New York’s bill remained in a senate committee, while Pennsylvania’s legislation had been referred to a house committee.Some of the largest celebrations are taking place inNashville, where Parton had lived since she was 18. The city is honoring the singer with pink lights and posters while handing out stickers, buttons and bookmarks.The Nashville celebration began with the unveiling of a new Dolly-themed license plate, with $25 from each plate sold going to support local Imagination Libraries. A downtown fireworks tribute is planned for 9.25pm.“It’s just bittersweet that Dolly isn’t here with us,” Nashville’s mayor, Freddie O’Connell, said during the event’s kick-off. “Today isn’t about the music or the fame, it’s about Dolly’s best gift to all of us: her kindness, the way she cared, the depths of her caring and the enduring lessons she taught us about how to care for one another.”View image in fullscreenTourists in Nashville, Tennessee, on 25 September 2026.Photograph: George Walker IV/APSouthwest Airlines also announcedplans to hosta Parton-inspired karaoke Friday for travelers and employees. Tennessee state and local officials are currently working to rename the airport after Parton.Elsewhere,New Orleanswill host a tribute led by the marching group Krewe of Dolly. The memorial parade will commence at 5pm that will pass through the French Quarter and end at the Jazz Museum.InSan Francisco, organizers are planning a public celebration in the heart of the city called Dolly Day, described as a celebration of life that will include “singing loud, dressing up and being a little kinder than usual in her honor”.On Thursday,U2announced a new album, entitled Carnaval de Luz, which will include the final recorded performance by Parton. Closing out the album’s 12 tracks is Torn, a duet performed by Parton and Bono. The song is described in press materials as “a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances”.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryU2CelebrityOhioLos AngelesSan FrancisconewsShareReuse this content

title: David Beckham takes £39m dividend as World Cup deals drive record profits | David Beckham | The Guardian
description: Former footballer appeared in about 12 ad campaigns this summer, pushing holding company’s revenue to $110.5m
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Former footballer appeared in about 12 ad campaigns this summer, pushing holding company’s revenue to $110.5m
Content: David Beckham at a Fifa Club World Cup group stage.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenDavid Beckham at a Fifa Club World Cup group stage.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPADavid BeckhamDavid Beckham takes £39m dividend as World Cup deals drive record profitsFormer footballer appeared in about 12 ad campaigns this summer, pushing holding company’s revenue to $110.5mMark SweneyFri 25 Sep 2026 06.27 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Beckham has taken a $51m (£39m) dividend from his business empire after a series of deals with brands for the Fifa World Cup.Beckham appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns across this summer’s tournament in the US, working with brands including Lenovo, McDonald’s, Bank of America, Verizon and the PepsiCo crisps brand Lay’s.The World Cup work helped to fuel a record year for DRJB Holdings, the commercial company for Beckham’s brands business, where revenues surged by a fifth to $110.5m last year, up from $92.3m in 2024.Pre-tax profits also climbed to a record $65.7m, a 46% increase on 2024.DRJB Holdings – which is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss – paid out $51.1m to shareholders last year, compared with $53m the previous year.View image in fullscreenDavid Beckham in a US advert for Stella Artois during the Fifa World Cup 26.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/GettyThe former England captain, who retired from professional football in 2013, sold a 55% stake in his businesses in 2022 to the US group Authentic Brands for £200m, meaning he took home 45% of last year’s total dividend.However, the Companies House filing, which will be published next week, showed a further $61.6m was paid in special dividends this year. This meant Beckham was paid out about $51m.Before this year’s World Cup the company secured partnerships including a multiyear deal with Bank of America: he became an ambassador for its global sports programme.The 51-year-old also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss, an eponymous range of spectacles for Safilo and a limited-edition Predator football boot with Adidas.He also struck a new deal for Beckham & Friends Live, a show on Paramount+ that was broadcast around the Uefa Champions League.Beckham featured in a Stella Artois campaign alongside the actor and producer Theo James to mark the beer’s partnership for the second season of Netflix series The Gentlemen.DRJB Holdings is jointly owned by Authentic Brands Group and Footwork Productions, controlled by David Beckham.View image in fullscreenBeckham with his new star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in Los Angeles in June.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APCorey Salter, the chief executive of entertainment at Authentic Brands, said Beckham was “one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more”.Salter added: “What these results show is that behind the Beckham brand is a strong and highly effective team within Authentic, set up with the financial discipline and strong fundamentals to continue to grow profitably through 2026 and beyond.”DRJB Holdings includes the Seven Global division, which contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas. The remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production company that made the four-partNetflix documentary Beckhamthat was released in 2023. It also producedVictoria Beckham’s Netflix documentary, which was released last year.David Beckham is also an investor in businesses including the supplement specialist IM8, which he co-founded in 2024, and the honey-based fruit snack firm BeeUp.Explore more on these topicsDavid BeckhamAdvertisingWorld Cup 2006newsShareReuse this content

title: MNEK on writing smash hits, battling self-doubt and his solo struggles: ‘I’m a fat Black gay man. Try selling that’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The artist has written for Beyoncé and been nominated for two Grammys, yet individual success has eluded him. Now he’s back with a new album that puts queer joy in the spotlight – and, he says, he’s finally ready to enjoy himself
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: The artist has written for Beyoncé and been nominated for two Grammys, yet individual success has eluded him. Now he’s back with a new album that puts queer joy in the spotlight – and, he says, he’s finally ready to enjoy himself
Content: Hot and heavy … MNEK.Photograph: Lewis VornView image in fullscreenHot and heavy … MNEK.Photograph: Lewis VornMusicInterviewMNEK on writing smash hits, battling self-doubt and his solo struggles: ‘I’m a fat Black gay man. Try selling that’Alim KherajThe artist has written for Beyoncé and been nominated for two Grammys, yet individual success has eluded him. Now he’s back with a new album that puts queer joy in the spotlight – and, he says, he’s finally ready to enjoy himselfFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a south-east London warehouse, Uzoechi Osisioma Emenike, more commonly known as MNEK, is sitting on a bench in a makeshift locker room surrounded by semi-naked men. One particularly muscular individual suggestively adjusts a jockstrap, while another, taller and toned, removes his vest before eyeing MNEK with a loaded gaze. It’s a lot of sexual tension for a Tuesday morning. But such is the life of a pop star on the set of a music video.“It is very gay, you’re not wrong there,” MNEK says, while getting his makeup done for the shoot. The video being filmed is for the fittingly titled Muscle Marys.., the third single from the 31-year-old south Londoner’s second album, Bulldozer!! In one corner of the warehouse, behind a large vanity curtain, a group of dancers are being hosed down while filming a shower scene. The water, a runner has assured me, is warm.The album is MNEK’s first solo record in eight years and its title is confrontational. “As a six-foot-four Black man, I am very conscious of the space I take up,” he explains. “I am often trying to squeeze myself down. I mean look at where we are right now …” He gestures at the low-ceilinged room. “Can I stand up straight in this space? But that’s the reality of being as large as I am. Bulldozer came about because it’s one of those words that I found very triggering. But because of that, it felt like the right title.”No one can argue against MNEK’s outsized impact on pop music. He signed his first publishing deal aged just 14, and as a writer-producer has worked with the likes of Beyoncé, Kylie Minogue, Madonna, Christina Aguilera, Little Mix and Flo. His songs – Never Forget You, a duet with Zara Larsson, and Head & Heart, a 2020 collab with DJ Joel Corry – have amassed more than 1bn streams. Earlier this year he was nominated for his second Grammy for Larsson’s song Midnight Sun, which he co-wrote and produced.As a solo artist, however, things haven’t always been so big. His debut album, 2018’s underrated Language, peaked at No 81. “I lost a lot of confidence after that,” he says. “I live every day knowing that most, if not all, of my money is made from being a writer and producer. But my solo music is also something I care about. Still, a lot of the time, I will be the only person vouching for me to make my own music.”double quotation markWhile there is a very rich queer culture within the Black community, there’s also a deeper history with homophobiaThe visuals and lyrics of Language were also explicitly queer, with one reviewer at the time suggesting the muted response to the record was a result of homophobia and racism. “When it comes to going to the public with my own music, I am a fat Black gay man. Try and sell that.” Still, as an artist, he wanted to be true to who he was. “I feel like [withholding my sexuality] is something that maybe could have benefited me, but now we’ll never know. I just didn’t want to be on stage singing about girls if it wasn’t my truth.”While MNEK says he began working on his second album just after Language came out, his poor mental health, the pandemic and other work commitments left him feeling he couldn’t make a coherent record. “I needed to figure out how to get back to the pure desire of wanting to make a project,” he says. A separation from his management helped. “It took me back to being 14. I was making music and there were no expectations other than me being excited about it.”That purity of intent paid off. Bulldozer!! is MNEK at the height of his powers: an electric rush of window-rattling grime, Godzilla-sized hooks, cavernous club bangers, oily UK garage and lushly layered harmonies. Sonically, it’s his personal and musical identity unapologetically stuffed into a hulking pop beefcake.View image in fullscreenSixpac … MNEK performing at Pride In London in July.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Getty ImagesIts themes are equally big. Songs such as The Wall!! address pushing through self-doubt (“Six foot four and I still got growing pains,” he sings), while both the braggadocious, Channel U-indebted Reverse!! and Dirty Little Secret!!’s stuttering R&B explore encounters with “DL trade” (men who sleep with other men secretly, or on the “down low”).Does he have experience with that community? “I have over the years. It’s not my reality right now. But it’s complicated. While there is a very rich queer culture within the Black community, there’s also a deeper history with homophobia, which starts with colonialism, of course. There are a lot of people who believe in the ‘batty man’ ideology and that being gay is a sin. Those God-fearing environments create DL people. It’s not about shaming anyone. I’m just saying: ‘You don’t have to drag me into it.’”There is also a sonic thread MNEK is pulling at, too. “Those songs are influenced by the grime and garage and two-step I grew up listening to,” he says. “I consider it dance music, as much as house and disco and all the different things I explore on the record. I wanted to claim some ownership of that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat has proved harder than anticipated. When he tried to clear a sample of Lethal Bizzle’s Pow! for Reverse!!, his request was shut down. “They weren’t comfortable with the lyrical content,” he says with a sigh. “Even though Pow! is hardly a song about morality, [queerness] is a no-go area in a lot of these communities.” Other requests were easier: Lady!! interpolates Geri Halliwell’s Bag It Up, with MNEK subverting Ginger Spice’s turn-of-the-millennium battle of the sexes into a song that embraces gender fluidity, while Oh No!! All the Boys!! samples the piano riff from the Clash’s Rock the Casbah.‘Men explicitly loving men is so threatening to the status quo’: why are gay male pop stars being shut out of the music industry?Read moreDesirability politics, meanwhile, come to the fore on Muscle Marys.., which addresses the toxicity of male body standards in the gay community, something MNEK has experienced first-hand. “There was one instance where I had hooked up with a guy. He was a total Muscle Mary, a quintessential LA gay,” he recalls. “I found his Twitter account. It turned out that he had tweeted saying: ‘Hey, this British musician is messaging me. I don’t think he’s that attractive, but should I do it just to say I did it?’”That’s horrible, I say. “It’s vile. In those intimate settings, of course there’s an element of transaction there, but you want to feel desirable.”Body image is something MNEK has struggled with his entire life. “I’ve always been fat. It’s something that you’re dealing with or running away from or keeping a tab on,” he says. “But I’ve taken up the gym, which has become part of the fabric of my life, as far as feeling confident about my body.”Just then, someone comes in to say they’re waiting for MNEK to film. The dancers have dried off and the locker room is set up. MNEK jumps up, tugging on a vest, protecting the white fabric from his dyed yellow hair (“It stains everything!”). Despite the simple get-up, he looks ready to be a pop star again. “I wish I hadn’t been so hard on myself [before] because I’m really fab and I’ve done really great things in my life. This time I want to really, really enjoy it.”Bulldozer!! is out now.MNEKtoursthe UK and Ireland to 15 November; tour starts Bristol.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockDance musicR&BinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songs | Taylor Swift | The Guardian
description: This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lows
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lows
