Content: ‘Like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love’ … Taylor Swift.Photograph: TAS Rights ManagementView image in fullscreen‘Like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love’ … Taylor Swift.Photograph: TAS Rights ManagementTaylor SwiftReviewTaylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songs(Republic)This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lowsLaura SnapesFri 25 Sep 2026 09.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne downside of turning your release strategies into scavenger hunts and layering clues within your work is that it invites enormous amounts of scrutiny about your potential motive. When Taylor Swift announced an expanded edition of last year’s critically malignedThe Life of a Showgirlthis week, subtitled The Encore, many fans instantly suspected one of two things: that it was designed to remind Grammy members of Showgirl’s existence during their voting period to determine next year’s nominees, or to oust country ingenue Ella Langley from herrecord-breaking US No 1 run.If that sounds cynical, it’s also worth remembering that when Swift announced Showgirl last year, she said that unlike her previous album,The Tortured Poets Department– a 16-track record immediately inflated to 31 songs on release day – the purposefully concise, 12-track Showgirl would not be expanded. (This didn’t stop her releasing34variants of the record, with various acoustic demos and so on, to juice sales.)After Showgirl had the biggest US opening week ever, Swift went to Sweden to celebrate with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback, she revealed this week. The trip was intended to be about reflection and gratitude, she wrote on Instagram. “But,” she continued, “there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: we wrote more songs.” One hesitates to liken Swift to Kanye West, but The Life of a Showgirl is starting to look a little more likeThe Life of Pablo, West’s endlessly extended seventh album.Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl review – dull razzle-dazzle from a star who seems frazzledRead moreA slipperiness has infected the whole endeavour, not helped by Swift’s initial promise that Showgirl was all “bangers” and about “keeping the bar really high”, a claim quickly dismissed: the record is a travesty, a word that feels particularly apt when you recallWood, a Bruno Mars-lite abomination about her now-husband Travis Kelce’s penis. And for an album that was supposed to be about the giddy highs of life on Swift’s own record-breaking Eras tour, it contained a tedious amount ofwell-worn score-settling. Adding four more songs written some time after the initial sessions further dilutes the record’s already flimsy premise.The most Swiftian thing about these four tracks is their visceral sense of course-correction. For all that Swift chafes against The Haters – more on them to come, shocker – she’s always reacting to criticism. Recall the scene from herMiss Americanadocumentary where she learns that her sixth album,Reputation, didn’t get nominated for the album of the year Grammy: “I just need to make a better record,” she says, visibly crushed. (That’s the folly of working like this: Reputation is her best record, and those voters are idiots.) Showgirl was panned for its excessive wordiness and defaulting on the promised bangers; these Encore songs largely pare back the verbiage and double down on hooks and firework-laden bridges, Swift’s metier. It’s like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer breathlessly flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love.Taylor Swift: Patient Zero – videoEvery Swift album except Reputation has a deluxe version, though just a handful of those bonus songs are keepers:Jump Then Fall(from Fearless),New Romantics(1989),Bigger Than the Whole SkyandWould’ve Could’ve Should’ve(Midnights). None of these new songs are destined to join those ranks, though Patient Zero comes closest. Hooked around a mournful and curiously processed Celtic fiddle sample, it recalls the spirit ofLover, where it felt as though Swift was trying out potential new sonic futures. Its pained chorus also evokes Tortured Poets’Fortnight: a slinky, low-key yet insidiously catchy melodic Möbius strip, with lyrics offering connection to a woman recently burned by an ex whose games Swift knows well.It’s one of two Encore songs that contain a palpable sense of humanity, unlike anything from its childish parent album.Pink Cloudingis a mature apology to a kind ex she let down – “Neither of us knew at the time / That I was a liar” – filled with the sort of regret that will never lose its shameful sting. Unlike Swift’s post-2020 turn to heavily detailed narrative writing, it’s written in a pure-pop form, braiding shades of pink and various flowers into a sweet and effective conceit without defaulting on emotional grace. Its ardent synth-pop, a nice balance of airy and punchy, also sounds a little like it could’ve lived next toCruel Summeron Lover, though truthfully it recalls Tegan and Sara’s classic 2013 album Heartthrob, which inspired Swift’s1989pop makeover.The beauty of Pink Clouding is that it sounds genuinely believable, a quality curiously missing from Swift’s songs about Kelce. Tortured Poets bonus trackSo High Schoolis as close as she’s gotten; the Showgirl songs about their romance framed it as a triumph over venal and conniving haters. It’s a very strange lens through which to write about supposed true love, and one she returns to here. The appallingCleveland!is all about how Kelce loves her despite internet commenters saying she can’t dance (a long-dead criticism) and that she’s annoying, and is sung with such oozing self-satisfaction it’s like being repeatedly poked and asked if it hurts. Spiritually, it is a cut-and-shut of two of her worst songs ever, Lover’sMe!(about being cringe but free) and Showgirl’sHoney(about other women being jealous haters). Despite her long-term collaborator Jack Antonoff not being part of the Showgirl era, it still sounds like warmed-over Bleachers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTaylor Swift: Cleveland! – videoIt is a mess of contradictions: it has an oddly sour tang for such a festive, all-bells-jangling confection, like biting into a lavishly iced cake to find the sugar swapped for salt. For a song about having found the one, its standards are barrel-scrapingly low: “You only need to find one person in this entire world / Who doesn’t find you completely insufferable!” she declares. Girl! Aim higher! Where on Honey, and other recent songs, she has proven strikingly eager to call other women bitches, here she coyly stops short of calling herself a “whore” and “bitch” in incomplete lines that make conspicuous features of those gaps.Taylor Swift’s singles – ranked!Read moreAnd for all that she laments the haters, she sure does write a lot of songs about them. The more dogshit like Cleveland! she releases, the more criticism it may garner, in turn generating inspiration for … more songs like this. It is Swiftian Groundhog Day: she seems unwilling or unable to extricate herself from the vast web of self-reference she now seems condemned to operate within, having reached the point in the corporate life cycle where novelty is all but exhausted and it’s easier to double down on core values.It’s hard to tell what any of this has to do with Showgirl (other than pushing the album back to No 1 until Christmas). Every song sounds as though it could have been appended to a different record. Closing trackBabylonis sub-Evermorein its overcomplicated narrative of a fractured family and grave, watery production. You could point to their very loose shared theme, each taking different angles on the gap between a facade and an intimately understood truth – though the greater truth affirmed by this batch of music is that the more Swift releases, the weaker her output gets. It doesn’t take any detective work to deduce that the healthiest thing for her creativity would be to let the curtain fall for a while.Explore more on these topicsTaylor SwiftPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new film | Crime films | The Guardian
description: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV
Author: David Smith
Headline: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV
Content: Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in PrimetimePhotograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenRobert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in PrimetimePhotograph: Courtesy of A24Crime films‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new filmExperts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TVDavid Smithin WashingtonFri 25 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAman from Long Beach, California, is here to have sex with someone he believes is a 13-year-old girl. When the journalistChris Hansenwalks in, the man’s stomach drops. He is caught, and it is the end of his life as he knew it. Hansen asks what his fate should be. “The electric chair?” he asks. No, replies Hansen. “Dateline NBC.”Primetime review – Robert Pattinson’s preening TV host hunts paedophiles but real drama proves harder to targetRead moreThis is the opening scene ofPrimetime, a film directed by Lance Oppenheim, released in the US this week (a UK release follows on 30 October). It explores how a network news show turned sting operations into must-see television, raising a host of ethical questions about justice, voyeurism and society’s willingness to dehumanise certain offenders for profit and entertainment.The swaggering Hansen is played byRobert Pattinson, whose recent movies includeThe Batman,The DramaandThe Odyssey. He delivers a line that captures the film’s argument about a societal turning point: “There used to be a pillory in every village. Now, there’s a television in every living room.” But the real Hansen, 67, hasbrandedthe movie an “insult” and “identity theft” without having seen it.Going head-to-head with ABC’s Lost in primetime, Dateline NBC’s To Catch a Predator was one of the defining TV hits of the US ratings wars of the mid-2000s, an era before streaming. The programme targeted men suspected of soliciting sex with minors in online chat rooms. Volunteers from the citizen watchdog groupPerverted Justiceposed as underage children, engaging adults in conversations and then arranging meetings at fake homes.There, decoy actors playing the supposed teenagers would be waiting. The men would be confronted on camera by Hansen while police officers stood outside, ready to make arrests. The formula proved hugely successful. By the 2006-07 season,To Catch a Predatorwas averaging about 7 million viewers an episode, turning Hansen into a star with his own catchphrase: “Have a seat.”David Osit, director of Predators, an acclaimed 2025 documentary about the show, says: “The show was sordid and creepy and amusing and you could find many different ways to relate to what was happening. You could identify with the parents, you could identify with Chris Hansen, you could identify with the schadenfreude of watching these men have the worst day of their lives.“You can see that even in the marketing for Primetime: a lot of it’s reposting old clips of To Catch a Predator. It’s quite clear that this still has an effect on people because it is at this nexus of discomfort and basic human instinct. In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs and we enjoy discomfort from a safe vantage point and that’s what the show was able to offer people.”View image in fullscreenTo Catch a Predator still taken from Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators.Photograph: Courtesy of DogwoofBut in 2006 the operation took a fatal turn.Bill Conradt, an assistant district attorney in Rockwall county, Texas, allegedly contacted a decoy posing as a 13-year-old boy but changed his mind. The team went ahead with the police operation at his home after he failed to appear at the sting house. Conradt killed himself as a local Swat team entered, with the television crew outside.The episode prompted a lawsuit that was eventually settled out of court, as well as a series of journalistic investigations including reports by ABC’s 20/20 and Esquire journalist Luke Dittrich, whose 2007 article,Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die, would later become a key source for Ajon Singh’s screenplay for Primetime. By 2008 To Catch a Predator had been cancelled.‘He stole the show’: do Oscars beckon for Robert Pattinson, star of four of the year’s biggest films – and Batman?Read moreBut years earlier, local law enforcement agencies across the US had already been quietly wrestling with the dawn of internet solicitation. In Kentucky, then attorney general Greg Stumbo oversaw a series of state-led sting operations aimed at snaring men suspected of soliciting sex with minors.Working alongside local officials – including Jerry “Peanuts” Gaines, the sheriff of Bowling Green – Kentucky’s bureau of investigation used a young-looking female agent to pose online as an underage teenager. The state partnered with Perverted Justice to engage men in online chat rooms and lure them to monitored locations. The stings resulted in more than 20 arrests in Kentucky.Stumbo recalls:“None of them had a criminal record. They were a firefighter, they were a university teacher – people that you just walk around and see every day on the street. It’s scary when you think about how many people like that there are out there who are predators for our children.”Only after Kentucky authorities concluded their stings did Hansen and his Dateline NBC crew arrive in Bowling Green to carry out interviews. Stumbo notes that state prosecutors kept tight control over their files, refusing to hand over criminal evidence tapes to network producers while trials were pending. But the message sent to potential offenders, Stumbo says, was immediate: “The talk was, ‘Don’t go to Kentucky. They’ll catch you if you go to Kentucky.’ That’s what we wanted the talk to be, obviously.”View image in fullscreenTo Catch a Predator still taken from Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators.Photograph: Courtesy of DogwoofAsked whether the sting setup – and the subsequent television spectacle – crossed an ethical boundary into entrapment, Stumbo is adamant. “Nobody ever came to me and said that and it wouldn’t do any good if they did. We didn’t do it for that purpose. We did it because we wanted that word that was spread through that community of people who look at those types of situations: don’t come to Kentucky.”And for the men caught on camera whose lives evaporated in an instant, Stumbo offers no quarter. “I’m a prosecutor. I probably am a little bit hard about stuff like that. I don’t find any excuse in that. Yeah, you feel sorry for anybody that stoops that low in life, but to intentionally want to go and do that type of activity with a minor, I have no sympathy for them.”Perverted Justice, founded by Xavier Von Erck, was also the engine behind Dateline NBC’s To Catch a Predator. Von Erck’s relationship with national media began in early 2004, following a series of stings with local television stations. In a single week CBS’s 60 Minutes II, ABC’s Primetime Live and NBC’s Dateline NBC asked him to replicate his model on a national network scale.Von Erck immediately knew which he would not choose. He says via email: “We had caught a national news producer for ABC News at our first sting in Milwaukee. He showed up to that very first sting house we ever did, and ABC News did not fire him despite our pressure campaign … So obviously I wasn’t going to work with Primetime Live.”Von Erck managed volunteers remotely, screening chat logs and enforcing boundaries, while operatives Frag and Del Harvey worked inside the sting houses with Dateline NBC producers. He recalls one particularly disturbing suggestion from a producer: that a target be encouraged to get into a hot tub with one of the female decoys. “We said no.”Von Erck fiercely defends Perverted Justice’s record, claiming more than 600 convictions, a 99.1% conviction rate and statutory changes in all 50 states. He dismisses accusations of entrapment, arguing that his operatives never made first contact and that convictions based on their evidence survived appeals.View image in fullscreenActors Bokeem Woodbine, Phoebe Bridgers, Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever at Venice film festival, 5 September.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageHe writes: “In fact, out of the dozens of cases in which convicted individuals desperately appealed to a higher court, convictions due to the evidence we supplied were *never* overturned. It is quite a silly notion to believe that someone can be ‘induced’ to want to sexually assault a 10-15 year old. It requires a specific predilection.”He says he spoke to Hansen only twice and regards To Catch a Predator as fundamentally dependent on his group work. “Without my organization, there was no To Catch a Predator possible at that time,” he says. “It would have been a tall reporter standing inside of a house interviewing no one.”That history is one reason Von Erck is so hostile to Oppenheim’s film. He accuses the filmmakers of inventing scenes, opinions and locations involving him. “I don’t regard ‘Primetime’ as being a movie made about the story of To Catch a Predator because from what I know from watching the trailer and reading reviews of the movie, it seems like most of the details of the movie are absurdly inaccurate when it comes to my organization in particular.“It feels like an oddly and purposely malicious portrayal, especially of myself, given that every review I’ve seen that mentions the way they have portrayed me is literally something I did not do, things I never said, and places I never was ever even physically at. Frankly, I find it bewildering that they are using my legal name and semi-likeness while completely inventing every opinion, statement, act and physical location that they portray me as in the movie.”The Guardian made repeated attempts to contact Oppenheim and Dittrich but without success. Hansen did not respond to requests for an interview. But he has used other platforms to condemn Primetime as an “insult” and complain that the actorDenis Learywould have been better casting than Pattinson.View image in fullscreenA scene from Primetime.Photograph: Courtesy of A24In aninterview with USA Today newspaperon Wednesday, Hansen said: “They wanted to exploit the brand that I’ve built over the last 45 years. You can decide whether that’s ethical or legal or identity theft or however you look at it. But it seems a little exploitive, as Hollywood often is.”Intriguingly, he has alsobought advertisingfor his true crime streaming network TruBlu to play before screenings of Primetime. The move strikes Osit, the director of Predators, as characteristically shrewd. “It does fit with the Chris Hansen I know,” he says. “That’s a savvy and intelligent thing to do for what Chris Hansen is interested in doing, which is to get people to see his investigations.”Osit argues that when commercial news networks commodified vigilante justice, they established a precedent that has only accelerated in the age of social media and streaming. In modern iterations of the format, networks and digital streamers no longer feel compelled to blur the faces of suspects or provide traditional journalistic safeguards. He argues that ethical qualms have increasingly been swept aside.“We’ve societally accepted that these men are not human beings. They’re not deserving of the same rights or protections that someone who committed a different kind of crime and has their face blown up on the internet might be. We’ve societally accepted it’s quite acceptable to shame these men and that is their punishment for this crime.”Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?Read moreOsit found Hansen to be a charismatic combination of both journalist and entertainer and does not think To Catch a Predator’s intentions were cruel. He admires Hansen’s ability to interact with people but does not agree with some of the ways that he conducts himself professionally.“If Chris was interested in ending child predation, the investigations wouldn’t still be going on,” Osit comments. “That’s not what we’re doing here. However, Chris has been told by many, many people over the years that they’re grateful for his investigations and those people exist. There are also many people who think that those investigations are problematic and then there’s a lot of people in between.”Ultimately, Osit contends, fixating on Hansen’s personal motives misses the more uncomfortable truths that To Catch a Predator exposed about its audience.“The more interesting question than who is Chris is who are we? Why do we enjoy this show? What do we get out of the show? What is this show reflecting about the society we live in where we sexualise teenage girls so much and yet create circumstances where we will ask people to show up to a house because they think it’s safe and people are playing these games on the internet where they’re pretending to be different ages?”Osit adds: “This is a world that we helped create as a society and those are more challenging questions to ask about who we are as human beings because it involves maybe interrogating how culpable we are in the culture that decides to treat young people as attractive objects for men who can’t get mental help to avoid being sucked into these issues. Those are questions that a movie is not going to deal with.”Primetime is out in the US now, in Australia on 29 October and in the UK on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsCrime filmsRobert PattinsonUS crimeThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma to The Moment: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder’s slasher spectacular, and Charli xcx’s mockumentary about her Brat summer. Plus, Sydney Sweeney’s immaculate conception
Author: Simon Wardell
Headline: Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder’s slasher spectacular, and Charli xcx’s mockumentary about her Brat summer. Plus, Sydney Sweeney’s immaculate conception
Content: A psychosexual blowout … Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: © MUBIView image in fullscreenA psychosexual blowout … Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: © MUBIThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevision & radioTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma to The Moment: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekGillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder’s slasher spectacular, and Charli xcx’s mockumentary about her Brat summer. Plus, Sydney Sweeney’s immaculate conceptionSimon WardellFri 25 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekTeenage Sex and Death at Camp MiasmaIn her previous two movies, indie director Jane Schoenbrun explored the uncanny spaces we inhabit between the internet, TV and our daily lives. For her dark and deliriousnew drama, she delves into movies and their unsettling hold on us. Hacks’ Hannah Einbinder plays Kris, an up-and-coming queer film-maker hired to reboot Camp Miasma, a “problematic” Friday the 13th-style slasher horror franchise. For research, she visits the original’s reclusive star, Billy (Gillian Anderson), who, bizarrely, lives in the film’s abandoned summer camp location. As the women get closer, reality and Camp Miasma’s grisly fiction start to blur in a giddy, psychosexual blowout.Friday 2 October, MubiThe MomentView image in fullscreenSpinal Tap-ish … Charli xcx in The Moment.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockIt’s hard to tell whether Charli xcx’smockumentaryis a way of summing up her world-exploding “Brat summer” of 2024 or razing it all to the ground. As it counts down to a big arena tour and its accompanying concert film, Aidan Zamiri’s tale flips between the musician being overwhelmed by her sudden celebrity and a string of comically terrible Spinal Tap-ish decisions (the Brat credit card for gay people is a highlight). Throughout, Charli does a good job of keeping us guessing as to what’s a fact and what’s not.Saturday 26 September, 6.35am, 1.30pm, Sky Cinema PremiereNickel BoysView image in fullscreenSublime … Ethan Herisse in Nickel Boys.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyBased on the Pulitzer prize-winning novel by Colson Whitehead, RaMell Ross’ssublime dramais, unusually, shot from the first-person point of view. It’s a bold move that pays off, as we’re immersed in the life of Elwood (Ethan Herisse), a Black student raised by his grandma (a standout Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor) in early 60s Florida. A miscarriage of justice sends him to a brutal, segregated reform school called the Nickel Academy. His only respite is a friendship with another inmate, Turner (Brandon Wilson), as he tries to work out how to live in a world intent on beating him down.Monday 28 September, 11.05pm, BBC TwoImmaculateView image in fullscreenA miracle awaits … Sydney Sweeney in Immaculate.Photograph: APThis ripepieceof nunsploitation from Michael Mohan owes a lot to Rosemary’s Baby – but the evil forces at play here are entirely Christian. Controversy magnet Sydney Sweeney plays a young American who arrives at a rural Italian convent to take her vows. Soon, however, she falls mysteriously pregnant. “It’s a miracle,” proclaim the mother superior, doctor and priests (including Money Heist’s Álvaro Morte) – but how did this virgin birth occur? With creaky doors and creepy sisters, it’s classic, bloodily accomplished horror.Monday 28 September, midnight, BBC Threeskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBetter ManView image in fullscreenCheeky chappy turned ape … Robbie Williams in Better Man.Photograph: Entertainment Film/SkyMichael Gracey’sfilmabout Robbie Williams sticks to the music biopic template of rise-fall-redemption, save for one aspect: he’s portrayed as a chimp. Manifesting Take That’s cheeky chappy as an ape provides a pleasingly surreal edge to the singer’s lairy tale – as well as giving Williams, who narrates, the chance to be amusingly self-deprecating. A fun, vibrant and silly film, with one set-piece, Rock DJ on London’s Regent Street, that’s the equal of La La Land’s freeway number.Thursday 1 October, 8.30am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereThe HoldoversView image in fullscreenWitty and bittersweet … Da’Vine Joy Randolph, Paul Giamatti and Dominic Sessa in The Holdovers.Photograph: Seacia Pavao/Focus Features/APAlexander Payne gets back with his Sideways lead, Paul Giamatti, for a witty, bittersweetstory. The actor is on fine misanthropic form as Paul Hunham, a widely disliked classics teacher at a New England boys’ boarding school in 1970. He is ordered to stay on site over the Christmas holidays to supervise the children who can’t go home, most problematically Dominic Sessa’s smart, sardonic teenager Angus. Also stuck there is grieving canteen manager Mary (an Oscar-winning Da’Vine Joy Randolph). Forced into uncomfortable proximity, the three slowly eke out an understanding.Thursday 1 October, 9pm, Film4The Last First: Winter K2View image in fullscreenA sobering cautionary tale  … The Last First: Winter K2.Photograph: Apple TV“No tents. No food. I think some people will die this night.” It’s a chilling start to Amir Bar-Lev’s sobering, cautionary documentary about the2021 raceto be the first to climb the world’s second highest peak, which resulted in five deaths. The copious interviews and footage (every team seemingly had a camera crew) focus mainly on the Icelandic/Pakistani trio of John Snorri and Ali and Sajid Sadpara. They got to base camp first but were soon joined by “rock star” Sherpa climber Nims Purja and, fatefully, a large commercial expedition of mostly amateurs.Friday 2 October, Apple TVExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: East of Eden to Kill Jackie: the seven best shows to stream this week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Florence Pugh shines as the icy sociopath at the heart of the Steinbeck classic, plus Catherine Zeta-Jones plays an international cocaine dealer in a truly bananas thriller
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Florence Pugh shines as the icy sociopath at the heart of the Steinbeck classic, plus Catherine Zeta-Jones plays an international cocaine dealer in a truly bananas thriller
Content: Plenty to like … Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in East of Eden.Photograph: Geoffrey Short/NetflixView image in fullscreenPlenty to like … Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in East of Eden.Photograph: Geoffrey Short/NetflixThe seven best shows to stream this weekTelevision & radioEast of Eden to Kill Jackie: the seven best shows to stream this weekFlorence Pugh shines as the icy sociopath at the heart of the Steinbeck classic, plus Catherine Zeta-Jones plays an international cocaine dealer in a truly bananas thrillerPhil HarrisonFri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekEast of Eden“A girl like that doesn’t just fall out of the sky.” Charles Trask has a bad feeling about Cathy Ames, the woman who has arrived, beaten almost to death, on the doorstep of the farm he shares with his brother Adam. But it’s too late – Adam is smitten and therefore doomed. Zoe Kazan is behind this adaptation of John Steinbeck’s study of family, free will and arbitrary evil. Her new twist is a closer focus on Cathy (played with icy sweetness byFlorence Pugh). She’s a more ambiguous figure here: not a purely sociopathic destroyer of lives but instead a ruthless survivor at all costs. The script doesn’t always do the ideas justice but there’s still plenty to like.Netflix, from Thursday 1 OctoberKill JackieView image in fullscreenAll in … Catherine Zeta-Jones as Jackie Price in Kill Jackie.Photograph: Unai MateoThis thriller starringCatherine Zeta-Jonesought to be the kind of cartoonish nonsense that, as long as you are willing to leave plausibility concerns at the door, is a source of endless fun. But the writing isn’t quite funny or smart enough for it to attain the brutally hilarious Killing Eve vibe it is clearly aiming for. If you manage your expectations, though, there’s still a good time to be had. Jackie is a dealer who has pivoted from cocaine into art. But assassins the Seven Demons didn’t get the memo: cue an ultraviolent, international game of hide and seek with Jackie as both hunter and quarry.Prime Video, from Friday 2 OctoberChilean Mine Rescue: Race Against TimeView image in fullscreenGripping … Chilean Mine Rescue: Race Against Time.Photograph: Miguel SoffiaSixteen years on,the rescueof 33 miners after 69 days spent trapped at the bottom of the San Jose mine seems even more extraordinary than it did at the time. With testimony from rescuers, relatives who were waiting anxiously and the miners themselves, this three-part series offers what can only be described as a deep dive. The most gripping segments are those detailing the underground survival effort, from the careful rationing of food to the filtering of water through socks. “I felt like I was in another dimension,” recalls one miner.Disney+, from Saturday 26 SeptemberOutsideView image in fullscreenLike I’m a Celebrity – with mud … Outside.Photograph: Charlie Woodward/Courtesy of NetflixA sequel of sorts to Netflix’s challenge show Inside (see what they did there?) devised by YouTube wags Sidemen. This show plunges various shrieking, content creators (including the likes of Dani Babes, Chloe Veitch and Lacy) into a forest where they will be tested by a series of daft, gross, infuriating games. There’s £1m up for grabs but the prize fund drains away if contenders can’t resist a few creature comforts. It aims for Squid Game: The Challenge with laughs and ends up more like I’m a Celebrity … with mud.Netflix, from Monday 28 Septemberskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Widower: Til Death Do Us PartView image in fullscreenDisturbing … Thomas Randolph in The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part.Photograph: NetflixThe story of Thomas Randolph is as bizarre as it is disturbing. Over several decades, Randolph married six times. Four of his wives wound up dead. Was he cursed? Or was he a serial killer? This startling documentary tracks the police and press investigation into a man variously described here as “jovial, smart and funny” and “very charming and witty” as he manipulates everyone around him, up to and including police officers. The storytelling is basic and unvarnished but the case itself is wild enough to make that essentially beside the point.Netflix, from Wednesday 20 SeptemberSomebody Knows SomethingView image in fullscreenOn a mission … Kara Chamberlain in Somebody Knows Something.Photograph: DisneyAbout 600,000 people are reported missing in the US every year. Many are found but thousands are not. This series follows law enforcement officer turned true-crime influencer Kara Chamberlain as she reopens some cold cases. They range from babies taken from cots to adults who went on holiday and never came back, but Chamberlain is an indefatigable sleuth – and if the mining of these stories for content feels a little queasy, it’s salient to note that Chamberlain herself was kidnapped as a teenager so, for her, the missions feel personal.Disney+, from Wednesday 20 SeptemberSchumacher 94View image in fullscreenHair-raising … Michael Schumacher at the Australian GP in November 1994.Photograph: Ercole Colombo/Studio Colombo/Getty ImagesThe 1994 Formula One season saw the first world title for a startlingly self-assured young German calledMichael Schumacher. His win in the first grand prix of the season in Brazil was the beginning of an era of domination. This documentary gets the inside track on his ascent and also examines the death of Ayrton Senna, the tragedy that clouded the season and which, as many contributors here suggest, transformed Formula One for ever. The race clips are hair-raising and confirm the suggestion that danger levels had peaked and something needed to change.Netflix, from Friday 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe seven best shows to stream this weekTV streamingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating stroke  | Michael Kiwanuka | The Guardian
description: The Mercury prize winner hasn’t been able to go home since falling ill last summer. In his only interview, he opens up about the ‘poignancy’ of finally releasing the new album his stroke shelved
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: The Mercury prize winner hasn’t been able to go home since falling ill last summer. In his only interview, he opens up about the ‘poignancy’ of finally releasing the new album his stroke shelved
Content: ‘I want to tell people why I haven’t been around’ …Michael Kiwanuka, pictured in March 2023.Photograph: Jodie CanwellView image in fullscreen‘I want to tell people why I haven’t been around’ …Michael Kiwanuka, pictured in March 2023.Photograph: Jodie CanwellMichael KiwanukaInterview‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating strokeJason OkundayeThe Mercury prize winner hasn’t been able to go home since falling ill last summer. In his only interview, he opens up about the ‘poignancy’ of finally releasing the new album his stroke shelvedFri 25 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the end of July 2025, Michael Kiwanuka was back home in Southampton after a series of European gigs. His 2024 albumSmall Changeshad been critically acclaimed and was kept off the UK No 1 slot only by Kendrick Lamar’s GNX. His fifth record, Fudge, was due that autumn. All was going perfectly for the virtuoso singer-songwriter, whose eccentric, genre-busting mix of psychedelic rock, prog soul, blues and gospel had marked him as a real one-off.Kiwanuka had been expected to appear at the All Together Now festival in County Waterford, Ireland, in the coming days, when anannouncementwas posted to his Instagram story: “We are so sorry to announce that due to continued illness, and on the advice of doctors, Michael will sadly be unable to perform at the rest of his scheduled festival performances throughout the rest of the summer and the shows in North America in October.”Until now, fans have heard nothing from – or about – Kiwanuka. Fudge wasn’t released and his social media channels fell silent. This week, Kiwanuka revealed the devastating reason: at just 38, he’d had a haemorrhagic stroke. His brief post updating fans on his health drew messages of support from the likes of Alicia Keys, Cat Power, Olivia Dean and Alabama Shakes.double quotation markI don’t know how long it will be until I can release another recordHis team tells the Guardian that he underwent emergency surgery and was then in intensive care for months to support his breathing. Kiwanuka has no memory of this. Once he was well enough to breathe on his own, he left the ICU and spent five further months in hospital before moving into a rehabilitation centre in Hampshire. In that time, he has not once been able to return home, and the trajectory of his rehabilitation remains uncertain.Kiwanuka is now releasing Fudge in October, and wanted to do one interview about the album. “It feels poignant to do it now after I got sick, because I don’t know how long it will be until I can release another record,” he says.View image in fullscreenKiwanuka at Primavera Sound in Portugal in June 2025, a month before his stroke.Photograph: Diogo Baptista/SOPA Images/ShutterstockI speak to Kiwanuka over the course of two 30-minute calls from his accommodation at the rehabilitation centre. The calls are off-camera, and he is accompanied by his wife, the Christian singer and worship leader Charlotte Kiwanuka. He has been determined to speak, though he is still in recovery. His speech is slow and fragmented; the traumatic details of his stroke are clearly off limits.Kiwanuka is famed for his introspection yet also fiercely protective of his privacy. Despite his success, he always enjoyed relative anonymity – he could still travel by bus or visit the pub without being swarmed. It means that going public about such a health crisis is a difficult step. But the vulnerability of this moment is tempered by a desire to connect with the world again.“It’s a bit nerve-racking,” Kiwanuka tells me. There is palpable reticence in his voice. “But it feels a bit like responsibility as well. I want to tell people why I haven’t been around. It’s been a while. And I think something that everyone can relate to is pain and struggle. That’s one thing all humans have in common. So I’m just sharing mine with the world.”Kiwanuka tells me the stroke was brought on byhigh blood pressure. He was unaware that he had the condition, having experienced no symptoms before the stroke. He does not know if his lifestyle or career contributed to it; naturally, the life of a touring musician is intense, with frequent early flights and late-night shows. “Quite a lot of work, quite tiring, but it was all exciting,” he says.He realises now that he was particularly at risk of a stroke because of the increased susceptibility to high blood pressure among Black African males. That’s also why he decided to go public. “If I’d known, I would have got checked out and been on medication to lower the blood pressure,” he says. He sounds overwhelmed and frustrated. “I wouldn’t have had a stroke. So I want to make Black people aware that you could be at risk.”Dr Maëva May fromthe Stroke Associationconfirms that the higher rate of high blood pressure and diabetes in Black African and African-Caribbean communities is a risk factor for strokes. What can be done about it? “We can make sure that people are measuring their blood pressure earlier, that we’re monitoring for any kind of developing diabetes earlier, that we equip people with the right information to take control of their health earlier,” she says.I do not disclose Kiwanuka’s identity to May, but mention his age and his work as a musician. “That is so young for a stroke,” she says. “There are some studies, especially in younger people who experience a stroke, [suggesting] that occupation may be tied to it, especially if you’re suffering high levels of stress, really long hours. We don’t know why that drives increased stroke, but we do think it’s a factor beyond the fact that, in general as a population, we’re just getting unhealthier. Though this is just emerging data – we don’t have really good answers yet.”It all feels maddeningly unfair. Kiwanuka is young, and he has two small children. In his words: “Things were going well before getting sick – the gigs were going well and the music was sounding good and seemed to be connecting with people, and that was a dream come true.”Before his stroke, Kiwanuka had been enjoying incredible success. His 2016 track Cold Little Heart went platinum in the US, partly thanks to its use on the opening credits of the TV drama Big Little Lies. In the UK, all four of his albums reached the Top 10; in 2020, his third,Kiwanuka, won the Mercury prize.He had also reached a newfound level of artistic confidence. He had a long-term creative partnership with the esteemed alternative hip-hop and neo-psychedelia producer Danger Mouse (Brian Burton). “When I was at school and I heard Danger Mouse’s music, I really connected to it because it seemed like someone who was Black, liked indie music, was in between two cultures,” says Kiwanuka. “So making songs like Lowdown, which was showcasing that with Brian, felt amazing.” And on his last tour, he strummed an acoustic guitar while wearing a kanzu tunic, reflecting his Ugandan heritage. “It felt great, felt really freeing and empowering,” he says.View image in fullscreenThere’s a real honesty to the playing’ ... Kiwanuka in the studio in August 2023.Photograph: Jodie CanwellThe creative process behind Fudge was different. His first self-produced record, it started life while he was partway through makingSmall Changes. Fudge, he told Mojo in 2025, in the only preview that ran before the record was pulled, was his chance to take a renegade approach, down to the title: “This is my life and screw everything, I don’t care.” In his downtime, he wanted to keep creating music “to keep the juices flowing”, he says today, and so he invited his live band’s multi-instrumentalist, Joe Connell, down to a makeshift studio in Southampton, which they named Dreamers. Soon, there were eight of them squeezed into this compact space. Kiwanuka had used his Mercury prize money to buy a mixing console, which became the centre of the record.In Dreamers, jamming sessions alchemised fresh melodies into new work. One night after dinner, he and the band were playing and the track Love in My Heart “came together like one brain. It was almost telepathic,” he says. He is most lucid when talking about music, clearly buoyed up by the memories; his voice lifts with excitement. “It sounded like we had rehearsed it but we hadn’t – it had only come from years of playing together, and it sounded larger than the sum of its parts.” It’s a slow-blooming, languorous seven-minute composition, Kiwanuka’s vocals floating over delicate psychedelic grooves that explode into rich orchestration.Pianist Steve Pringle played the contemplative outro. “The sound is one of my favourite parts of the album,” says Kiwanuka. “All the music sucks into one and you hear this beautiful piano piece that he just improvised on the day. You can only get these special moments when you’ve got a relationship with musicians you’ve played together with so much.”It was this moment that convinced Kiwanuka that these sessions weren’t just some romantic indulgence, but the makings of his next album, one looser and more unstructured than ever before. Fudge builds on the direction he set with Small Changes, with his musical output becoming smaller and more personal, rather than bigger and more commercial: he calls it “a continuation of the focus on the melody of the song, the lyrics and the voice, as opposed to big production”. The closeness between Kiwanuka and his band meant that much of the album came together live in the studio, in inspired bursts. He cites the unadorned, heartfelt Move in my Direction: “I played guitar and sang with the string quartet at the same time in the room. That was special. That string moment was written on the spot as well. There’s a lot of that in this album: a real honesty to the playing, sort of blurring the lines between composition and performance.”Fudge was completed before Kiwanuka’s stroke, but it is difficult to listen to without finding new resonances in light of his illness. He now finds a double meaning in some of its lyrics. On California, he muses on the idea of home: “California rise again / Be my sweet medicine I need / California to live again.” Parts of Small Changes were recorded in Los Angeles, but Kiwanuka says this track wasn’t really about the state: “It’s funny, the word California just sounded good in that part of the song and I couldn’t think of anything else. But that bliss that comes with being in California, I was thinking of that – it feels like eternal sunshine, good food, fresh weather, blue skies.” Does this song make him think quite differently about home now? “Sort of,” he says. “Just being with people you can be yourself with. That sort of blissful state.”Perhaps the most poignant is the bluesy track Stars, on which he sings: “I remember when I played I used to feel / Now I don’t feel a thing.” With its unruly guitar solos set against more tonal strumming and percussion, it conveys a sense of discord, of being lost. “That’s a bit more resonant now,” Kiwanuka says. It was written many years before it found a home on Fudge. “I wrote that at a time when I hadn’t written songs for a while. I thought I’d lost the ability to write good music,” he says. “I used to focus on my feelings a lot to get music out. And for a while, quite a few years ago, that didn’t seem to work. But I feel like that will work even more now.”View image in fullscreenKiwanuka performing on the Pyramid stage at Glastonbury in 2024.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianIt is not yet clear what the future of Kiwanuka’s music will be. For now, rehabilitation is a day-by-day process. He is incredibly thankful for the care and support he and his family have received from the NHS and medical professionals. “People have been helpful and kind and diligent and patient,” he says. “But it’s been hard as well. Things like sessions of rehab every day, which can get tiring.” What do the rehab sessions involve? “A lot of stretches and getting your body back in shape. The brain injury affected some of the pathways to parts of my body, so I’ve been working on that.” Charlotte reminds him to mention speech therapy. “There was a point where my volume was really low when I spoke because I had a breathing tube, so that affected my vocal cords. I had to re-energise those.”But music has also aided his recovery. “Singing along to my favourite songs, that’s helped a lot.” What kind of music? “Some Bob Dylan songs, because they are easier to sing,” he laughs, “because it’s more like talking. Some stuff off [the Beach Boys’] Pet Sounds, like I Just Wasn’t Made for These Times. I love the lyrics on that album. Very melancholy, so it reflected how I felt in recovery.” Singing has helped him to talk, improving his vocal volume. And some of the breathing exercises to rebuild his stamina are the same as those he would do on tour, such as blowing bubbles through a straw into a cup: “It soothes your vocal cords.”double quotation markThere’s some days of hope, some days of real anger, some days of sadness and loss and griefWriting has also aided him emotionally. “There was a point in hospital where I had a notepad and I wrote lyrics down every day,” he says. The brain damage from the stroke affected the regulation of his tears, meaning he would cry uncontrollably, all the time, over anything. “So I wrote about crying and how it’s OK to cry and how it feels when you finish crying. You feel better. I never used to cry that much. My brain just didn’t have a filter for that any more.”Still, even if creativity can help him process those emotions, it does not give him total control over them. “There’s some days of hope, some days of real anger, some days of sadness and loss and grief,” he says. “But it feels quite therapeutic to feel emotions so heavily, and the crying, quite soothing.”View image in fullscreen‘It was almost telepathic’ ... Kiwanuka and his collaborators recording Fudge.Photograph: Jodie CanwellThe extent to which Kiwanuka’s stroke has affected him physically is not made clear to me beyond what I can infer from his speech. Even though he is partially disclosing what has happened to him, he is clear that it’s not an invitation for intrusion or speculation. But no doubt fans and well-wishers will be wondering if a sustained return is possible. He can’t truly know yet, and all live commitments are indefinitely on hold, but his ambitions have not disappeared. “I still have as much drive to create good music as I’ve ever done,” he says. He imagines himself leaning more into collaboration, recruiting musicians to play the instruments that he usually plays, and cutting down on travelling and antisocial hours.‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 yearsRead moreFudge was created to convey a sense of optimism and play, hence its sweet name. Its artwork, by Kiwanuka’s friend Stevie Gee, is a vibrant, psychedelic portrait of a bespectacled Black man surrounded by bright pink swirls. Releasing this album is one way of reclaiming the fun and freedom that had become so important to Kiwanuka. “A stroke can take away a lot of things, but it can’t take those songs away,” he says. “So I’ve got hope from that. Who I was still exists in those songs and in that music.”Fudge is released via Polydor on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMichael KiwanukaStrokeMercury prize 2020Pop and rockSoulIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the defiant queer dancehall of Destin Conrad and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Every one of the Grammy-nominated Floridian’s songs reveal a different side of him. His latest album, Roadrunner, is all languid reggae basslines and come-hither lyricism
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: Every one of the Grammy-nominated Floridian’s songs reveal a different side of him. His latest album, Roadrunner, is all languid reggae basslines and come-hither lyricism
Content: ‘Celebrating his Jamaican roots and queer identity’ … Destin Conrad.Photograph: RyderView image in fullscreen‘Celebrating his Jamaican roots and queer identity’ … Destin Conrad.Photograph: RyderAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the defiant queer dancehall of Destin Conrad and the week’s best new tracksEvery one of the Grammy-nominated Floridian’s songs reveal a different side of him. His latest album, Roadrunner, is all languid reggae basslines and come-hither lyricismOlive Pometsey,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromTampa, FloridaRecommended if you likeKwn, Tyla, OdealUp nextPerforming in Dallas, Texas, 1 NovemberDestin Conrad has had a busy couple of years: three albums, one Grammy nomination and a string of collaborations with fellow R&B up-and-comers such as Bellah and Nia Smith. Pick any record and you’ll hear a different side of the 26-year-old. His spring 2025 debut Love on Digital pays its dues to the genre that raised him while swerving derivative cliches with small production quirks – a vocal glitch here, a skittering Jersey beat there. Last summer’s Whimsy is a sprawling alt-jazz album that waswritten in two weeks, inspired by his time in a high-school jazz choir. A year later, Roadrunner arrived as a celebration of his Jamaican roots and queer identity – all languid reggae basslines, gyrating dancehall rhythms, drinks-in-the-air swagger and come-hither lyricism.Roadrunner doesn’t gloss over reggae and dancehall’s history of homophobia, nor does it simply condemn it. On Chi Chi, Conrad interpolates the notorious chorus of TOK’s Chi-Chi Man, flipping its calls to burn anyone seen driving with gay men into a brag: “Yes, I know they don’t wanna see me drivin’ / So I make sure I drive off in a Benzy.” He makes defiance against bigotry seem easy – fun, even – and spends the rest of the album revelling in that freedom. “I know I make them nervous,” he winks over the throbbing sub-bass of Nervous. “You want fi control me,” he moans on Obsessed. Granted, those last two lines are about flexing on peers and teasing lovers. But what’s a turn up without a little bump and grind?Olive PometseyThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenMadonna and Charli xcx.Photograph: Ricardo GomesMadonna and Charli xcx – Danceteria Afterhours“I get off the train, Hackney Wick / I’m sweet 15 in a weird outfit”: Charli blends her origin story into the Confessions II highlight, PC Music and “flavoured cocaine” mingling with Basquiat and Haoui Montaug.LSJane Remover – Beauty SleepHeavily compressed even by her standards, the US singer-producer condenses her digicore-hyperpop style into a seething, tinny cube of sound – but graces it with one of her loveliest melodic top lines.BBTLily Konigsberg – Free ByrdIf your song centres around the word “free”, it’d better feel that way. Konigsberg fulfils the brief with a winsome, characterful indie jangler about betting on herself over a too-safe relationship.LSTegan and Sara – Our Year (ft Lights)Another song eyeing the exits, set to wistful, jewel-toned synths and balmy horizon fantasias that make the Quin twins’ notion of quitting a tired town almost viscerally alluring.LS​Catherine Elicson – FigureThe front person of estimable Philly garage rock band Empath strikes out solo, defugging her band’s haze for a plaintive ballad on lo-fi electric guitar, with Vini Reilly-ish soloing.BBTMorphine – CocoonFrom a forthcoming rarities album, Cocoon revels in the sleazy, disarmingly seductive brew of sax, idle crooning and heavy bass that made the Boston band – and late frontman Mark Sandman – so brilliant.LSSpace Afrika – Pretty Gospel (ft Kiala Ogawa)Surfacing out of the cold, slow currents of ambient, post-rock and dub on the Mancunians’ new album Quiet Storm is this jazz ballad, with Ogawa’s kindly yet melancholy vocals reminiscent of Cleo Sol.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jae Stephens: Audacity review – a thrilling lesson in why more debut albums should go for broke | Music | The Guardian
description: After five EPs in in seven years, the Dallas native with the big voice pours everything into this bonkers cauldron of maximalist R&B and hyperactive pop
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: After five EPs in in seven years, the Dallas native with the big voice pours everything into this bonkers cauldron of maximalist R&B and hyperactive pop
Content: Audacious … Jae Stephens.Photograph: Courtesy of Cass MeyersView image in fullscreenAudacious … Jae Stephens.Photograph: Courtesy of Cass MeyersMusicReviewJae Stephens: Audacity review – a thrilling lesson in why more debut albums should go for broke(Def Jam)After five EPs in in seven years, the Dallas native with the big voice pours everything into this bonkers cauldron of maximalist R&B and hyperactive popShaad D'SouzaFri 25 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is so, so much happening on Jae Stephens’ debut album Audacity. Thankfully, it seems like mess is her medium. Although the 29-year-old Dallas native is often sold as a big voice – and she undoubtedlydoeshave a big voice – her debut album has more in common with hyperactive, magnetic records such as PinkPantheress’s Fancy That or Salute’s True Magic: recent albums whose need for speed and sweetly toned maximalism fostered an irrepressible sense of personality.View image in fullscreenThe album artwork for Jae Stephens, Audacity.Photograph: Courtesy of Cass MeyersStephens is an apt case study of a career in the contemporary pop industry: she started writing, producing and performing alone in her room, and dropped a whopping five EPs in the seven years before Audacity’s release. She has written with a host of pop also-rans and, inexplicably, hosts a music interview podcast. But listening to Audacity forces me into that age-old cliche: why isn’t this artist a bigger star?Opener Crush is simultaneously loud and minimal, hypnotic in its rhythm but melodically aloof and laid-back. No One Knows My Name and Attaboy! feel like classic 2000s R&B tracks played at double speed during the best DJ set ever. But even when Stephens slows down a little, as on I Miss the City, she refuses to let things get too by-the-book, layering bounce hi-hats over her frustrated, yearning lyrics as the song crests. The whole record is bonkers and, for once in pop, makes good on its title. It’s the sound of an artist finally getting her shot, and refusing to squander it.Explore more on these topicsMusicR&BPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Norma Tanega and Aida Pavletich: Saturday Dancer review – cult pop songwriter’s wonky collaborations | Music | The Guardian
description: This reissue of late 80s and early 90s recordings of wonky, nocturnal keyboard and drum machine experiments is immersed in swampy synth and noir-ish eccentricity
Author: Safi Bugel
Headline: This reissue of late 80s and early 90s recordings of wonky, nocturnal keyboard and drum machine experiments is immersed in swampy synth and noir-ish eccentricity
Content: Artists and friends … Aida Pavletich, left, and Norma TanegaView image in fullscreenArtists and friends … Aida Pavletich, left, and Norma TanegaExperimental album of the monthMusicReviewNorma Tanega and Aida Pavletich: Saturday Dancer review – cult pop songwriter’s wonky collaborations(Freedom to Spend)Far from her conventional 60s and 70s hits, Tanega joined up with a friend for an endearingly eccentric ‘rap opera’ spanning swampy synths and sardonic showtunesSafi BugelFri 25 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps you know Norma Tanega for her chirpy 60s folk pop, such as Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog, which charted in the US and Canada. Or perhaps you know her swooning ballads from the 70s, which have had a streaming-aided resurgence in popularity. Lesser known are her wonky, nocturnal keyboard and drum machine experiments, recorded between the late 80s and early 90s with friend and writer Aida Pavletich. Together, the pair produced a trio of tapes on a four-track in Tanega’s home studio, which are now being reissued.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Saturday Dancer by Norma Tanega and Aida PavletichThe first of the three, Saturday Dancer, is billed as a “rap opera”, which gives a sense of the album’s theatrical tone, if not the genre. Over 19 scuzzy and shapeshifting vignettes, the duo narrate a noirish night out on the town, from stripteases and sticky tables to the dread that seeps in when the lights come on – with some frankly bizarre tangents. The lo-fi instrumentals are suitably delirious, with clattering, likely improvised percussion and eerie synths lurking somewhere between strange and seductive.Amplifying the eroticism are Pavletich’s esoteric commentaries, which channel the seedy, drawling monologues of Angel Corpus Christi or Little Annie. The jagged instrumentation references everything from primitive post-punk to children’s music, while tracks such as Eryngo and Angel call to mindPatrick Cowley’s swampy synth atmospheres. The eccentricity peaks on electronic whirlwind Danse Macabre and White People’s Music, a sardonic take on a show tune with a dizzying country interlude.The brilliant, smoky title track is the clear highlight – and the first song, meaning momentum wavers somewhat thereafter. You wonder whether the label would have been better off exercising more curatorial input, cherrypicking the standouts across all three tapes into a single, better focused compilation. That said, the project is an exciting artefact: an insight into the minds of two boundary-pushing artists.Also out this monthSinkronia, the new record from Basque musicianIker Munduate, is a delightful listen (Hegoa). Inspired by minimalist compositions, these nine instrumentals are spacious but warm, layering bleary-eyed synths and hazy Durutti Column-style guitars with xylophone, hand drums and other simple percussive arrangements. The combination evokes a wistful feeling well-suited to the change of seasons. Another highlight isArchives, the fifth album from long-distance experimental trioVanishing Twin(Fire Records). Broadcast are a clear influence on this set of gorgeous psych-pop tracks, but conventional structures are sent off-piste by warbling electronics and glitching samples. BristoliansTara Clerkin(ofher eponymous trio) andMemotonemet up for a studio day last summer with just their clarinets and a few pedals. That session has materialised in For Clarinets (Bliss Archive), a charming collection of slow-building, occasionally sprightly, improvisations. Foggy samples of rainfall, woodwind and distant voices enhance the DIY atmosphere.Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental album of the monthExperimental musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My generation of novelists is dying’: Rose Tremain on 70 years of writing, and late-life inspiration | Books | The Guardian
description: As her latest novel about Daphne du Maurier is published, the bestselling author reflects on age and creativity – and why at 83 she has no plans to stop
Author: Rose Tremain
Headline: As her latest novel about Daphne du Maurier is published, the bestselling author reflects on age and creativity – and why at 83 she has no plans to stop
Content: ‘Do readers still love us?’ … Rose Tremain.Photograph: Ali Smith/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘Do readers still love us?’ … Rose Tremain.Photograph: Ali Smith/The ObserverBooks‘My generation of novelists is dying’: Rose Tremain on 70 years of writing, and late-life inspirationAs her latest novel about Daphne du Maurier is published, the bestselling author reflects on age and creativity – and why at 83 she has no plans to stopRose TremainFri 25 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy generation of writers is dying. Of Granta’s fabled list of 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, six are gone, including our most princely satirist, Martin Amis. We’re all approaching birthdays where the cake is too small for the candles. Some of us are wounded: Salman Rushdie by an attacker’s knife, Julian Barnes lives with blood cancer, others with the fatal hurt of being forgotten.But what’s the likely fate of those of us who are surviving – for now? Do readers still love us? When Barnes announced that he was signing off because of illness, was he also intuiting that the younger generations had heard enough from us old birds and geezers who were young when Sean Connery had dimples, when David Hockney first coloured his hair yellow?The answer is probably “yes”. But here’s what I believe: contrary to what publishers hope and expect, serious writers don’t think obsessively about readers, or even about sales, royalties and prizes. What we talk to each other about, what we dream of, what we can’t live without is the work itself. When I endured a terrifying procedure for pancreatic cancer in 2019 and contemplated the likelihood of dying in Addenbrooke’s hospital, I spent wide-awake nights mourning not only the people I love and the places that are precious to me, but the end of storytelling. Ideas for stories have peopled my life since the age of 12, when I wrote my first play at boarding school. My existence devoid of these would definitely feel what Amis once called “thin”.From interviews Hockney gave towards the end of his 88 years, when yellow had turned to white, we gleaned a fine understanding of the elderly artist’s unflagging commitment to a day-by-day engagement with his art. The simplicity of the Hockney philosophy – “I wake up. And I go to work” – enabled him to rival Picasso with the vastness and variety of his output. He lived and breathed painting. The idea that he would suddenly stop doing this he would surely have thought plain stupid, and I’m with him on that. Though there can be a falling-off in the work of artists and writers as they age, this is by no means inevitable; the reasons for keeping on are not too hard to find.double quotation markMy latest project brings together both the young playwright that I once was and the elderly novelist I am nowCertainly I’m getting towards the end of my life, but why should what remains of it be stricken by the loss of the one constant that has kept me company for 70 years, since that first little school play? To those who might imagine me in “retirement” tending my garden in Norfolk, existing only through this and through the lives of my daughter and my grandchildren, I need to explain that ideas for novels and stories still arrive in my head all the time, like supplicants at the gate. They beg to be let in. Where would all this clamour go if I shut them out?This may be delusional, but I don’t believe the work done in the last third of my life is inferior to that done near its beginning. Critical reaction to my later novels –The Gustav Sonata(2016),Islands of Mercy(2020),Lily(2021) andAbsolutely and Forever(2023) – was very positive and these books were written on the kind of creative high that I never experienced in my early writing days. In contrast, there were a few writers on the Granta 1983 list who had already foreseen a golden road ahead. Amis and McEwan seemed to arrive on the scene as fully fashioned geniuses, nudging literary fame in their 20s. Rushdie, too, had by then published his Booker sensation, Midnight’s Children, and was clearly a star.The rest of us lined up in their wake. I’d published only two books and still felt uncertain that I really understood the form of the novel well enough to write anything worth keeping. I retreated back to play writing, this time for the BBC radio drama department, and was surprised to win an award for one of the best radio plays of 1984 for Temporary Shelter, starring the wonderful late Roy Kinnear (Rory’s Dad) as a naive English tourist facing up to the shortcomings of his life on a French campsite.View image in fullscreenSome of Granta’s 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, including Julian Barnes (back, centre), Martin Amis (middle, right) and Rose Tremain (front, centre right).Photograph: Snowdon/Camera PressWhen, in 1988, I had the idea for my “breakthrough novel”,Restoration, I remember that I drew on one of the themes explored in Temporary Shelter:the protagonist as a shambling man who finds himself in a world he doesn’t understand and who makes a spectacular mess of things until he begins to learn the lessons his own nature is ready to teach him. But by this time I’d begun to learn lessons of my own about what kind of novel I wanted to write.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI inclined towards the epic rather than the miniature. History’s great canvas was a constant lure, yet my opinion on historical research is that it has to be done thoroughly and then almost abandoned, to let the imagination do its essential work. (Kipling described this process as lighting a great fire and then working only with its riddled embers.) Humour had to be part of the storytelling mix and could play a lovely melody above the bass notes of tragedy. Above all, I understood that to live with a work of fiction for the many months that it takes to complete it, one has to love it quite passionately and be comfortable with all its moods and habits, or – as Colm Tóibín puts it with delicious domestic flair – one has to stay for long periods of time in one’s “mental pyjamas”.My mental pyjamas are on, then, but is it time to put everything to bed? This may be stubborn, but I don’t feel that it is. My latest project brings together both the young playwright that I once was and the elderly novelist I am now. The new book is titledThe Housekeeper, and is a reimagining of the inspiration behind Daphne du Maurier’s classic novel Rebecca. It began as a short story in 2014, but I have now brought it to life not only as a novel but also as a screenplay for a film, directed by Richard Eyre and starring Anthony Hopkins and Helena Bonham Carter. I’ve been enthralled by the script work. It takes me back to standing in the wings of the school stage, hearing my own words spoken aloud for the first time.The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain is published by Chatto & Windus.
