title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley; The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett; Cold Sunset by William Boyd; The Occidental Book of the Dead by T Geronimo Johnson and The Last Tenant by Eva Björg Ægisdóttir
Author: Laura Wilson
Headline: Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley; The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett; Cold Sunset by William Boyd; The Occidental Book of the Dead by T Geronimo Johnson and The Last Tenant by Eva Björg Ægisdóttir
Content: Julia McKenzie in the TV adaptation of Agatha Christie’s Marple: A Caribbean Mystery.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJulia McKenzie in the TV adaptation of Agatha Christie’s Marple: A Caribbean Mystery.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockCrime and thrillers roundupFictionReviewThe best recent crime and thrillers – review roundupMurder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley; The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett; Cold Sunset by William Boyd; The Occidental Book of the Dead by T Geronimo Johnson and The Last Tenant by Eva Björg ÆgisdóttirLaura WilsonFri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenMurder at the Grand Alpine Hotelby Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, £22)This, the first Miss Marple continuation novel, must have been a more difficult undertaking than a new Hercule Poirot; furnished by Christie with a cartoonist’s worth of exaggerated traits, the Belgian detective is surely easier to bring off the page than the unassuming but observant elderly spinster. Foley makes a commendable attempt, removing Miss Marple from the postwar austerity of St Mary Mead to the comparative luxury of the Swiss Alps. Although we are introduced to the unnamed body in the gondola cabin at the start, an immediate backward shift for a two-day lead-up means Miss Marple has little actual detecting to do until about halfway through the proceedings. Employing four narrators rather dilutes things, as well as necessitating a considerable amount of Murder of Roger Ackroyd-style withholding of information, but Foley’s Miss M shows her true colours when – of course – the hotel gets cut off from the outside world, and provides a solution worthy of the Queen of Crime herself.View image in fullscreenThe Silent Appealby Janice Hallett (Viper, £20)Bestseller Hallett’s latest novel reunites us with amateur dramatic group the Fairway Players, first encountered in her debut novel, The Appeal. This time the play is The Hollow, dramatised by Agatha Christie from her novel of the same name, and, as before, lawyers Charlotte and Femi are called upon to review the mountain of emails, online messages and police reports through which the story is told, in order to figure out exactly what happened. All we know at the start is that “a brutal murder was committed” and Hallett slowly but expertly ratchets up the tension as clashes over casting, power plays, marital suspicions and distrust of newcomers create an entire gallery of potential murderers and murderees. The epistolatory method may not be for everyone, but Hallett excels at the form – these missives are variously funny, sinister, heartfelt and thoroughly human in their relatable pettiness – and the plot is well up to her usual standard.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: PRCold Sunsetby William Boyd (Viking, £20)Boyd’s third novel to feature British travel-writer-cum-spy Gabriel Dax takes place in 1964. Initially on the trail of a wartime double agent for the Soviet Union, who operated out of Bletchley Park, our man is then sent to Moscow in order to exfiltrate repentant double agent Kit Caldwell, who promises to offer up secrets in return for sanctuary back in Blighty. Naturally, none of this goes according to plan … Boyd is an accomplished storyteller, excellent on period detail and often funny – the dinner party of self-important Hampstead literati is particularly good – and one can’t help taking proprietorial pleasure in seeing Dax’s tradecraft gradually improving, although he remains alarmingly in thrall to his MI6 handler and on/off lover, Faith Green, who continues to run rings round him. I’d recommend reading this superb series in order.View image in fullscreenThe Occidental Book of the Deadby T Geronimo Johnson (Abacus, £25)Taking place in a lightly fictionalised version of Atlanta, Georgia, the central storyline in this wide-ranging juggernaut of a third novel seems superficially straightforward. In 2005, after 13 years in the police force, Black officer George Washington Jonson finds himself in hot water when his redneck rookie partner shoots and kills a white teenager. In due course, a film version of this event and its aftermath serves up an acceptable narrative about racism and corruption. But in the second half of the book, hero-of-the-hour Jonson gives us his own version of the story, which the film-makers told faithfully “except for that fairytale series finale and a couple other facts Hollywood found inconvenient”. The truth, which is much more complex, is a lot less comfortable: internalised racism, overlapping identities, double standards and the sheer messiness of people’s lives are laid bare in an immersive and thought-provoking read.View image in fullscreenThe Last Tenantby Eva Björg Ægisdóttir, translated by Victoria Cribb (Orenda, £9.99)The final book in Ægisdóttir’s award-winning Forbidden Iceland series sees Detective Elma Jónsdóttir investigating the case of two skeletons – a woman and a baby, buried some years apart – which have been discovered at a long-abandoned farmhouse in the country outside Akranes, the small west coast town where she works. The farmer who owned it had a reputation for cruelty, but he is long dead, and his son never returned to claim the place. Elma tries to find answers, but is distracted by problems at home – might her partner be having an affair? Meanwhile, single mother Karitas and her young son, Bessi, are in Akranes for a fresh start, but her eccentric landlord’s behaviour is becoming disturbing. Missing family members, people living with past trauma, and the insidious damage caused by secrets abound in this atmospheric and powerful novel.Explore more on these topicsFictionCrime and thrillers roundupreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Can’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius? | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon
Content: Kylie performing in 2000.Photograph: Paul Bergen/RedfernsView image in fullscreenKylie performing in 2000.Photograph: Paul Bergen/RedfernsBook of the dayPop and rockReviewCan’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius?The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie iconJack ParlettFri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 02.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘There’s an anxiety in declaring oneself a Kylie fan,” wrote the late San Francisco poet Kevin Killian (who nonetheless once published an entire collection devoted to the singer). Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmament has often felt more precarious than that of other artists, perhaps because of her past as a soap star, and the schmaltz of some of her early material with Stock Aitken Waterman.But she has always displayed a canny self-awareness, alongside a willingness to push the envelope. It’s evident in her knowing rendition of I Should Be So Lucky as a bad poem at the Royal Albert Hall in 1996, and her many collaborations with experimental dance producers. Then there’s her instinct for giving fans what they want: inarguable bangers, like those of her 2000s imperial phase, that also possess an offbeat, idiosyncratic quality, true of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and of her 2023 viral hit, Padam Padam.Michael Cragg’s illuminating new book explores Kylie’s multiple selves, her talent for shapeshifting, and the question of why she has been persistently underrated. He makes the case that the most easily maligned aspects of her music – frivolity without subtext, fun without an underlying seriousness – are precisely what makes it so pleasurable and available for camp reclamation, its apparent disposability capable of being recast as a virtue.double quotation markThis project is unambiguously the work of a superfan and scholar of popThe Aussie girl next door is thus a different kind of gay icon to club kid Madonna, a grittier figure who looms large here, and whose own acts of reinvention have been considered not just the work of an entertainer, but of an auteur. This comparison is also a matter of taste, of course; in a particularly juicy quote included in the chapter on Kylie’s appeal among gay audiences, singer Rufus Wainwright describes her “as the anti-Madonna. She is what she is and there is no attempt to make quasi-intellectual statements to substantiate it. She is the gay shorthand for joy.”As to what makes a gay icon, Cragg nimbly tackles the question by including a committee of different voices on the subject, just as he threads his chapters through with interviews. These generate intriguing discoveries and esoteric insights from people as diverse as textile designers, academics and film-makers, all of whose work has been informed by Kylie in some way. While this can slightly disrupt the flow of the book, it also captures the communal ethos that is key to fandom.Cragg’s prose is appealingly breezy, its register more Popjusticethan Pitchfork, but never less than earnest. This projectis unambiguously the work of a superfan and scholar of pop, for whom the question of Kylie’s legacy is a high-stakes one. His book is animated by a level of devotion that may not be unique to queer culture, but is certainly one of its hallmarks. There are many reasons we worship our icons in precisely the ways we do, and Cragg’s personal disclosures about his mental health, his early experiences of the closet, and his relationship with his husband provide a touching backdrop to this portrait of why Kylie matters. As does the section reflecting on Kylie’s breast cancer, how it humanised her in the public eye, fostering greater awareness of the disease and underlining the importance of early screening.That an artist like this has the ability to bring people together might seem like an obvious point, but Cragg urges us not to underestimate “what an amazing service that is”. I finished his book with a newfound appreciation not only of her artistry, but of what she has meant to so many people. She is a singer whose generosity and mutability has allowed her fans to feel whatever they need to feel, nowhere more so than when she performs All the Lovers at her live shows, and arms sway in unison, the song’s lyrics capacious enough for multiple readings, about the adversities of queer life and all of those we have loved and lost.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJack Parlett is the author of Flamboyance: The Art of Burning Brightly (Granta).Can’t Get You Out of My Head: In Search of Kylie by Michael Cragg is published by Faber (£25).
