title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | Games | The Guardian
description: The game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane
Author: Patrick Lum
Headline: The game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane
Content: ‘The simple act of flying around looks astounding’ … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoView image in fullscreen‘The simple act of flying around looks astounding’ … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoGamesReviewAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasyPlayStation 5, Xbox, PC (version played); Bandai NamcoThe game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy planePatrick LumFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe core appeal of any Ace Combat game lies in the moment when the beautiful clouds part, the sunlight glints off your perfectly rendered state-of-the-art fighter jet, and guitar-shredding music kicks into overdrive as your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane. All of that is 100% present in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. What’s new is the way it delivers its unexpectedly compelling story.Set in the Earth-like alternative world of Strangereal, where every country is absolutely obsessed with fighter planes and giant superweapons, Ace Combat drafts you into the role of a fake ace pilot called the Wings of Theve – a propaganda invention to raise the morale of a besieged nation, similar to real-life rumours about Ukraine’sGhosts of Kyiv. You rapidly find yourself becoming an actual legendary pilot, soaring through the skies with your buddies and raining hell upon your oppressors as everybody cheers on the radio. Speaking of ghosts, you have one in your ear – your predecessor, whom nobody else can hear, a gravelly voice waxing lyrical about flying, war and whatever else is on his mind as you flit about.Despite slavish devotion to the accurate depiction of military hardware, Ace Combat has always been more concerned with making flying fun than sticking to realism. Simplified, more intuitive controls and training scenarios are available to help ease beginners into the pilot’s seat, while as a series veteran I was happier with the expert control scheme, which opens up more complex manoeuvres like missile-evading rolls and zero-G turns. Importantly, the simple act of flying around looks astounding; action replays unerringly choose the best camera angles to make you look like a true ace (instead of someone simply doing their best not to smash straight into the ground).This is a game all about dogfighting, but there’s a pleasing variety of mission types ranging from bombing runs and escorts to more convoluted scenarios such as taking out a giant, railgun-equipped “land battleship” rampaging through a city’s streets, or hunting radar-invisible supersonic planes by trying to spot their tell-tale contrails. It’s all thrilling stuff; the game is perfectly tuned to generate high-tension, blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through endless rains of missiles while an orchestra goes absolutely wild and a well-produced radio drama plays out over the open airwaves.It can all get a little confusing in the heat of battle, especially in the first-person cockpit view (which I otherwise highly recommend). Deciphering what the game is telling you to aim for next amid the visual clutter can be a trial – a button to target priority mission objectives directly wouldn’t have gone amiss. The clouds, too, can disorientate; I have never seen skies as gorgeous before, but you’ll soon learn to read the atmosphere for its tactical considerations as much as for its beauty.Gameplay innovations are more incremental than sweeping. You can issue commands to your wing-mates, as in much earlier games in the series, but new to AC8 is environmental destruction. Some buildings and vehicles crumble when damaged: falling debris or explosions can trigger devastating chain reactions and you are no longer forced to target weak points to do damage to larger vessels, though it usually remains more efficient. Your plane can also glance off surfaces, taking a bit of damage, which is a relief; in previous entries you would explode instantaneously if your wing so much as clipped a tree branch.View image in fullscreenImpactful … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoLarger, more impactful changes are reserved for how the game tells its story. AC7’s cut-scenes were closer to motion comics than movies, which worked fine for mission briefings but less so for anything involving human emotion. Here, fully animated first-person segments meld with more traditional cinematic cut-scenes (and some really effective smash-cutsbetweenscenes) to really bring your wing-mates and the drama to life. Enemy incursions might occur during routine landings or refuelings, too, keeping you on your toes.Ace Combat has always owed a debt to the movie Top Gun, and AC8 borrows liberally from the more recent sequel Top Gun: Maverick, with closeup pilot face-cam shots and a handful of story beats lifted straight from the film. Dialogue can be a bit clunky (again like Top Gun, or perhaps Metal Gear Solid); characters will occasionally pause midway through an otherwise natural-sounding conversation to deliver some convoluted plot exposition or an ideological clanger. But between the truly amazing shot framing and cinematography, emotive motion capture and voice acting, the series’ trademark soaring music and a story that actually sticks the landing, I ended up oddly moved. This is not something you necessarily expect from an arcade flight combat sim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnfortunately I was unable to try the game’s online multiplayer mode, Ace Combat Online, which was only available for a very short time during the review period. But even leaving that aside, AC8 is a triumph, a perfectly composed symphony of fire and steel that absolutely soars.Released on 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesAdventure gamesArcade gamesSimulation gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears | Games | The Guardian
description: I’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played together
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: I’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played together
Content: ‘We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun’ … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.Illustration: APView image in fullscreen‘We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun’ … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.Illustration: APGamesPlaying video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tearsDominik DiamondI’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played togetherFri 25 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTShareIhave spent the last three weeks living with my 22-year-old son in a two-bedroom flat he has dubbed the ”brotel”. We cook curries and watchLanterns. We barbecue meat and analyse Tarantino movies. We get pizza and we play video games. Boy, do we play video games!The first game I ever played in co-op with him was Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 in 2009, when he was five. He wasn’t the most accomplished sidekick, notsogreat at placing a mobile gun turret while under fire from what seems like a bazillion enemy soldiers, but we had a laugh. It started the video game bond between us before his sister introduced him to Banjo-Kazooie and Rayman, and he stopped being a preschool warmonger. Probably for the best. So how would it be tackling the same game nearly two decades later?We start with the two Special Ops missions we used to play. We never completed them because, once again, he was five – and I am left-handed, which makes me rubbish at joypad-controlled first-person shooters without the help of auto targeting. Thankfully, one of those circumstances has now changed.View image in fullscreenGuard dogs in the snow … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s Evasion mission.Photograph: ActivisionThe first mission is officially called Evasion, but to us it has always been “the guard dogs in the snow”, because they got us every time we played. Our initial attempts highlight the differences between us as gamers. And men, if I’m being honest.I am paranoid. I sense calamity around every corner, so I creep forwards, mostly crouching, frequently crawling on my belly, slowly and carefully scouting for enemies using my sniper scope. Charlie is running through the level firing from the hip likeLeeroy bloody Jenkins. Which means he alerts all the dogs, who for some reason are able to smell me from miles away and nom nom nom me to oblivion.We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun.Teamwork eventually emerges through compromise. He holds back a bit, I grow less timid. I snipe from a distance, he finishes them off up close. And, most importantly, we take out the guard dogs first. We realise that was where we went wrong two decades ago. These dogs are superhuman. I would love a level where you got to play as them.We finally complete the mission. It has only taken us 17 years! We go straight into the other level that we never conquered: Homeland Security, AKA “defend the garage from five waves of attack”. This takes a fair few goes, but we have such great communication by this time that it’s never a chore. We leap from our twin La-Z-Boy chairs in celebration when we win.We gambol through mission after mission. Suspension, AKA “bridge with helicopters”, is a riot from start to finish. We have a great rhythm. I bazooka from afar, Charlie sprints in to mop up. In Snatch and Grab, we take a computer file then boot it from an aircraft graveyard, avoiding helmeted Juggernauts; it’s pure unadulterated gaming joy. Even when, once again, we fail.As I am writing this, thanks to whatever AI is lurking in my computer scanning everything I type or possibly even think, an article pings up about the online gaming cheat industry, which is now apparently worth $8.5bn. I’m sure there are reasons why people invest so much money in cheating – but talk about ripping the soul out of something fun.View image in fullscreenA familiar sight … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s multiplayer.Photograph: ActivisionI have loved these last few weeks gaming with my son. I feel like I have gone back to basics. After decades as an uptight stressed dad, I am finally carefree, because I have recently gone back to working for myself. And I am a very forgiving boss. Sitting there with pizza, beer and another bloke, playing games till the wee small hours without a care in the world … this is what gaming was like for me when I was my son’s age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m not sure you ever top that period in your life as a gamer – when you get that first job that allows you to leave home, get your own place, buy whatever game you want and play it to your heart’s content, before you become burdened by the responsibilities of relationships, mortgages, parenthood and, worst of all, ambition.When those things arrive, you are lucky to squeeze in an hour of play here and there. You just try to get as far through a game as you can in that time because you don’t know when the next free hour will come, and you still feel guilty because you feel you should be doing something more grownup instead. You know, something that might help pay the rent.Now, though, I am back in gaming heaven. It won’t be for ever: my son and I are due to move to different parts of the world in a few months. But he turns to me after one session and says that he will look back on this as some of the best times we ever had together.I turn my head because I am still a Scottish dad and I don’t want him to see me cry. Even if those tears are the most beautiful big, happy ones.Dominik Diamondis on tourwith his show Dominik Diamond Sings the Video Games from 29 September to 6 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyShooting gamesParents and parentingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Table 17 review – a tasty romcom served with dazzle and cheek | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Marisha Wallace and Jamael Westman play exes who reconvene over dinner in Douglas Lyons’ sparky old-school charmer
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Marisha Wallace and Jamael Westman play exes who reconvene over dinner in Douglas Lyons’ sparky old-school charmer
Content: Dinner for two … Jamael Westman as Dallas and Marisha Wallace as Jada in Table 17 at Kiln theatre.Photograph: Steve GregsonView image in fullscreenDinner for two … Jamael Westman as Dallas and Marisha Wallace as Jada in Table 17 at Kiln theatre.Photograph: Steve GregsonTheatreReviewTable 17 review – a tasty romcom served with dazzle and cheekKiln theatre, LondonMarisha Wallace and Jamael Westman play exes who reconvene over dinner in Douglas Lyons’ sparky old-school charmerArifa AkbarFri 25 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis incorrigibly likable romcom comes to the UK with a series of sold out runs in New York and Los Angeles in its wake. You can see why: it slips down as easily and pleasantly as an old-school, Saturday-night TV meet-cute. Except writer Douglas Lyons’ story is a meet-again-cute because the couple at its centre are exes.It has been several years since air steward Jada (Marisha Wallace) and aspiring music producer Dallas (Jamael Westman) felt the sting of each other’s betrayals. Now they are sitting at table 17 to hash out unfinished business – and maybe relight the fire?We first meet them moments before the nervy reunion. What plays out is sparky fun, spanning the couple’s history in a similar manner to Nick Payne’s Constellations, sliding from present to past and back.Its ambition to double up as a serious relationship drama is not always met because of the imbalance of cutesy humour. The play treads similar ground to such recently successful romantic two-handers as Benedict Lombe’sShiftersbut is not as emotionally freighted, and nor does it have the larger social framework. The point here, it seems, is to entertain with comedy and elicit sentiment from romance.It works to please the crowd and melt your heart a little by the end, the actors raising the effect of the too-soft humour to make lines sound more sparkling than they are. Unfaithful acts and insecurities generate the drama, although this couple remain a little too generic.Under the direction of Zhailon Levingston, the dazzle around the script does a good job, from the music (Chaka Khan’s I’m Every Woman and some nostalgic 90s numbers) to sharp lighting design by Matt Haskins and freeze-frames that denote movement between present and past. Amy Jane Cook’s set design is the most dazzling of all – a horseshoe-shaped banquette, jauntily positioned, that revolves through the timelines and a sultry stage lit up by neon.View image in fullscreenShow-stealer … Michael Rishawn.Photograph: Steve GregsonThere are plenty of cheeky theatrical touches as Wallace and Westman make lightning-quick work of returning to the past and changing costumes, as well as giving soul-baring asides to us, in the middle of an emotionally dissembling scene. Michael Rishawn, who takes on several ancillary parts, almost steals the show with his gay restaurant host, who has a backstory of unwelcome singledom that you want to hear more about – maybe more so than the break-up-make-up drama of the couple.Still, there is great, energetic acting from the leads: the always magnetic Wallace, in a non-singing role here, oozes charisma although you do want her to burst into song in the vein of the Kiln’s previous romantic two-hander,Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York). Westman fills Dallas with life, sensitively balancing his ridiculousness with his depth of emotional injury.It’s feelgood fare that has you rooting for the couple, and leaves you thinking that in spite of their mutual hurt, they may just be meeting up again this time next year.AtKiln theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Kiln theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hallé/Wong review – MacMillan’s new symphony centres a great concert hall’s birthday celebrations | Classical music | The Guardian
description: James MacMillan’s sixth symphony proved an intricate, intriguing and forward-looking work. It was well paired with Stephen Hough’s exuberant ‘Emperor’ piano concerto and a Liszt rarity
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: James MacMillan’s sixth symphony proved an intricate, intriguing and forward-looking work. It was well paired with Stephen Hough’s exuberant ‘Emperor’ piano concerto and a Liszt rarity
Content: Britain’s best acoustic? … Manchester’s Bridgewater Hall, with the Hallé orchestra.Photograph: Alex Burns/HalléView image in fullscreenBritain’s best acoustic? … Manchester’s Bridgewater Hall, with the Hallé orchestra.Photograph: Alex Burns/HalléClassical musicReviewHallé/Wong review – MacMillan’s new symphony centres a great concert hall’s birthday celebrationsBridgewater Hall, ManchesterJames MacMillan’s sixth symphony proved an intricate, intriguing and forward-looking work.  It was well paired with Stephen Hough’s exuberant ‘Emperor’ piano concerto and a Liszt rarityAlexandra CoghlanFri 25 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe complain a lot about concert halls in the UK. The acoustics of the Barbican, Royal Festival Hall and Royal Albert Hall; the practicality of Usher Hall and St George’s Bristol;thoseseats at Snape Maltings, andthatfoyer at Birmingham’s Symphony Hall. But do we really have it so bad?As Manchester’s Hallé opens its season with a celebration of 30 years of the Bridgewater Hall, it’s a good moment to remember what we’ve gained in the three decades since a car park became Britain’s best acoustic. A flagship London hall may still be a fantasy, but with Gateshead’s Foster-designed Glasshouse, Saffron Hall, Kings Place and Milton Court all opening their doors since 2000, it’s hard to feel despondent.The Hallé and principal conductorKahchun Wongcelebrated their home’s birthday with a major new commission – James MacMillan’s sixth symphony. After a cycle of symphonies that seemed to work up to the choral epic of 2019’s fifth, the sixth feels like a new beginning.There are echoes of both Elgar’s Enigma Variations and Britten’s The Young Person’s Guide in a work that looks simultaneously in and out: inward to the family members who inspired four short, expositionary movements – the key to the wild parade that follows – and outward to the composers who inspired the fifth movement’s subsequent textural and formal manipulations.View image in fullscreenClever choices … Kahchun Wong conducts the Hallé.Photograph: Alex Burns/HalléThe effect is disorienting. There’s a pastoral, folk-inspired trio of flutes, a buzzing swarm of muted brass, a peal of gongs, bells and bowed vibraphone, and a yearning solo cello. And, standing apart from the rest, a Debussyean duet for harp and piano. How are we to assemble the fragments? Optimistically, MacMillan and an incisive Wong seem to urge. Low woodwind and trombones (together with a nagging siren) may attempt to pull us under, but surging life-force in brass-gilded climaxes pushes valiantly back. Tempests rage, but the still, small voice of the alto flute gently persists.What a clever choice to frame the symphony with a rare performance of Liszt’s compact epic Les Préludes (brass resplendent in the narrative highs, strings fretting convulsively in the lows) and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No 5: battles, both, for man’s survival and supremacy. Perhaps egged on by this cumulative energy, we got a more robust “Emperor” from soloist Stephen Hough than usual, his opening cadenza flinging down a gauntlet gleefully plucked up by Wong and his players in a heroic duel that climaxed in an exuberant, close-combat finale.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicHallé OrchestraJames MacMillanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Phil Wang: Uh Oh review – how to achieve an eighth of an orgasm, and other millennial myths | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The standup delivers older and wiser musings and mockery, whether it’s about taches, a passion for Gail’s or a distaste for cyclists
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: The standup delivers older and wiser musings and mockery, whether it’s about taches, a passion for Gail’s or a distaste for cyclists
Content: ‘Revelling in life’s mundanity’ … Phil Wang.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreen‘Revelling in life’s mundanity’ … Phil Wang.Photograph: Matt StrongeComedyReviewPhil Wang: Uh Oh review – how to achieve an eighth of an orgasm, and other millennial mythsSoho Theatre Walthamstow, LondonThe standup delivers older and wiser musings and mockery, whether it’s about taches, a passion for Gail’s or a distaste for cyclistsAnya RyanFri 25 Sep 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLots has changed in the world ofPhil Wangsince his last tour. He has mastered the art of growing a moustache, for one. He’s bought a house in a “cool” part of London, where he lives with his houseplants and, oh, the world has tipped considerably to the right. So what does this mean for the ever-even-tempered comedian, now officially in the territory of an ageing millennial?Largely, more of the observational routines that have made his name. We get his classic riffs on what it means to be both British and Chinese, his thoughts on gentrification – you best believe he wants a Gail’s in Peckham – and his resentment at finding his views becoming progressively less progressive. All of it is gently mocking: mainly of himself, but of others, too, to varying degrees of effect. A bit about cyclists, who are apparently asking for a death wish by venturing out on a 2D vehicle, feels more snarky than he may have intended. But his David Bowie impression could use a stage all of its own.It might not push the boundaries. But, at his heights, Wang is a king of linguistics and loopholes. Why, he asks, is being described as a person of colour perfectly acceptable, but “coloured person” deeply offensive? Of course he thinks about his girlfriend when he masturbates – it’s just that his mind wanders to whether she will walk in and catch him doing it. Revelling in life’s mundanity, he makes it bloom into material.‘Audiences no longer laugh if you call their town crap’: can Phil Wang heal divided Britain?Read moreIt is a show strung together by the nagging feeling that things have got worse. Long gone are the days of sweeping millennial myths, when we were told we could achieve one-eighth of an orgasm through a spidery hand gesture performed by our classmates. Now, he’s at the stage of mourning the loss of his once-slender neck. There’s something bleakly moving about Wang’s grownup outlook: the realisation that everything he thought those wild parties and long conversations with his parents were leading to was actually just the thing. It’s a lesson in living in the moment. And a taste of the halcyon days of youth comes at the close of a pondering show, if not a consistently revelatory one.On tour until 23 MayExplore more on these topicsComedyPhil WangSoho theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: K-art, William Kentridge and a Turner prize worth getting excited for – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Korean art rewinds 2,000 years, Kentridge enters another dimension and Rodinesque ghosts make a bid for art’s most prestigious gong
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Korean art rewinds 2,000 years, Kentridge enters another dimension and Rodinesque ghosts make a bid for art’s most prestigious gong
Content: Behind the mask … Kira Freije at the Turner prize 2026 at MIMA, Middlesbrough.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBehind the mask … Kira Freije at the Turner prize 2026 at MIMA, Middlesbrough.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianArt Weekly newsletterArt and designK-art, William Kentridge and a Turner prize worth getting excited for – the week in artKorean art rewinds 2,000 years, Kentridge enters another dimension and Rodinesque ghosts make a bid for art’s most prestigious gong –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekTurner prizeKira Freije creates a waste land peopled by Rodinesque ghosts in the machine, Simeon Barclay meditates on masculinity, Tanoa Sasraku takes on big oil and Marguerite Humeau gets lost in wonderland in the most exciting Turner prize in years.MIMA, Middlesbrough, from26 September until 29 MarchAlso showingKoreaA survey of 2,000 years of Korean art, belief and philosophy – but will it be as big as Bayeux?British Museum, London, from 1 October until 31 JanuaryFail We May, Sail We MustArtists from Salvador Dalí to the 18th-century British painter George Romney star in another eclectic dip into artist Glenn Brown’s impressive collection.Brown Collection, London, until 7 AugustMark Wallinger: Circling the SquarePaintings and a film from the Turner prize winner, that explore abstraction and the vitality of nature with a nod to Dylan Thomas.Paul Stolper Gallery, London, until 24 OctoberWilliam Kentridge: A Nicely Built CityA new animated film by this artist who takes drawing into new dimensions gets its world premiere.Goodman Gallery, London, until 7 NovemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonGoons in the military fatigues and wraparound shades beloved of ICE agents ride around in a clown car – a pretty clear comment on contemporary US. Elsewhere a solitary figure amid the ruins of Stonehenge is overwhelmed by the universe – are we now lost in in cosmic speculation? Welcome to the abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling world of Nicole Eisenman.Read our review here.What we learned101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser has had an amazing lifeSophie Calle has stalked people, posed as a hotel maid to get into rooms and filmed her mother’s last breath in the name of art, but she has no regretsDutch sculptor Magali Reus reimagines rubbish into vast versions of sardine tins and fishing luresA new Magritte exhibition showcases his surrealist brilliance and his occasional trashThe Greek PM has said a deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reachedBeverly Buchanan’s ramshackle mini barns memorialise the survival of enslaved peopleskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRachel Kneebone’s porcelain sculptures are edgy and marvellousMasterpiece of the weekAn Elderly Man as Saint Paul by Rembrandt, probably 1659View image in fullscreenPhotograph: SuperStock/AlamyYou can see he’s wearing archaic garments and has religious trappings that identify him as the early Christian Paul, but all that slips your mind compared with this man’s incredibly real, suffering face. Paul, who set out some of the Church’s most severe views on matters including sexuality, doesn’t usually come across as anything like as doubtful or hesitant as this pensive soul. He is surrounded by the shadows of evening, or night, or death, and in his eyes you see a world of cares and regrets. Rembrandt has no respect for the conventions of art or storytelling that would make this a picture of Paul and allow us to move on after recognising that: instead he wants you to be shocked into recognition of the human predicament. You are held by this face, dragged behind the painting, into the man’s mind or soul or whatever we call the essence of the human. Nothing else, for Rembrandt, is worth making art about.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsTurner prizeAwards and prizesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen
Content: Catherine Corless and Liam Neeson at the Dublin gala screening of The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: GEMC/GMD/BackgridView image in fullscreenCatherine Corless and Liam Neeson at the Dublin gala screening of The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: GEMC/GMD/BackgridMovies‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave filmCatherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screenRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiam Neesonstill remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign byCatherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”View image in fullscreenLiam Neeson, the producer of The Lost Children of Tuam, says he felt a deep sense of obligation to expose the truth.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDbIt prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.The result, nine years later, is The LostChildrenof Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961.View image in fullscreenCatherine Corless at the site of the former mother and baby home in Tuam, County Galway, where it is believed 796 infants were buried.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianAn international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children sincestarting work last year– the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died.It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions acrossIreland. Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it.View image in fullscreenMonica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, in a scene from The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: Element PicturesIn her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.”The film, based on theNew York Times article by Dan Barry, tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished.Early reviewsof the film, which was written byRebecca Lenkiewiczand directed byFrank Berry, say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actorMonica Dolangiving a powerful central performance.View image in fullscreenDirector Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson promote The Lost Children of Tuam in Toronto.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb“She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?”Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said.Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said.View image in fullscreenMonica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, with fellow actor Lalor Roddy, who plays a character called John, in a scene from the film.Photograph: Element Pictures“We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.”Berry, the director, said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.”This article was amended on 25 September 2026. The last image in the article is of Monica Dolan with Lalor Roddy, who plays John, not with Andrew Bennett, who plays Aidan Corless, as an earlier caption said.Explore more on these topicsFilmIrelandLiam NeesonChildrenCatholicismReligionChristianityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list | Prix Goncourt | The Guardian
description: Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media
Content: The author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesPrix GoncourtNovelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listThélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social mediaPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorFri 25 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.View image in fullscreenThe novel on display inside a bookstore in Paris.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersAllegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”View image in fullscreenOrélien at Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque this week.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesThe author of the anonymous X account was lateridentified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaroas one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokeism” on film and TV.On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged caution over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.Libération alleged inan articlethat the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”The Canada-based publisher said it was important not tojump to conclusions, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me,” adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.Explore more on these topicsPrix GoncourtAwards and prizesPlagiarismFictionFranceAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: The comedians turning AI anxiety into punchlines: ‘It’s so good, it’ll completely alter our grasp on reality’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Across videos, standup and cartoons, humorists are skewering big tech’s attempt to make AI ubiquitous and inevitable
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Across videos, standup and cartoons, humorists are skewering big tech’s attempt to make AI ubiquitous and inevitable
Content: ‘[The comedy] effectively punctures tech CEOs’ relentless narrative: that artificial intelligence represents humanity peaking.’Photograph: marwanshaffey/alberta.tech/the_varunrana/theharrisaltermanView image in fullscreen‘[The comedy] effectively punctures tech CEOs’ relentless narrative: that artificial intelligence represents humanity peaking.’Photograph: marwanshaffey/alberta.tech/the_varunrana/theharrisaltermanAI (artificial intelligence)The comedians turning AI anxiety into punchlines: ‘It’s so good, it’ll completely alter our grasp on reality’Across videos, standup and cartoons, humorists are skewering big tech’s attempt to make AI ubiquitous and inevitableMatthew Cantorin Los AngelesFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Best case scenario, we never have to do any admin again,” saysan AI CEO. “Worst case, we all die.”A young manstruggles to the top of a beautiful mountain, words echoing in his ears: “AI will most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there will be great companies created.” At the top of the mountain, he triumphantly holds up a sign: “Build a datacenter here.”On the New York subway, posters herald what appear to be AI startups. “What if forks were spoons?” asks an ad for Cutlery.ai. Another advises viewers that Ziplink is now known as Froggle.The posters are real, but the companies aren’t; the CEO and datacenter scenarios are social media sketches (though the “great companies” quote is agenuine piece of wisdomfrom Sam Altman). It’s all part of a recent wave of comedy inspired – but absolutely not generated – by AI.The comedy extends across all forms of media: social videos,standup,songs,humor columns,comic stripsandart installations. It takes aim at companies’ attempts to make AI ubiquitous, thedangers of believingits every word, its threats to society and the environment. It effectively punctures tech CEOs’ relentless narrative: that artificial intelligence represents humanity peaking; that it is inevitable and all-powerful; that we have no idea where it’s going and it could kill us all, but for some reason it is absolutely essential to pursue.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIt’s no surprise that a topic as pervasive as AI in 2026 would end up in comedians’ crosshairs. A MarchGallup pollfound 79% of Americans believe AI will reduce jobs. In aCNN pollthis week, 81% of respondents said they were more concerned than excited about how the technology could “fundamentally change our way of life”. Only 11% of Americans would support the building of a datacenter locally, according toUMass Amherst. Meanwhile, a handful of impossibly wealthy weirdos wander between podcasts and conference stages boasting about their plans to fundamentally alter what it means to be human.One way to expose the absurdity of the AI companies’ story is by exposing the flaws in their products.Ty Eveland, for instance, trolls AI doctors and HR professionals – the video bots you might awkwardly encounter at a virtual doctor’s appointment or job interview. Asked about marketing, he tells one bot interviewer he takes “everything with a grain of salt and maybe a little bit of pepper”. The bot, portrayed as a generically handsome blond man, responds earnestly: “When you say you take things with a grain of salt and pepper, what does that actually mean for a brand’s social media strategy?”If bots are approaching superintelligence, this one has clearly been left behind.35:15Can you stop AI datacenters? Comedian Charlie Berens thinks so – Stateside with Kai and CarterOther comedians parody the user experience: the comedian Aya Huseen, repeatedly popping out from behind a door,personifiestech companies’ desperate attempts to get users hooked on new AI features: “You sure you don’t want to try it with AI?” “This would be so much funner with AI.” “Just try generating it with AI.” The comedianTom Nestor imagines“how people who love AI think we see them,” telling a friend on the phone: “Do you know what I also really like? It’s not so good now but in years to come it’ll get so good that it’ll just completely alter people’s grasp of reality.” Inthe Atlantic, the humorist Alexandra Petri recounts a dream in which everything in her life has pivoted to AI, from children’s books – Goldilocks and the 4.5 Bears – to her cereal, which features “subtle changes in the recipe, such as the nuts now being the hard, metal kind”.Pro-human comedians have also taken aim at AI’s artistic pretensions. “If you are somebody who uses ChatGPT to generate videos, images, art, text, in an artistic capacity, to write for you, you are not somebody who deserves to be taken seriously,” said the comedian Caleb Hearon in a serious momenton his podcast. Acomic striptitled “AI Design Logic” puts it more succinctly: “Get me a cheese pizza,” a diner tells a waiter. When the pizza arrives, the customer takes credit, exclaiming: “Wow, look what I made!” It’s simple, scathingly effective, and highly meme-able. Even more succinct isa T-shirt wornby the actor Ayo Edebiri: “Do not talk to me about AI. I will kill myself.”double quotation markThe message that I want people to take home is to actually understand what they’re asking AI [and] what the limitations of it areAlberta DevorThe Altmans and Musks of the world may be louder than these comedians, but the collective weight of their jokes provides a counterbalance to the pro-AI declarations. “I would like to think that some of these [companies] are looking at the ridiculousness of where we’re at” and might be swayed by the success and relatability of comedy mocking their products, saysMarwan Shaffey, whose videos include a takedown of a water-guzzling Google in 2026, with its Gemini-generated search resultsthat are more about vibes thanaccuracy. “It does seem like the sentiment is changing, but I think it will take time.”Comedy, of course, can cut through the noise in a way that serious lectures may not. That has been the experience of Alberta Devor, who spent six and a half years as a software engineer at Google. Inone recent video, she offers a cool hack for when someone asks you a tricky question: instead of pulling out your phone and asking AI, it’s actually possible to use the LLM in your brain to produce a response. When a colleague wonders what “EOD” means, she immediately tells him. “How’d you ask Claude that so fast?” he asks. “I trained a model in my head,” she replies. “I just consumed a lot of media, a lot of books.”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueDevor herself is a regular AI user. Still, she’s concerned about overreliance on the products, whether they’re being used to seek information or to code. “The message that I want people to take home is to actually understand what they’re asking AI, to actually understand what the limitations of it are,” she says in an interview. Her serious videos on these topics often meet with some backlash.Comedy, she says, tends to find a more open audience. “It makes people want to engage more, and then you can start to get through to these more complex ideas,” she says. “Like maybe we should be using our brain.”Not all the AI takedowns are themselves digital. The New York subway signs are the brainchildren of two comedians, Harris Alterman and Dave Ross, who designed a campaign mocking the inscrutable – and insufferable – language of bus-stop tech ads and San Francisco billboards.View image in fullscreenA fake tech subway ad by Harris Alterman and Dave Ross.Photograph: Harris Alterman/Harris Alterman and Dave Ross“It was the quickest writing and creative process I’ve ever had,” Ross said. The tech advertising tropes were so clear, and so different from how any human has ever talked, that it was easy to satirize. “We made a big Google Doc of every keyword from all these things – ‘agents’, ‘democratize’ – and then we made 50 frameworks of these ads”: “finally, X that you can Y, or from X to Y in just one Z”. They rearranged and filled in the frameworks, Mad Libs-style, and had them printed.Initially, the concept just seemed funny. “The more I talk about this, and it’s been months now, the more I realize just how disgusted I am with it,” Ross says of the ads’ language, which is “borderline offensive to the human brain”.Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it allRead moreOther comics are equally clear-eyed in their message, and more direct in their advocacy. The British comedian Cody Dahler, condemning “techy tits” such as Palantir CEO Alex Karp, AKA “evil Art Garfunkel”, for creating systems “designed to set fire to everything we value as human beings”, hasdirectly urged followersto speak out.Charlie Behrens of Wisconsinhas led a fight against datacenters in that state. His parody news broadcasts – warning it could soon be “goodbye, America’s dairyland and hello, America’s motherboard” – led to him headlining gatherings of hundreds.Sure, it may be “a little lofty to expect that your comedy could topple a billion-dollar corporation”, as Ross says. But we shouldn’t underestimate the power of comedy wielded en masse. Altman, the human face of ChatGPT, was recentlypresentedwith a clip of Husk,a former landscaperwho recently reached a million followers, asking the bot to time a supposed long-distance run, which it got wildly wrong. Altman appeared sheepish: “It’s a known issue.”Ross doesn’t believe comedians should be seen as philosophers, but it would be “wonderful”, he says, if humor “woke up an understanding in people’s minds that they’re also upset, and drove them toward questioning” our AI future.It’s easy to feel helpless against a tide of supposed robotic inevitability. But each small act of comedy offers permission to question our self-appointed AI overlords – a little win for the humans.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComedyAdvertisingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for the Pogues | The Pogues | The Guardian
description: Ahead of a greatest hits tour, original members Spider Stacy and James Fearnley will join us to answer your questions
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Ahead of a greatest hits tour, original members Spider Stacy and James Fearnley will join us to answer your questions
Content: The Pogues in 1984: Shane MacGowan, James Fearnley, Jem Finer, Andrew Ranken, Spider Stacy and Cait O’Riordan.Photograph: Steve Rapport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Pogues in 1984: Shane MacGowan, James Fearnley, Jem Finer, Andrew Ranken, Spider Stacy and Cait O’Riordan.Photograph: Steve Rapport/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewThe PoguesPost your questions for the PoguesAhead of a greatest hits tour, original members Spider Stacy and James Fearnley will join us to answer your questionsBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 25 Sep 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenShane MacGowandied in 2023, you’d be forgiven for wondering whether the Pogues could carry on, given what a singular frontman he was – and given the band had been dormant since 2014. But grounded by original members James Fearnley, Jem Finer and Spider Stacy, the Pogues have been playing hugely acclaimed reunion gigs in recent years with various guests sitting in for MacGowan – and as they go on a greatest hits tour around the UK this autumn, Fearnley and Stacy will be joining us to answer your questions.The Pogues’ history stretches back to the late 70s when MacGowan, Stacy and Finer played together in London; Fearnley, meanwhile, was a member of MacGowan’s punk band the Nips.The Pogueseventually formed in 1982, investing the traditional music of their Irish heritage with the energy of the city’s punk scene.They released debut album Red Roses for Me in 1984, the following year’s Rum Sodomy & the Lash took them into the UK Top 20, and then 1987 brought Fairytale of New York, their eternally popular Christmas song. The brilliant but wayward MacGowan was eventually fired from the group in 1991, and Joe Strummer stepped in for a time before being replaced by Stacy; the band soldiered on for another couple of albums before splitting in 1996.But while there have been no more studio albums, the Pogues reformed in 2001 and played on and off until 2014. After MacGowan’s death, the richness of the band’s catalogue and the originality of their takes on Irish folk standards was brought into renewed relief; concerts celebrating 40 years since Red Roses for Me were warmly received, with the Guardian’s Patrick Clarke saying in afive-star reviewof a London date: “It could so easily have been a pale imitation, glorified karaoke. And yet, it’s utterly triumphant.”Their greatest hits tour promises a “superlative collection of special guest musicians and singers, among them the cream of the current generation of Irish artists”, and before it kicks off on 28 November, Fearnley and Stacy will answer your questions about the band’s history and future. Post them in the comments below before 4pm BST on Monday 28 September, and their answers will be published later in the week.Explore more on these topicsThe PoguesFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockFolk musicShane MacGowanIrelandcalloutShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have a blowtorch at uni’: what do students eat apart from pesto pasta? | Food | The Guardian
description: Students are too broke or busy having fun to eat well, right? Wrong: some find cash and time for creme brulee and duck eggs
Author: Lauren Bravo
Headline: Students are too broke or busy having fun to eat well, right? Wrong: some find cash and time for creme brulee and duck eggs
Content: Illustration: Tim AlexanderView image in fullscreenIllustration: Tim AlexanderFood‘I have a blowtorch at uni’: what do students eat apart from pesto pasta?Students are too broke or busy having fun to eat well, right? Wrong: some find cash and time for creme brulee and duck eggsLauren BravoFri 25 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis month marks 20 years since I arrived at university in London, with an Ikea saucepan set, a six-pack of Pot Noodle and a trusty jar of pesto to my name. I was a student now, and I intended to eat like one.But what did that mean? Where to my parents “student food” had hippyish connotations – lentils and ancient grains, communal pots of unidentifiable greige – by 2006 the stereotype had evolved to mean convenience and speed. Frozen pizza, potato waffles, mountains of pesto pasta – if we were eating at all, that is. As a 2000s girl with a 2000s diet mentality, I’ll admit that part of me hoped university would mark a turning point where I started having so much fun that I forgot to think about food. No such luck. What followed instead were probably the most formative eating years of my life; I don’t remember a single line of Beowulf, but those early tastes of independence are seared into my memory for ever.Far from swapping food for booze, student nightlife opened doors to new culinary delights: there was a vogue for bars and clubs with barbecues in the yard, or a man in a cloakroom hatch selling McCain Micro Chips for a quid. I discovered that kebabs could taste of fire and adventure, not animal welfare violations. By the end of the first year, all my vintage dresses bore oil stains like medals of honour.My new friends and I invented an official fourth meal of the day:pstub. Short for post-pub, it was coined to name those sacred meals eaten after midnight, which started as street hotdogs and hasty fridge-raids, but soon evolved into feasts more memorable than the nights themselves. Vast trays of crisp nachos, elaborate toasties, curry mopped up with bread stolen from someone else’s cupboard, a 3am roast chicken. Pstub had rules, it had ceremony, it had – oh, brave new world – a thriving Facebook page.There were wholesome habits, too. Brisk Sunday walks across Hampstead Heath, rewarded by soporific pub roasts; enough hummus and falafel to keep an army regular; pick-and-mix sushi from the new breed of chains springing up across the city. “Look at me, Worthing”, I would think, administering my tiny plastic bottle of soy sauce. Eating eel.Having to shop, cook and budget for myself for the first time, I discovered new passions for tinned sardines, fish-finger sandwiches and omelettes zhooshed-up with sweet chilli sauce. Sainsbury’s Basics 8p chicken noodles soon became a staple, so I could save my loan for this newfangled thing called brunch. Meeting other students also expanded my horizons. Before encountering themiddle-middle classes at uni, I’d never eaten real butter, and I didn’t know anyone could make yorkshire puddings exceptAunt Bessie. I learned that what I thought of as a bagels was just bread with a hole in it – nothing like the warm, chewy wonders we’d queue for on east London’s Brick Lane and eat on the back seat of the N253, chunks of salt beef falling into our hair.Food was a way to bridge cultural gaps and forge new friendships. On my first-year corridor alone were students from lands as distant and thrilling as China, Poland, Japan, the Czech Republic and Hull. My nextdoor neighbour, a Hongkonger, and I began a tradition of monthly dinners in Chinatown, where she would order and I wouldn’t ask questions. On her watch I tried tripe, chicken feet, soup dumplings and lilac-huedubetea. I returned the favour by introducing her to Fray Bentos tinned pies.Two decades later, though, what are students eating? Legend would have us believe Gen Z are all matcha-swilling, fibremaxxing wellness nuts who choose sushi over chicken nuggets – does that mean student food culture as we knew it is dead? Is it all poké bowls and functional mushrooms now? Not according to Alex Harvey, founder ofThe Student Food Project, which provides online recipes and runs cookery workshops on campuses across the country. “There’s greater awareness around health and wellness, but I wouldn’t say student eating habits have dramatically shifted off the back of that,” he says. “If they have, it’s only people in a financial position to make that possible.” With fees now three times higher than mine, plus the cost of living about 80% more expensive, today’s undergrads are feeling the pinch more than ever. “Students have always had to budget, but it’s now becoming a constant worry,” says Harvey, who is still gathering results from the project’s Student Food Survey (the first in the UK), but about 40% of respondents so far say they’ve gone to bed hungry or skipped meals because they couldn’t afford food.But that doesn’t mean they can’t afford principles. Since 2021, the climate-focusedPlant-Based Universitiescampaign has seen 29 student unions across the UK and Europe vote to make their campus catering 100% plant-based. Meanwhile, institutions themselves are making an effort to equip students with cooking skills to save them money, keep them healthy and help form social bonds. “We’re increasingly seeing universities doubling down on food as an area of their wellbeing programmes,” says Harvey, who has seen his busiest year yet. “As loneliness and isolation form an increasing part of student life, food has that ability to bring people together.”But while my beloved 8p noodles now cost 50p and my favourite kebab shop was bulldozed for the Elizabeth Line, it’s nice to know some things haven’t changed. “A lot of student staples remain incredibly popular,” says Harvey. “Pesto pasta is still top of the list.View image in fullscreenStudent eating.Illustration: Tim AlexanderFood for thought: what students are really eating‘I might be the only person who has a blowtorch at uni’Aaron Godwood, 20, from Cambridge, is in his third year studyingcomputerscience andmathematics at theUniversity of Bath“I couldn’t really cook before I came to uni. In the weeks before I started, my older brother gave me lessons so I could make a few basic meals: spaghetti bolognese, chilli, fajitas, that kind of thing. But now I’m in my third year, and I’ve discovered I really like cooking. One of my favourite meals to make is gyros, either with chicken or halloumi. I eat a lot of halloumi. There’s a bean and halloumi stew that I make all the time, and, of course, a lot of pasta too. Across my campus, I’d say pesto pasta is probably the most widely eaten dish.“I might be the only person who has a blowtorch at uni. My favourite dessert is creme brulee, and when I tried making it without a blowtorch, it was just terrible. So when I had a bit of money for my birthday, I thought: I know what I’m spending that on.”“One of my housemates is also really into cooking, so we’ll swap recipes and teach each other how to make new dishes. And often we’ll do big group meals where we all contribute a dish. Cooking for other people is one of my favourite things to do; it’s a bit like showing someone a film you really love. It’s introducing them to a little bit of your world.“I’ll get food on a night out maybe twice a week. My mates and I always go to the same kebab shop in Bath, and always get the same order: chips with chilli sauce and garlic mayo.“I try to set a weekly food budget of about £40, but I don’t really stick to it. If I want to cook something nice that costs a bit more, I see it as an activity in itself. I’ll happily spend an extra £5 on ingredients and have fewer drinks in the pub to balance it out.“I don’t consciously think about the health credentials of what I’m eating, but a lot of the food I cook is naturally pretty healthy – a lot of beans, lentils and veg. But I’m glad I’m not a gym bro who only cares about food as fuel. Sometimes you’re out on campus and you’ll see someone whose lunch is a plain chicken breast. That can’t be nice.”View image in fullscreenStudent eating.Illustration: Tim Alexander‘It’s a lot of toast, a lot of cereal’Archie Marks, 20, from Worcester, is in his final year studying Englishliterature attheUniversity of Birmingham“I love an Aldi pizza. Pesto pasta has always been a mainstay for me, or just pasta with oil and cheese, and I quite like a stir-fry, because it’s easy. But that’s it for cooking, if I’m honest. It’s a lot of toast, a lot of cereal.“I try to budget for about £30-35 per week on groceries, and get a takeaway or eat out maybe once a week. Post-night out, we always go to Mamma Mia, which is a local institution. It’s one of those takeaways that sells a bit of everything – it does the best pizza I’ve ever tasted, and for about a fiver. It’s so trashy, but when you’ve had a few it’s an absolute godsend.View image in fullscreenArchie Marks: ‘I love an Aldi pizza!’Photograph: Archie Marks/The Guardian“I think money is on the mind of every student. I’m not exactly living off scraps – I buy strawberries out of season and stuff like that – but I don’t go crazy. I spend a lot of money on concert tickets, so often I’ll just live off whatever I have in the cupboard to afford them. Recently I went to see Harry Styles, which was worth a few weeks of beans on toast.“I’ve been vegetarian for five or six years, and my parents instilled in me the value of good nutrition and getting my five a day, so that’s kind of second nature. But the idea of Gen Z as clean-eating wellness types could not be further from the truth. It’s a lot of faff, and it can get really expensive. Sometimes I’ll be at pre-drinks and we’ll play a game of: ‘what has everyone eaten today?’, and I’ll realise I’ve had two slices of toast and an apple.“But two things can be true at once. Budget is a big factor for students, but by the same token there is a lot of going out for coffee, going for sushi, splurging on food every once in a while. It’s something to get you through, isn’t it?”‘For lunch I’d have avocado toast with a boiled duck egg’Hannah Austin, 20, from Wellingborough, is in her third year studyinggamesart atNottingham Trent University“In my first year, I put less time into cooking than I do now, but I did a lot of meal prepping. Usually for breakfast I’d make a dairy-free yoghurt bowl, then for lunch I’d have avocado toast with a boiled duck egg, or a cheese and tomato toastie with plant-based ‘bacon’ on the side. For dinner I’d typically make a veggie gyro bowl using oyster mushrooms as a meat substitute, some sort of pasta, or if I really couldn’t be bothered, noodles. I am definitely more adventurous now in terms of what I make, and it’s something different every day.“During the day I prefer quick things – I almost always have a sandwich of some sort (smoked salmon and cream cheese bagel, say, or a caprese sandwich) for lunch. I go through a lot of pesto, basil, rocket, prawns and salad veg; they’re my favourite ingredients. Buying fish in supermarkets gets expensive, so I found a well-priced fishmonger nearby.View image in fullscreenHannah Austin: ‘Price is important to me, but I care about quality more.’Photograph: Michael Davis/The Guardian“I wouldn’t describe myself as a foodie, but it depends on who you ask. My friends would tell you that I’m always cooking something a bit extravagant (by student standards). In my first year, one of my flatmates would eat plain pork chops every single day for dinner. I cooked him chicken wings one night and he loved them, so I taught him how to make them and let him use my seasonings.“I’m usually quite good at sticking to my food budget of £40 per week. Most of my friends spend less, but I have food allergies, which mean I have to buy more expensive alternatives. I definitely need to adjust my budget, though – my most recent food shop had gone up by £7, despite buying all the same things. Price is important to me, but I care about quality more. I don’t really travel, and I don’t go on nights out, so I save a lot of money that would otherwise be spent on drinks.“I’d say uni has positively influenced my eating. I get very lazy when I’m at home. But there’s not much I’ve picked up from living with others, except red pesto. It’s good, but I still prefer green.”Explore more on these topicsFoodStudentsHigher educationPastaPizzaNoodlesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: a brain surgeon dropped part of my skull on the floor | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I was a healthy 34-year-old when a mass of blood vessels ruptured in my brain. It took three neurosurgeons and a risky 16-hour operation to fix me
Author: Amy Swales
Headline: I was a healthy 34-year-old when a mass of blood vessels ruptured in my brain. It took three neurosurgeons and a risky 16-hour operation to fix me
Content: ‘I’ve never felt sorry for myself’: Tom Park-Paul, with his dog Binks, near his home in West Yorkshire.Photograph: Rebecca Lupton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ve never felt sorry for myself’: Tom Park-Paul, with his dog Binks, near his home in West Yorkshire.Photograph: Rebecca Lupton/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: a brain surgeon dropped part of my skull on the floorI was a healthy 34-year-old when a mass of blood vessels ruptured in my brain. It took three neurosurgeons and a risky 16-hour operation to fix meTom Park-PaulFri 25 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a Sunday in May 2017, I was at the gym and using a chest press when there was this pop. It wasn’t a sound – it was more like a sigh in my body. There was no pain, but I went limp. I shuffled along the wall to some mats. I thought I was having a stroke, but I wasn’t slurring and my eyes and arms seemed fine. But my left leg felt numb – it was the weirdest feeling. Lying on my back with my legs bent, both knees stayed upright when I looked at them. When I looked away, the left one fell to the side.I ended up in A&E for hours at nearby St Thomas’ hospital in London. I was 34, healthy and had started regaining feeling in my leg, so they theorised it was a bruised spine and thought it was safe to discharge me. Overworked staff and shift changes meant that when MRI images of my brain went missing, nobody tracked them down.At a follow-up appointment days later, my partner, Luke, argued with the consultant. I was still struggling to walk, and assuming I’d had a stroke caused by a blood clot, the consultant wanted to prescribe a high-dose blood thinner. However, Luke – an ICU nurse at the time – demanded a scan.He saved my life. I returned from a CT scan to find the consultant looking pale: they had found a massive bleed on my brain and were sending me to specialists at King’s College hospital. Blood thinners might have killed me.View image in fullscreenTom Park-Paul after the surgery.Photograph: Tom GremlinTests confirmed an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) – a mass of tangled blood vessels – had ruptured close to the part of the brain that controls motor function in my limbs, causing a stroke. The consultant neurosurgeon and AVM expert rated it 4 out of 6 on the Spetzler-Martin grading system, which measures complexity, location and size.double quotation markThe surgeons considered 3D-printing a replacement and putting the skull back in months later, but instead cleaned itGrade 4 is typically considered too risky to remove. But I was young; he said if I was game, he was, too. Without surgery, there was the risk of another serious bleed.The operation required three neurosurgeons plus supporting teams of anaesthetists and nurses, so it couldn’t happen until July. Those weeks of waiting were hard. My limp disappeared, but knowing the AVM could pop again was terrifying.The surgery lasted more than 16 hours, and afterwards Luke was called and told it had gone well. However, the doctor sheepishly added: “There’s something we have to declare. We’re really sorry, but we dropped his skull.”Right at the end, the piece they had taken out got knocked to the floor. Infection was the concern, so they considered 3D-printing a replacement and putting it in months later, but instead cleaned it and dosed me up with extra antibiotics.I found out days later, when I was woken from my induced coma. But it meant nothing to me because I was on so many drugs, hallucinating visions and crying uncontrollably whenever I was happy or thankful.I didn’t care. Even now, I find it hilarious that my skull has been on the floor. I love to imagine them picking it up, dusting it off, and saying, “Five-second rule!” The surgeons had pulled about 100 metres of blood vessels out of me for 16 hours. They were exhausted. And they fixed me.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘I love to imagine them picking up the bit of skull, dusting it off, and saying, “Five-second rule!”’Photograph: Rebecca Lupton/The GuardianRecovery wasn’t easy. Relearning how to walk was horrible, and I was exhausted for months. For a long time, whenever I tilted my head I could hear brain fluid gurgling. I still have loss of proprioception in my left foot – without looking directly at it, I can’t control it, so I can’t drive manual cars.Experience: I fell 12 metres and smashed my pelvis into piecesRead moreI’ve never felt sorry for myself, because I’m just so grateful. It brought Luke and me closer: we got engaged weeks after surgery and married in 2021.I later learned that, once in surgery, they discovered the AVM was bigger and more complex than first thought. The consultant neurosurgeon now uses my case as evidence that larger AVMs can be removed successfully.While recuperating, I came across a study that said survivors of life-threatening situations are some of the happiest people. I feel that deeply. You couldn’t design a better life-changing experience. Skull-drop included.As told to Amy SwalesDo you have an experience to share?
