title: From chunky knits to go-anywhere boots: 52 women’s autumn wardrobe updates (some are even free) | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Forget a head-to-toe overhaul. Whether it’s swapping loafers for lace-ups or mixing your metals, try these styling tweaks to give your look a fresh seasonal spin
Author: Melanie Wilkinson
Headline: Forget a head-to-toe overhaul. Whether it’s swapping loafers for lace-ups or mixing your metals, try these styling tweaks to give your look a fresh seasonal spin
Content: Composite: Edward Berthelot/Getty Images, Christian Vierig/Getty Images, Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Edward Berthelot/Getty Images, Christian Vierig/Getty Images, Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFashionFrom chunky knits to go-anywhere boots: 52 women’s autumn wardrobe updates (some are even free)Forget a head-to-toe overhaul. Whether it’s swapping loafers for lace-ups or mixing your metals, try these styling tweaks to give your look a fresh seasonal spinDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereMelanie Wilkinson, introduction byJess Cartner-MorleyFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou know what I always think looks really chic? When someone is dressed timelessly, but with just one element that brings the outfit bang up to date. A look that is 90% personal style, 10% zeitgeist. That is such a good formula.Being head-to-toe in new trends is not cool these days. It can look a little overeager, and your clothes end up wearing you rather than the other way around. But a look that plays it completely classic can feel a little safe.What works is when you see someone who has hit the sweet spot: clothes that radiate personality and confidence, but with a little something extra that lets the world know they are alive to the current moment. That is the person in the room I want to go and chat to.So, most of your new autumn look is simple: you do you. All you need is one or two updates. Like swapping your loafers for a lace-up. Swapping your oversized blazer for a more fitted silhouette. Try a different pair of glasses. It could be as simple as a coloured sock, or a string of beads added to your necklace stack. Or a no-shopping-required styling update: a low ponytail is the new slicked-back bun. The point isn’t to change your look, just to make it shine. All you need is a fresh idea or two – and we’ve got 52 for you right here.Women’s wardrobe updates for autumnA funnel-collar jacket (with a formal twist)These technical-looking jackets are set to be what the quilted jacket was to 2025, ie, spotted in every train carriage for the foreseeable. They work well with slimline black trousers and kitten heels to offset the sportiness.View image in fullscreen& Other Stories jacket£119 at & Other Stories£119 at AsosThe barelythere silky blouseA romantic blouse is perfect for those evenings when all you want to wear is jeans and a nice top.View image in fullscreenAnthropologie satin blouse£98 at Anthropologie£98 at NextFocus on the collarView image in fullscreenStick your neck out with a dash of colour, and layers, around the collar.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesIt’s the centre of attention this season. Aim for layering with pops of colour – eg, a red rollneck under a blue shirt, under a navy jumper. Or double up on a polo shirt. Sounds weird. Looks good.Cool pyjamasIf a long-sleeved PJ set leaves you hot and restricted, then these cotton trousers paired with a vest are the perfect jewel-coloured alternative.View image in fullscreenChelsea Peers stripe pyjama set£58 at Chelsea Peers£58 at John LewisEmbrace the high-lowView image in fullscreenMix not match: fashion editor and blogger Tamu McPherson selecting striking combinations.Photograph: Christian Vierig/Getty ImagesA parka with a pretty slip dress, a smart wool coat with tracksuit bottoms … sometimes combinations that sound wrong on paper look best in real life.A funnel-neck dressThe season’s favourite neckline as seen on a chic midi dress – this would look great with a blazer and knee-high boots.View image in fullscreenNobody’s Child jersey dress£79 at Nobody’s ChildAchunkycardieIf your body temperature is set to changeable and you need an easy layer to throw on and off, opt for a chunky cardigan. Finisterre’s Mora crewneck is made of 100% fine merino wool, so it is naturally breathable.View image in fullscreenFinisterre cardigan£135 at FinisterreFlowery underwearNew season, new pants. These ditsy floral designs are fun, colourful and will jazz up the most boring bra.View image in fullscreenStripe& Stare knickers, four pack£50 at Stripe & StareSky-blue knitwearMake this two-tone blue melange jumper a new cosy favourite. The fresh shade is cheering and will still work with all your neutrals.View image in fullscreenCos cashmere jumper£249 at CosOpt for barrel-leg leatherLeather trousers can be intimidating, but a barrel-leg shape makes them a bit more casual, which in turn makes them a tad easier to wear.View image in fullscreenM&S faux leather trousers£36 at M&SThe 1990s jeanBritish shirting powerhouse With Nothing Underneath has pivoted to denim. I love this Crawford high-waisted straight-leg style. It hits your ankle in just the right place to wear with flat shoes.View image in fullscreenWith Nothing Underneath jeans£150 at With Nothing UnderneathA prom-style corsageMatthieu Blazy’s clever design details at Chanel are beginning to influence the high street. Get ahead of the curve by pinning a fabric flower corsage to your favourite blazer or dress.View image in fullscreenFlower corsageFrom £26.95 at V V RouleauxChic ballet flatsIf it still feels a bit early to be rummaging around in your sock drawer, put the idea of boots on the backburner and swap your summer slides for a leather pump. The almond cut of this pair is particularly flattering.View image in fullscreenNext flat shoes£46 at NextDitch theLabubuBag charms are getting a bit more grownup. Think sleek and silver rather than novelty. This design is based on a meditative mandala.View image in fullscreenBag charm£39 at LiffnerMix up your glassesA fresh pair of spectacles is an easy way to update your look. The autumn colourway is less harsh than black, and the aviator shape is a classic.View image in fullscreenBlack Eyewear glasses£197 at Black EyewearLook for lace-upsYou heard it here first: lace-ups are the new loafer. A derby shoe is a great choice if a brogue feels a bit formal. They’re a bit chunkier, so will give you a tad more room between the sole of your shoe and the bottom of your trousers. Useful in the rain.View image in fullscreenTommy Hilfiger shoes£140 at Tommy Hilfiger£140 at AsosMix your metalsLove both gold and silver jewellery? There’s no need to pick a side. Break the outdated fashion rule by mixing them instead.View image in fullscreenGold and silver bangle£295 at Astley Clarke£295 at SelfridgesChunky hoopsThe red and gold two-tone effect will glimmer under candlelight. Makes cosy suppers even more enticing.View image in fullscreenWhistles two-tone earrings£28 at WhistlesDip a toe into the heel trendAfter a few years of purely flat shoes, we’re starting to creep back into heel territory. If anything over about an inch and a half feels like madness, ease yourself in with a ballet-style block heel. It’s just a pump with a bit of lift. Honestly.View image in fullscreenH&M slingback heels£27.99 at H&MChunky red socksThe British brand Aries does excellent socks (alongside sweatshirts and tees), often with a fun twist. These burgundy towelling ones will add impact to trainers and clogs.View image in fullscreenAries socks£19 at Slam Jam£22 at AriesA clip-onAirPodspouchThis will add a little fun to your trusty shoulder bag. Clip it to the base of your handbag strap, and you will never have to rummage around for your headphones again.View image in fullscreenAnya Hindmarch eyes earphones case£95 at Anya Hindmarch£95 at John LewisPair sparkly socks with slingbacksWe all know how much a bright sock can enliven a boring loafer. But have you tried wearing a party sock with a basic slingback? It’s like a whole new shoe for less than a tenner. Look for glittery socks, or ones like these with tiny pearls.View image in fullscreenM&S embellished socks£6 at M&SThe modern broochDesigners including Giorgio Armani and Tory Burch championed brooches on this season’s catwalks. Add your own finishing touch with a pebble-shape version. A sculptural design feels less fusty and more fashion.View image in fullscreenUO pebble brooch£12 at Urban OutfittersA rope necklaceTake jewellery inspiration from the Celine catwalk with its shells, cord and gold trinkets. Layer this over your current necklace stack for a similar effect.View image in fullscreenMassimo Dutti necklace£50 at Massimo DuttiA bright notebookLean into the back-to-school feeling with fresh stationery. A vivid notebook is easier to spot at the bottom of a bag.View image in fullscreenSmythson notebook£75 at SmythsonAn investment buyThere’s something so versatile about a leather bomber jacket. Wear it open, closed, with wide-leg trousers, even over a glitzy party dress. It’s a splurge, yes, but we’re in this for the long haul, and it will only look better with age.View image in fullscreenLeather bomber jacketskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£449 at ArketKeep it looseComfort doesn’t have to mean casual. Ease yourself back into the idea of a waistband with a pair of relaxed wool and linen mix trousers. They look smart with a knit, too.View image in fullscreenComfortable trousers£165 at the White CompanyColour block your lookView image in fullscreenBlock party: try styling strong, vibrant colours together.Photograph: 305pics/Getty ImagesFollow Mugler and Marc Jacobs’ lead and style bold, bright colours together. Try a purple skirt with a pink top, or chartreuse with bright blue.Roll up, roll upView image in fullscreenSleeve notes: turn up coat cuffs to show off the top that lies underneath.Photograph: Raimonda Kulikauskienė/WireImageAdd an extra point of interest by rolling up the cuffs of your coat so the cuffs of a shirt or long-sleeved dress peek out from underneath.The school tripwindcheaterLightweight and water-repellent, but with a warm fleece lining, this nostalgically 90s windbreaker will even scrunch up pretty small so you can pop it in a tote bag.View image in fullscreenUniqlo fleece-lined blouson£49.90 at UniqloWear purpleIf there’s one colour to lean into now, it’s regal purple. Ease yourself in by pairing it with blacks and browns, or go full maximalist by clashing it with red and yellow.View image in fullscreenBoden cashmere v-neck£129 at Boden£129 at NextA cream sweatshirtTorn between a sweatshirt or a chunky knit? Do you want to feel pulled together or comfy casual? This knitted sweatshirt in a gorgeous buttery shade is going to make those decisions on an autumnal morning obsolete.View image in fullscreenJigsaw sweatshirt£139 at Jigsaw£139 at M&SLayer your LBDSheer is here to stay this season, and you can still make it work without flashing your underwear. Wear this LBD over a slightly shorter black slip, or style it over trousers.View image in fullscreenSusamusa sheer dress£175 at Susamusa£175 at LibertyCount the ways with a silk scarfOver the past year, we have been tying silk scarves to bags, knotting them round our necks and wearing them as belts. title: Cocktail of the week: Eleanore’s apple highball – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A classy autumnal aperitif with a pleasingly bitter zing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A classy autumnal aperitif with a pleasingly bitter zing
Content: Eleanore’s apple highball.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenEleanore’s apple highball.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Eleanore’s apple highball – recipeA classy autumnal aperitif with a pleasingly bitter zingJohanna ColeFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI adore calvados, and this highball was built off the back of a love for calvados and tonic. This refreshing aperitif expands on that idea andfeels really quite sophisticated in comparison.Apple highballServes1For the apple syrup250g eating apples, washed – we use braeburns250g caster sugarFor the drink25ml calvados– we useAvallen20ml Lillet Blanc15ml apple syrup(see above and method)15ml freshlemon juice1 dash orange bitters– we useRegans’1 dash champagne, to taste1 dash tonic water, to taste1 twist lemon zest, to finishFirst make the syrup. Dice the apples, core, peel and all, put them in a saucepan, and add the sugar and 100ml water. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring, for about 10 minutes, until the apples are soft and the sugar has dissolved. Fine strain into a clean jar, seal and store in the fridge, where the syrup will keep for up to four weeks (it’s also lovely diluted with sparkling water).To build the drink, put all the liquids bar the champagne and tonic into a cocktail tin filled with ice and give it a short shake. Strain into a small chilled highball glass filled with fresh ice and top with a dash each of champagne and tonic.Give it a quick stir, squeeze the lemon zest over the top, to express the oils (if you like, drop it into the drink afterwards), and serve.Johanna Cole, general manager,Eleanore, EdinburghExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodFruitAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for Belgian buns  | Cake | The Guardian
description: These old-school classic treats may struggle for attention among today’s more Instagram-worthy cardamon buns, but they’re simple to make and divine to devour
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: These old-school classic treats may struggle for attention among today’s more Instagram-worthy cardamon buns, but they’re simple to make and divine to devour
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s Belgian bunsPhotograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s Belgian bunsPhotograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotCakeBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for Belgian bunsThese old-school classic treats may struggle for attention among today’s more Instagram-worthy cardamon buns, but they’re simple to make and divine to devourBenjamina EbuehiFri 25 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBelgian buns are among a dying breed of bakes, forgotten about in favour of pretty cinnamon and cardamom buns and creative laminated doughs. I’d love to see more of these old-school, classic treats in bakeries, not least because they’re really simple to make. There are no twists or extra frills, just soft, buttery dough swirled with lemon curd and juicy sultanas. The icing glaze and cherry on top are essential, though, for maximum eating pleasure.Belgian bunsPrep5 minProve2 hr 30 min+Cook1 hr 15 minMakes8320g strong white bread flour,plus extra for dusting40g castersugar1½ tsp instant yeast¼ tsp fine sea salt100ml milk, warmed50ml water2 large eggs, 1 beaten for the egg washZest of 1 lemon40g unsalted butter, softened3-4 tbsp lemon curd70g sultanasFor the glaze120g icing sugar1-2 tbsp water8 glacé cherriesPut the flour, sugar, yeast and salt in a large bowl or stand mixer, and mix briefly to combine. pour in the milk, water, one egg, and the lemon zest, and stir until the mixture comes together into a shaggy dough. Knead by hand for eight to 10 minutes (or in a stand mixer for about five minutes), until you have a soft dough, then leave to rest uncovered for five minutes.Pat the dough flat on a lightly floured work surface and smush the butter all over the top. Fold the dough over itself, then knead again; it’s a messy job, but use a dough scraper to scrape the surface often and it will eventually all come together. Once the butter is completely incorporated and the dough looks silky and shiny, put it in a lightly greased bowl, cover and leave to prove in a warm place for two to three hours, until puffy and nearly doubled in size.Knock the air out of the dough, then tip it out on to a lightly floured work surface. Roll it out to a roughly 35cm x 25cm rectangle, then spoon the lemon curd on top and spread it out evenly. Sprinkle the sultanas all over.Starting from one long side, roll the dough into a log and put it seam-side down on a work surface. Use a sharp, serrated knife to slice the log into eight pieces, then arrange these on a large, lined baking tray. Cover loosely with clingfilm and prove again for 25-35 minutes, until puffy.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Brush the tops and sides of the buns with a little egg wash, then bake for 10 minutes. Turn down the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and bake for another 10-15 minutes, until the buns are golden brown. Remove and leave to cool while you make the icing.Put the icing sugar in a bowl and stir in the water a tablespoon at a time, until it’s a thick but pourable consistency. Spoon a dollop of icing on to each bun, letting it fall into the folds, then top with a cherry. Leave the icing to set before eating.Explore more on these topicsCakeThe sweet spotFoodBakingSnacksDessertFruitEggsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The lure of the loo: how restaurant bathroom design went wild | Food | The Guardian
description: Restaurants are giving their bathrooms a makeover: plush or pared back, flatteringly lit or full-on disco camp, a TikTokkable loo is now part of the hospitality experience
Author: Jimi Famurewa
Headline: Restaurants are giving their bathrooms a makeover: plush or pared back, flatteringly lit or full-on disco camp, a TikTokkable loo is now part of the hospitality experience
Content: The OTT-opulent bathrooms at Bacchanalia restaurant in London’s Mayfair.Photograph: Johnny StephensView image in fullscreenThe OTT-opulent bathrooms at Bacchanalia restaurant in London’s Mayfair.Photograph: Johnny StephensFoodThe lure of the loo: how restaurant bathroom design went wildPlush or pared back, flatteringly lit or full-on disco camp, a TikTokkable loo is now part of the hospitality experienceJimi FamurewaFri 25 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Bourdain was typically forthright when it came to his expectations for the toilet facilities in a food business. “I won’t eat in a restaurant with filthy bathrooms,” wrote the late chef and author, in his seminal, turn-of-the-millennium memoir Kitchen Confidential. “This isn’t a hard call. They let youseethe bathrooms. If the restaurant can’t be bothered to replace the puck in the urinal or keep the toilets and floors clean, then just imagine what their refrigeration and work spaces look like.” Setting aside the fact that, in later life, Bourdain softened his stance (“Some of the best food experiences I’ve ever had [have been in] places where they really don’t give a shit [about bathroom cleanliness],” were his words in a 2018 interview) his initial take tells us plenty about what the average customer historically demanded of restaurant restrooms. They needed to be clean. They needed to be functional. They needed, at a push, half-decent hand soap and the faint, reassuring waft of pine-scented floor cleaner.View image in fullscreenThe futuristic egg-pods at Mayfair brasserie-cum-gallery Sketch.Today, things could hardly be more different. Where once restaurant toilets tended to be a boring, unglamorous afterthought, in recent years, they have emerged as arguably the most unexpectedly attention-grabbing room in the building: atmospherically distinct sites of creativity and muscle-flexing design, where lavish amenities, bespoke lighting, custom soundscapes, selfie mirrors and all manner of other eye-catching flourishes abound, and are documented by social media channels, such as@LoosOfLondon(TikTok followers: 78k).Nip off to spend a penny at Michelin-starredTimberyardin Edinburgh and you’ll be plunged into an atmospherically shadowy space, soundtracked by the discordant pops and burbles of grapes fermenting. Do the same at Oxford’s south-Indian spotDosa Darlingsor Soho’s neo-trattoriaOsteria Vibratoand you’ll hear, respectively, Stephen Fry’s booming narration of the Harry Potter audiobooks and the swelling sound of opera. The practice of rigging lavatories with a disco soundtrack and flashing lights activated by a button – as seen atBarbara’s Bier Hausin Birmingham, plus outposts of Bavarian cabaret barAlbert’s Schloss– is so commonplace that it has almost become a cliche. From palatial TikTok-bait boudoirs (see the sprawling, uplit powder rooms in Mayfair’sBacchanalia) and horror-themed mini cinemas (MeatLiquor spin-offBloodSportsin London’s Covent Garden) to the unexplained shrine to former basketball player Dennis Rodman (there is genuinely one of these in London haute rotisserie jointStory Cellar), the world of modern restaurant bathrooms is in the grip of an unlikely, ever-intensifying arms race waged with luxury mouthwash dispensers, avant garde music, and soft-lit mirrors that are so flattering they might as well be enchanted. So how did we get here? And how far is too far, when it comes to turning these functional ablution chambers into noisy Instagram backdrops or giant art installations?View image in fullscreenLilibet’s washrooms are ‘gilded, azure-hued and inspired by the young Queen Elizabeth’s love of decorative china’.Naturally, social media has had a huge impact, pioneering toilet interiors – particularly the futuristic egg-pods at Mayfair brasserie-cum-gallerySketch– showing other operators how to turn a utilitarian amenity into a canny, digital age attraction. Yet, beyond all the hastily installed flower walls and neon signs, there is another significant factor. Namely, a post-Covid, industry-wide shift towards dining spaces that are more immersive, memorable and unapologetically atmosphere-forward.“We’ve become fascinated with the tiny details that add up to make a difference in a restaurant,” says Jo Radford, head sommelier and co-founder at Timberyard, and creator of its viniculture-themed bathrooms. “The amount of time that a guest is in the building with food in front of them is quite a small portion of their overall time with us, so we were looking at all those other touch points and how we could elevate things.” The result was the unexpected onslaught of scent, purposefully impeded sight (“environmental health told us that the lights might be so low that it wasn’t safe,” adds Radford with a sheepish chuckle) and sound that acts as both talking point and nudging link to the earthy seriousness of Timberyard’s wine programme. But the use of a wash of loud, discordant noises also serves another function. “It definitely helps in terms of audio privacy, ” he notes, highlighting the fact that a lot of these loud, characterful soundtrack choices often act as a kind of sonic veil against some of the grimmer realities of shared lavatories.More generally, the seclusion and privacy afforded by toilet facilities – plus the access flex of a selfie from within a hot new opening – is something that restaurant interior designers and operators are identifying, leaning into and playing with. “The bathroom is a little space where you can take time to look after yourself and maybe muck around and have an Instagram moment,” says hospitality designer Russell Sage, a more than 20-year veteran of the industry with clients including Gordon Ramsay and Angela Hartnett. “It’s increasingly become about giving people their own time, getting the lighting right, and making sure they feel a million quid by the time they step back into the restaurant.”Nowhere is this more true than atLilibet’s, a maximalist seafood restaurant in Mayfair that Sage worked on ahead of its opening late last year. Beyond the fact that its gilded, azure-hued restrooms are inspired by the young Queen Elizabeth II’s love of decorative china (a whole new kind of “royal flush”), they also feature mirrors that are lengthening and slimming. “There have definitely been enquiries from people about whether they can buy one from us,” says Sage. “We just thought, people want to look fabulous, so let’s make a mirror that guarantees you look even more fabulous.”View image in fullscreenHold my martini: Ellie’s Bar’s bathroom.Expensively wrought trick mirrors, opulent miniature spas and panoramic “loos with a view” like the ones atop20 Storiesin Manchester, many of the restrooms in this new wave default to the luxurious, but it’s notable that even smaller, scrappier businesses are getting in on the act. Cal McRae, owner of Zillennial-coded Dalston barEllie’s, had already been experimenting with time-sensitive crimson lighting and video installation, when he noticed an issue with one of the bar’s signature, budget-friendly cocktails. “We had these beautiful martini glasses that cost £7, the martinis themselves were £8, and by the end of the weekend the majority of these expensive glasses would be smashed all over the toilet floor,” he explains. “I was adamant that [we not use cheaper glasses] and that it was worth the cost, but by the end it was like, this is so stupid.” The solution was to build a custom martini-holder rack into the area above the sink; a feature that not only helped preserve Ellie’s glassware but became a much-photographed encapsulation of its dishevelled cool, written up in international publications like the hugely influential New York culture SubstackFeed Me. “I was absolutely buzzing off the back of that,” says McRae. “And it was nice to find this practical solution to a problem, that was interesting from a design point of view and became a bit of a talking point.”That Ellie’s viral martini-holders were needed in the first place reminds us of one of the abiding realities of toilets in restaurants and bars: they are often magnets for illicit behaviour, drunken damage, petty theft and other miscellaneous forms of unobserved wildness. “We’ve had someone rip off all the framing around the sink. And in the first week I heard about two people having sex in there which, honestly, is a massive achievement for a bar owner,” says McRae, laughing. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this tendency towards chaos and the basic importance of lavatories have caused some problems for this new generation of immersive facilities. Late last year, the Manchester branch of bougie steakhouse chainThe Cut and Craftimplemented a five minute time-limit on their Instagrammable toilets; this spring, veteran restaurateur Jeremy King revealed he’d had to ban filming and hire extra security at his Bayswater grand cafe,The Park, because of the number of influencers arriving with suitcases, tripods and sound systems for prolonged video shoots in the handsome, honey-toned restrooms. Even something as pointedly mischievous as the screamingly camp disco loos in branches of Albert’s Schloss – with two adjacent toilets in the ladies with a big “push for disco” button beside them – has needed occasional policing. “Now and again, we’ll get four girls going in there with a bottle of prosecco and there’ll be a big queue after 20 minutes,” says James Plant, head of openings and innovations at Albert’s Schloss. “So we make sure we have toilet attendants, to give them a gentle knock and a nudge.”Yes, these “influencer bans” often become a handy bit of additional publicity for the restaurant, but does the need for them also show us that the trend for ostentatious loos and logo-embossed selfie mirrors in restaurants and bars may already be circling the drain? McRae, founder of a bar so cool it was the venue for Charli xcx’s wedding party, certainly thinks so. “I hate the idea of putting a bar or restaurant name on a mirror,” he says. “I understand that a lot of people that come in might put [a photo] on Instagram, and that can help build a following. But it just feels so forced.”View image in fullscreenThe ‘screamingly camp disco loos’ at Albert’s Schloss, Liverpool.Conversely, Sage believes that the kind of amplified, TikTok-ready bathroom aesthetic he employed in Lilibet’s will only become more commonplace. “It’s the world that we’re in now,” he says. “Going to a restaurant is not a cheap business, so we owe it to people to give them a good experience, turn up the volume and really put on a show. Ten or 15 years ago it was all about exposed brick and how dreary we could make everything look. I loved it at the time, but we’re now in an era where people are in search of a little bit of glamour, fun and enjoyment.”The truth probably lies somewhere in the middle. Even if there is an active retreat from disco lights, selfie mirrors and some of the more gimmicky plays for virality that have dominated the world of restaurant bathrooms in recent years, we’ve passed a point of no return when it comes to bathroom design. Plush or pointedly stripped back; flatteringly illuminated or cast in a sexy, candlelit gloom; fitted with a Bond villain-worthy tank of live piranhas (as at Nikkei-themed Mayfair spotPirana), or ornamented with nothing more than stacked pyramids of loo paper. Even a quieter aesthetic choice is still an aesthetic choice. And in an economically pressured era when hospitality businesses have to use every marketing tool at their disposal, a bathroom that has to be experienced to be believed is both added value and a kind of irresistible, dangled lure.“We want to give people a stolen moment,” says Radford. “There’s nothing like seeing one of our guests returning from the bathroom, turning to the rest of the table and saying: ‘You need to go downstairs and experience that.’” Expect to see more and more restaurateurs continuing to turn their own facilities into the kind of miniature worlds that spark this level of unexpected ardour and intrigue. And if your dining companion suddenly disappears mid-meal for a prolonged toilet break – well, it’s no longer guaranteed that it’s a bad sign.Explore more on these topicsFoodRestaurantsHospitality industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Capital gains tax: how it works, and the pros and cons of another rise | Capital gains tax | The Guardian
description: Increasing the rate of CGT is one of the levers available to the chancellor as he considers revenue-raising options
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Increasing the rate of CGT is one of the levers available to the chancellor as he considers revenue-raising options
Content: Recent data from HMRC showed revenue from CGT was up 89% in 2024-25 after changes in tax policy.Photograph: Mykhailo Polenok/AlamyView image in fullscreenRecent data from HMRC showed revenue from CGT was up 89% in 2024-25 after changes in tax policy.Photograph: Mykhailo Polenok/AlamyCapital gains taxExplainerCapital gains tax: how it works, and the pros and cons of another riseIncreasing the rate of CGT is one of the levers available to the chancellor as he considers revenue-raising optionsHeather StewartEconomics editorFri 25 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCapital gains tax (CGT) has been widely cited as a possible revenue-raiser as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to deliver a tough budget next month. How does it work, and what are the pros and cons of raising it further?What is CGT?When you sell an asset – whether it’s a share, a business, or a buy-to-let property – you pay capital gainson the uplift in its value since you bought it.It’s not quite that simple: you can reduce your CGT bill by deducting losses made on other investments, and the costs of investing in improving a property. But essentially, it’s a tax on the profits realised when an asset is sold.The rate of CGT is now 18% for basic-rate taxpayers and 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. There’s an even higher rate, of 32%, for City fund managers who take their earnings as a share of profits in a controversial system called “carried interest”.All those rates have gone up significantly since Labour came to power in 2024, as Rachel Reeves, the previous chancellor, chose to tax wealth more heavily – the basic rate was previously 10%, for example.Recent data from HMRC showed the take from CGT was up 89% in 2024-25 as a result of these and other changes, which have also included cuts to the tax-free personal allowance for CGT, begun under the last Conservative government.Who is calling for CGT to rise?Thinktanks and politicians across the lefthave argued that it is unfair to tax the gains from holding an asset at a lower rate than a salary that has been earned by working. (The basic rate of income tax is 20%, for example.)Another argument – advanced by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) – is that it distorts behaviour: incentivising people to hold on to assets inside a business, for example.Back in May, when Wes Streeting had his eye on the Labour leadership, he called CGT“the wealth tax that works” – in contrast with the prospect of setting up an entirely new tax.Given Streeting’s position towards the right of the Labour party, his backing for higher rates of the key tax underlined how widespread the view is within the party.The first secretary, Louise Haigh, argued in an article in the journal Renewal, before she took on her powerful role in Andy Burnham’s cabinet, that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”.She said such a change was necessary to “shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy”.Other advocates of equalising CGT and income tax rates include the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at Warwick University (CenTax), the Resolution Foundation, and the TUC.What are the downsides?Business lobby groups argue that higher rates of CGT would disincentivise just the kind of productive investment the UK needs to generate stronger economic growth.As Lena Levy, the deputy director of policy at the British Chamber of Commerce, puts it: “Speculation over changes to capital gains tax in next month’s budget is only adding to the huge uncertainty for people looking to invest, grow or sell a business. The UK’s capital gains taxes are already above the OECD average of 20%.”The prospect of another rise – along with a slew of other tax reforms since 2024 – is also cited as one reason that high net worth individuals might choose to leave the UK.And there would be fears, too, that some wealthy individuals would be able to dodge the new higher rates through other forms of tax avoidance, undermining it as a revenue-raising strategy.Are the pitfalls avoidable?Fans of equalisation say yes: Prof Arun Advani, of CenTax, says there’s no point just raising CGT rates without reforming the “base” – the rules that determined what it is charged on.He suggests apackage of reforms, to be implemented alongside a rise in CGT rates.As well as making the system fairer, the aim of these would be to prevent potential revenues leaking out – with an “exit tax” levied when wealthy individuals move elsewhere, for example, and by removing the exemption that now applies to inherited assets.And the changes would also be intended to incentivise productive investment better, by including an “investment allowance” that would mean CGT was only paid on gains made over and above the general rate of asset inflation across the economy.These and other CGT reforms have been widely discussed – a version of them was recommended in the IFS’s authoritative Mirrlees review of the UK tax system way back in 2011, for example.But in 2024, Reeves opted for the simpler halfway house of just raising the rates. Healey could do the same, or wait until the budget next spring to undertake more comprehensive reform.What are Healey’s other tax-raising options?The most straightforward would be the big money-raisers – income tax, national insurance or VAT. Income tax is expected to raise about £330bn this year, for example; capital gains tax roughly £22bn.Burnham has ruled out breaking the Labour manifesto promise to leave these untouched, however, so if Healey wants to raise taxes he would have to look elsewhere.Other much-discussed possibilities include a bank windfall tax, or tweaking Reeves’s upcoming “mansion tax” so that it applies to more homes, and/or at a higher rate.Does he have to raise taxes?It depends on how far off course the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) believes Healey is from meeting Labour’s fiscal rules, and how slim a margin against those rules he is willing to accept.And that depends crucially on how the OBR interprets a slew of recent data – in particular, eye-wateringly high energy prices that have also spooked government bond markets and driven up the cost of borrowing.Treasury insiders suggest the budget will be relatively narrowly focused – on fiscal devolution, for example – with some big decisions, such as when the UK should aim to be spending 3% of GDP on defence, deferred into 2027.But a particularly bleak fiscal forecast, or a decision to take more drastic action to cushion consumers from looming energy bill rises, could yet prompt a more radical statement on 28 October. In that case, CGT may seem like an obvious lever to pull.Explore more on these topicsCapital gains taxTax and spendingTaxJohn HealeyBudgetLabourEconomic policyexplainersShareReuse this content

title: From bling and birds to ‘really fancy armour’ – the best dressed characters of the Bayeux tapestry | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Medieval experts talk us through the fashion of the near-1,000-year-old embroidered work, and what it says about the characters wearing it
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Medieval experts talk us through the fashion of the near-1,000-year-old embroidered work, and what it says about the characters wearing it
Content: The prosperity of England … Part of scene one of the Bayeux Tapestry, showing King Edward with Harold Godwinson.Photograph: Bayeux Museum - Ville de BayeuxView image in fullscreenThe prosperity of England … Part of scene one of the Bayeux Tapestry, showing King Edward with Harold Godwinson.Photograph: Bayeux Museum - Ville de BayeuxFashion Statement newsletterFashionFrom bling and birds to ‘really fancy armour’ – the best dressed characters of the Bayeux tapestryMedieval experts talk us through the fashion of the near-1,000-year-old embroidered work, and what it says about the people wearing itDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereEllie Violet BramleyFri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlood, booze, arrows and boats; these are what you might typically imagine when you think of the Bayeux tapestry, which has become one of the hottest historical tickets since it went on display at the British Museum in London this month. But what about the hair?“The Anglo-Saxons all have these little moustaches, which are brilliant. And then the Normans have these funny haircuts with the back of their heads shaved,” saysProf Laura Cleaver, an expert in medieval manuscripts at the Institute of English Studies.And the clothes? There are crowns and tights, and brooches that wouldn’t look out of place anchoring one ofColman Domingo’s lapels at the Oscars.The 70-metre-long embroidery – it’s famouslynot, in fact, a tapestry– was stitched almost 1,000 years ago and tells the story of the Norman conquest.But its clothes, while not always an accurate reflection of what people actually wore, give us codified hints about status, power and who was wealthy enough to own – and flaunt – the medieval equivalent of designer pieces. So, with the help of a clutch of medieval experts, here are the tapestry’s most stylishly, interestingly, or illuminatingly dressed characters.King Edward (the Confessor)Depicted in the first scene, Edward the Confessor (pictured top), who is king when our story begins, looks smart. Wearing a crown, holding a sceptre and with nifty stitching on his shins, he presides grandly over the opening of the tapestry.According to Gale Owen-Crocker, professor emerita of Anglo-Saxon Culture at the University of Manchester, he’s wearing “the most elaborate dress in the whole tapestry”. Plus “he’s seated on an elaborate lion-headed and footed bench in a magnificent building”. All in all, some serious optics.The get-up and the furniture befit the story: “That’s the opening scene,” says Owen-Crocker, “and that is the prosperity of England. That’s what the two contenders [Harold and William] are going to be fighting for, a magnificent kingdom like this. So Edward’s dress and his whole setting is a preliminary for what it’s all about.”Harold GodwinsonView image in fullscreenThe 11th century’s must-have accesory  … Harold Godwinson (later Harold II) holding a hawk while riding.Photograph: Photo 12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesHarold Godwinson, a powerful earl, brother-in-law to Edward, and rival to William the Conqueror, appears frequently throughout the tapestry. But it’s this scene, where he’s on his way to the south coast with his followers, to which Prof Leonie Hicks, a medievalist at Canterbury Christ Church University, is drawn.The outfit isn’t the most interesting thing here, though; the accessory is. Hawks were a status symbol – the medieval equivalent of a Birkin or a Rolex – because “hunting with hawks was an aristocratic pursuit”. Not only that, but Harold’s also on a stallion – a Tesla or a Range Rover today, perhaps – and the stallion has a swanky saddle (not to labour the point, but think leather, heated seats).All of this adds up to say “this is absolutely somebody who’s going to play an important part in the story,” says Hicks. He goes on, of course, to become the last crowned Anglo-Saxon king of England, until his death at the Battle of Hastings.Count Guy of PonthieuView image in fullscreenPattern clash … Count Guy of Ponthieu.Photograph: Bayeux Museum, Ville de BayeuxFrench nobleman, Count Guy of Ponthieu, is the figure in this scene with the axe, pretty tunic-style garment and stripy tights that give Main Character Energy. He is not, explains Cleaver, “somebody that we think of now as being a big part of this. But when Harold, at the start of the story, goes over into Normandy, he gets captured by Guy, who then takes him to Duke William’s.”“He’s wearing something absolutely unique,” says Owen-Crocker: “some kind of a patterned or scaled garment” and “differently coloured, two-tone garters”. What it represents, she says, “is an attempt to make him look really fancy” but in a way that, in modern parlance, takes the mickey out of him. He was, she says, “considered to be effeminate or generally lacking in manliness”, which at the time was a reason for ridicule in ways similar to today’s manosphere.To a modern audience he might just look like he’s mastered the art of pattern clashing. But according to Owen-Crocker, “he is a character that the designer seems to want to satirise, to make him look a fool”, and that would have been legible to a medieval audience through his outfit.Duke William of NormandyView image in fullscreenCloak and dagger … William the Conqueror.Photograph: Bayeux Museum, Ville de BayeuxDuke William of Normandy, who goes on to become William the Conqueror, is on the far left on a great big stallion. Which tells us instantly that he means business in this tale of shifting power. (Guido, by contrast, is depicted elsewhere in the tapestry “on a mare with a donkey’s ears”, according to Owen-Crocker; the final jab “in a series of put-downs”.)William has “got ribbons attached to his cloak … those are pretty unusual”, she continues. Apparently a Roman imperial style, this denotes power. If the ribbons weren’t enough, William’s also wearing a cloak with a gold border, a double gold belt, and spurs. “They’re all subtle indicators of relative status,” says Owen-Crocker. Even if you don’t remember your year 7 history, you might pick up that this French nobleman is going places.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBishop Odo of BayeuxView image in fullscreen‘Really fancy armour’ … Bishop Odo of Bayeux.Photograph: Bayeux Museum, Ville de BayeuxAccording to Owen-Crocker, Bishop Odo of Bayeux (in the centre on a black horse) is “galloping on to the battlefield to rally the troops in a heroic sort of way”. He’s wearing what Hicks describes as “really fancy armour”. There’s a good reason that might be: it’s believed the tapestry was commissioned by Odo, William the Conqueror’s half-brother, or, says Hicks, “someone close to Odo, so he wanted to be depicted in a flattering light”.As a person, she thinks “he was quite flamboyant”, and his armour here is certainly that. While most of the other men on the tapestry wear fairly identikit chainmail, Odo looks strikingly different.Plus, Owen-Crocker says: “His horse, in this sort of flying gallop, is one of the longest images in the tapestry. And it’s a really virile stallion, if you look closely at that part of it.” Manspreading, the medieval way; he, and his horse, are quite literally taking up space.Archbishop StigandView image in fullscreenTonsured hair and in a millefeuille of liturgical layers … Archbishop Stigand.Photograph: UniversalImagesGroup/Getty Images“Stigand is the archbishop,” says Hicks. “On the tapestry, he’s the one who crowns Harold after Edward the Confessor dies and Harold assumes the throne.” Given that Stigand (pictured on the far right) is “in some of the sources, a very problematic character … having Harold crowned by him is a way of maybe ‘casting shade’, as the young people say.”Nevertheless, he looks legit. He is, she says, wearing his “liturgical garments … a maniple over his left arm [a little short scarf] … his chasuble and his alb and his stole and his special pallium, which is a marker of him being archbishop”. According to Martin Bostal, director of the museum of Bayeux and expert in medieval archeology, “the depiction of the clergy is, in fact, quite close to what is described in texts from the period”.Arguably most striking to a modern audience, though, isn’t Stigand’s millefeuille of liturgical layers, but his tonsured hair. It’s an unfortunate style but apparently again something that would mark him out as a member of the clergy.AelfgyfaView image in fullscreenA rare Bayeux woman … Aelfgyva.Photograph: Bayeux Museum, Ville de BayeuxThe tapestry has slim pickings when it comes to women –there are just three on the central frieze. One is fleeing a burning building with her child, another, according to Hicks, is thought to be Queen Edith, “who’s sitting at the front of Edward the Confessor’s bed as he lies dying, warming his feet in her lap”.But Aelfgyva, who is standing under the arch here, is worthy of some attention. As Hicks puts it: “We’ve got this really weird scene with a heavily veiled woman, wearing the sort of flowy garments that women are depicted wearing in the pre-conquest artistic style.”Frustratingly, the men around her steal a lot of thunder. “There’s a priest in secular clothing who’s touching the side of her face, and then in the bottom margin – this is the very famous bit – there’s a very prominently naked bloke mirroring the posture of the priest.” It might, says Hicks, “be a reference to some kind of sex scandal”.But Aelfgyfa’s statement sleeves are making their own bid for attention. For Martin Bostal, director of the museum of Bayeux and expert in medieval archaeology, it seems plausible “that the tapestry is depicting the attire of the wealthy class, as such loose sleeves would be unsuitable for manual labour”.Their material extravagance, Owen-Crocker adds, is “what you call conspicuous consumption of cloth”–using lots of not-strictly-necessary (and expensive) fabric to show off your wealth. The medieval precursor, perhaps, to today’s logo-drenched designer wear.To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure and your wardrobe dilemmas solved –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everything is golden’: readers’ tips for a great autumn day out in the UK | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: With autumn officially here, our readers savour days of fruitful mellowness, from Cornwall to Loch Lomond
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: With autumn officially here, our readers savour days of fruitful mellowness, from Cornwall to Loch Lomond
Content: Orange hills, cold air and dramatic clouds at Loch Lomond.Photograph: David Robertson/AlamyView image in fullscreenOrange hills, cold air and dramatic clouds at Loch Lomond.Photograph: David Robertson/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Readers' travel tipsUnited Kingdom holidays‘Everything is golden’: readers’ tips for a great autumn day out in the UKWith autumn officially here, our readers savour days of fruitful mellowness, from Cornwall to Loch LomondTell us about a great wellness experience– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 02.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGambling on sunshine at Loch LomondI love Loch Lomond in autumn. I’d start with a walk around Balmaha village and a stretch of theWest Highland Way, pretending I’m there for the scenery rather than earning the right to eat something massive afterwards. Autumn is when it looks best: orange hills, cold air, dramatic clouds and the constant Scottish gamble of whether you’ll get sunshine, sideways rain, or both within 10 minutes. I finish, if I’m not driving, with a wee dram to properly round things off.PeteCornwall’s wild autumn seasView image in fullscreenThe coastal path from Godrevy.Photograph: Peter Lane/AlamyThe rough beauty of Cornwall’s sea views appeals to me. A great autumn day involves walking along the staggered cliff edges betweenGodrevy and Portreath. The isolated nature of the coastal paths makes me feel as if the sea is singing just for me, while below the waves go wild, waiting to be admired. On this walk, you will be rewarded with the most breathtaking views, lone benches and burnt orange sunsets.OliwiaA hydro-powered house in NorthumberlandView image in fullscreenCragside was a technological marvel of the 19th century, with hydroelectric power and hydraulic gadgets.Photograph: Jonathan Ayres/AlamyWhen I first visited the National Trust’sCragsidein Northumberland, a staff member at the entrance made the bold claim that it was “the best place in England”. In autumn you can really see their point. The estate’s 1,000 acres are covered with a huge variety of trees that transform the landscape into a mixture of reds, oranges and deep greens, contrasting perfectly with the often misty Northumberland weather. It’s a perfect autumn day trip for woodland walks, possibly stopping for a picnic at one of the many lakes or gardens, and visiting the extraordinary hydro-powered Victorian house with its pioneering gadgets.EverlyProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.- back sections make it manageable without losing the drama.Bonita PhilpDeep in the forest in the Scottish BordersView image in fullscreenLichen on fir trees in the Glentress Forest.Photograph: Tom Richardson Scotland/AlamyGlentress Forestin the Scottish Borders is hard to beat on a crisp autumn day. Start with a walk or mountain-bike ride through the forest, when the trails are surrounded by copper, red and gold, and climb high enough for brilliant views across the Tweed valley. Afterwards, warm up with coffee and something sweet at the cafe before heading into nearby Peebles for a wander along the river and around its independent shops. It feels properly remote despite being less than an hour from Edinburgh. And, whether you’re cycling or walking, autumn is when the forest is at its most spectacular.Remi LapeyreBirmingham’s secret oasisView image in fullscreenWinterbourne Gardens.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyWinterbourne House and Gardenat Birmingham University is a wonderful little oasis in Edgbaston, just outside the city centre. A beautiful Arts and Crafts style house, set in stunning gardens, it is a lovely place for a wander and is especially beautiful on a sunny day in early autumn when everything is golden. See herons at the reservoir, talk to friendly robins by the walled garden and browse the bookshop. Have coffee there and then head into nearby Harborne for lunch or dinner.RachelRivers and ruins in a Lancashire valleyView image in fullscreenThe River Roddlesworth near Darwen.Photograph: Walker/AlamyRocky Brook is the name given by locals to the River Roddlesworth, which flows through a wonderful wooded valley at the edge of the West Pennine Moors. The woodland, planted by Liverpool Corporation Waterworks, provides plenty of autumn colour. A network of paths allows exploration of the woods and the ruins of Hollinshead Hall and well house. There’s a public car park, cafe and pub (theRoyal Arms) at Ryal Fold, and for those who walk north-west through the woods there’s also theHare & Houndsat Abbey Village. Four buses a day run from Blackburn to the Royal.Graham Deanskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTwisted oaks and fungi in the Peak DistrictView image in fullscreenSessile oaks in Padley Gorge.Photograph: Septemberlegs/Getty ImagesTheLongshaw estatein the Peak District is perfect for an autumn stroll. Both Oaks Wood and Bolehill Quarry have a huge variety of fungi in their hidden depths. The twisted oak trees inPadley Gorgelook at their most spectacular on early autumn misty mornings. It’s easy to explore pathways on the estate with the friendly free social walk every Wednesday. Finish a wonderful day with a treat in the cafe.KatharineA lime tree avenue in NottinghamshireView image in fullscreenClumber Park’s avenue of trees is one of the longest in Europe.Photograph: Eye35 Pix/AlamyClumber Parkis a must-visit at this time of year. The National Trust property features peaceful woodlands with golden leaf carpets, crisp lakeside views and an ornamental bridge. You’ll want to keep your camera handy as you enter a double tree avenue of 1,296 limes stretching three miles (one of the longest in Europe), which provides a gorgeous golden canopy. The walled kitchen garden is a favourite with its massive apple collection and seasonal displays. The apple juice I’ve tried here is some of the best I’ve tasted.AsmaA Roman autumn at Hadrian’s WallView image in fullscreenLate autumn at Steel Rigg.Photograph: Donaleen Shiell/AlamyMy perfect autumn day iswalking Hadrian’s WallfromSteel Rigg, when the moorland turns copper and gold and every climb rewards you with another enormous Northumberland view. Pack a flask, sturdy boots and something waterproof – the weather changes its mind even faster than I do. You only pay for parking, and shorter out- andWinning tip: Steaming through north WalesView image in fullscreenThe Llangollen Railway.Photograph: Paul Weston/AlamyMy perfect autumn day out is a trip on theLlangollen Railwayin north Wales. There’s something magical about travelling through the Dee valley on a steam train when the leaves have turned orange and gold. We start in Llangollen, grab something warm to drink, then climb aboard for the journey alongside the River Dee, watching the autumn scenery through the window. Afterwards, we wander around Llangollen, exploring the little shops. It’s simple, nostalgic and feels like autumn properly arriving – especially when you hear the steam train whistle through the valley.ChelseaView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysReaders' travel tipsAutumn walksDay tripsWalkingWalking holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: After a fiery summer, I’m choosing resilient crops to future-proof my garden | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: From kale to hostas, there are many vegetable patch options that are hardy, low-maintenance and delicious
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: From kale to hostas, there are many vegetable patch options that are hardy, low-maintenance and delicious
Content: New hosta shoots can be sauteed like any spring greens.Photograph: Zoonar RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew hosta shoots can be sauteed like any spring greens.Photograph: Zoonar RF/Getty ImagesGardening adviceAfter a fiery summer, I’m choosing resilient crops to future-proof my gardenFrom kale to hostas, there are many vegetable patch options that are hardy, low-maintenance and deliciousClaire RatinonFri 25 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 06.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’d have to have been living under a rock (which would have been a cool and sensible place to dwell) to not have felt the intensity of the heatwaves this summer. I’ve yet to meet a plants person who isn’t concerned by the impact of the changing climate on the living things we share the planet with – as well as our fellow humans. If one had any doubts, the sight of parched grasslands and garden plants withering to a crisp should have set those aside.As I’ve shared in previous columns, this summer I was sparing with what I watered. I emptied the water butts and only used mains water on plants that were likely to survive and provide a harvest. Any sign of floundering and the crops were for the chop – sorry, stunted courgettes! And if you’ve been reading my column for a while, you’ll also know that I turned over one of my annual beds to golden raspberries and tayberries this year in a bid to have more plants that are less needy. So you can imagine my joy when I saw that brilliant gardener Jack Wallington has written a book that delves deep into this low-impact, resilient approach to edible gardening. Perfect timing.double quotation markHostas are not just beautiful ornamental plants for shady borders – they, too, are edibleWhile I’m familiar with many of the crops Jack writes about, there are a good number that I didn’t even realise were edible! For example, I had no idea there were edible varieties of stonecrop (also known as sedum). Its succulent leaves can be picked as and when needed, and have a mild taste that makes them an ideal addition to a well-dressed salad. These plants are easily grown from seed and I can testify to this given how readily they pop up, self-seeded, around my garden, sometimes out of gravel. Leaf cuttings also take readily.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s time for a Gardeners’ World that reflects Britain’s gardens in all their messy, realistic chaos | Claire RatinonRead moreHostas are not just beautiful ornamental plants for shady borders – they, too, are edible. New shoots that emerge in spring can be sauteed like any spring green, and made more delicious with a dash of soy sauce. If you beat the slugs and snails to their leaves, they can be thinly sliced and added to salads.I was once gifted some perennial kale cuttings and still kick myself for not doing a better job of rooting them, as I adore a brassica and would be grateful to have one that lasts for a decade. Perennial kale needs the same kind of care as other brassicas – protection from cabbage whites and pigeons, and support when mature – but nothing more. ‘Nine Star’ (a perennial brassica Jack describes as “broccauli”, due to its florets that taste like a cross between broccoli and cauliflower) is similarly resilient.As well as making space for more water butts and considering what seeds I may not sow next season, I’m going to be making plans to add more resilient crops. I hope you will be too.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: Before Hastings was the Battle of Stamford Bridge. And it happened right here, 960 years ago today | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Low Catton, East Yorkshire: It was King Harold’s last taste of victory. How chilling it is to visit this unassuming spot and imagine the bloody scene back in 1066
Author: Amy-Jane Beer
Headline: Low Catton, East Yorkshire: It was King Harold’s last taste of victory. How chilling it is to visit this unassuming spot and imagine the bloody scene back in 1066
Content: The Stamford Bridge battle site on the River Derwent.Photograph: Amy-Jane BeerView image in fullscreenThe Stamford Bridge battle site on the River Derwent.Photograph: Amy-Jane BeerCountry diaryArchaeologyCountry diary: Before Hastings was the Battle of Stamford Bridge. And it happened right here, 960 years ago todayLow Catton, East Yorkshire:It was King Harold’s last taste of victory. How chilling it is to visit this unassuming spot and imagine the bloody scene back in 1066Amy-Jane BeerFri 25 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 04.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe field with freshly sprouted winter wheat sloping down to the River Derwent looks ordinary; however, today feels anything but. Just standing here, strange chills are swarming through my body and converging in my chest.It happenedhere.I’m standing on what has recently been identified as thebattleground of Stamford Bridge, where on 25 September 1066 an English army led by Harold Godwinson surprised and devastated the Viking and rebel forces of Harald Hardrada and Godwinson’s brother, Tostig. A famous victory, but short-lived: Harold’s luck ran out catastrophically just three weeks later at Hastings.Despite many aspects of the battle being colourfully documented, the land around the modern village of Stamford Bridge has never offered any physical trace . But in 2022, the metal detectorists Simon Richardson and John Benfield turned their attention a mile downstream, where traces of Roman settlement hinted at a second ancient crossing point.Their systematic search has since yielded anastonishing arrayof 11th-century Saxon and Viking weaponry: spear points, arrow tips, an axe head, sword and scabbard fragments, scraps of chainmail. There can be no doubt that this is the place.View image in fullscreenThe Battle of Stamford Bridge, portrayed in the style of the Bayeux tapestry by the Stamford Bridge Tapestry Project. The large figure in the centre is a Norse ‘berserker’ under attack from the English army.Photograph: Chris Rock/The Stamford Bridge Tapestry ProjectI walk upstream to cross the river and loop back to the spot where the Roman bridge must have stood. New signs forbid digging and unauthorised metal detecting, but there’s no prohibition on imagination, and mine is in overdrive, conjuring roars, screams and gasps, the thwack of metal on metal, metal on bone; the reek of sweat and mutilated flesh. Are these insouciant crows descendants of those who feasted then? Were there slim-bodied fish (bleak, a friendly angler tells me) in the water then as now, to taste the blood?There hasn’t been a bridge here for centuries, so to return to my starting point I undress, stuff my clothes in a drybag and slip into the river. Cool green water carries me under the sun-dappled boughs of goat willow and oak where dragonflies and bumblebees cruise, but my mind is winding along the silty bed below, peering at bent and corroded weapons untouched since they were dropped.What was really won that day 960 years ago, I wonder? Because right now, I am more aware than ever that England is a dream, and the battle for her is still going on.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsArchaeologyCountry diaryRural affairsBayeux tapestryHeritagefeaturesShareReuse this content
