title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada
Content: A map labeling Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ is displayed as Donald Trump signs an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House on 27 August 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA map labeling Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ is displayed as Donald Trump signs an executive order in the Oval Office of the White House on 27 August 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesMichiganMichigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweatersJane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with CanadaLucy CampbellFri 25 Sep 2026 18.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CEO of aMichigancredit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to sayLake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sureCanadawill.”The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deletedaccording to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role inhostingthousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw,Michigan– said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smithtold the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said astatementfrom the organization shared on social media.After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive orderchangingLake Ontario’s name to Lake America.Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” hewroteon X.Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compelCanada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.Explore more on these topicsMichiganUS politicsDonald TrumpCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alberta’s self-image as world’s only rat-free region shattered by discovery of rat | Canada | The Guardian
description: Province’s rat patrol called in to investigate as town of Bowden announces discovery of dead vermin
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Province’s rat patrol called in to investigate as town of Bowden announces discovery of dead vermin
Content: Alberta’s formidable geography has stymied the infiltration of the vermin into the province – until now.Photograph: Dave Chidley/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlberta’s formidable geography has stymied the infiltration of the vermin into the province – until now.Photograph: Dave Chidley/AFP/Getty ImagesCanadaAlberta’s self-image as world’s only rat-free region shattered by discovery of ratProvince’s rat patrol called in to investigate as town of Bowden announces discovery of dead verminLeyland CeccoFri 25 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common withAntarcticaand the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats.But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of adead ratand called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate.“If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.”Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found.‘I love rats but we can’t live with them’: the headache of rising rodent populations around the worldRead moreBut as global temperatures increase, rat numbershave surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years.Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all.“Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide.It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation.In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south.In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats.The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found;made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents.Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats.But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice.Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaMammalsWildlifeAnimalsUrbanisationHealthAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Polo barrels towards Baja California region of Mexico | Hurricanes | The Guardian
description: Area’s second-most intense hurricane on record being fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Area’s second-most intense hurricane on record being fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters
Content: Cleaning up after Hurricane Polo hit Playa Azul in Lazaro Cardenas, Michoacan state, Mexico, on Thursday.Photograph: Enrique Castro/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCleaning up after Hurricane Polo hit Playa Azul in Lazaro Cardenas, Michoacan state, Mexico, on Thursday.Photograph: Enrique Castro/AFP/Getty ImagesWeather trackerHurricanesAnalysisHurricane Polo barrels towards Baja California region of MexicoEd Walton for MetDeskArea’s second-most intense hurricane on record being fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific watersFri 25 Sep 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.20 EDTShareHurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region ofMexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.InIndia, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, inPortugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.Explore more on these topicsHurricanesWeather trackerExtreme weatherEl Niño southern oscillationMexicoAmericasIndiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: A TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway October’s presidential vote in favour of Lula’s far-right opponents
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: A TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway October’s presidential vote in favour of Lula’s far-right opponents
Content: Supporters of opposition presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro march with an effigy of US president Donald Trump holding a doll depicting Brazilian president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva earlier this month.Photograph: André Penner/APView image in fullscreenSupporters of opposition presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro march with an effigy of US president Donald Trump holding a doll depicting Brazilian president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva earlier this month.Photograph: André Penner/APBrazilLula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in electionA TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway October’s presidential vote in favour of Lula’s far-right opponentsTom PhillipsandTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroThu 24 Sep 2026 23.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva’spresidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election.The accusation came ina campaign advertthat was published on social media on Thursday night by Lula’s team and will air on television on Friday amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote.The TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation.“Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to coloniseBrazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video.The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement.‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to powerRead moreWriting on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”.“If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added.With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington’s apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports.View image in fullscreenWorkers prepare electronic voting machines during a sealing operation before being used in the first round of Brazilian elections.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersSpeaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US’ perceived meddling, telling delegates: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.”Earlier this week,dozens of Democratic party congresspeoplewrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration’s “apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine”Brazil’s elections through what they called a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil”.The narrator of Lula’s campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling.They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil’s intelligence agency warning of a “critical level” of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump’s vice-president JD Vance.Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to “alert the Brazilian people” to the ideologically-driven US campaign. “We don’t believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,” Valadares said.“President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,” added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday.Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil’s election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump’s behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. “They want to interfere in Brazil’s elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,” Santos claimed in a social media video.Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.”In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsBrazilTrump administrationAmericasUS politicsLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China | China | The Guardian
description: While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Content: Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExpectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesChinaAnalysisPomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for ChinaAmy HawkinsSenior China correspondentWhile US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issuesKey takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in WashingtonFri 25 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIf the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying anextraordinary degree of deferenceto Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.View image in fullscreenExpectations going into the summit were low.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesOne of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White HouseaccusedChina of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit withChinain 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?Read moreWith the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary trucein Busanlast year.That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.View image in fullscreenFor China, the lack of big news from the state visit is a win in itself.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAOn Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”Explore more on these topicsChinaXi JinpingDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS foreign policyAsia PacificanalysisShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma  | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race
Content: Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, during a meeting on artificial intelligence at the UN general assembly on Wednesday. Australia’s government healthcare system was hacked by an OpenAI agent in June, it was revealed this week.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreenSam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, during a meeting on artificial intelligence at the UN general assembly on Wednesday. Australia’s government healthcare system was hacked by an OpenAI agent in June, it was revealed this week.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemmaAs the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI raceBen Dohertyin SydneyFri 25 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Australian prime minister,Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US andChina– would dominate the world’s response to the new technology.“The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said.“The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.”Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by anOpenAIagent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestAgain he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI todevelop too fast without guardrails”.China’s president,Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in WashingtonRead moreBut the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he wouldonly encourage, not restrain, the AI race.Alarms soundingTo little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed.There was, the panel, said: “no assurancethat humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”.The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month.Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent hadhacked medical dataheld by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare.No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”.OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September.It was another week before the Australian people were told.Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person.The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows theHugging Face incidentin July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face.TimelineThe OpenAI Medicare hackShowJune 2026The hackOpenAI agent hacks into Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.August 2026The discoveryOpenAI becomes aware of agent hack.10 September 2026Email sentOpenAI email Services Australia's public portal.11 September 2026Email receivedServices Australia checks email and identifies the issue.15 September 2026The notificationServices Australia notifies Australian Signals Directorate, and ASD do further work to verify the incident.17 September 2026Minister informedGovernment services minister, Katy Gallagher and her ministerial office are advised of the hack and further investigate the seriousness of the incident.18 September 2026Formal briefingGallagher receives formal briefing from services Australia.18 September 2026-19 September 2026The discussionsGallagher notifies prime minister, deputy prime minister and home affairs minister. Discussions take place between ministers, Services Australia and ASD.18 September 2026The technical briefingOpenAI provides first technical briefing with Services Australia, the first direct sharing of information from Open AI to Services Australia.23 September 2026The checksGovernment waits for confirmation about risks of announcing information publicly and ensuring it is in interests of national security.24 September 2026The announcement6am Australian eastern standard timePM Anthony Albanese announces breach in New York.10.45amDeputy PM Richard Marles and  Gallagher address Australian media.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections.“The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.”Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this weeksigned a statementarguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed.“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”Too soon?Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control.Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”.“As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry.View image in fullscreenElon Musk has said AI would probably be beyond human control within a decade, and that humanity should ‘enjoy the ride’.Photograph: Susan Walsh/APElon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”.Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”.“I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots.“If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.”Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous | Kenneth RothRead moreDonald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it shouldnever be reined in.“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said.Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”.“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”.“Whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsAnthony AlbaneseMedicare AustraliaOpenAIXi JinpingDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate science | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions
Content: The autonomous vessel being deployed by the CSIRO in waters off Hobart for its months-long mission.Photograph: CSIROView image in fullscreenThe autonomous vessel being deployed by the CSIRO in waters off Hobart for its months-long mission.Photograph: CSIROAustralian climate and environmental reportingClimate crisis‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate sciencePowered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissionsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockFri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap aroundAntarcticaand may not return for months.The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth.Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross.The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks.Possums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat lossRead moreDr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.”She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months.View image in fullscreenThe vessel has a heavy keel to keep it upright and a solar sail to power it.Photograph: CSIRO AAPPThe autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction.“It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.”Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play inglobal heating.“The ocean is doing all of us a great service by absorbing about a third of anthropogenic or human emissions every year,” Shadwick said, and the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, played a significant role. “If we want to continue to rely on this ocean service of absorbing our human emissions, we need to understand how it might change in the future.”Crewed research vessels that travelled between Hobart and Antarctica traversed only a limited patch of the ocean, she said. The autonomous craft would gather data over a greater distance and time, including crucial measurements during the polar winter.The vessel is the first in a fleet of four. Others are planned to be launched at three-monthly intervals. They will be spread across the Southern, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, particularly during winter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe approximate route the vessel will travel to circumnavigate Antarctica.Photograph: CSIROThe scientists will be able to access information in near real time via a mission portal, and once the vessels return to home base, all data and observations will undergo quality checks before they are made available for further research.Dr Pep Canadell, a chief research scientist at the CSIRO, said for every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, about 500kg were removed by ocean and forest sinks. “This is like a 50% discount on climate change,” he said.But the amount absorbed by the oceans could change due to multiple drivers: warming waters, westerly winds, melting ice, ocean acidification and the hole in the ozone layer. Observations would enable scientists to more accurately model these processes and understand how they could change in the future, he said.Solar and wind generation meet record 80% of power demand on Australia’s national gridRead moreThe University of New South Wales professor Matthew England, who studies the role of ocean circulation in global climate but was not involved in the research project, said measuring how much the oceans absorbed and how that was changing was critical.“We’ve obviously got a surge of emissions going into our atmosphere. Both the terrestrial vegetation on land and the oceans absorb a big chunk of that,” he said. “We need to track that carbon uptake and understand exactly how big the absorption is. If it starts to decline in a significant way, then it tells us that we have an even bigger problem of carbon emission reductions.”The Southern Ocean was “inhospitable” with huge swells, gale force winds, sea ice and storms. “These are very tough measuring conditions for a research vessel.” So gathering data using an autonomous vehicle, without burning fuel, was “an incredible deployment of technology”, he said.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisAustralian climate and environmental reportingAntarcticanewsShareReuse this content

title: NSW crackdown on ‘AI-doctored’ real estate listings hits mural-covered wall | Housing | The Guardian
description: Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fake
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: Apartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fake
Content: The Leichhardt property – about 12km away from Bondi – has a view of an outdoor mural of the famous beach.Photograph: realestate.com.auView image in fullscreenThe Leichhardt property – about 12km away from Bondi – has a view of an outdoor mural of the famous beach.Photograph: realestate.com.auHousingNSW crackdown on ‘AI-doctored’ real estate listings hits mural-covered wallApartment with strange view singled out in government’s fight against deceptive ads – but real estate agent says photo is no fakeGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastIma CaldwellFri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNew South Walesgovernment’s crackdown on “AI-doctored” rental listings has hit a wall, after it made an example of a supposedly manipulated ad that turned out to be a genuine photograph of a $5,000 courtyard mural of Bondi beach.In a media release on Friday announcing protections against misleading rental ads, the state government provided a link to a property in Leichhardt, claiming it was an “AI-doctored rental listing in Sydney’s inner west”.But the listing agency IB Property denied the images were altered.Half of young Australian adults now live with their parents – and it’s not hard to see whyRead moreA spokesperson confirmed the photograph showed a mural of Bondi beach on an internal courtyard wall visible through the unit’s windows, rather than a false digital depiction of coastal views.“We can confirm that the image has not been altered or digitally generated using AI, Photoshop or any other image-editing software,” the spokesperson said.View image in fullscreenThe apartment’s original view, when listed in August 2014.Photograph: realestate.com.auLeichhardt is about 12km away from Bondi beach.When Guardian Australia visited 2/14 Norton Street, the artwork was not visible from the street. IB Property explained the mural sits within an internal courtyard and provided photos taken inside the unit confirming it remains in place.“The mural was commissioned and paid for by the landlord at a cost of approximately $5,000, and we can also confirm that there are no plans for it to be removed,” the spokesperson said, adding that the property was leased in February 2026 and had not been advertised since.View image in fullscreenA photo from 2026 showing a different view from the kitchen windows.Photograph: IB PropertyThe better regulation and fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose office issued the media release, didn’t respond directly to questions from Guardian Australia about the mural, but issued a subsequent statement on Friday afternoon.“Every renter knows the frustration of seeing a property online, only to turn up and find it looks nothing like the listing,” Chanthivong said.“These laws are about putting an end to misleading practices and making sure renters get a fair go. We will always stand on the side of renters.”Tackling ‘housefishing’Despite the mix-up, the new laws target an increasing issue.Under the legislation, real estate businesses in NSW will face fines of up to $22,000 for failing to disclose digitally altered or AI-generated property images.The legislation targets therapid rise of “housefishing”– where digital alterations distort the true size and condition of a home.View image in fullscreenNSW fair trading minister Anoulack Chanthivong says ‘we will always stand on the side of renters’.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPChanthivong said the new laws would establish strong protections against misleading property marketing and support ethical AI use. The regulations take effect in early 2027.Virtual staging v distorting realityThe legislation arrives as artificial intelligence embeds itself in property marketing nationwide.Tim McKibbin, the chief executive of the Real Estate Institute of NSW, said generative AI complicates pre-existing digital enhancement in the industry.“This technology has been available for some years now – people have used Photoshop,” he said. “People were removing trees and removing telegraph poles … clearly that is false and misleading.”McKibbin draws a line between virtual staging and false advertising.“I’ve seen instances where agents have put furniture into the photographs. Now, that is merely giving you an indication of what you could do,” he said.Stewart Bunn, of First National Real Estate, said consumer trust was being tested by poor industry examples, referencing a 2024 instance where an LJ Hooker branchused AI to generate a listing with nonexistent schools.“We have seen examples across the industry where AI-generated images have depicted renovations that have not occurred, furnishings that create an unrealistic impression of scale, landscaping that does not exist or finishes that materially differ from the actual property,” Bunn said.“The best practice is simple: if a buyer would be surprised by what they see when they arrive at the property, the advertising has gone too far.”AI ‘hallucinations’An RMIT Universityreportled by Dr Leah Li, funded by the Australian Property Institute, found a “significant lack of sector-specific AI frameworks to guide responsible AI practice within the property profession”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPublic confidence remains fragile: a2026 Cotalitystudy showed only 40% of Australians trust AI-generated outputs, compared with 62% in Canada, 52% in the US, and 46% in the UK.Dr Shuai Wang, a research fellow at the University of Queensland, said generative AI systems prioritise visual appeal over accuracy. In real estate, this can manifest as “hallucinations”.“AI hallucinations can occur when AI-generated images introduce features that were never part of the property,” Li said, fundamentally changing a prospective tenant’s perception of “size, layout, condition, or amenity”.Leo Patterson Ross, the chief executive of the Tenants’ Union of NSW, said deceptive imagery could artificially inflate rental markets “by inflating the number of people who appear interested in a place and increasing pressure on someone to rush to put in an application or even offer above the advertised rent”.Patterson Ross said stricter measures were necessary, rather than just disclosure. “The bill only requires disclosure of the use of digital alterations. We think any use of imagery that misrepresents the property should be disallowed.”Li said a long-term solution would require national coordination combining “transparency requirements, professional accountability, industry standards, regulatory oversight and consumer education”.“Trust does not come from simply adopting AI; trust comes from transparency about how AI has been used and confidence that it is being used responsibly.”‘Haunted houses with a digital paint job’For tenants navigating tight rental markets, AI distortion has added a frustrating layer of deception.Roxanne Gardiner, 26, said AI-generated imagery was “rife” during her search for a rental in Brisbane’s eastern suburbs.“I was constantly getting scammed by listing photos,” she said. “What’s so embarrassing is we didn’t even realise one of the first houses we saw was AI until we rocked up there.“The AI furniture is not accurate to the rooms and would usually make them look bigger than they were.”Beyond virtual staging, Gardiner observed artificial greenery and soft lighting that changed the true character of a home.“It feels cheap … lazy and insulting,” she said. “We just stopped going to AI listings, period. We started asking: ‘What are they compensating for?’”Gardiner eventually signed a lease on an unedited property within three days of manually filtering out AI-altered ads.Matt Stitt, 25, faced similar issues searching in south Brisbane.“Listings had completely replaced floorboards to look new, edited in area rugs that near-covered entire rooms,” he said. “It was such a waste of time seeing these haunted houses with a digital paint job.”Crackdown on data collection and hidden feesThe NSW legislation also protects privacy for more than 2.3 million renters by curbing excessive data harvesting. Landlords and property managers must use standardised application forms, banning requests for personal photos, social media handles, tattoo details or children’s information.Sensitive identity documents, such as driver’s licences and passports, will only be collected from the single preferred applicant prior to lease signing, eliminating roughly 187,000 document collections annually, according to the government.AI could be a bubble and is not yet making Australia more productive, Michele Bullock saysRead morePenalties for privacy breaches will reach up to $11,000 for individuals and $49,500 for corporations. The legislation also mandates the disclosure of embedded utility networks upfront, so tenants know if they’ll be locked into a gas or electricity supplier.Chanthivong said privacy protections built on broader rental reforms, including fee-free payment options and ending no-grounds evictions.“Whether you have a tattoo, or what school your kids go to, is not relevant to whether you’ll be a good tenant.”Explore more on these topicsHousingNew South WalesReal estateNew South Wales politicsAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list | Prix Goncourt | The Guardian
description: Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media
Content: The author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesPrix GoncourtNovelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listThélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social mediaPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorFri 25 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.View image in fullscreenThe novel on display inside a bookstore in Paris.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersAllegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”View image in fullscreenOrélien at Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque this week.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesThe author of the anonymous X account was lateridentified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaroas one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokeism” on film and TV.On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged caution over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.Libération alleged inan articlethat the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”The Canada-based publisher said it was important not tojump to conclusions, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me,” adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.Explore more on these topicsPrix GoncourtAwards and prizesPlagiarismFictionFranceAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years
Content: Pope Leo delivers a speech at the Elysée Palace in Paris.Photograph: Maurizio Brambatti/APView image in fullscreenPope Leo delivers a speech at the Elysée Palace in Paris.Photograph: Maurizio Brambatti/APPope Leo XIVPope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visitPontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 yearsAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 25 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leohas warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines” as he addressed global concerns over the dangers ofartificial intelligenceat the start of a three-day visit to France.“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for people to be educated in ethical discernment, capable of seeing what is morally right,” he said in a speech at the Élysée.At a second address on Friday, the 71-year-old head of the Catholic church insisted that new technologies must “remain at the service of the human person rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice” in remarks to a gathering at the Paris headquarters ⁠of the UN culture and education body, ⁠Unesco.“Every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics,” he said. “Certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought: intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.”He added: “While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and when deemed no longer productive, rejected and discarded.”Leo also criticised world leaders who disrespect the ⁠rule of ⁠law, without naming individuals. “Instead of ​respecting ‌the law, ‌those in power invoke ‌it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself ‌as though it were a commodity to be ​bought and sold,” he said.Leo, who became pope in 2025, ⁠has been critical of the direction ​of ​global leadership in ​recent months. He ​said ‌the world was “being ​ravaged ​by a handful of tyrants” last April.View image in fullscreenPope Leo with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and his wife, Brigitte Macron, at the Élysée.Photograph: Maurizio Brambatti/APThe first official papal visit toFrancein 18 years comes as Emmanuel Macron’s decade in office draws to an end ahead of next spring’s French presidential election, for which the far-right, anti-immigration Marine Le Pen is polling high. Pope Francis did not make a full state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame Cathedral in 2024.After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right toassisted dying, the pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.”A key moment of the three-day visit will be a giant outdoor mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde.The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, on Friday urged Paris to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide. On Monday, he will deliver a speech on European peace in the eastern city of Metz as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues into its fifth year.Leo called on the world not to ⁠become indifferent to the pain caused by “the scourge of war”.He told Macron and other French politicians: “I urge you ‘… never to grow resigned to the prospect of war or to ⁠consider it ‘inevitable’.”Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide, where he will privately meet seven victims of clerical sex abuse. After some survivors’ groups suggested a larger number of survivors should have been canvassed, the Catholic church said the pontiff was seeking in-depth dialogue with individuals.France’s Catholic bishops’ conference has agreed to provide compensation after a 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials.In recent years, further accusations have emerged, including against workers at the elite Catholic boarding schoolNotre-Dame de Bétharram, near Lourdes.On his flight to Paris, Pope Leo told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt tobar US mediafrom the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures.Asked by a CNN reporter about Donald Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media were welcome on his plane. “I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVFranceEuropeAI (artificial intelligence)The papacyCatholicismUnesconewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo warns against AI and says technology ‘must remain at service of humans’ during first visit to France – as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: The pope gives landmark speech on AI development and Europe’s future
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: The pope gives landmark speech on AI development and Europe’s future
Content: 09.54 EDTTechnology 'must remain at service of humans,' and not become instrument of 'domination and injustice,' Pope Leo warnsIn his deliberations on what it means to be human,Pope Leosays “we are all born naked and in need; poor by birth, in need of bread, and words, and words of care and affection.”Only through becoming adult, “we risk forgetting it,” with people’s “humanity betrayed or cast aside, exploited or deceived.”“Life is no longer understood as a gift, but as a commodity. It is no longer viewed as a summons to care and responsibility, but as a product to be exploited.”He “to be human is to be free by nature,” and to “recognise [life’s] grandeur” and “immense potential.”But he says “to be human … implies a responsibility before history,” as “the human being is one who grows, learns, and works with both hands and mind.”He then talks about the tragedy of the second world war, when “humanity had come to realise that scientific progress, when severed from wisdom, can turn into a weapon of destruction.”He says 80 years later, the founding charter ofUnesco– built on that recognition – still stands.Turning to the issue of technology, he says “our efforts in this domainmust ensure that new technologies remain at the service of the human person, rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice.”In a strong passage, he warns:“Over the centuries, many tasks once performed by human beings have been entrusted to machines whose capabilities and applications have continued to expand. More recently, certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought intelligence.At the same time, however,our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.The paradox has become increasingly evident.While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiencyand, when deemed no longer productive, the rejected and discarded.”Share

title: Meloni accused of ‘running scared’ with cap on foreign children in classrooms | Italy | The Guardian
description: Critics say decree also banning burqa in schools shows Italian PM worried about losing far-right voters in next year’s elections
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Critics say decree also banning burqa in schools shows Italian PM worried about losing far-right voters in next year’s elections
Content: Giorgia Meloni speaking on Italian TV on Tuesday. She has claimed the new measures ‘do not divide but genuinely help to integrate’.Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/APView image in fullscreenGiorgia Meloni speaking on Italian TV on Tuesday. She has claimed the new measures ‘do not divide but genuinely help to integrate’.Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/APItalyMeloni accused of ‘running scared’ with cap on foreign children in classroomsCritics say decree also banning burqa in schools shows Italian PM worried about losing far-right voters in next year’s electionsAshifa KassamEuropean community affairs correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Italian government has been accused of ramping up divisive rhetoric to try to court far-right voters ahead of next year’s general election after it passed a decree aimed at capping the number of newly arrived migrants in classrooms and banning the burqa and niqab in schools.The prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who leads the far-rightBrothers of Italyparty, said her government had approved what she called “commonsense measures that do not divide but genuinely help to integrate”.Writing on social media, she said the measures included: “A limit of 30% in classrooms for students who do not adequately know Italian, plus tools to learn our language and a halt to burqas and niqabs in school.”The announcement was a toned-down version of comments she had made earlier in the week at an event organised by Brothers of Italy’s youth division. “It cannot be that in the classroom it is Italian children who feel left out because they’ve become the minority,” Meloni said as she vowed to “legally set the number of foreign students per class”.Thursday’s decree also sets out that in cases where students show persistent problems with integrating or struggling to learn the language, their parents will be referred to social services and will have to take free literacy and Italian language classes. Parents’ failure to comply could result in fines of up to €1,000.The education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, said the measures, set to take effect in the 2027-28 school year, would affect about 1,000 classrooms, or about 0.3% of the total nationwide.Rights campaigners were swift to link the measures to next year’s election, in which Meloni’s premiership isfacing an unexpected challengeron the right.“She’s creating an emergency that is not a real emergency at all,” said Daniela Ionita, of the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, pointing out that an estimated 60% of the pupils who could be described as foreign were born in Italy butfaced a myriad of hurdleswhen it came to accessing citizenship. “Because there are now new parties pushing from the right, I think Meloni is scared,” she said.View image in fullscreenJannatur Nayeem, 33, an Italian citizen of Bangladeshi origin, chats with other mothers as they wait for a sports session to end at a school in Rome on Thursday.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APThe government said students born and raised in Italy or who had attended at least two years of nursery school or completed three years of schooling in Italy would be exempt from the measures.Ionita said the ramped-up rhetoric was an attempt by the government to mask how little it had accomplished during its time in power. “If you remove every decree linked to security or to migrants, the government’s political and economic programme will fall apart, and very little concrete remains of one of the longest-serving governments of the last years in Italy,” she said.Marco Tarchi, a political scientist who focuses on the extreme right and teaches at the University of Florence, said the measures were “undoubtedly” driven by fears of a new political challenge on the right.Since February, a new party, Futuro Nazionale (FN), has galvanised the extreme right, withpolls suggestingit could capture about 8% of the vote in an election expected as early as spring 2027.Led by Roberto Vannacci, a former army general best known for self-publishing a book rife with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism, the party’s popularity in polls has eclipsed that of Brothers of Italy’s two coalition partners, the League and the conservative Forza Italia.View image in fullscreenRoberto Vannacci’s party Futuro Nazionale has galvanised the extreme right.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersThose who have shifted allegiances include some who had enthusiastically lined up behind Meloni years agoas she spokeof “ethnic substitution” and vowed to install an all-out naval blockade to prevent migrant arrivals from north Africa.Tarchi said: “Many of the FN’s potential voters are former supporters of Giorgia Meloni’s party who are disappointed that, once in power, the leader softened many of her previous stances regarding the European Union, which she had harshly criticised; immigration, on which she had made radical proposals that were later abandoned; and other issues.”He said Vannacci had capitalised on this, capturing voters with an extreme manifesto that promised “remigration” and limits on the number of foreigners in the country, as well as curtailing LGBTQ+ rights and negating the right to abortion. He said that in order to win back this support, Meloni may have to adopt positions closer to those she held in opposition.A glimpse of what this could look like came this summer when Meloniseized on the sudden entryof tens of thousands of people into the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta in north Africa, said Elisa De Pieri, a researcher at Amnesty International.“Meloni immediately exploited the situation in Ceuta, which had absolutely nothing to do with Italy and nothing to do with the Schengen space, but she made it into a supposed crisis for Italy,” she said. “And so that’s the mode that I think we’re going to see in the next months.”De Pieri predicted that Meloni “won’t be talking too much” about Italy’soffshore detention agreement with Albaniaon the grounds that it had not been as successful as she would have hoped. “It’s been very costly, and it’s been struck down repeatedly by national and international courts,” she said.View image in fullscreenA reception camp for migrants transferred from Italy in Gjader, Albania, in 2024.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersInstead, she expects Meloni will adopt a more aggressive tone on migration more generally, leading to a polarising electoral campaign that would have a disproportionate impact on migrant communities.The view was echoed by critics of the new measures who pointed out the rarity of burqas or niqabs in Italian classrooms and said the government was simply repackaging previous, unenforced policies, given that the 30% threshold was previously floated by the education ministry in 2010. Save the Childrensaidthe overall impact would be to “create ‘first-class’ and ‘second-class’ students”.The leader of the Democratic party, Elly Schlein, described the decree as “shameful” and accused the government of “living on a different planet”. She said Italian parents were grappling with a very different set of issues, citing crumbling school buildings, the high costs of textbooks and low teacher salaries.“Faced with all this, the government’s response is to kick foreign children out of the classroom,” Schlein said. “Who do they think they’re kidding? After four years of cuts and no serious investment in school buildings, they’re inventing a witch-hunt that targets the youngest children.”Explore more on these topicsItalyGiorgia MeloniBrothers of ItalyThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tall, dark and hated: plan to renovate ‘Paris’s ugliest building’ put on hold | Paris | The Guardian
description: Tour Montparnasse modernisation project at a standstill after clashes over pricing and other issues
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Tour Montparnasse modernisation project at a standstill after clashes over pricing and other issues
Content: The Tour Montparnasse in the Paris skyline. It has been emptied and closed for renovation.Photograph: Bim/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Tour Montparnasse in the Paris skyline. It has been emptied and closed for renovation.Photograph: Bim/Getty ImagesParisTall, dark and hated: plan to renovate ‘Paris’s ugliest building’ put on holdTour Montparnasse modernisation project at a standstill after clashes over pricing and other issuesAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 25 Sep 2026 07.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been called a carbuncle on theParisskyline, a sombre skyscraper where visitors to its viewing platform often joke that the city looks better when you can’t see the building itself.The much-maligned Tour Montparnasse, a lone, dark monolith with tinted windows rising above a historic neighbourhood in the south of the city, is once again at the centre of controversy after its long-awaited renovation was halted this week because of disagreements between its many private co-owners.The tower, which opened in 1973, is the tallest skyscraper in inner-city Paris and is also considered its ugliest building.View image in fullscreenParis’s tallest inner-city skyscraper is due to undergo a massive structural transition.Photograph: Frédéric Vielcanet/AlamyFor more than a decade, plans have been thrashed out to overhaul the building and brighten its looming presence and modernise the area around it. Architects had planned to entirely refit the 210-metre structure with a new glass exterior, adding vegetation throughout, with a garden terrace on the 16th floor and an agricultural greenhouse at the top. The plans included a hotel on three floors of the 59-storey building, as well as new office and leisure spaces.But alongside a significant operation to remove asbestos, the estimated price of the project more than doubled to €800m (£688m).The building’s private co-owners, which include French investment funds and insurers, met this week for a final vote on the start of a first phase of renovation, with asbestos removal, interior stripping and a partial facade removal. After clashes over plans and pricing, more than three-quarters of the co-owners voted against the project.It was the last opportunity to launch the project before the building permit granted for the tower’s renovation expires at the end of November. There are now concerns that the building, which has been emptied and closed for renovation, will loom deserted. This summer, fire officers intervened after bits of glass fell off the building and landed on the street below, although no one was hurt.View image in fullscreenA design for the renovation of the Tour Montparnasse.Illustration: RPBW“Everyone needs to come to their senses,” said Philippe Goujon, the rightwing mayor of Paris’s 15th district where the tower is located. He told Agence France-Presse: “I cannot accept seeing a project that took 10 years to develop thrown away, or allowing this world-renowned landmark to fall into neglect.”Four of the co-owners who still want a renovation, including the tycoon Xavier Niel, said in a joint statement: “We would like all the co-owners, financial partners and public authorities to meet soon to examine all the solutions to transform the Montparnasse Tower.”Some co-owners hope that a new, scaled-down project could be agreed upon.View image in fullscreenMany commercial spaces within the tower have been left derelict.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamySeparately, the architect Renzo Piano has been tasked with overhauling the shopping centre beneath the tower and other buildings nearby, opening up new pedestrian spaces and moving from grey concrete to a greener, planted space. Local officials want to avoid delays to that project if the tower’s renovation stalls.The office of the Socialist mayor of Paris,Emmanuel Grégoire, said it wanted “an alternative solution to be proposed” so the site does not stay at a standstill.Opposition councillors on the left have suggested the “obsolete” tower should instead come down and be replaced by a park that would have a cooling effect during summer heatwaves.Explore more on these topicsParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
Content: People in Iran’s capital, Tehran, walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople in Iran’s capital, Tehran, walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranAnalysisTrump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midtermsPatrick Wintourin New YorkIran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTLast
