Dole, an Irish multinational producer of fruits and vegetables,started eradicating paraquatfrom its fields 19 years ago. A2007 emailbetween Syngenta executives about Dole’s decision notes a need to try to “influence” Dole’s press release on the matter “to ensure its not too damaging”.Through it all, the US EPA has taken the position that paraquat is an important tool for farmers and evidence about serious chronic health impacts is lacking, though the agency does restrict paraquat use to certified applicators and has put limits on how it can be applied to try to reduce inhalation and absorption through the skin. But the agency still allows paraquat to be sprayed from the sky on farm fields.In its 2021 decision, the EPA said there was insufficient evidence of links between paraquat and Parkinson’s and also insufficient evidence of a range of other health problems. The “human health database for paraquat is considered complete”, the agency said in its decision.Several health advocacy groups challenged the EPA’s decision in court, leading the EPA to say it needed time to “further consider substantive issues”. Last November, the agency asked paraquat manufacturers to provide additional data on paraquat volatilization to help understand exposure risks to people living beyond areas where paraquat is sprayed.View image in fullscreenLee Zeldin, the EPA administrator, speaks at the agency’s headquarters on 18 February 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Getty ImagesThe EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, then made a statement on social media in January this year saying the agency was making a decision to “freshly reassess” the safety of paraquat as part of an effort to recognize the “Make America healthy again” (Maha) movement. But an EPA spokespersoncontradicted Zeldinat the time, saying the administrator had been referring to the volatilization data.Paraquat was a prime example of the weaknesses in the current regulatory system, said Ted Schettler, a former physician who serves as science director for theScience and Environmental Health Network, a group that advocates for precautionary health policies.“[This situation] illustrates the public health risks of allowing the US EPA to be the sole arbiter of pesticide safety,” he said. “Untold numbers of people could have been prevented from developing Parkinson’s disease, not to mention other illnesses, if the agency had done its job of protecting public health.”This story is co-published with theNew Lede, a journalism project of the Environmental Working Group

title: White House television pool resumes after banned news outlets regain access | Media | The Guardian
description: Trump’s media ban resulted in an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the UN general assembly
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Trump’s media ban resulted in an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the UN general assembly
Content: Journalists gather in a press briefing room in the White House on 24 September 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJournalists gather in a press briefing room in the White House on 24 September 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesMediaWhite House television pool resumes after banned news outlets regain accessTrump’s media ban resulted in an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the UN general assemblyJeremy Barrin WashingtonFri 25 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe primary White House television pool has resumed filming administration events after a court ruling temporarilyoverturneda Trump administration ban on CNN a day earlier.In an unprecedented move, the pool – which also includes NBC, ABC, CBS andFox News– ceased recording and transmitting White House footage on Monday, in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico, which had been banned by Trump from the building over what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”The decision meant that, for much of this week, there was no high-quality pool footage of White House events and the president’s movements, though some smaller outlets attempted to provide coverage.With the pool still inactive on Thursday afternoon, that meant that a significant presidential event, a summit with Xi Jinping, China’s president, did not receive video coverage on the leading television networks. ABC had been listed as the TV pooler for the day, but held off until the network received assurances thatCNNwould be let back into the pool.Tensions between the media and the administration were further exacerbated on Thursday evening when journalists for CNN and MS Now weredenied accessto the White House state dinner in honor of Xi. The journalists were blocked despite a ruling earlier in the day from a federal judge who granted a request by CNN, MS Now and Politico to force the White House to restore their access for the next two weeks while the case plays out.Although television networks remain apprehensive, a producer forCBSNews confirmed that the network would be serving as the TV pooler for the day as scheduled, according to an internal note obtained by the Guardian.“The plan is to return covering the President in a normal capacity with a full crew,” the note read, with the pool covering Trump and Xi arriving at the South Portico for tea and a tour of the National Archives.Pamela Brown, a CNN anchor, told viewers on Friday morning: “CNN’s access to the White House has been restored, and the TV pool appears to be functioning as normal.”The resumption ends – for now – an extraordinary standoff between the US’s biggest media companies and theTrump administrationthat led to an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the United Nations general assembly.For decades, the five networks have shared the cost and responsibility of providing footage of the president that is carried by news outlets worldwide.Pool subscribers had originally received a note on Monday from Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who is now serving as the TV pool chair, saying that it would cease operations. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” he wrote in a memo. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.”Explore more on these topicsMediaUS politicsCNNFox NewsCBSDonald TrumpUS television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rules | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City face substantial sanctions from the Premier League after an independent panel found they had broken rules over financial fair play
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Manchester City face substantial sanctions from the Premier League after an independent panel found they had broken rules over financial fair play
Content: Manchester City celebrate with the Premier League trophy in 2018. Later that year the league began its investigation into the club.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester City celebrate with the Premier League trophy in 2018. Later that year the league began its investigation into the club.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesManchester CityManchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rulesCity face sanctions after more than 100 rule breachesClub insist on innocence and are expected to appealMatt Hughes,Paul MacInnesandWill UnwinFri 25 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of more than a hundred charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, throwing English football into turmoil.The serial champions now face the possibility of being relegated from thePremier League, or expelled from the competition altogether, after a verdict in the biggest disciplinary case in the history of the sport was finally delivered.Manchester City timeline: trophies, transfers and more than 100 chargesRead moreNeither party was willing to publicly confirm the outcome on Friday with an appeal process expected to be pursued imminently by City. Two years after the hearings first began, however, there is now some clarity as to the scale of City’s rule-breaking.The 134 charges made against City cover the seasons 2009-10 to 2022-23 and cover a number of areas, with the most serious relating to claims that the club failed to provide “accurate financial information” to the league during this time. From season 2009-10 to 2022-23 inclusive City won seven Premier League titles, a Champions League, three FA Cups and six League Cups.A City spokesperson said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”The Premier League did not comment, citing the confidential nature of the case. Club executives are understood to have learned about the outcome following a shareholders’ meeting in central London on Thursday and subsequently signed non-disclosure agreements.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Andy Burnham was asked about the news on Friday evening. The prime minister told ITV Granada Reports: “I’ve only just been made aware of it – I think these are reports at this stage. But if they’re confirmed, obviously I will want to look at the report of the independent commission.“People shouldn’t jump to those kind of conclusions. I know, this has been a long process between the club and the Premier League. I think quite a contested process. So I don’t think it’s as simple as jumping to conclusions. I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”The verdict was reached more than three and a half years after the 134 charges were first brought and more than two years since disciplinary hearings began. According to the Premier League rulebook, the appeal process has a stricter time frame, whereby any party who wishes to appeal a decision by a judicial panel must do so by email within 14 days of a decision being announced. Under rule W.86 any hearing should conclude no longer than 12 weeks after the first appeal is submitted. Any decision by the appeal board must also be published, alongside full written reasons, within 30 days of the conclusion of the hearing.Should City fail in their appeal, the judicial panel would then be expected to produce its verdict on the level of sanction applied to the club. Premier League rule W.64 describes the list of punishments available to a panel. Alongside levying a fine, any disciplinary committee could first suspend a club from competition, or levy a points deduction, or in the most extreme circumstances expel a club from competition altogether.Such is the scale of the charges brought against City that there is no direct comparison to be made with other disciplinary cases. The recent case involving Chelsea, who were found to have breached the FA’s rules on agents on 74 occasions, resulted only in a cash fine of £10m but Chelsea were adjudged not to have gained significant sporting advantage from their actions and were praised for self-reporting the misdemeanours, which had occurred under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. Neither of these factors would appear to apply in the City case, given the systemic claims of financial misreporting and the fact that a majority of the charges related to a failure to comply with league rules.The unprecedented catalogue of charges related to five distinct areas of alleged rule-breaking. More than 80 charges related to a club’s obligation to act in “the utmost good faith” when relaying information to the Premier League and to give complete disclosure of any information requested. These claims pointed towards the league’s belief that City had given an inaccurate picture of the club’s financial situation and withheld documents that might have cast greater light on it.The rest of the charges related to alleged breaches of profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) and the related Uefa financial fair play regulations. Finally, 20 charges related to the club’s obligation to provide “full details of … remuneration”, with breaches being claimed in the rules relating to the payment of players and managers.The extent of the charge sheet reflected a process that had been a decade in the making. Uefa found City in breach of FFP in 2014, a decision which resulted in City paying a €20m fine. The Football Leaks affair, in which millions of private documents relating to football clubs and players were hacked and made public in 2015, led to reporting on City’s affairs and a new investigation from Uefa. By 2020, Uefa had suspended City from the Champions League for “overstating its sponsorship revenue in its accounts”. This suspension was overturned by City on appeal to the court of arbitration for sport.In December 2018 the Premier League began its own investigation into City. A highly secretive inquiry, which required legal action by the Mail on Sunday to prove it was taking place, it is believed to have been inspired by the Football Leaks revelations and resulted, four years later, in City being charged.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancesFinancial fair playnewsShareReuse this content

title: The age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted now | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Friday’s verdict against Manchester City changes everything we understood about their era and Premier League title triumphs
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Friday’s verdict against Manchester City changes everything we understood about their era and Premier League title triumphs
Content: ‘There could yet be a dramatic reversal of the verdict against Manchester City but for now this is a good day for football.’Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘There could yet be a dramatic reversal of the verdict against Manchester City but for now this is a good day for football.’Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesManchester CityThe age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted nowBarney RonayFriday’s verdict against Manchester City will change everything we understood about their Premier League title triumphsFri 25 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWelcome, then, to the age of asterisk. Whatever punishmentManchester Cityand their owners receive at the end of this process, the fact remains, everything is tainted now.Overturn the tables, scatter the gold coins. Throw your medals in the bin. You cheated to win them. Whatever that thing was, it’s done. Stolen glory, stolen income, stolen joy. Every chant, every “we won the lot”, every awkward documentary scene about the deep, throbbing heart of this empire of love. It all looks odd, sinister, cold, sloppy, but also, and this is always the best response, utterly absurd.We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rightsRead moreThis is not over of course. We still work on the principle of innocent until repeatedly proven guilty, pending mega-bucks final appeals. There could yet be a dramatic reversal at the next stage. And if so, fair enough. Trust the process. So for now we must also asterisk the asterisk. It should also be pointed out that City still deny all allegations, even when proven at the first instance. They have also, in fairness, not been found guilty of all of those 100-plus charges. Maybe the club can spin this, take the positives, a vital away charge to take into the appeal.But for now this is a good day for football. And also a good day for, of all things, the world. ThePremier Leaguemay seem an unlikely revolutionary. But in the age of despotism, of endless chatter about the decline of the rules-based international order, any tribunal that finds a fund back by the one of the United Arab Emirates’ ruling families guilty of breaches of minor but still vital sporting regulations deserves its own statue outside the Royal Courts of Justice. People in wigs: not always slaves to power, or indeed the enemies of the people.View image in fullscreenSergio Agüero scores his title-winning goal in added time against Queens Park Rangers in May 2012.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersMainly this is a great day for the Premier League, which must be commended above all for its refusal to bend. There has been frustration at the time it has taken to reach this verdict. Technically it is a full eight years since Der Spiegel published the first allegations of industrial-scale cheating. And spare a thought here too for Rui Pinto, the original whistleblower, currently in witness protection after being found guilty of information-related offences. This verdict suggest football’s greatest vigilante was also right, or right enough. Raise a glass, José Bloggs of Oporto, or whatever you go by these days.That extreme delay is simply another consequence of taking on an entity that is willing to spend so aggressively on the world’s most energetic lawyers, to threaten to bankrupt the organisation it signed up to serve and nourish. It always seemed worrying that an accusation of not cooperating with financial reporting, a charge that on the face of it could be cleared up in half a day, should take three years to reach a verdict.But this is testimony to the lawfare-level response. In this context, and pending a proper sanction, the entire case speaks to the basic sanctity of the rule of law, of applying the same rules to all irrespective of status, a small but high-profile rejection of the idea wealth and political heft can steamroller regulation and process.And that punishment really is key. Because everything is on the cards here, not least the much‑trailed potential destruction of the brand. There has always been a whispered suggestion the league is taking a hammer to its own knees in this process. That thing we sold you all those years? Well, it’s not straight. The product you paid for and believed in wasn’t real.Arguably everyone who bought a Sky Sports subscription in that period now has a legal claim against City. I signed up for sport. This was an exhibition event. But the Premier League has been rigid in the right way. What is that legacy actually worth, how much more damaged will it be, if its owners shy away from their own rules and allow the serial champions to shortcut their way to plastic success? The answer is: very little. At that point we may as well all turn off the lights and abandon the stage to the world of scripted product.It is important in all this to spare a thought for City fans, who are innocent of anything other than wanting their team to win and believing the evidence presented to their eyes. There will be some who see conspiracy, because they want to, who choose to fight on, or pretend not to understand. We live in an age when even billionaire inherited rulers get to style themselves as victims of oppressive power structures.View image in fullscreenManchester City players celebrate the first of Pep Guardiola’s Premier League titles on the Etihad Stadium’s pitch in May 2018.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesBut the fact is the rules do matter, even if you think they shouldn’t exist. They matter because other teams were abiding by them. Other teams didn’t buy players, lost bidding wars, lost games and league titles by fine margins during a period when one team was saying, well, thanks but no thanks. This is why cheating matters. You can disagree with the offside law and try to get it changed. But if you just ignore it and keep on hammering the ball into the net, you’ve destroyed your own sport.City’s fans deserve sympathy generally. They don’t run the club, they simply support it. They have been loyal to their owners, even while those owners, on the basis of this decision, were turning the club into a toxic entity, a parasite on its host and on the basic idea of sport. What is the right response to this? Some will simply feel sad at the tarnishing of memories.But there is also a legitimate suggestion it is time for those owners to sell up and move on. This has been a disgraceful episode in so many ways: the casual cheating, the refusal to mitigate or compromise, the assault on English football, the attempt to bleed the rest of the field dry.The fact is anyone with an interest in justice, equality and abiding by universal rules, should be pleased with this result, including City fans. Although there is of course still a huge opportunity for the process to hole itself below the waterline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuilt followed by a minor slap on the wrist. This would asterisk the asterisk, would provide a complete reversal of all that goodwill. What would be the point of going through this only to blink at the sanctions stage? And yes, this is the job of an independent tribunal, but the league will have agency in how this is interpreted, through its submission and its evidence.View image in fullscreenMohamed Salah celebrates putting Liverpool 2-1 up against Wolves on the last day of the 2022-23 season. Manchester City took the title by one point.Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesAnd there is very little mitigation here. Not reporting financial information might sound trivial in another sphere. But in football, where success is defined by expenditure, this is deliberate and highly effective deceit. City have continued to spend freely, to win things under this shadow, in a space where more than simply results and titles are at stake. Football is a zero-sum game. When you cheat, you’re taking money and opportunities out of the pockets of others.Not to mention glory, happiness, life chances, things people work and bleed for all their lives. In their place you’re introducing failure, doubt, career regression, moving home, moving jobs, cutting ties, losing connections, all based on skewed results on a sports field, all based on cheating.The list of teams that might have won league titles in those years reads: Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal. Perhaps these clubs will even consider suing City for compensation. The Premier League could pre-empt this by stripping titles and reallocating glory. That still feels like an overload of asterisks. But this is what happens when you cheat. You degrade the experience for everyone.Everything you need to know about Manchester City’s hearing and chargesRead moreThere are two final things worth saying. Last month Bloomberg reported that the UAE had been in touch with the UK government expressing concerns about the Premier League process, and potentially, it was implied, damaging the prospect of that wider relationship.If true, and it is simply a suggestion, this would demonstrate yet another profound misunderstanding of the culture you’re buying into. The law is not supposed to bend to power and influence. Does anyone actually want to live in a world where this is the case?But then, it is also worth remembering that skimping on some financial rules is hardly the worst thing the UAE has been accused of in those years. There are accusations of supporting the bloodshed in Sudan, as well as numerous human rights abuses, the curtailment of dissent and massive social inequality.Whatever its ultimate outcome the entire process stands as a warning for every sport with it eyes in a spin at the offer of transformative financial investment. Look very hard at who you get into bed with. Jam today, pain tomorrow. And it never, ever comes for free.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFootball politicsPremier LeaguecommentShareReuse this content

title: 55,000 fans and nowhere to hide: what it’s like to play in basketball’s biggest arena | Basketball | The Guardian
description: The sprawling Philippine Arena hosts games in a country of fanatical basketball fans. Jamie Malonzo was lucky enough to play there in a Game 7
Author: Jacob Uitti
Headline: The sprawling Philippine Arena hosts games in a country of fanatical basketball fans. Jamie Malonzo was lucky enough to play there in a Game 7
Content: Justin Brownlee of Barangay Ginebra San Miguel is mobbed by the fans after Game 7 of the 2023 Commissioner's Cup Finals.Photograph: Xinhua/Rouelle Umali/Xinhua/AlamyView image in fullscreenJustin Brownlee of Barangay Ginebra San Miguel is mobbed by the fans after Game 7 of the 2023 Commissioner's Cup Finals.Photograph: Xinhua/Rouelle Umali/Xinhua/AlamyBasketball55,000 fans and nowhere to hide: what it’s like to play in basketball’s biggest arenaThe sprawling Philippine Arena hosts games in a country of fanatical basketball fans. Jamie Malonzo was lucky enough to play there in a Game 7Jacob UittiFri 25 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamie Malonzo got there early, one of the first players to arrive. He knew this was a different thing altogether. He knew the 55,000-capacity Philippine Arena was something else.As Malonzo warmed up, the crowd began to file into the stands for Game 7 of the PBA Commissioner’s Cup. Fans tried to get his attention, yelling and waving their arms madly. This game, Malonzo knew, would be unlike any other he had ever played in.“For me, warming up in there was not about trying to warm up my body. It was more about practicing cancelling out the outside noise – it was like practicing a different part of your brain,” the Seattle-born forward says of the game in January 2023.When the game started, things didn’t get any easier.“It was definitely hard to hear,” the 30-year-old says. “I remember that being a problem.”In fact, Malonzo and his team had to invent hand signals to combat the fan volume.“When you were on the court and you look up and you see these people way, way, way, way, up there in the upper bleachers cheering – it was crazy,” he says.Today, most professional basketball arenas seat between 10,000 and 20,000 people. The capacity at Madison Square Garden, for example, is 19,812 for New York Knicks games. The Philippine Arena seats nearly three times that.Until this month, it was the largest indoor arena in the world. (TheKJC King Domein Davao City opened on 1 September, also in the Philippines, and holds a whopping 75,000 people.)“In other places, soccer is the biggest sport,” says Malonzo, whose mother was born in thePhilippinesand moved to Seattle as an adult. “But that same enthusiasm other places have around the world for soccer is equaled in the Philippines for basketball.”While Malonzo now plays in Japan, he spent four years playing in the Philippines. There, he saw it all.“If you look at the poorest streets of the Philippines, if you look at the richest streets,” Malonzo says, “anywhere from the poorest to the richest area codes – you’re always going to see a basketball hoop kids can play on.”Basketball started to grow in the Philippines during the American colonial period in the early 1900s. Founded in 1975, the PhilippineBasketballAssociation (PBA) was Asia’s first pro basketball league. It has hardcore fans, brilliantly named teams – from the Magnolia Chicken Timplados Hotshots to the Rain or Shine Elasto Painters – and very specific rules: for example, certain competitions limit the height of foreign players. The national team has also recently featured several acclaimed NBA players, including former NBA sixth man of the year Jordan Clarkson.Malonzo found success in the league, perhaps most notably in that raucous Game 7 in 2023, when he scored 22 points and grabbed 17 rebounds, earning the Best Player of the Game nod.“I’m pretty familiar with the place,” Malonzo says, with a laugh. “It was the arena I won my first championship in the Philippines, which meant a lot for me.”Originally slated for 13 January, that particular Game 7 was pushed back two days because of demand for tickets, and it ended up being the most attended PBA game in history.Malonzo’s Barangay Ginebra San Miguelbeat Bay Area Dragons– a guest team from Hong Kong that season – 114-99 in front of 54,589 people. The game broke the previous PBA record of 54,086 fans, set six years prior.“It was for sure nerve-wracking,” Malonzo says. “When you think about how many people are there watching you – it’s so intense. Any little movement you make is noticed bythat manyfans.”The O’Dea High School graduate, who was taken second overall in the 2020 PBA draft out of college, says it took time to adjust to the tens of thousands watching. “It just took a few good plays to settle in, to kind of get comfortable,” he says.Soon, though, he realized most of the fans were cheering for his team. They wanted the team from Hong Kong, who boasted two former NBA players, to go down hard. And go down hard they did.View image in fullscreenJapeth Aguilar of Barangay Ginebra San Miguel dunks during Game 7 of the PBA Commissioner’s Cup.Photograph: Xinhua/Rouelle Umali/Xinhua/Alamy“When you realize the fans are with you and cheering you, it makes it special, for sure,” Malonzo says. “It was really important that we got the win in front of our crowd. To this day, I’ve never even come close to a crowd that capacity. It was huge!”Malonzo was a star during his time in the Philippines, where fans treat their basketball players like idols – literally. “That’s the word they use all the time,” Malonzo says. “Idols.”Eldridge Recasner, who enjoyed a number of years in the NBA with teams such as the Atlanta Hawks and Houston Rockets, later played in the Philippines. The point guard was in the country in 1992.“As soon as I walked off the plane, everybody knew who I was,” Recasner says.Chris McCullough, who was drafted by the Brooklyn Nets in 2015 and played 59 games in the NBA, agrees. “The way they love basketball out there, it’s unheard of,” says McCullough, who won a PBA championship in 2019. “It’s more than in America – they live and die with it.”When he first arrived in the country, Malonzo says he wasn’t quite sure what he was getting himself into. He didn’t want to play in Europe and he didn’t particularly want to try out for the NBA’s G League. Instead, he chose to honor his roots.“I felt like I wanted to do something meaningful,” Malonzo says. “I felt like going back to my mom’s home country – that meant more to me than playing in a place like Europe.”He played for several years for the country’s national team before more recently deciding to sign a contract this year to play in Japan. But it was while playing for the Philippines that he suited up and played in the giant 55,000-person venue for a second time, just a month after that famous Game 7.“Carmelo Anthony was at that game,” Malonzo says. “He’s my favorite player of all time. Yeah, that arena is a special place for me.”In the Philippines, basketball players almost can’t fathom their impact on the community, Malonzo says. Impoverished people spend their last bit of money on game tickets. They travel from far and wide, often by rickety bus, just to watch.“Some of these people don’t haveanything,” Malonzo says. “So, if you’re able to give back to some of them at the games – if they ask for pictures, autographs, I try to always stop. I just want to be able to give back.”Malonzo remembers a key play during that Game 7 in 2023. Early on, he got the ball and took it to the rim for the game’s first dunk.The crowd erupted.“You could feel how crazy it was,” he says. “It’s safe to say you could actuallyfeelthe crowd.”But in the Philippines, that’s just how it goes. Basketball brings people together.“That’s the beautiful part about it,” Malonzo says.Explore more on these topicsBasketballPhilippinesAsia PacificUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meet the USMNT’s next generation: a cheat sheet for 12 new players in camp | USA | The Guardian
description: Each of these (mostly) teenaged newcomers have shown promise and could make their US debuts soon
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: Each of these (mostly) teenaged newcomers have shown promise and could make their US debuts soon
Content: Crystal Palace's Zavier Gozo, Red Bull New York’s Julian Hall and Neil Pierre of the Philadelphia Union could make their USMNT debuts in this window.Composite: Reuters; Imagn Images/Reuters; Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCrystal Palace's Zavier Gozo, Red Bull New York’s Julian Hall and Neil Pierre of the Philadelphia Union could make their USMNT debuts in this window.Composite: Reuters; Imagn Images/Reuters; Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesUSAMeet the USMNT’s next generation: a cheat sheet for 12 new players in campThese (mostly) teenaged newcomers have shown promise and could make their US debuts soonSign up for our free soccer newsletter, for US readersJeff RueterFri 25 Sep 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States men’s national team’s stars of tomorrow will debut en masse over the coming multi-week Fifa window, with Mauricio Pochettino calling in 13 players who have yet to debut.Cavan Sullivan, at 16 years old, is the headliner, and we’ve gone deep into what makes him specialhere. But he’s far from alone. Consider this a cheatsheet to get to know all the new guys on the back of their performances at the club level.All data pulled fromFutiunless otherwise noted.View image in fullscreenDiego Kochen of FC Barcelona during a warm-up.Photograph: Álex Caparrós/Getty ImagesDiego KochenGoalkeeper, Lyngby (loan from Barcelona), 20 years oldIt’s tough to say exactly how Kochen’s first club run-out away from Barça is going, as Lyngby plays in the Danish Superliga – one of many leagues lacking in robust publicly available data. The club, just promoted from the second division, have won just one of nine games to date, conceding 16 goals from 116 shots for a 0.14 rate that’s joint-worst in the league. These are surely among the lumps both Lyngby and Barcelona are willing to let Kochen take as he gets some needed professional seasoning.Those numbers might not jump off the page, but Kochen’s profile still makes him a tantalizing prospect for a program that has been without an obvious starter in goal since Tim Howard’s retirement a decade ago. The Miami-born Kochen already got valuable reps as a training-only member of the World Cup squad. Scouting reports from Europe suggest he’s already proactive about stopping crosses, a good sign considering his slim build. It will be fascinating to finally get an up-close look at what Kochen is all about, should Pochettino give him some minutes.View image in fullscreenBrian Schwake is in the middle of an historic MLS season for a goalkeeper.Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty ImagesBrian SchwakeGoalkeeper, Nashville SC, 25 years oldThis installment’s relative “unc”, Schwake joined Nashville in 2025 after some successful loan stints in Scotland and two years with Castellón. He’s first-choice this season, and has backstopped Nashville to MLS’s best record with a credible shot at setting a new single-season points record.Schwake’s rate of 0.81 goals allowed per game jumps off the page, though it’s a metric that is equally attributable to the defense in front of him. What separates Schwake from the pack is that he still keeps clean sheets under a greater shot volume, while he also offers capable cross claiming and is tidy with his distribution to minimize mistakes. Not quite a late bloomer, but an experienced pro with room to grow, especially in possession.View image in fullscreenFrankie Westfield could fill a gap at right back for the US.Photograph: Howard Smith/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesFrankie WestfieldDefender, Philadelphia Union, 20 years oldRight back has quietly been among the thinnest parts of the US player pool for multiple cycles, especially considering Mauricio Pochettino has wisely recast Sergiño Dest as a winger given his subpar defensive awareness. Enter Westfield, a member of last year’s U-20 World Cup squad who’s thriving in his first season as Philadelphia’s preferred starter.Westfield does a lot of what coaches hope for from a modern full-back. He lobs in 3.62 crosses per 90, in the 98th percentile of MLS full-backs, while he’s also increasingly comfortable with switching play to the opposite flank. What sets Westfield apart from his peers is his progressive passing. Rather than relying on carries and one-twos to work upfield, Westfield takes the initiative himself.View image in fullscreenIllustration: FutiWith a quarter of the MLS season remaining, only three players have sprayed more progressive passes: Carles Gil (attacking midfielder and the 2021 MLS MVP), Joaquin Pereyra (winger and currently second in MLS with 12 assists), and Lionel Messi (some guy you might have heard about). No other defender ranks in the top eight. For a US team that struggled to build up the right flank throughout the World Cup, Westfield offers a potential solution.View image in fullscreenNeil Pierre towers over most of the competition at 6ft 7in.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesNeil PierreDefender, Philadelphia Union, 18 years oldThe towering 6ft 7in defender was heralded asarguably the Philadelphia Union academy’s best center-back prospectbefore making his first-team debut; no small claim given the club’s development of USMNT regulars Mark McKenzie and Auston Trusty. After spending part of 2026 on loan at Lyngby, Pierre returned to Philadelphia this summer and swiftly became its goalscoring ace on set pieces.Pierre is more than just a tall target to win headers and dunk on opponents, though. Interim manager Ryan Richter has given Pierre license to be the backline’s proactive passer - he directs 38% of his distribution upfield, in the 88th percentile among MLS center-backs. His profile is generally of a front-footed defender, ranking in the 95th percentile for high defensive actions and the 97th for balls won in midfield.Much of the lead-up to this window has lamented Noahkai Banks’ decision to commit to Germany rather than the nation he represented at the youth levels. If Pierre can continue to round out his defensive and passing chops, he could help make Banks’ about-face a footnote.View image in fullscreenPeyton Miller has been a standout for the Revolution in MLS play.Photograph: Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesPeyton MillerDefender, New England Revolution, 18 years oldEver since Alphonso Davies left Vancouver for Bayern Munich, MLS has seen several homegrown left-backs plucked by European suitors. This group – which includes Caleb Wiley, John Tolkin, George Bello, Sam Vines, and Kevin Paredes – has seen mixed returns over time, with Luca Bombino and Max Arfsten becoming the latest with their summer moves to Stoke City. Miller is assessed to have arguably the greatest ceiling of the bunch.That is, if he continues to play there. Increasingly operating as a right winger since the World Cup break, Miller has rare goalscoring potential for a player in his position. A brace against Orlando brought his season tally to seven, having also notched four assists predominantly from cutbacks and squared passes into the box. If he does play left-back for the US, those instincts could be handy as an alternative to the better-rounded Antonee Robinson.View image in fullscreenMathis Albert is still on the fringes at Borussia Dortmund.Photograph: Hendrik Deckers/Borussia Dortmund/Getty ImagesMathis AlbertMidfielder, Borussia Dortmund, 17 years oldAlbert has split billing with Cavan Sullivan as this US generation’s headline attackers, but while Sullivan is able to enjoy regular starts in MLS, Albert is still largely a training player, not even starting regularly with Dortmund II.And yet, the talent that earned hima Bundesliga debutat a younger age than Christian Pulisic and Gio Reyna is unmissable. Once part of the LA Galaxy academy, Albert takes to the wing with mazing intentionality, able to dribble upfield with ease thanks to his unusually effective acceleration with the ball at his feet. Beyond that, much of his skillset is yet to be determined, especially in terms of figuring whether he’s more likely an upfield advancer, a chance-creator, or a finisher.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenZavier Gozo has made two Premier League appearances so far for Crystal Palace.Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty ImagesZavier GozoMidfielder, Crystal Palace, 19 years oldIn any other window, Gozo’s senior international debut would almost certainly serve as the headline inclusion – he may be best positioned among the baker’s dozen of newcomers to stick around immediately and for the long haul. While he’s been an infrequent contributor to Palace thus far, his decisiveness and ability to wring threatening shots from seemingly unpromising sequences is a rare danger.View image in fullscreenIllustration: FutiGozo warranted lateconsideration as a World Cup wild-cardthanks to a red-hot start to the MLS season with Real Salt Lake. He has the tricks and ingenuity to catch opponents off-guard with his dribbling, and his MLS side got some strong shifts from him at right wing-back, as well. That only enhances his versatility, meaning he could work into Pochettino’s plans at multiple spots.View image in fullscreenAdri Mehmeti has won praise for his work in possession.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockAdri MehmetiMidfielder, Red Bull New York, 17 years oldArguably the league’s best midfield prospect since Tyler Adams, Mehmeti is a fixture of the Red Bulls’ engine room. Currently a lean six feet tall, he already serves as the team’s epicenter in possession, leading the team in touches and responsibly linking the defensive line to the attack. It’s a role he’s taken to with unusual grace for a player his age who only made his MLS debut in the 2026 season opener, operating with poise more commonly seen from players with at least 100 senior matches to their name.View image in fullscreenAdri Mehmeti distribution map, showing a lot of upfield passes from the middle of the pitch.Illustration: FutiPart of Mehmeti’s precocious approach relies on how he positions himself to collect passes, consistently changing his posture to leave opponents in two minds about what he’ll do next. When New York is in the final third, he’s already shown off a knack for threading through balls to create chances. His time with Red Bulls head coach Michael Bradley should be crucial in rounding out his midfield approach, invaluable tutelage from arguably the United States’ greatest box-to-box midfielder.View image in fullscreenBrooklyn Raines could figure into the US plans at the 2028 Olympics.Photograph: Andrew Katsampes/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesBrooklyn RainesMidfielder, New England Revolution, 21 years oldRaines is one of a few players brought in with an eye toward the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. Born in Monrovia, Liberia, he spent crucial time developing at the Barça Residency Academy in Arizona, the same program that yielded Bournemouth full-back Julian Araujo and RSL playmaker Diego Luna. Operating on the right of the Revolution midfield, Raines is a tidy passer with baked-in instincts to recirculate.Just 22.1% of his passes are directed upfield, fourth-lowest among 75 qualified midfielders. Instead, Raines’ instinct is often to carry the ball into the final third – an invaluable trait for a possession-dominant team that often faces mid-to-low defensive blocks, as the US often does in Concacaf play. Raines ranks in the 76th percentile of midfielders for progressive carrying, and offers an option for indirect dead ball service.View image in fullscreenCole Campbell at the Bundesliga 2026/27 match between FC Schalke 04 and SV Elversberg at Veltins-Arena.Photograph: Jan Fromme/firo sportphoto/Getty ImagesCole CampbellWinger, SV Elversberg, 20 years oldCampbell first drew attention as part of German Bundesliga side Dortmund’s conveyor belt of dribbly American wingers. A summer move to recently promoted Elversberg has resulted in way more minutes on the field, with Campbell scoring his first Bundesliga goal last month in a win over Bayer Leverkusen. Fitting the Dortmund archetype, Campbell is a direct winger who looks to get past his defensive mark to find dangerous areas in and around the box.Elversberg manager Vincent Wagner encourages his charges toplay without fear, and the Houston native revels in that mentality. In a small sample, Campbell has already shown plenty of initiative to get on the ball in the final third, while looking more inclined to try his own shot than set up a teammate.View image in fullscreenJustin Ellis has partnered well with Antoine Girezmann in Orlando.Photograph: Mark Thorstenson/Orlando City/MLS/Getty ImagesJustin EllisForward, Orlando City, 19 years oldEllis is the latest player whose career has benefited from playing with Antoine Griezmann, who joined Orlando over the summer. Despite entering the 2026 season with just two MLS minutes on his ledger, Ellis has already played 11 assists in his first full season, including eight since Griezmann’s post-World Cup arrival.Born in Wellington, Florida, Ellis has quickly established himself as an ideal running mate whenever Orlando is on the break. It’s fair to call him more “tricky” than outright quick, as his nimble movement and quick acceleration separates him from marks more often than downhill running. Time will tell whether Ellis eventually settles in as a finesse striker or more of an attacking midfielder, but for now, he’s another option to put a backline on skates.View image in fullscreenJulian Hall is still being pursed by Poland to join their national team setup.Photograph: Gordon Donovan/NurPhoto/ShutterstockJulian HallForward, Red Bull New York, 18 years oldSo unmissable was Hall’s early season form that the Polish federation presented Hall’s mother with a national team jersey bearing her maiden name, Zakrzewski. Hall, a dual citizen, has yet to fully commit to either country, but Poland head coach Jan Urban will be closely counting Hall’s cap tally closely – an appearance in all four friendliescould permanently tie his futureto the United States. While his form dipped this summer alongside all of the Red Bulls, Hall’s call felt inevitable thanks to 10 goals and five assists in 2,198 MLS minutes this season.Thus far in his young career, Hall’s calling card has been his preternatural reading of space and knack for slipping into scoring positions before opponents see it coming. While some center forwards largely stay in the middle of the park and others drift in from a half space to catch a goalkeeper off-center, Hall is happy to flow from sideline to sideline to get involved. From there, his interplay can get him into prime scoring territory: eight of his 10 goals this year have come from shots inside the six-yard box.Also of note: Hall was named inlast year’s Guardian Next Generation list– the next edition of that will be out soon.Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsMLSfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carlos Alcaraz leads by example as Europe take early lead in Laver Cup | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Team Europe led Team World 3-1 after the first day of the Laver Cup, with Carlos Alcaraz featuring in the doubles with Jakub Mensik
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Team Europe led Team World 3-1 after the first day of the Laver Cup, with Carlos Alcaraz featuring in the doubles with Jakub Mensik
Content: Carlos Alcaraz and Jakub Mensik celebrate after winning their doubles match against Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz and Jakub Mensik celebrate after winning their doubles match against Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersTennisCarlos Alcaraz leads by example as Europe take early lead in Laver CupEurope lead Team World 3-1 after opening dayAlcaraz wins doubles match with Jakub MensikTumaini Carayolat the O2Fri 25 Sep 2026 18.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time Casper Ruud had completed his typically tenacious comeback to capture victory in the opening scuffle of this year’s Laver Cup,Carlos Alcarazwas on the floor. The Spaniard had worked harder than any other player on the sidelines as he repeatedly cheered, animated the crowd and offered a steady stream of thoughtful tactical advice to his teammate. He reacted to Ruud’s triumphant final smash with a jubilant scream, his legs dramatically giving way as he slid down his seat on to the ground.Alcaraz is well aware of his status as the leading star of this year’s event, and in his third Laver Cup outing, the seven-time grand slam champion at times practically took on the role of Europe’s third coach behind Yannick Noah and Tim Henman. This provided a number of insightful glimpses into the way he sees the sport. During one exchange with Ruud, Alcaraz suggested that the Norwegian should attempt more down-the-line backhands and drop shots to draw Francisco Cerundolo, his opponent, into uncomfortable positions on the court. Whether Ruud possesses the skillset to follow Alcaraz’s tactics is another question, but the reasoning he gave for those suggestions was particularly interesting: The ultimate goal, Alcaraz said, should be to “make [Cerundolo] think a little bit more.”Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worthRead moreOn the opening day of the Laver Cup Team Europe established an early 3-1 lead over Team World and the focus of this weekend at the O2 Arena is on the two teams rather than any one player. However, in some ways this week carries greater individual significance for Alcaraz than anyone else. While the other players are moving towards the final stretch of a long, gruelling season that has taken them around the world, Alcaraz is still just finding his way back. With the season nearing its conclusion, Alcaraz has minimal time to rediscover his top form.Alcaraz and Jakub Mensik’s 6-4, 6-4 win over Alexander Bublik and Taylor Fritz marked just the second competitive appearance of Alcaraz’s comeback after being sidelined for four and a half months, from April till August, due to a right wrist injury. His first tournament at the US Open two weeks ago, ended in remarkable fashion: Alcaraz beaming in the corridor after losing a fifth set tiebreak against Ben Shelton at 3.33am, so happy he was to be healthy, tussling with top players in front of passionate fans and feeling like himself on the court again.Coming back from lengthy injury layoffs is challenging for all players and it can take time for many to find their form and rhythm. However, his time away also presents a rare opportunity. The indoor swing at the end of the year remains the one stretch of the season that Alcaraz, the youngest man to ever achieve the career grand slam, is yet to conquer. The faster indoor conditions have sometimes exposed Alcaraz more temperamental serve in the past, but his diminished form at this stage of the season has often been a consequence of his physical and mental fatigue.For once, he is fresh. Alcaraz returns to the Laver Cup attempting to take a step towards finding his form after such a disruptive injury and finish the season as triumphantly as it began: “I know that I have really important tournaments ahead of me, tournaments that I really want to win at least once, and if we see the record for me, the last part of the season it’s never been my good point,” he said. “But hopefully, right now that I’m just fresh mentally, physically, I’m feeling great. So hopefully, I’m gonna do great tournaments and try to find my good tennis again soon.”View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz (second left) celebrates with Rafael Jodar, Flavio Cobolli and Alexander after Casper Ruud’s victory.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersAfter Ruud’s tight 6-7 (4), 6-4, 10-8 win over Cerundolo and Team World Brandon Nakashima’s 6-1, 3-6, 10-7 win over Mensik, the evening session was defined by one statement performance, a reminder that despite the fact that although Alcaraz is still just 23 years old, an even younger Spanish talent has arrived. On a day that Jannik Sinner announced his withdrawal from the upcoming Beijing Open on Friday, extending his injury layoff to three months, and during an overall depressing ATP season ravaged by so many injuries, the ascension of the 19-year-old Rafael Jodar has been one of the brightest developments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJodar marked his O2 Arena debut with a near flawless performance, picking apart Bublik’s game with his spotless, destructive shotmaking off both wings, and he wreaked havoc on one of the biggest serves on the tour as he led 6-2, 4-0 before closing out a 6-2, 6-3 win. Jodar’s stratospheric level of play was best reflected in the raised eyebrows and shocked facial expressions from the groups of players spread across both team benches. Back in the warm-up room, as he prepared for his upcoming doubles match, the Spaniard’s performance surely provoked a few more vigorous fist pumps from his elder countryman, who by comparison is now an old veteran.Explore more on these topicsTennisCarlos AlcaraznewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel’s match with Republic of Ireland will be an eerie occasion as political debate rages on | Republic of Ireland | The Guardian
description: Despite fierce opposition to the Nations League encounters across Irish society, a boycott has not materialised
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Despite fierce opposition to the Nations League encounters across Irish society, a boycott has not materialised
Content: Republic of Ireland players look deflated after their opening Nations League defeat by Kosovo on Thursday.Photograph: Valdrin Xhemaj/ReutersView image in fullscreenRepublic of Ireland players look deflated after their opening Nations League defeat by Kosovo on Thursday.Photograph: Valdrin Xhemaj/ReutersRepublic of IrelandIsrael’s match with Republic of Ireland will be an eerie occasion as political debate rages onDespite fierce opposition to the Nations League encounters across Irish society, a boycott has not materialisedPaul MacInnesFri 25 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe match is being played in a neutral country and the stands are likely to be empty but Sunday’s Nations League fixture between Israel and theRepublic of Irelandwill nonetheless have the eyes of the world upon it.Since February’s draw paired the sides against each other, voices across Irish society have demanded a boycott of the match. The Republic of Ireland’s governmentsays Israel is committing genocidethrough its military action in Gaza, and the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) wants Israel suspended from international competition. But unless Ireland’s players decide not to take the field in the Hungarian city of Debrecen, the match will go ahead.Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for corner flag celebration in defeat by AustriaRead moreThe debate over these two upcoming games, with Ireland to “host” Israel in a return fixture behind closed doors in the Serbian town of Backa Topola on Sunday week, has continued for months. But the temperature has risen as the first fixture approaches. Remarks made by the Ireland head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, that his side were “playing against genocide” prompted a stern response this week from the Israel Football Association (IFA), which accused the Icelander of “ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity”. Hallgrímsson was thenbacked publicly by the Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, who described the IFA’s remarks as “unacceptable” and said they should be withdrawn.At the same time as Martin’s intervention his government faced protests by Irish fans who want the game called off. One organisation, Stop the Game, criticised the “hypocrisy” of Irish sports ministers announcing they would refuse to attend the fixture on principle, while also failing to support a boycott. Another group, Irish Sport for Palestine, published an open letter signed by more than 160 athletes calling for the players to act where their leaders wouldn’t. “Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do,” the letter said. “Through your leadership and courage it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game.”It is clear that all this scrutiny is being felt by Hallgrímsson’s squad. Before Thursday night’sNations Leaguedefeat in Kosovo, Dara O’Shea said the squad had found themselves in a “difficult” and “unusual” position, and had agreed to decide a collective approach to the match in Debrecen. “It’s something that can’t be brushed over,” O’Shea said. “Whatever decision that we go through as players is taken as one and everybody’s view is respected as well.” That decision is expected to stop short of a boycott, however. The midfielder Jason Knight, speaking after Thursday’s game, said: “I don’t think the game should be going ahead but it is going ahead.”View image in fullscreenSaied Abu Farchi of Israel was sent off after his goal celebration led to a second booking during the defeat by Austria on Thursday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APIt has been a winding road for the FAI to get to this point. Last November its general assembly voted to request that Uefa suspendIsraelfrom its competitions for a breach of its statutes. At the same time its president, Paul Cooke, said Ireland would play Israel if drawn against them in Uefa competition. In June the FAI said Uefa had granted a request that its home fixture be played in a “neutral venue and behind closed doors” owing to the “operational challenges” of delivering a fixture against Israel on home soil. In July, at an extraordinary general meeting, FAI delegates confirmed their support for playing the fixture, voting in favour by 68% to 32%. The given justification related to concerns over “the profound impact that any non-fulfilment of Uefa fixtures would have on Irish football as a whole”.Those calling for a boycott have pushed back on the concerns “nonfulfilment” would have had on Irish prospects, pointing to recent punishments meted out to Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia. Those three each boycotted fixtures against Belarusian teams and Uefa responded with the traditional sanction of a 3-0 walkover and, in one case, a €5,000 fine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIrish media will limit their engagement with the match, with the broadcaster RTÉ showing the game live but with no studio coverage and with commentary from the international feed. Israel, meanwhile, are expecting no more than 100 supporters to attend this “home” match, with the tickets largely purchased by fans living in Hungary. Each of these elements will further contribute to what is likely to be an eerie encounter in Debrecen. Both teams need a win after opening defeats, Israel losing in Austria, but there can have been few international matches where the result has been of less import to those watching.Explore more on these topicsRepublic of IrelandIsraelNations LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Falcons trample punchless Packers as Bijan Robinson runs riot in Penix return | NFL | The Guardian
description: Atlanta outrushed Green Bay 242-17 as Robinson starred and Michael Penix Jr returned from a torn ACL in a 35-14 rout at Lambeau Field
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Atlanta outrushed Green Bay 242-17 as Robinson starred and Michael Penix Jr returned from a torn ACL in a 35-14 rout at Lambeau Field
Content: Bijan Robinson celebrates with Atlanta Falcons teammate Chris Lindstrom after scoring a fourth-quarter touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field.Photograph: Geoff Stellfox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBijan Robinson celebrates with Atlanta Falcons teammate Chris Lindstrom after scoring a fourth-quarter touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field.Photograph: Geoff Stellfox/Getty ImagesNFLFalcons trample punchless Packers as Bijan Robinson runs riot in Penix returnRobinson rushes for 194 yards and two touchdownsPenix throws TD pass in return from torn ACLPackers’ 13-game home-opener winning streak endsAgenciesThu 24 Sep 2026 23.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBijan Robinson rushed for 194 yards and two touchdowns as the Atlanta Falcons capitalized on the return of quarterback Michael Penix Jr and trounced the punchlessGreen Bay Packers35-14 on Thursday night.Atlanta (1-2) erased an early 7-0 deficit by scoring 27 straight points to take control amid a chorus of boos at Lambeau Field. The Falcons outrushed the Packers 242 yards to 17.Former NFL star Antonio Brown to avoid possibility of 30 years in prison with plea dealRead moreGreen Bay (1-2) lost a home opener for the first time since falling 30-22 to the San Francisco 49ers in 2012. The Packers had won 13 straight home openers from 2013-25 to share theNFLrecord with the Miami Dolphins, who also won 13 in a row from 1976-88.Penix went 18 of 25 for 256 yards with one touchdown and an interception in his first action since tearing the ACL in his left knee during a loss to Carolina on 16 November. Atlanta (1-2) had struggled to produce any offense whatsoever with Cooper Rush starting at quarterback the first two weeks of the season.That wasn’t a problem Thursday.Robinson and Drake London became the first teammates to each compile at least 150 yards from scrimmage against the Packers at Lambeau Field. London caught nine passes for 194 yards.Green Bay’s Jordan Love went 28 of 53 for 312 yards with two touchdowns and an interception. MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson combined for 17 yards on eight carries.Love was working behind an offensive line missing left guard Aaron Banks and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, who tore his patellar tendon Sunday and will miss the rest of the season. Banks was dealing with a toe injury.Jager Burton, a rookie fifth-round pick from Kentucky, made his first career start at left guard, and 2025 second-round selection Anthony Belton started at right tackle.The lack of discipline that hindered Green Bay in its first two games cropped up again Thursday.View image in fullscreenMichael Penix Jr celebrates after leading the Atlanta Falcons to a 35-14 victory over the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field.Photograph: Mike Roemer/APGreen Bay led 7-0 and had forced an apparent third-and-11 incompletion late in the first quarter when Brenton Cox Jr was called for roughing the passer. Robinson delivered a 55-yard carry on the next play to set up his own three-yard touchdown run.The Packers had committed an NFL-high 26 penalties through the first two weeks of the season.Robinson long run allowed Atlanta to take a snap inside an opponent’s 20-yard line for the first time this season. Atlanta had been the first team since the 2008 Rams not to run any plays in the red zone through the first two weeks of a season.Atlanta dominated the rest of the first half and led 17-7 at the break.Nick Folk put Atlanta ahead by hitting a 44-yard field goal with 4:48 left in the second quarter. After Atlanta’s Zach Harrison blocked Trey Smack’s 47-yard field-goal attempt, Penix threw a five-yard touchdown pass to Austin Hooper on third-and-goal with 59 seconds left in the half.Green Bay wasted a red-zone opportunity on its first drive of the second half when Love couldn’t connect with Christian Watson in the end zone on fourth-and-1 from the 7. Atlanta extended the lead to 24-7 on its next possession, as Brian Robinson’s seven-yard touchdown run capped a 10-play, 92-yard drive.Folk added a 31-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter before Love threw a 15-yard touchdown pass to Matthew Golden with 8:18 remaining. Bijan Robinson capped the scoring with a two-yard TD.Explore more on these topicsNFLAtlanta FalconsGreen Bay PackersUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A lot of people counted me out’: Ashley Sanchez on goal records, grit and potential USWNT return | NWSL | The Guardian
description: After playing zero minutes at the 2023 World Cup, Sanchez embraced a new club and a new position. Now she’s making NWSL history in North Carolina
Author: Abigail Segel
Headline: After playing zero minutes at the 2023 World Cup, Sanchez embraced a new club and a new position. Now she’s making NWSL history in North Carolina
Content: Ashley Sanchez leads the NWSL’s Golden Boot race with 19 goals on the season.Photograph: Matt Kelley/NWSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAshley Sanchez leads the NWSL’s Golden Boot race with 19 goals on the season.Photograph: Matt Kelley/NWSL/Getty ImagesNWSLInterview‘A lot of people counted me out’: Ashley Sanchez on goal records, grit and potential USWNT returnAbigail SegelAfter playing zero minutes at the 2023 World Cup, the attacker embraced a new club, a new mindset and a new position. Now she’s making NWSL history in North CarolinaFri 25 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a familiar sight: Ashley Sanchez running at the left post, controlling a lofted cross, deftly finding a window between defenders and taking a quick shot to the inside of the far post beyond the reach of the goalkeeper. It’s how the North Carolina Courage winger has scored so many of her 19 goals this year. This would be her 20th, tying Temwa Chawinga’s 2024 record for most goals scored in anNWSLseason.But on Saturday against Gotham, it wasn’t meant to be. As Sanchez celebrated with her teammates and fans in the WakeMed Soccer Park stands updated their handmade “Sanchez Goal-O-Meter”, the center referee was summoned to the VAR monitor, and the goal was called off; Sanchez’s teammate Gianna Paul was a touch offside when the play began. No tied game, and no tied record.Saloons, school and specialty coffee: NWSL players enjoy new era of side hustlesRead more“I was just happy to tie [the game] up,” Sanchez told the Guardian of the moment the ball went in the net. “I honestly wasn’t really thinking about what that would mean until after, and I was like, ‘Oh, dang, I could have done it.’ It was a good goal. I was really upset that we didn’t tie the game up right then and there.”If that 20th goal comes, it’ll have been worth the wait. The same could be said of Sanchez’s season, the seventh of her professional career. She was on the US women’s national team’s 2023 World Cup roster, but didn’t see any playing time in Australia and New Zealand. Five months after that, after a dynamite four years with the Washington Spirit, she was traded to North Carolina without warning.Now, in the best form of her life, Sanchez, 27, doesn’t think about that turbulent year much. “I feel like I’m past that point. But when I look back at this season I’m like, ‘I guess I had to go through some tough times to get here.’ I always felt like there was a reason that I had to go through them – maybe that was character-building, or not taking things for granted,” she said. “When I look back now, I’m really happy those things happened because I have perspective now. But definitely at the time, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is the worst thing that’s ever happened to me.’”“I’ve always kind of felt like there was something bigger that was going to happen. I just felt like I needed to stay patient and have trust that whatever God was doing in my life was for a reason,” she said. “I tried to lean on to that because you can get really caught up in, ‘Oh my gosh, these things keep happening to me, and it’s really hard.’ And it was really hard. But I was very patient and I controlled what I could, and that was my effort.”The effort has paid off. Sanchez has already broken at least two records: the most NWSL goals scored in one season by an American, and most goals by a Courage player in one season.View image in fullscreenNo American player has scored more goals this NWSL season than Ashley Sanchez.Photograph: Jacob Kupferman/NWSL/Getty ImagesFor Sanchez, her goal tally has come as a welcome surprise. But someone in Cary, North Carolina, saw it coming. Mak Lind, the Courage’s first-year head coach, told Sanchez during preseason that she’d have a 20-goal season. “I was laughing,” Sanchez recalled of the moment. “He was like, ‘I don’t know why you’re laughing. I’m being serious.’”At the time, she thought about the players with NWSL goalscoring records and thought Lind’s statement was “insane”. Entering this year, Crystal Dunn and Alex Morgan held the American single-season record, with 15 goals in 2015 and 2022, respectively; Chawinga and Sam Kerr were the only players to score 17. Sanchez had never scored more than five in one season.“There’s a reason that there are these records that nobody’s touched,” she said. “It was my first time professionally playing on the wing. So I was like, ‘Hopefully I’ll score a lot of goals, but I don’t know if I’m going to hit 20.’”As it turns out, playing on the left wing is what unlocked the former attacking midfielder as a scoring virtuoso. “My coaches have helped me with a lot of little things that really helped me improve: my timing, what to look for, making runs in behind defenders, and different things like that,” she said. “But ultimately I do feel like this position really suits me and the skillsets that I have, and a lot of it does feel like second nature to me.”Sanchez’s natural instincts are a joy to watch. When she’s making a run, she considers if the defender is coming toward her, creating room for her to run in behind them once the ball arrives. “As soon as I’m dribbling, it’s just pretty natural for me. I don’t really know what I’m thinking in the moment, but as soon as I see them bite is when I’m like, ‘Now I can go,’” she said. “I basically just wait for them to make a move, and then I decide which way I’m going to go, whether that’s to the left or the right. Sometimes they give me the right [side] unexpectedly: ‘Guess I’m gonna take a shot now.’”After enough of those shots went in, about halfway through the season, Lind reminded Sanchez of his prediction. “I still didn’t think I was going to be able to double what I had already done,” she said.But soon enough, she couldn’t deny that her goalscoring pace was on its way to breaking records. “Sometimes some of these records seem untouchable, and then you just start picking away at it, and you’re like, ‘I guess I’m a little bit closer than I thought,’” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLind is the seventh head coach Sanchez has played under in her seven seasons in the NWSL. That managerial revolving door can make for difficult conditions to improve as a player, and Sanchez said it’s especially tough when coaches change midseason. It hasn’t been that way with Lind. The Lebanese-Swedish manager, in his first year in the NWSL, has offered stability to a team that had an abrupt head coaching change in the middle of 2025.View image in fullscreenAshley Sanchez last appeared for the USWNT in October 2024.Photograph: Hannah Peters/Getty Images“He’s just a really good person,” Sanchez said. “And I think when we all talk about it – he’s just so nice – we’re just like, ‘We need to protect him.’”The team’s respect for Lind as a person translates to respecting him as a coach, and it motivates the team on the pitch. “It’s the first time that I’ve been like, ‘Wow, I do want to win for him.’ … He puts a lot of trust and confidence in me and I want to reward how he treats his players,” Sanchez said. “He’s definitely the kindest coach I’ve ever had in my life.”Sanchez is happy to keep scoring if it means helping the seventh-place Courage reach the playoffs, but racking up goals and records isn’t her focus. “I think that the season I’ve had is already so great. And I just try to tell myself if it ended right now, I would still be happy,” she said. “And all the other stuff is kind of just extra at this point.”Chicago Stars make a splash as Vlatko Andonovski joins as chief soccer officerRead moreThere’s also the question that has swirled around American women’s soccer conversation for months now: will Emma Hayes call up Sanchez for the USWNT’s friendlies against Spain next month? Hayes has been clear that she has shifted from widening the national team pool to narrowing in on her roster for next year’s World Cup, and Sanchez’s last international appearance was in October 2024. But her club performance begs for attention.On Tuesday afternoon, Sanchez said she hadn’t yet heard from Hayes. While she’s thought about getting the call-up, she’s not dwelling on it. “The only thing I can do is just make it as hard as I possibly can for [Hayes] to make her decisions, and put myself in the best position to get called in or play in these games,” Sanchez said. “But ultimately it’s up to her and I have to be comfortable with it maybe not being good enough.”“For me to be able to get called back in – I think a lot of people, and maybe even myself, kind of counted me out. I think it would just be a testament to going through a little bit of a tough time and still being able to find your way back,” she added. “But I also think this season has been so incredible that even if I didn’t, I would still be so proud of what I’ve been able to do. It would feel like a little bit of an extra cherry on top. Obviously I would like to, but we’ll see.”Explore more on these topicsNWSLWomen's footballUS sportsUSA women's football teaminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli hits wall as George Russell takes F1 Azerbaijan GP pole | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kimi Antonelli crashed out in Q1 while his Mercedes teammate George Russell was in brilliant form, taking pole in Baku by 0.837 from Charles Leclerc
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Kimi Antonelli crashed out in Q1 while his Mercedes teammate George Russell was in brilliant form, taking pole in Baku by 0.837 from Charles Leclerc
Content: George Russell with his pole position award after qualifying for the F1 Azerbaijan GP.Photograph: Bryn Lennon/Formula 1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell with his pole position award after qualifying for the F1 Azerbaijan GP.Photograph: Bryn Lennon/Formula 1/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli hits wall as George Russell takes F1 Azerbaijan GP poleChampionship leader Antonelli crashes out in Q1Mercedes teammate takes pole by 0.837 from LeclercGiles RichardsFri 25 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor all his youth, such has been Kimi Antonelli’s consummate control this season he has barely put a foot wrong. In qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, however, he was given a salutary reminder that the full-on commitment that makes him so engrossing to watch can still bite.The F1 championship leader was disconsolate at being eliminated after hitting the wall in the first session but with his Mercedes teammateGeorge Russellon pole it has set up a potentially fascinating showdown for Saturday’s race.George Russell on pole for Azerbaijan GP after F1 leader Antonelli crashes out – live updatesRead moreAntonelli’s error was uncharacteristic and, he conceded, unnecessary. He knows his lead in the championship – 81 points over Russell – is such that he need take no chances, especially at a track where Mercedes enjoy such a huge advantage over their rivals. Russell’s pole, an immense lap of the street circuit in Baku, was eight-tenths clear of Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc in second, the largest margin to pole of the season.Antonelli has been a revelation in only his second season in F1 with eight victories so far but on Friday in Baku he was sat disconsolately trackside after only 11 minutes of running. A little too eager into the 90-degree left-handed turn one, he clipped the barrier.He took damage to the track rod and a puncture and while he attempted to bring the car home, he was told to park up by a race engineer Pete Bonnington. “We can’t fix this, mate,” Bonnington said. The 20-year-old’s time was enough to see him through to Q2, in which he took no part. Finishing in 16th and angry with himself he held his hands up to the error, caught out as the grip ramped up.“I turned in and suddenly I had a lot more front end than the lap before and touched the wall,” he said. “Mistake from my side, very unnecessary. I’m very mad about it and we’ll try to do better tomorrow. We’ll try our best to recover as many places as possible.”The mistake is Antonelli’s only serious error this year since he crashed in final practice at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix and he was understandably crestfallen, aware a fractional misjudgment had been enormously costly.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli’s broken front left is clearly visible as he tries in vain to get back to the pits.Photograph: Michael Potts/LAT ImagesRussell in is every position to take advantage and to try to claw back some of the points he desperately needs to keep the title fight alive but Antonelli knows that the race is far from a write-off.At Monza hecame back from 19th to take victoryand Baku, with its long straights, has similarly generous opportunities for overtaking.
