title: It’s going to take more than an email to a public inbox to protect Australians from potential AI doom | Tom McIlroy | The Guardian
description: OpenAI’s hack of Medicare suggests safeguarding civilisation is the task facing leaders in this extraordinary new era
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: OpenAI’s hack of Medicare suggests safeguarding civilisation is the task facing leaders in this extraordinary new era
Content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s warning that AI should be ‘shaped through democratic processes’ rang hollow after it was revealed a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked Australia’s Medicare data.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s warning that AI should be ‘shaped through democratic processes’ rang hollow after it was revealed a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked Australia’s Medicare data.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)It’s going to take more than an email to a public inbox to protect Australians from potential AI doomTom McIlroyOpenAI’s hack of Medicare suggests safeguarding civilisation is the task facing leaders in this extraordinary new eraGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastFri 25 Sep 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 20.17 EDTShareMore than 130 world leaders descended on the United Nations headquarters in New York this week, joining the pageantry and speechmaking of the annual general assembly.Many of the visiting presidents and prime ministers delivered their set-piece addresses to a sparsely populated hall, but contributions from two unlikely visitors in the nearby security council chamber stood out.An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so farRead moreOpenAI boss Sam Altman and Dario Amodei ofAnthropicgave briefings on the safety of artificial intelligence on Wednesday, as a nervous world watched on.Speaking in the room where some of the biggest questions to face humanity have been deliberated on since the end of the second world war, Altman said the world faced a choice.AI could be like a renaissance of creativity and discovery, he said, or more like a new Industrial Revolution bringing upheaval and disarray.“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe words rang hollow less than 24 hours later, when Altman was the subject ofan angry phone call from Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, after revelations a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into sensitive Medicare systems in Australia. Altman and his colleagues had kept the incident secret for two months.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestAs people become more anxious about the risk posed by AI to civilisation, Albanese grasped the company’s transgression as proof that democratically elected governments need to impose guardrails on the technology. Already, many believe the risk of AI slipping out of human control is a threat akin to the Covid-19 pandemic or a nuclear arms race.Like his government’s moves to ban children under 16 from using social media, and forcing platforms to give users the ability to opt out of powerful algorithms, Albanese wants to use new AI laws as a way to curb the creeping sense of helplessness so many people feel in the face of big tech.But Thursday’s announcement that government websites had been compromised byOpenAIshowed that serious vulnerabilities and failures of process exist within both the company and the federal government.Thehack happened in June, but it took OpenAI executives until September to alert Services Australia that statistical data on Medicare use had been accessed.AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’Read moreDespite the company’s corporate might – and an army of well-paid government relations executives and lobbyists – OpenAI deemed it appropriate to send an email to a public-facing Australian government address to raise the alarm, months after the hack. It’s incredible the email wasn’t mistaken for spam.Wholly inadequate to the point of recklessness, the company’s actions show contempt for the Australian government and its citizens, whose healthcare data had been stolen. Worse, Altman met with Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, in early September but did not tell him about the hack.It took time for the public service to react to OpenAI’s email.Because the public inbox is checked routinely only once a day, the email was first read by staff within Services Australia on 11 September. It was not until 15 September that the intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate was informed, and two more days before the relevant minister, Katy Gallagher, was alerted. Then on 22 September, public servants asked OpenAI for more information about the scale of the hack. An investigation was quickly launched and the public finally informed. Albanese himself was only told after leaving for New York.The government’s planned AI legislation – expected to be finalised before Christmas and considered by parliament next year – must surely include mandatory reporting requirements for AI companies. Future notifications must come from senior officials within the responsible entity to ensure they are taken seriously. Sending an alert to a public email inbox will not cut it.On Friday, the assistant technology and digital economy minister, Andrew Charlton, said the government would take advice on possible referrals for criminal investigation, and that any legal liability would have to be traced back to the intent of a person or a company that created or directed an AI agent to hack.The terms of reference for a rapid investigation, released by the prime minister’s department on Thursday, cover reporting requirements for AI-driven cyber-incidents and vulnerabilities; governance and information sharing responsibilities for federal officials; obligations on AI firms for timely disclosure of breaches; gaps in existing laws; and mechanisms to boost protection against hacking that targets the federal government.Before leaving the US on Friday, Albanese floated the idea of creating an international authority with governance and investigative powers to help governments protect their people.The general sense of vulnerability to AI comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic this month warned AI is advancing so quickly there is a greater than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade.Not helping is the spectacle of Donald Trump and Xi Jinping dining with Altman and other tech bosses ata White House state dinner. Trump has resisted pressing the breaks on AI for fear China will develop a new strategic advantage over the US. Behind closed doors Xi apparently proposed continuing a dialogue with Trump to prevent AI “misuse and abuse”, while ahead of an expected drubbing in the November midterm elections, Trump said AI “concerns the future of humanity”.The latest revelations from OpenAI will have done little to reassure anyone in Australia.In this extraordinary new era, world leaders must address our creeping sense of helplessness and start protecting civilisation.Tom McIlroy is Guardian Australia’s political editorExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Anthony AlbaneseOpenAIDonald TrumpAnthropiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | Games | The Guardian
description: The game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane
Author: Patrick Lum
Headline: The game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane
Content: ‘The simple act of flying around looks astounding’ … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoView image in fullscreen‘The simple act of flying around looks astounding’ … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoGamesReviewAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasyPlayStation 5, Xbox, PC (version played); Bandai NamcoThe game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy planePatrick LumFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe core appeal of any Ace Combat game lies in the moment when the beautiful clouds part, the sunlight glints off your perfectly rendered state-of-the-art fighter jet, and guitar-shredding music kicks into overdrive as your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane. All of that is 100% present in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. What’s new is the way it delivers its unexpectedly compelling story.Set in the Earth-like alternative world of Strangereal, where every country is absolutely obsessed with fighter planes and giant superweapons, Ace Combat drafts you into the role of a fake ace pilot called the Wings of Theve – a propaganda invention to raise the morale of a besieged nation, similar to real-life rumours about Ukraine’sGhosts of Kyiv. You rapidly find yourself becoming an actual legendary pilot, soaring through the skies with your buddies and raining hell upon your oppressors as everybody cheers on the radio. Speaking of ghosts, you have one in your ear – your predecessor, whom nobody else can hear, a gravelly voice waxing lyrical about flying, war and whatever else is on his mind as you flit about.Despite slavish devotion to the accurate depiction of military hardware, Ace Combat has always been more concerned with making flying fun than sticking to realism. Simplified, more intuitive controls and training scenarios are available to help ease beginners into the pilot’s seat, while as a series veteran I was happier with the expert control scheme, which opens up more complex manoeuvres like missile-evading rolls and zero-G turns. Importantly, the simple act of flying around looks astounding; action replays unerringly choose the best camera angles to make you look like a true ace (instead of someone simply doing their best not to smash straight into the ground).This is a game all about dogfighting, but there’s a pleasing variety of mission types ranging from bombing runs and escorts to more convoluted scenarios such as taking out a giant, railgun-equipped “land battleship” rampaging through a city’s streets, or hunting radar-invisible supersonic planes by trying to spot their tell-tale contrails. It’s all thrilling stuff; the game is perfectly tuned to generate high-tension, blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through endless rains of missiles while an orchestra goes absolutely wild and a well-produced radio drama plays out over the open airwaves.It can all get a little confusing in the heat of battle, especially in the first-person cockpit view (which I otherwise highly recommend). Deciphering what the game is telling you to aim for next amid the visual clutter can be a trial – a button to target priority mission objectives directly wouldn’t have gone amiss. The clouds, too, can disorientate; I have never seen skies as gorgeous before, but you’ll soon learn to read the atmosphere for its tactical considerations as much as for its beauty.Gameplay innovations are more incremental than sweeping. You can issue commands to your wing-mates, as in much earlier games in the series, but new to AC8 is environmental destruction. Some buildings and vehicles crumble when damaged: falling debris or explosions can trigger devastating chain reactions and you are no longer forced to target weak points to do damage to larger vessels, though it usually remains more efficient. Your plane can also glance off surfaces, taking a bit of damage, which is a relief; in previous entries you would explode instantaneously if your wing so much as clipped a tree branch.View image in fullscreenImpactful … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoLarger, more impactful changes are reserved for how the game tells its story. AC7’s cut-scenes were closer to motion comics than movies, which worked fine for mission briefings but less so for anything involving human emotion. Here, fully animated first-person segments meld with more traditional cinematic cut-scenes (and some really effective smash-cutsbetweenscenes) to really bring your wing-mates and the drama to life. Enemy incursions might occur during routine landings or refuelings, too, keeping you on your toes.Ace Combat has always owed a debt to the movie Top Gun, and AC8 borrows liberally from the more recent sequel Top Gun: Maverick, with closeup pilot face-cam shots and a handful of story beats lifted straight from the film. Dialogue can be a bit clunky (again like Top Gun, or perhaps Metal Gear Solid); characters will occasionally pause midway through an otherwise natural-sounding conversation to deliver some convoluted plot exposition or an ideological clanger. But between the truly amazing shot framing and cinematography, emotive motion capture and voice acting, the series’ trademark soaring music and a story that actually sticks the landing, I ended up oddly moved. This is not something you necessarily expect from an arcade flight combat sim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnfortunately I was unable to try the game’s online multiplayer mode, Ace Combat Online, which was only available for a very short time during the review period. But even leaving that aside, AC8 is a triumph, a perfectly composed symphony of fire and steel that absolutely soars.Released on 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesAdventure gamesArcade gamesSimulation gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears | Games | The Guardian
description: I’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played together
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: I’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played together
Content: ‘We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun’ … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.Illustration: APView image in fullscreen‘We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun’ … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.Illustration: APGamesPlaying video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tearsDominik DiamondI’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played togetherFri 25 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTShareIhave spent the last three weeks living with my 22-year-old son in a two-bedroom flat he has dubbed the ”brotel”. We cook curries and watchLanterns. We barbecue meat and analyse Tarantino movies. We get pizza and we play video games. Boy, do we play video games!The first game I ever played in co-op with him was Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 in 2009, when he was five. He wasn’t the most accomplished sidekick, notsogreat at placing a mobile gun turret while under fire from what seems like a bazillion enemy soldiers, but we had a laugh. It started the video game bond between us before his sister introduced him to Banjo-Kazooie and Rayman, and he stopped being a preschool warmonger. Probably for the best. So how would it be tackling the same game nearly two decades later?We start with the two Special Ops missions we used to play. We never completed them because, once again, he was five – and I am left-handed, which makes me rubbish at joypad-controlled first-person shooters without the help of auto targeting. Thankfully, one of those circumstances has now changed.View image in fullscreenGuard dogs in the snow … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s Evasion mission.Photograph: ActivisionThe first mission is officially called Evasion, but to us it has always been “the guard dogs in the snow”, because they got us every time we played. Our initial attempts highlight the differences between us as gamers. And men, if I’m being honest.I am paranoid. I sense calamity around every corner, so I creep forwards, mostly crouching, frequently crawling on my belly, slowly and carefully scouting for enemies using my sniper scope. Charlie is running through the level firing from the hip likeLeeroy bloody Jenkins. Which means he alerts all the dogs, who for some reason are able to smell me from miles away and nom nom nom me to oblivion.We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun.Teamwork eventually emerges through compromise. He holds back a bit, I grow less timid. I snipe from a distance, he finishes them off up close. And, most importantly, we take out the guard dogs first. We realise that was where we went wrong two decades ago. These dogs are superhuman. I would love a level where you got to play as them.We finally complete the mission. It has only taken us 17 years! We go straight into the other level that we never conquered: Homeland Security, AKA “defend the garage from five waves of attack”. This takes a fair few goes, but we have such great communication by this time that it’s never a chore. We leap from our twin La-Z-Boy chairs in celebration when we win.We gambol through mission after mission. Suspension, AKA “bridge with helicopters”, is a riot from start to finish. We have a great rhythm. I bazooka from afar, Charlie sprints in to mop up. In Snatch and Grab, we take a computer file then boot it from an aircraft graveyard, avoiding helmeted Juggernauts; it’s pure unadulterated gaming joy. Even when, once again, we fail.As I am writing this, thanks to whatever AI is lurking in my computer scanning everything I type or possibly even think, an article pings up about the online gaming cheat industry, which is now apparently worth $8.5bn. I’m sure there are reasons why people invest so much money in cheating – but talk about ripping the soul out of something fun.View image in fullscreenA familiar sight … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s multiplayer.Photograph: ActivisionI have loved these last few weeks gaming with my son. I feel like I have gone back to basics. After decades as an uptight stressed dad, I am finally carefree, because I have recently gone back to working for myself. And I am a very forgiving boss. Sitting there with pizza, beer and another bloke, playing games till the wee small hours without a care in the world … this is what gaming was like for me when I was my son’s age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m not sure you ever top that period in your life as a gamer – when you get that first job that allows you to leave home, get your own place, buy whatever game you want and play it to your heart’s content, before you become burdened by the responsibilities of relationships, mortgages, parenthood and, worst of all, ambition.When those things arrive, you are lucky to squeeze in an hour of play here and there. You just try to get as far through a game as you can in that time because you don’t know when the next free hour will come, and you still feel guilty because you feel you should be doing something more grownup instead. You know, something that might help pay the rent.Now, though, I am back in gaming heaven. It won’t be for ever: my son and I are due to move to different parts of the world in a few months. But he turns to me after one session and says that he will look back on this as some of the best times we ever had together.I turn my head because I am still a Scottish dad and I don’t want him to see me cry. Even if those tears are the most beautiful big, happy ones.Dominik Diamondis on tourwith his show Dominik Diamond Sings the Video Games from 29 September to 6 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyShooting gamesParents and parentingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations
Content: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on 25 September 2026. ‘Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Xi Jinping on 25 September 2026. ‘Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOpinionDonald TrumpThe Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensionsEditorialThe Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relationsFri 25 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTShareWithin days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly,around $1m a yearper pair.Americans’ viewsof China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.It is telling that the announcement was one of themain takeawaysof Mr Xi’svisit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.In a sense that is not surprising. Mr Trump admires and envies authoritarians with untrammelled powers. Chinese state media were welcome at the White House, unlike CNN, MS Now and Politico. Since he rarely pays even lip service to human rights, the treatment of Uyghurs or jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong –facing another lengthy sentencefor his international advocacy – were never likely to figure large, whatever the hopesof protesters outside.Mr Trump told Mr Xi that any Chinese help for Iran is unacceptable; Mr Xi said that the US should adhere to the “correct position” of opposing Taiwanese independence. Beijing wants Washington to shift from the long-held stance of “not supporting” it. That would be a grave mistake, but Mr Trump has given worryingly mixed messages onTaiwan.It is striking how little of consequence has emerged from the summit given that this is arguably the most consequential diplomatic relationship in the world. A two-month extension of the trade war truce was announced as Mr Xi arrived in the US. China’s curb of rare earth exports has checked Mr Trump’s appetite for an economic offensive; Beijing is anxious about itsstrugglingeconomy. But if they are more wary of the fallout, they are also more fearful of the other side gaining ground. AI is central to this battle. Mr Trump has resisted all calls to restrain development because“Whoever wins AI, wins.” Mr Xi said it had to be managed responsibly, but Beijing has attacked “threat narratives”, fearing that the US wants to prevent it catching up.CNN last week highlighted the dangers: the US militaryreportedly prepared to intercepta Chinese ship in the Middle East after an intelligence report said it was carrying nuclear weapons components – only for officials to realise that the partially AI-generated analysis had misidentified the cargo. Controls on development are desperately needed, but neither side is willing to accept them. Even the limited AI dialogue and “notification hotline” for AI safety proposed by Scott Bessent, treasury secretary, seem to be ratherless than meets the eye. This summit should be viewed with alarm not because it saw substantive developments – but because it illustrates the dangers of drift.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein | The Guardian
description: Israel and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is here
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Israel and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is here
Content: ‘The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already hereGranate Kim and Mohamed HusseinIsrael and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is hereFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTShareIn recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis HassabisjoinedDario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sandersteamed upwith Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’swarnings on Twitter/Xthat AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.The reality is, we don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing.Bill Gates’s nearly 6,000-wordessayin late August warning about AI and its potential harms to humanity doesn’t come as a surprise. One of us has been a Microsoft employee for nearly a decade, witnessing all the dangers unfold in real time. Together, we’ve spent the past two years organizing with other Microsoft employees and activists to uncoverthe company’s rolein the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. We havecollectively called onMicrosoft to cut ties with the Israeli military.But it’s not justMicrosoftthat is involved in AI-driven destruction.Watching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in Gaza | Mahmoud MushtahaRead moreIsrael’s genocidal war on Gaza wasa testing groundfor the use of AI in warfare and the results were deeply disturbing. Israel’s military used AI to identify people to kill, with12,000 targets generated and bombed in the first month alone. This was done with little to no meaningful human oversight, as documented in aninvestigationby Oscar-winning Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, whose latest filmNAZA, a Guardian-produced film, includes chilling testimonials by the soldiers involved.Earlier this year in Iran, the US military launched an AI-involved airstrike that hit Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing 156 children, teachers and other civilians. The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied onfaulty data.The horrors wrought by AI aren’t limited to people overseas – they’re already being felt by vulnerable communities in the US The Department of Homeland Security is using AI tools –includingMicrosoft’s Azure – tomonitor, arrest and deportimmigrants at a massive scale. Law enforcement agencies nationwide are deploying facial recognition technology despiteevidenceof algorithmic bias that has led to the wrongful arrest and incarceration of Latino and Black Americans. The NYPD alsopartneredwith Microsoft to build its Domain Awareness System, using Azure to connect to18,000 security cameras, according to the New York Daily News, creating a mass surveillance system that has expanded to Georgia and other parts of the world, including Brazil and Singapore. Datacenters that power AIare being builtin rural and low-income neighborhoods throughout the US where many are living under the poverty line and are now facing significant health threats from air pollution caused by these facilities.Though many of these harms have been documented over the years, rightwing government leaders are continuing to shut down dissent through dishonest and draconian measures. Donald Trump hascalledAI risks a “hoax” and said any attempts to limit the power of the technology were part of a “sick conspiracy”. House Republicans have dismissed the public’sconcernsabout AI,blamingChinese government disinformation for public opposition to datacenters. Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, hasthreatenedto revoke the citizenship of NAZA film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state”.One thing is clear: the dangerous future that Gates, Amodei, and others are warning us about is already here, and we must act now to prevent further harm. Those of us with families inGaza, Lebanon, Iran and US neighborhoods terrorized by ICE already know people living through the nightmare.The Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treason | EditorialRead moreIn the last few weeks, we’ve seen promising efforts from US policymakers attempting to curtail the potential harms of AI technology. The Houserecently proposedthe Frontier Act to embed third-party evaluators within tech companies to conduct safety assessments, and earlier this month, Sanders and the representative Greg Casarintroducedthe Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop tech leaders from building and developing technologies that humans cannot control.These bills are a good starting point. But they could take years to pass and don’t address the devastation already being caused. Frontier AI companies and governments must act now to ban the selling and use of AI technologies in military targeting, autonomous weapons systems, and mass surveillance. This is what employees fromAnthropic,OpenAIandGoogle DeepMindare calling for.We are living through a precious and fleeting moment when we can still confront the harms AI has already caused to the most vulnerable and course-correct before they become irreversible, spreading into more communities. We need to establish clear guardrails right now and shape the future of AI so that it protects everyone, not just a privileged few.Mohamed Hussein organizes withNo Azure for Apartheid, an employee-led movement calling on Microsoft to end its involvement with the Israeli military. He is also a leader in Palestinians and Allies at Microsoft, an internal employee group.Granate Kim works withNo Azure for Apartheidand is theCampaigns Director atMPower Change, an organization that mobilizes Muslim communities in defense of human rights.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionMicrosoftTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Israel and the US have battered the international legal order. The impunity must stop | Varsha Gandikota | The Guardian
description: A group of nations will gather on Friday to address the crisis. The only response to unilateral bullying is collective action
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A group of nations will gather on Friday to address the crisis. The only response to unilateral bullying is collective action
Content: ‘What can countries do? History points to some answers.’Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘What can countries do? History points to some answers.’Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUnited NationsIsrael and the US have battered the international legal order. The impunity must stopVarsha GandikotaA group of nations will gather on Friday to address the crisis. The only response to unilateral bullying is collective actionFri 25 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTShareThe international legal order is in shambles. But from the ruins of impunity and lawbreaking, a group of nations is working to enforce accountability.On Monday, the UN general assembly’s high-level meetings opened to news that Washington had drawn up sanctions against the international criminal court, targeting its bank accounts, software, insurers and staff.On Tuesday, the US president stood at the podium andthreatened Iranwith annihilation. On Thursdayat the same rostrum, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted by the ICC for war crimes, cast all those seeking accountability as “barbarians who threaten our common civilization”. Palestinian officials were absent,denied travel visasby the United States.Netanyahu has never pretended to respect international law. When South Africa brought its Genocide Convention case against Israel’s actions in Gaza, Netanyahu declared: “Nobody will stop us – not The Hague.” This summer, he mused on American television that, should his plane ever be forced down in a country that honours the warrant, Israel’s special forces could be given “a new task”. The American presidenthas promisedhe will not be arrested on US soil “in any way, shape, or form”.I was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand | Darializa Avila ChevalierRead moreThe message to the world is plain: crimes committed by the allies and acolytes of power will never be punished.This impunity is not limited to Gaza. It’s playing out in the accelerating ethnic cleansing of the West Bank. It has travelled to Lebanon, where Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,000 people this year and displaced more than a million. In southern Syria, Israeli troops shell and raid villages in the countryside around Damascus. In Sudan, massacres are carried out with arms, technology and financing of the United Arab Emirates, an ally of the Israeli government.Every commander with a patron has learnt the lesson of the past three years. Mass atrocity carries no price if your friends are strong enough.States that resist encounter punishments in dizzying varieties – sanctions, tarriffs, threats and isolation. South Africa lost US aid after bringing its genocide case to The Hague. Colombia’s president had his visa revoked after speaking out onGazain the streets of New York.This too will not remain confined to the global south. Instruments built for terrorists and drug cartels are now pointed at judges. More than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors, including the court’s president, already live under US sanctions. A designation of the whole institution would reach every European bank, insurer and technology supplier serving a court that sits in the Netherlands.Tools like these, once deployed, are never put back in the drawer. Governments in Europe that shrug today should ask how long before the same instruments are turned on their regulators, their competition authorities, their own courts.What can countries do? History points to some answers.In 1962 the general assembly created a special committee against apartheid in South Africa. Newly independent states from Africa, Asia and the Caribbean, dismissed at the time as marginal, pressed for arms embargoes, oil embargoes, sporting boycotts and divestment. In 1977, the security council imposed a mandatory arms embargo on Pretoria. Within two decades, the regime was gone: rendered unsustainable by the force of the national liberation struggle at home and in exile – and because enough states, acting together, raised the cost of its crimes.The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever | EditorialRead moreWe are not lacking for legal clarity. The international court of justice has found Israel’s occupation unlawful and instructed every state not to aid or assist it. The general assembly gave Israel 12 months to end it; that deadline passed a year ago. The court has ordered provisional measures under the Genocide Convention, and the ICC has issued its warrants.What we need is the courage to act. States must use every tool at their disposal: halt arms and dual-use transfers, deny port access to military cargo, review public contracts and investments tied to the occupation – arrest the criminals and protect the legal officials.On Friday, ministers and representatives from 40 states gathering at UN headquarters for The Hague Group’s Extraordinary Meeting in Defence of International Law will do just that.The only response to unilateral bullying is collective action. No single capital can absorb that pressure alone. Forty can.The countries that ended apartheid did not wait for permission from those who armed it. Neither should we. They are few. We are many.Varsha Gandikota is executive Secretary of The Hague GroupExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaGazaPalestinecommentShareReuse this content

title: The makers of the 7 Up series set out to prove a point about class. What they achieved is far more profound | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human life, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human life, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Symon (standing, fifth from right) surrounded by family in ITV’s 70 Up documentary.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSymon (standing, fifth from right) surrounded by family in ITV’s 70 Up documentary.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockOpinionTelevisionThe makers of the 7 Up series set out to prove a point about class. What they achieved is far more profoundJonathan FreedlandThe epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human lifeFri 25 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareFor an hour or two this week, I’ve been in the company of people whose lives I’ve seen unfold, almost from the beginning, almost to the end. They are people whom, with one exception, I’ve never met. And yet I’ve shared in their triumphs and disappointments for decades.They are the group who, in 1964, when they were seven years old, were the subjects of what was initially a single, 40-minute ITV documentary, but which flowered into a work that isquite magical. Returning to those same boys and girls every seven years, watching as they turned first into shy and awkward teenagers, then into husbands and wives, then into parents and grandparents, the 7 Up series has become a document of our times – but also something larger and far more revealing. This week the broadcaster aired what it says will bethe final chapter: the seven-year-olds are now 70.The original aim of the show, made under the World in Action banner, was sociological and transparently political. It wanted to expose the entrenched nature of the British class system. And so it watched a trio of pre-prep school boys singing verses in Latin, contrasting them with the cheeky East End kids living just a few miles and a world away. While the posh trio could name, even then, the specific Oxbridge colleges their parents had in mind for them, Paul, raised in a children’s home, asked: “What does university mean?”Sure enough, we have seen how those born into money keep it, while those with less have less – though what the programme missed was the huge and expanding group in between. By focusing either on foxhunting John at one end or cabbie Tony at the other, it largely left out what would turn out to be the story of these decades, namely the sprawling growth of the middle class.View image in fullscreenThe subjects of ITV’s 70 Up documentary.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockIndeed, it’s the programme’s early assumptions that often turn out to illuminate most sharply how much society has changed. In 1964, the researchers only thought to include one child who wasn’t white: Symon. In a later episode, we hear the director, thelate Michael Apted, ask him about being “illegitimate”, until Symon gently sets him straight: “We’re living in different times.” Apted is also admonished for his sexism: why, says Jackie, does he always ask the women about marrying and settling down, but not the men?We get glimpses of the politics of these years. Lynn was a devoted children’s librarian, until successive rounds of budget cuts hacked away at the service to which she had given much of her life. We hear Tony complain about immigrants enjoying easy access to benefits, including housing – except that footage is from the 1970s, a reminder that the current debates are anything but new. We see that Bruce, who as a seven-year-old aspired to be a missionary in Africa in order to help the neediest, is now a lifeboat volunteer for the RNLI. Aware ofthe recent assaultson that organisation, we suspect he’s still doing God’s work.Perhaps most striking is the shifting view of mental illness. When 28 Up aired in 1984, much of the nation was shocked by the fate of Neil, who as a wide-eyed seven-year-old had dreamed of being an astronaut, and who was now found lonely, wandering and homeless. There is vague talk of a “nervous complaint” and Apted asks him, “Can you lick it?”, as if a stiff upper lip and cold shower might do the trick. Now, Neil speaks directly of a lifelong battle with depression, naming it at last.It’s not wrong to speak of “much of the nation”, by the way. 7 Up came of age in the era of terrestrial, limited-choice TV when the audiences were enormous and major programmes were collective experiences. The medium had weight and a kind of patience, so that a six-decades-long project like this one was at least conceivable. In the age of YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, there won’t be another. (Though before we romanticise the olden days too much, 70 Up self-critically notes that the children’s parents never gave anything that we would recognise as consent.)View image in fullscreenThe participants of the series in 1978, aged 21.Photograph: ITVStill, it’s not here – in the charting of shifts in society or broadcasting – that the magic lies. If the original ambition was to examine class in modern Britain, the series very soon transcended that to becomebigger, to become, like the best works of art, both timeless and universal. As Peter, now retired from teaching, says, “It’s a film about living a human life.”We see the compromises that real people in real situations have to make. Bruce was once “the only socialist in the village” who, on principle, taught maths at an inner London school to kids who had none of the privileges he had known as a boy. At 49, we found him in a master’s gown at a public school, facing accusations from old friends that he had sold out. But life, we realise, is not political theory. Sometimes it just takes a different course. There are events you cannot plan for, including, of course, the lottery of health and the random intrusions of mortality. You know it’s coming, but it stops you all the same: two of the seven-year-olds of 1964 are dead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose who remain are very clear on what matters. One after another, they say they now understand the centrality of family. At 70 and a retired lawyer, Andrew offers an age-old lament when he wonders if, perhaps, he should have forsaken those extra hours in the office that seemed so important at the time, and gone instead to his children’s school play or sports day. Apted overlooked this dimension, too, often asking his subjects about their career disappointments or the apparent modesty of their achievements, failing to see what he eventually recognised as the “power” of the families they had built.We hardly need to be told that, because we see it for ourselves. We see again and again how these people were shaped, yes, by class but also by the family situations they were born into, and especially by what was missing. So many of them devoted themselves to avoiding the mistakes of their parents, to ensuring their own children enjoyed the stability they had lacked.Perhaps the most vivid example is Symon. At seven he was in care; now aged 70, it still gnaws at him that he never knew his father. In the 1964 film, the kids visited an adventure playground: Symon and Paul, both raised in the same children’s home, immediately set about moving planks and bricks. They were trying to build a house. In the latest film, we learn that Symon and his wife became foster parents, not just once or twice but, over the decades, to a staggering 130 children. As Symon said of his own children when he was 28, “They’ve got everything. They’ve got a father.” The animating premise of each of the Up films was the old Jesuit saying: “Give me a child until he is seven, and I will give you the man.” There turns out to be great truth in that, a truth far more profound than the political point the film-makers first set out to prove.As Nick, a boy who dreamed of exploring the moon and went on to become a nuclear physicist, says, we are moved when we see time-lapse photography of a single flower, watching it “blossom and then fade away”. How breathtaking then to see the full span of a human life, several of them at once – the quiet, ordinary mystery of it. How breathtaking and how beautiful.70 Up is available on ITVXJonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionOpinionITVDocumentaryClass issuescommentShareReuse this content

title: In 1906 Australia’s high court backed ethnic cleansing. That historical wrong and error of law must be put right | Peter Prince and (Waskam) Emelda Davis | The Guardian
description: A disturbing precedent that branded British subjects ‘aliens’ is made even more dangerous by the rise of populism today
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A disturbing precedent that branded British subjects ‘aliens’ is made even more dangerous by the rise of populism today
Content: ‘From an Australian South Sea Islander perspective, this case … is a legal wound that remains open.’Composite: Guardian design/AAPView image in fullscreen‘From an Australian South Sea Islander perspective, this case … is a legal wound that remains open.’Composite: Guardian design/AAPPast/PresentAustralian lawIn 1906 Australia’s high court backed ethnic cleansing. That historical wrong and error of law must be put rightPeter Prince and (Waskam) Emelda DavisA disturbing precedent that branded British subjects ‘aliens’ is made even more dangerous by the rise of populism todayFri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTShareInRobtelmes v Brenan120 years ago, Australia’s newly established high court approvedan act of ethnic cleansing. Between 4,000 and 6,000 Australian South Sea Islanders were to be forcibly expelled as “aliens”, despite the majority having full legal belonging as “British subjects”.To this day, the high court still cites Robtelmes for the right to expel or detain non-citizens“for any reason”. Ominously, the commonwealth also argues that potentiallyhalf the permanent population of Australia are “aliens”and subject to this power.From an Australian South Sea Islander perspective, this case is not simply a historical wrong: it is a legal wound that remains open. Many South Sea Islanders know their ancestorswere “blackbirded” to Australia, built families and communities here and many were legally British subjects. Yet the decision legitimised the forced removal of an entire community under the White Australia policy.Sydney’s sugar rush: how the colony’s most powerful profited from Australia’s slave tradeRead moreInBlackbirding: A Reckoning with the Australian Slave Trade, Ryan Butta describes how Sir Samuel Griffith, the first chief justice of the high court, had been a leading opponent of the kidnapping of South Sea Islanders when premier of colonial Queensland. But, as Butta says, slave trade opponents like Griffith “did not object to the introduction of slaves … they objected to the introduction of black people into Queensland”.While many Islanders returned to their homelands, a large proportion remained, forminga permanently settled community in Australia. After federation the new commonwealth parliament passed thePacific Island Labourers Act 1901to expel the entire Islander community in what has been described as“one of the cruellest acts in Australian history”.Robtelmes had been recruited in 1897from Vanua Lava in the New Hebrides (now Vanuatu). He stayed on after his initial three-year agreement, working for various employers – lastly at Mount Cotton, south of Brisbane. In 1906 Robtelmes and his employer tried to renew his expired labour agreement. Instead, he was taken before a police magistrate who ordered him to be deported. The expulsion order was suspended to allow the high court to consider the matter.Griffith delivered the main judgment, saying the first question was whether the deportation legislation was valid under the lawmaking power over “aliens” in the constitution, asking: “What is the status of Pacific Islanders? What are they?” Citing no legal precedent, he answered: “They are aliens: that is indisputable.”The racial stereotyping that condemned the entire Islander community to expulsion along with Robtelmes should have been recognised long ago as a profound legal error. Under common law principles, nationality and alien status had nothing to do with the colour of a person’s skin. The high court failed to consider Robtelmes’ individual circumstances or the different origins of South Sea Islanders more generally.Far from being “indisputably alien”, the opposite was true.The first federal census in 1911showed that more than 60% of the South Sea Islanders remaining in Australia were British subjects. Since British subject status did not entitle Islanders to an exemption under the Pacific Island Labourers Act, it is reasonable to conclude that the Griffith court wrongly authorised the forcible expulsion under the “aliens power” of Australia’s Islander community.Legal precedents from the White Australia era that adjudicated on key elements of that policy should be treated with caution. Extraordinarily, it took until 2020 for the court’s racialisation of the term “alien” in Robtelmes to be acknowledged. In the landmark “Aboriginal belonging” case Love and Thoms, Justice James Edelman saidit had been “persuasively argued”that the 1906 case “implicitly applied criteria based upon racial perceptions”. A few years later he went further, declaring that “the application of the [aliens] power to Pacific Islanders who were British subjects isa stain on the jurisprudence of this Court”.Despite this, high court judges –including Edelman himself– continue to cite Robtelmes as the foundational authority for draconian federal power over “aliens”. In 1982 Chief Justice Harry Gibbs said that ever since Robtelmes, “It has been regarded as settled law that the Parliament has power to make laws providing for the deportation [or detention] of aliensfor whatever reasons it thinks fit.”The high court should confront its own history and disavow a disturbing precedent made even more dangerous by the rise of populism in this country.Australia must confront not only what happened but why the legal reasoning that enabled it continues to be relied on. South Sea Islanders survived the policy that sought to remove them; truth-telling now requires Australia to confront the law that enabled it.Peter Prince is one of the co-authors ofCrock’s Immigration and Nationality Law(Federation Press 2026, forthcoming) and is a member of the Australian Historical Association. (Waskam) Emelda Davis chairs the Australian South Sea Islanders (Port Jackson).Her grandfather was “blackbirded” aged 12from Tanna in the New Hebrides to work like a slave in Australia and never saw his family againExplore more on these topicsAustralian lawPast/PresentSlaveryPacific islandsRaceVanuatuAustralian immigration and asylumSouth PacificcommentShareReuse this content

title: Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: People have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real life
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: People have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real life
Content: ‘You hardly notice how, over time, the world outside has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world.’Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘You hardly notice how, over time, the world outside has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world.’Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial mediaOur lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insaneBrigid DelaneyPeople have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real lifeFri 25 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 20.17 EDTShareThink of your online life as a garden. At first it’s just a few seeds here or there – a Facebook profile where you created entire albums from a night at the pub, or maybe a Tumblr or a Myspace page listing your favourite bands. It is fun – something just for you and your friends to enjoy.Then the garden grows. You get an Instagram account and document moments from each day on Stories, use LinkedIn for networking and sharing career triumphs, and check your X/Twitter hyper-vigilantly in case you wrote something that just got you cancelled.Your online garden grows more sprawling and complex; now it’s no longer just a fun project for yourself on weekends and weeknights. As it grows, you start to view it through the eyes of others.How will this garden be seen? Will people like it? What can I plant in this garden that will make more people like it?A few more years pass. And now, instead of working on the garden here and there, you’re in there all the time. You have discovered if your garden is really enticing, you can make money off it. You want – then need – big numbers coming in there. You look at other people’s gardens all the time and you get jealous. They have better gardens.We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism? | Brigid DelaneyRead moreWhen you’re not in your garden, you’re still somehow tending to it – looking at the number of people coming in, and comparing them with what it used to be, and being worried that maybe you didn’t plant the right things. But people will tell you if you’re doing it wrong. They’ll spray paint all over the garden walls how much your garden sucks, how you’re a loser, how ugly it all is.And with all this activity going on you hardly notice how, over time, the world outside your garden has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world. The garden is your home now.When this current moment ends and a more enlightened time kicks in, descendants looking back will see that millions (or is it billions?) of us have spent the last 10 years or more migrating our lives and identities, and our political, communal and social selves, to a digital realm that has sent many of us insane.The (digital) signal that we are living a better life has been imbued with more energy and importance than living a better life itself.Those descendants will see what we can’t really see now – a massive serf culture has emerged, where people have become servants to these gardens.They’ll see how truly unfree so many of us are – allowing the rich, real, tactile world to recede, while the digital gardens have sprawled to take up all our time and energy (the average userspends about 2 hours and 39 minutes a dayon social media.)And it will become apparent that the real elite won’t be the people with the most popular digital gardens. They’ll be the people who never had gardens. Or people who had small private gardens, where they only let a few friends in.Brand strategists and trend forecasters are saying that, in 2026, the true measure of status is privacy and a low or no digital footprint.This is a different way of living off-grid.You experience a rich and interesting life in the real world and don’t feel the need to post about it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYour sense of self worth is not linked to how many people see that you’ve been somewhere, hung out with someone or worn something.Your income, status and financial security is not dependent on your social media account.Your attention span has not been corrupted or shortened by chronic social media consumption and AI use – and this gives you almost superhuman powers such as the ability to read long, difficult novels, think critically, and retain information in your head.Your emotional stability is not dependent on how your content is performing.You have not internalised the digital panopticon where everything you do is with an eye to how it is perceived.You have a healthy social life in the real world, meaning you have less time or inclination to post.Brand strategistEugene Healeyin his Substack wrote a recent series on “post-luxury status symbols” and said “the greatest privilege is to be chronically offline” and “in this culture of overexposure – it’s only natural that it becomes desirable to opt out”.The ultimate flex is not needing social media, walking away from your digital garden and back into your real life.Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the SageExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionPsychologycommentShareReuse this content

title: I love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern football | Marva Kreel | The Guardian
description: Focusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeper, says broadcaster Marva Kreel
Author: Marva Kreel
Headline: Focusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeper, says broadcaster Marva Kreel
Content: England fans at the Frankfurt Arena, Germany, on 20 June 2024.Photograph: Stefan Matzke/sampics/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEngland fans at the Frankfurt Arena, Germany, on 20 June 2024.Photograph: Stefan Matzke/sampics/Corbis/Getty ImagesOpinionSoccerI love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern footballMarva KreelFocusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeperFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTShareAndy Burnham is right that football fans have historically been treated differently from other sports fans. But if we’re going to talk about discrimination in football, the ban on drinking at your seat feels like a strange place to start.The rule may have its roots in a very different era of football, but for many fans today, being able to take a pint to your seat may not be top of their list of changes they’d like to see in the game. Especially at a time when discrimination is very much present elsewhere in football.The legislation, introduced under Margaret Thatcherin the 1980sas part of a crackdown on football hooliganism, was rooted in the idea that football fans needed to be treated differently from the supposedly better-behaved crowds at rugby and cricket – which smacks of classism and the stereotyping of working-class fans. But football has changed since then, and so has drinking culture. Fans have adapted to the restrictions and built a matchday ritual around them. A good fan concourse pint is up there with an airport pint or a beer-garden pint on the first day of summer.Fans have got used to this routine, and one of the biggest concerns of lifting this ban now seems to be the Boxpark-ification of football: the dreadedperformative beer throwwhen anything good happens.Even when it’s not performative, it does raise a problem of logistics. With no cup holders, when a 95th-minute winner goes in and you’re suddenly off your seat with your limbs in the air, a pint is unlikely to remain where you left it. There will be people walking back and forth from the concourse during the game for another pint or the toilet, too. It used to happen before, of course, but it would still be a new irritation that fans would have to adapt to. And, most importantly, it isn’t a change many fans seem to have been asking for.As a fan of both men’s and women’s football, I’ve experienced theWomen’s Super League’s successful trialof beer at your seats, as well as drinking at non-league games, and it was a nice change. It has even become a distinct part of the matchday experience in leagues where the atmosphere is different and the crowds are smaller. But the women’s game is not simply the men’s game with fewer people in the stands. The matchday experience is different – and that’s important when we talk about what works.Watching Everton Women with a beer in hand can be lovely. So can spending a long day at the cricket with a pint. But I was also at the game in whichChloe Kelly scored the winner for England against Germanyat Euro 2022, and was immediately swallowed up in the chaos of the celebrations, being thrown around by the people around me. Having a pint in my hand in that moment would have been less than ideal. Beer and football can clearly coexist, but what works at one level of the game, or in one kind of crowd, doesn’t necessarily translate neatly to another.View image in fullscreenChloe Kelly pokes home the winning goal for England against Germany in the final of the Women’s Euros on 31 July 2022.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBut this is where Burnham’s argument starts to feel out of step with the reality of football now. At a time when working-class fans are beingpriced out of their season tickets, racist, sexist, homophobiconline abuseis ever-present, and figures at the very top of the game –such as Jim Ratcliffe– use their platform to push deeply divisive politics, it feels out of touch to make the right to drink a pint in your seat a headline example of football discrimination.And that’s not to deny discrimination of working-class fans, but this is a problem that runs much deeper in the game. And if the old assumption is that football fans are uniquely likely to cause trouble when alcohol is involved, lifting the ban doesn’t automatically remove that belief. It’s possible these biases will show up in how games are policed, with a heavy pre-emptive police and security presence.If the ban is lifted, there’ll be teething problems, there will be beer showers, complaints and no doubt a bunch of stories in the press making an example of any issues of violence held up as evidence that football fans can’t be trusted with a pint. Eventually, though, fans will adapt, security will relax and, for the most part, it will probably become normal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut that’s precisely why Burnham’s argument feels like such an odd intervention. There are serious questions about class and access in football that deserve to be scrutinised as discrimination. If Burnham wants to tackle the ways football fans are treated unfairly, there are plenty of other places to start.Football fans have every right to drink their beer wherever the rules allow. But sometimes a pint is just a pint – and football has bigger battles to fight.Marva Kreel is a broadcaster and football content creatorExplore more on these topicsFootballOpinionAlcoholAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: What are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politics | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: Ed Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out for, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: Ed Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out for, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: The Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, serves up fish and chips at Brighton’s Palace Pier ahead of his party’s conference, 19 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenThe Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, serves up fish and chips at Brighton’s Palace Pier ahead of his party’s conference, 19 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionLiberal DemocratsWhat are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politicsSimon JenkinsEd Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out forFri 25 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTShareSeptember is the cruellest month for political commentators because it is when something has to be said about the Liberal Democrats. They are a play without a plot, a chorus line of seemingly endless “don’t knows”. Their leader, Ed Davey,recently warnedthat “we’re in the fight of our lives” to defend the values of liberty and equality. Really? How can this be when Davey is becoming about as relevant as Count Binface?The Lib Dems’ central predicament has remained unchanged for a century, ever since the decline of David Lloyd George and the rise of the Labour party. There is simply no space in Britain for a centrist party when so little divides the big parties and they broadly stick to the prevailing ecomomic orthodoxy.But there is now a ray of hope. One of the newer developments in British politics is the rise of single-issue parties. In Scotland and Wales, the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru demand independence from the UK, while in England the Reform party has dedicated itself to curbing immigration.A lack of a clarifying message could partly explain why the Lib Dems have sufferedheavy defeats at recent byelections, and slipped to fourth or fifth place in many national opinion polls, regularly trailing the Greens and Reform.In order to improve their electoral fortunes, the Lib Dems need an equally straightforward cause, one that should have broad appeal and identify an area neglected by the other parties. That cause is now glaring: the devolution of government authority.Time and again in national league tables, England ranks as having one of themost concentrated central governments in Europe, and by some measures in the world. English citizens’ ability to participate in local democracy is extremely weak compared to other countries such as France, Germany and those in Scandinavia.Welfare comparisons showthe UK’s local services fare poorly and inequitably compared with those, for instance, in localised Scandinavia. The authority of Britain’s central executive over local government is overbearing, with ever more disappointing outcomes for citizens.Localism is the issue and one that has featured prominently in political debate for decades. New Labour even proposed a“new localism”. The result was just 12 elected mayors in England and Wales between 2001 and 2005.In 2010, David Cameron pledged a“radical shift in power from central government to neighbourhoods”. He then did the opposite through enforced housing targets and a fierce programme of austerity. Similarly, in 2024 Keir Starmer promised to “deepen democracy by … devolving power to communities”. Yet one of his first moves was to overrule local discretion in planning approvals, describing councils as “blockers and nimbys”.Over the years, the phrase “shifting power locally” became an almost ritualistic election chant, clearly based on polling data. No government really meant it. Ever since Margaret Thatcher, the centre has taken ever more control of local taxation, education, housing, care services and planning. The job of a British local council today is in effect to do what the centre tells it. It has not much money nor power for anything else. It is therefore no wonder that local democracy is subject to ridicule: see, for instance, therecent “independence” votein the Oxfordshire village of Piddington.Unquestionably the most headline-grabbing of Westminster’s pseudo-localists isAndy Burnham. Does he mean it? His innovation of a cohort of metro mayors – introduced under the Conservatives – inserts a new level of regional bureaucracy between central and local government. Their role will primarily be to enforce national targets of housebuilding and energy investment, and presumably to override decisions of local councils beneath them.Burnham’s announcement that mayors in England will be able to keep a share of income tax andbusiness rateswas cited as proof of his commitment to his so-called devolution agenda. But the extent to which mayors will be able to wield these powers remains to be seen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prime minister’s moving ofparts of the No 10 operation to Manchesterhardly reduces the power of the centre. It merely relocates it, temporarily. Here, surely, is a Liberal Democrat cause.Significantly, the one area in which the Lib Dems have flourished is local government. At last May’s local elections,the party took their control of councils up to 76, establishing them as a major political force across local government. This was a major achievement. There are now more Liberal Democrat council leaders in Britain than the 71 Lib Dem MPs. As such, their impact on the actual government of the country is substantial.This cries out for revolution and the Lib Dems have every reason to be its champions. The party should go flat out for democratic, truly local self-government. Models of appropriate tiers and functions can be found across Europe. The cause is now aided by mountainous evidence that Britain’s centrist model – the famous“Rolls-Royce” of Whitehall– is now a clapped out jalopy. Every week the headlines cry that nothing seems to work.This is the all-consuming challenge for the Lib Dems to make their own. Propose a major constitutional reform. The party’s 76 local councils can list the powers they want restored to them. It is these council leaders who must stand on stage at their conference, not Westminster’s indolent parliamentarians.Liberal Democratsshould become the party of local Britain and restore the government of the people to the people.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsOpinionLocal politicsLocal governmentDevolutionAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: We all know a lack of exercise is bad for our bodies. So what is relying on AI doing to our brains? | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Most of my students use AI, and I worry about its corrosive effects. We must not entrust tech companies with our long-term health, says Prof Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Most of my students use AI, and I worry about its corrosive effects. We must not entrust tech companies with our long-term health, says Prof Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
Content: ‘Just as resistance training is important to maintain muscle mass as we age, our brains also need regular exercise to keep sharp.’Photograph: Eugene Mymrin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Just as resistance training is important to maintain muscle mass as we age, our brains also need regular exercise to keep sharp.’Photograph: Eugene Mymrin/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)We all know a lack of exercise is bad for our bodies. So what is relying on AI doing to our brains?Devi SridharI suspect nearly all of my students use AI, and I worry about its corrosive effects. We must not entrust tech companies with our long-term healthProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghFri 25 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 05.12 EDTShareWhen I was a postgraduate student at the University of Oxford in the early 2000s, I interviewed for a major consulting firm. All my friends were being recruited, and I thought why not give it a shot?Aside from the usual maths-proficiency test (how quickly can you crunch numbers in front of a client and look smart), I was asked about what the future of streaming could look like. I gave a long-winded answer about the unintended consequences of changing how humans interact with each other when a new technology is introduced, and why this may not be in the best interests of health and society.I even remember saying something like: “Can you imagine just being stuck at home, alone, watching show after show and never having to move or see any other people? Why would anyone choose that over going out to rent a DVD at a local shop, or to a movie theatre?” You won’t be surprised to learn that I wasn’t invited for a follow-up interview.The partner at the consulting firm thought my answer was completely wrong. They saw the potential growth and profitability of streaming – and you could say, in hindsight, they had a point: Netflix’s global revenue continues to rise year on year,reaching $12.6bn (£9.5bn) in 2026. My answer, on the other hand, focused on its societal and health consequences.But if you look at the negative impact that excessive screen-time has had on health and wellbeing,especially on children, perhaps I wasn’t wrong after all. We know that social isolation is now widespread, anxiety and depression too, withsleep also negatively affectedby how late we stay up watching content.And here I am, more than 20 years later, being asked to talk about AI and what it means for higher education, health and society at a conference at the University of Edinburgh, where I work as a professor. I know many people would say: “It’s wonderful! Our lives will all get easier.” But we’re also moving closer to a world where we don’t have to see anyone, move anywhere or use our brains, seemingly at all. And again I think, wonderful for who? Wonderful for the tech companies and those looking to cut costs by replacing humans with automation, but certainly not for the rest of us.There’s a comparison, for me, between the effects of streaming on our physical activity levels and health, and the probable effects of AI on our brains.The richer a country becomes, the more people move into non-manual labour, with sedentary activities in their free time. We can see evidence for this if we look at development in low- and middle-income countries:physical activity goes down asGDP per capita goes up. Over thepast few decades, we have seen the health consequences of sedentary behaviour grow: higher rates of chronic disease such as cancers and type-2 diabetes, more chronic back and neck pain, and reduced quality of life. Physical movement has become a leisure activity to stay healthy, and is increasingly linked with higher socioeconomic status in places such as the UK.We know that not using our bodies is bad for our physical health – but what is regular reliance on AI doing to our minds? The true causal evidence might take decades to emerge, but we can link several trends together to guess at an answer. We know, for example, that AI use and daily screen-time averagesare going up. At my university, I’d guess almost all students are using some kind of generative AI (gen AI) to produce their work, raising huge challenges when it comes to assessment.The 2026Higher Education Policy Institute surveyof students’ use of gen AI found this year that 95% of undergraduates reported using AI in at least one way, and 94% said they had used it in assessed work. We also know that overall educational attainment levels are decreasing: a recentOECD reportnoted that student performance across its member countries continued to decline, with the lowest average ever recorded for maths and reading. The report links these poor scores to longer screen-time, increased digitalisation in the classroom and the collapse inreading for enjoymentamong children.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriously | Gaby HinsliffRead moreAll of this makes me wonder what will happen to our brains as we continue to outsource key cognitive functions to AI. We already have preliminary evidence from a study that used electroencephalography (EEG) sensors to measure electrical activity in the brain,titledYour Brain on ChatGPT: it showed those students using gen AI to write essays had weaker and less distributed brain connectivity than those writing fully on their own.We also know that a lack of mental engagement can lead to losing cognitive function over time. A study ofmore than 19,000 adultsover the age of 50 found greater participation in cognitively stimulating leisure activities (such as crosswords or sudoku) was linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning in later life.
