Just as resistance training is important to maintain muscle mass as we age, our brains also need regular training. Use it or lose it.As we look to the future, will thinking, reading, writing and actively using our brains become activities from a bygone era? If we stop using our brains to think, socially interact, concentrate or problem-solve, what will be the impact on our quality of life and our chances of ageing healthily? Will we see a rise in chronic disease linked to the brain?And, maybe just as importantly, does anyone even care? It’s certainly not the concern of tech companies, which are in an arms race to go faster. And so we’re heading in that direction and being told it’s all wonderful. Yes, it is wonderful for certain tech companies. And probably terrible for the mental health and wellbeing of the rest of us.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionHealthNeuroscienceMental healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Plans are under way to finally help Britain’s unemployed young people – will Labour pull it off? | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Alan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it through, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Alan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it through, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: People at the London Job Show in Westfield shopping centre, London, 15 May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople at the London Job Show in Westfield shopping centre, London, 15 May 2026.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The GuardianOpinionLabourPlans are under way to finally help Britain’s unemployed young people – will Labour pull it off?Polly ToynbeeAlan Milburn is preparing to implement his report to bring young people back into work. Let’s hope the government will see it throughFri 25 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTShareAs certainly as the moon pulls on the tides, Labour governments improve the lives of the poorest children. Just as surely, Conservative governments pull back and reverse the good done. Here we go again: despite the social devastation caused by George Osborne’s cuts last time, Kemi Badenoch announces that she wants to imposecuts to universal creditfor the poorest if she gets the chance.She doesn’t do subtle, none of Iain Duncan Smith’s cruel-to-be-kind routine, but goes straight for populist rabble-rousing, stirring up fact-free contempt for anyone on benefits, with aproposed banon buying cigarettes and alcohol, or gambling, with benefit money. Welfare, she says, must not be “a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered”. As with all crude rightwing populism, the harm she does spreads hatred of the weak. In this most unequal country, it encourages bullies to kick downwards, stifling more generous human instincts.Here’s how the pendulum swings: NewLabourlifted nearly a million children out of poverty and set up 3,500 Sure Start centres, which supported families from birth. David Cameron and Osborne swept all that away with billions of pounds in benefit cuts directed at families, tipping more children into food-bank poverty.Naturally, this Labour government has swung the pendulum back, taking 450,000 children from destitution by removing the Tory two-child benefit cap – albeit with too much delay. For the first time ever, the universal credit standard allowance will permanentlyrise above inflation, with free breakfast clubs for all primary schoolchildren in England, half a million more children eligible for free school meals in England, cheaper school uniforms and Best Start family hubs opening.But Labour has been bequeathed the worst fallout from 14 Tory years. The nearly 1 million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – are a legacy of Tory rule. Labour has made turning the tide on thoseaged 18 to 24its flagship goal, hoping that numbers fall fast by the next election. Can it be done?The man who says it can is most in demand at meetings around the Labour conference next week. Alan Milburn’sencyclopaedic reporton the problem revealed the myriad reasons why so many of the young get left in limbo.Next month, before the budget, he will publish the plan for what’s to be done. I hear intense negotiations are in progress, down to the wire because this is in effect a white paper, not a report to gather dust but one ready to be implemented at once, with costings pre-agreed with PM, chancellor and relevant ministers. Milburn knows the system, and he is determined to short-circuit any blockers.Here’s the problem. His diagnosis points to everything from inequality and profound deprivation to mental illness, failures of the education system, refusal of employers to offer first breaks, falling apprenticeships, lack of early support in areas where many families are in trouble, and declining youth services. Neets are the fallout from deep social dysfunction, accelerated by the cuts.Which will be the first priorities? It has been good to see Lucy Powell, the education secretary, start right away on new vocational GCSEs, which Milburn thinks will keep pupils engaged instead of dropping out. Copying the Dutch system of intensive one-to-one personal support will getNeets into training or work. That needs upfront investment from the new chancellor, John Healey, who is said to agree, even though he knows the results take time. The quid pro quo expected from Neets is a “duty to engage”, so they must take part in the help offered, as all benefits are always conditional, with penalties as a backstop. Milburn’s research defies Badenoch’s kneejerk nastiness, as he finds84% of Neetswant urgent help into work.Success will be judged by falling numbers of Neets, but there is the “stock and flow” question: preventing more from joining tomorrow’s list starts at the very earliest years. Children who are not school-ready at ages four to five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet at ages 16 to 17, as Milburn said in the report. That’s not certain destiny, but it is a high risk.The good news is that Milburn will reset the nursery system that currently discriminates against the poorest. He tells me he is shocked that only68% of childrenare school-ready, even after they have had a year in reception at primary school. He tells me he will be announcing a new target of 90% to reach that level by five years old: all research shows how investment at the earliest age yields most.What would that take? The nursery system inherited from the Tories deliberately holds back the most deprived children by denying funded nursery hours in England to most children with a non-working parent. Here was Tory thinking: both parents must work to stop lazy mothers idling in nail bars while the state acts as childminder. But deprived children with non-working parents need nursery education to close the growing gap between them and the rest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere’s how it works: a child with working parents can get 30 hours of free nursery care from the age of nine months up to primary school. Only some disadvantaged two-year-olds can qualify for 15 hours a week, but that entitlement now reaches“fewer than 30% of two-year-olds”,says theInstitute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).This means that children of the best-off are eight times more likely to benefit from state-funded nursery than the most disadvantaged children,says the New Economics Foundation. As the IFS says, the system “almost by definition excludes the poorest families”. No wonder primary headteachers I have spoken to say they can immediately tell which children have had full nursery education, which have had a little, and which have had none.Sarah Ronan, the director of the Early Education and Childcare Coalition, tells me pithily: “Imagine denying the poorest children access to primary education. We just wouldn’t stand for it. Yet we allow that to happen in the early years while we wring our hands about school-readiness and scratch our heads about Neets.”The head-scratching may be over when Milburn’s report lands. Meanwhile, Badenoch has little to say about Neets, but her wider plans for the jobless see no investment in training or extra support into work. Reform UK dared to sayshe didn’t go far enough. There it is: the age-old divide, psychological and emotional as well as political, between the left’s practical social policy to lift people up and the right’s punitive desire to give every underdog a kick.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionYoung peopleUnemploymentcommentShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it  | Will Hutton and Andy Haldane | The Guardian
description: Nationalisation is not the ultimate answer for companies like Thames Water – but they could be run for the public benefit, say journalist and economist Will Hutton and former chief economist of the Bank of England Andy Haldane
Author: Andy Haldane
Headline: Nationalisation is not the ultimate answer for companies like Thames Water – but they could be run for the public benefit, say journalist and economist Will Hutton and former chief economist of the Bank of England Andy Haldane
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionUtilitiesAndy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through itNationalisation is not the ultimate answer for companies like Thames Water – but they could be run for the public benefitWill Hutton is a journalist and political economist. Andy Haldane is a former chief economist of the Bank of EnglandWill HuttonandAndy HaldaneFri 25 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.47 EDTShareView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham came to power promising greater “public control” over the UK’sutilities, such as water and energy. His reasons for doing so were to cut what is described as the “privatisation premium” paid for public services by consumers, and to improve their quality. The plight of thestricken Thames Waterexemplifies the scale of those problems.Yet two months on, the government has failed to provide any real clarification of whatit means by “public control”, beyond stating that this may not necessarily mean public ownership of these companies. One option under discussion is tobuild a network of regional political bodiesto hold water companies to account. But such a step would not, by itself, confer the control needed to meet the prime minister’s objectives. Meanwhile, in a febrile environment for borrowers, uncertainty about “public control” is imposing real costs, both on those companies affected and the UK government.As a result of this uncertainty, bond issues by utility companies that would have financed investment are being deferred and their costs are rising.Thames Water is in a state of suspended animation, in part because no one knows what its ultimate proposed ownership and regulatory structure will be. With public ownership not having been ruled out, its potentially significant cost is another factor adding to pressures in UK government debt markets.In the face of these mounting costs, there is a strong case for the government to quickly clarify its intentions. Whatshouldit mean by public control of utilities, in order to secure the best possible services at a reasonable cost?Good governance typically involves seeking an appropriate balance between incentives and expertise. For public services, this means a set of incentives well aligned with the interests of customers – namely, the general public – while having the expertise to deliver services effectively.This underlines the perils of the privatised model. For example,Thames Wateris owned by a consortium of investors, including highly leveraged hedge funds. This governance structure has no shortage of high-quality financial expertise. Unfortunately, this highly “innovative” (and leveraged) financing structure is singularly ill-suited to a low-risk public utility; investor incentives are horribly misaligned with the public good.Full nationalisation faces the opposite problems. In this scenario, the company’s incentives would be aligned, by statute, with the public good. But without commercial discipline and expertise, there are fewer reasons to expect it to be run expertly and efficiently. Past experience – from British Rail to British Steel to British Leyland – demonstrates this risk.For public utilities, then, “public control” should mean seeking governance structures with aims that are aligned with those of the general public. This should not be mistaken to mean that the public sector itself should necessarily play a central role in owning or operating the company. This erroneous belief is costing the UK (and the utilities) dear, and needs dismissing once and for all.View image in fullscreenProtesters ask for Thames Water to be nationalised outside the high court in London, February 2025.Photograph: Victoria Jones/REX/ShutterstockHaving done so, what alternative governance structures strike a better balance than the extremes of nationalisation or privatisation? Aligning the incentives of utilities with those of the public could be done most easily and effectively by turning them into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim.This has the advantage that it could be introduced within the current ownership and licensing regime. While not without potential legal challenge, in principle it would not require expensive compensation to shareholders who have already considered a level of regulatory risk when making their investment. The government itself could take a special or “golden share” at a nominal cost of £1, of the type used to maintain BAE Systems and Rolls-Royce (and latterly Royal Mail) in domestic ownership.Importantly, the utility companies would go beyond “benefit” or B Corps (obliged to display high standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability), and instead would have more demanding governance requirements, tailored to their needs and standards. These could be taken off the shelf – for example, Ofgem already requires energy companies to comply with certain international environmental standards – or alternatively, stakeholders could work together to develop industry-specific standards.With this core structure, there are various ways the governance regime could be enhanced. For example, utilities could be required to have a minimum fraction of their shares publicly listed and traded, which would help transparency and market discipline. Publicly quoted utilities have tended to outperform the alternatives across all metrics.To strengthen further public incentives, executive pay could be linked to public-benefit outcomes. This could also be achieved by requiring each utility to create an independent customer group and incorporating its views in all dimensions of the companies’ decision-making. There is good evidence across the utilities of customer involvement improving outcomes.Lastly, this would imply a paradigm shift in the culture and architecture of regulation, currently alternating between regulatory capture and mutual distrust, which has palpably failed. Public-benefit utilities would be constitutionally obliged to want the same outcomes as public-interest regulators. Open-book accounting would be routine as regulator and regulated both prioritised the delivery of high-quality public services.There is an urgent need for the government to clarify its intention around public control before uncertainty imposes further costs on fragile utilities and public finances alike. A public-benefit structure would, we believe, achieve a much better balance between public-good incentives and operational expertise at a much lower cost for consumers, investors and the government. It would be measured in single pounds rather than hundreds of millions. Burnham won power by daring to be different. Daring to be different – within practical bounds – should also inform his approach to public control of utilities.Will Hutton is a journalist and political economist and host of the We Society podcast. Andy Haldane is president of the British Chambers of Commerce anda former chief economist of the Bank of England

title: Berlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma Aydemir | The Guardian
description: Elif Eralp wants lower rents and more public housing. It’s not rocket science but mainstream parties still don’t get why they are failing, says Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir
Author: Fatma Aydemir
Headline: Elif Eralp wants lower rents and more public housing. It’s not rocket science but mainstream parties still don’t get why they are failing, says Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir
Content: ‘Elif Eralp put housing at the centre of her campaign. For weeks Berlin was flooded with portraits of her wearing a nameplate necklace with the wordMietendeckel(rent freeze).’Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Elif Eralp put housing at the centre of her campaign. For weeks Berlin was flooded with portraits of her wearing a nameplate necklace with the wordMietendeckel(rent freeze).’Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersOpinionGermanyBerlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housingFatma AydemirElif Eralp wants lower rents and more public housing. It’s not rocket science but mainstream parties still don’t get why they are failingFri 25 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTShareHope is a fragile thing. You can only hold on to it as long as you find reasons to believe tomorrow can be better. A woman, for instance, who has the resources and opportunity to rent her own flat will be more likely to leave her abusive husband and recover. A pupil who has their own room and desk to do their homework might find more meaning in thriving at school. And an elderly person who can afford to live in a neighbourhood where they feel safe and connected is less likely to become isolated and depressed.It’s not by chance that the examples above all revolve around the same topic. Affordable housing is possibly the most personal and most urgent social issue of our time. In Berlin, a city where 85% of residents live in rented accommodation, rents have risen by almost70%in the past 10 years. And that is despite arent control lawthat has been in effect since 2015. How? Loopholes and illegal practices have allowed property owners to continue putting pressure on the housing market. The social anxiety caused by this crisis, far from affecting just low-earners and single-parent households, affects vast parts of the middle class, too.So what does a political party need to do to get into power in the state of Berlin? It’s really not rocket science: focus on the housing crisis, provide solutions and avoid distractions by political opponents. This is exactly what the leftwing party Die Linke has been doing for months. The result of last Sunday’s state election is striking: for the first time, Die Linke, with 25.7%, became the strongest party in Berlin. Not because everyone who voted for it suddenly agreed with everything else the party stands for. But because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.The result is also remarkable because Germany is at a historic turning point: on the same day as the Berlin election, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged – with 38% – as the largest party in a state election inMecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Just two weeks previously, it had secured a victory inSaxony-Anhaltwith almost 44%. While the centrist parties, in an attempt to win back their voters, are desperately mimicking the AfD’s ideas and rhetoric on migration, Die Linke could set an example in Berlin for the rest of the country: by actually listening to people’s worries and working on ideas to improve their lives sustainably, instead of scapegoating.The party’s lead candidate, Elif Eralp, could become not only Berlin’s first mayor from the left since Germany’s reunification in 1990, but also Berlin’s first mayor ever with a migration background. Born in Munich, she is the daughter of Turkish socialists who fled following the military coup in Turkey in 1980. Eralp put housing at the centre of her campaign. For many weeks the whole city was flooded with giant portraits of the 45-year-old wearing an optimistic smile and a golden nameplate necklace with the wordMietendeckel(rent freeze).Eralp’s programme was clear from the start: lower rents, more public housing and the implementation of Berlin’s2021 referendumin which a majority voted for more public ownership of housing to alleviate the accommodation crisis. It’s not a completely new world that Eralp promises. All she had to do was simply speak about the one we are already living in.But winning an election is one thing. Governing is another. Die Linke may have won the most seats, but it lacks a majority to run the state on its own. To turn its campaign promises into policy, Eralp has to negotiate with other parties, particularly the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. While Berlin’s Greens have already spoken out in favour of a progressive coalition, the SPD isdeeply divided.Die Linke’s top priority is aradical ambition:it would involve the compulsory purchase of the housing portfolios (which exceed 3,000 apartments) of large private real estate companies and their transfer into a democratically controlled non-profit, public body. The SPD’s approach is to regulate the housing market much more strongly, expand public housing and potentially introduce a rent cap. Which sounds like everything that has already failed in the last decade.At the same time, Die Linke enters negotiations under a microscope. Political opponents are questioning whether the party’s positions are compatible with democratic values, while controversies surroundingantisemitismand parts of the party’s political culture have become a major subject of public debate. Antisemitism is, historically and today, a problem inherent in German society as a whole, one that also exists within Die Linke and should be combated more decisively. However, theuproarabout antisemitic rappers and an organised crime member who was spotted at Die Linke’s election party seem like sham debates that overshadow the actual conflicts of interest.Meanwhile, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has already stated, in response to the Berlin elections, that afederal lawcould be passed to prevent the expropriation of privately owned housing. Markus Söder, leader of the state of Bavaria, announced financialconsequencesfor Berlin, if the “extremist”, “antidemocratic” and “antisemitic” Die Linke were to govern the capital. No such measures were announced for potential AfD-governed states, of course.It is hardly surprising that conservatives are now foaming at the mouth, given that for decades they have been pursuing policies that benefit those who profit from the housing crisis. Yet, more and more Social Democrats are alsoup in arms, putting pressure on their party not to form a coalition with Die Linke.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd this is where hope becomes fragile again. Because Eralp now has to do something harder than naming a problem: she has to find coalition partners, and for that she has to compromise – without making her voters feel betrayed. Now that would be a radical act, indeed.Fatma Aydemir is a Berlin-based author, novelist, playwright and a GuardianEuropecolumnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionEuropeHousingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songs | Taylor Swift | The Guardian
description: This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lows
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lows
Content: ‘Like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love’ … Taylor Swift.Photograph: TAS Rights ManagementView image in fullscreen‘Like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love’ … Taylor Swift.Photograph: TAS Rights ManagementTaylor SwiftReviewTaylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songs(Republic)This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lowsLaura SnapesFri 25 Sep 2026 09.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne downside of turning your release strategies into scavenger hunts and layering clues within your work is that it invites enormous amounts of scrutiny about your potential motive. When Taylor Swift announced an expanded edition of last year’s critically malignedThe Life of a Showgirlthis week, subtitled The Encore, many fans instantly suspected one of two things: that it was designed to remind Grammy members of Showgirl’s existence during their voting period to determine next year’s nominees, or to oust country ingenue Ella Langley from herrecord-breaking US No 1 run.If that sounds cynical, it’s also worth remembering that when Swift announced Showgirl last year, she said that unlike her previous album,The Tortured Poets Department– a 16-track record immediately inflated to 31 songs on release day – the purposefully concise, 12-track Showgirl would not be expanded. (This didn’t stop her releasing34variants of the record, with various acoustic demos and so on, to juice sales.)After Showgirl had the biggest US opening week ever, Swift went to Sweden to celebrate with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback, she revealed this week. The trip was intended to be about reflection and gratitude, she wrote on Instagram. “But,” she continued, “there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: we wrote more songs.” One hesitates to liken Swift to Kanye West, but The Life of a Showgirl is starting to look a little more likeThe Life of Pablo, West’s endlessly extended seventh album.Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl review – dull razzle-dazzle from a star who seems frazzledRead moreA slipperiness has infected the whole endeavour, not helped by Swift’s initial promise that Showgirl was all “bangers” and about “keeping the bar really high”, a claim quickly dismissed: the record is a travesty, a word that feels particularly apt when you recallWood, a Bruno Mars-lite abomination about her now-husband Travis Kelce’s penis. And for an album that was supposed to be about the giddy highs of life on Swift’s own record-breaking Eras tour, it contained a tedious amount ofwell-worn score-settling. Adding four more songs written some time after the initial sessions further dilutes the record’s already flimsy premise.The most Swiftian thing about these four tracks is their visceral sense of course-correction. For all that Swift chafes against The Haters – more on them to come, shocker – she’s always reacting to criticism. Recall the scene from herMiss Americanadocumentary where she learns that her sixth album,Reputation, didn’t get nominated for the album of the year Grammy: “I just need to make a better record,” she says, visibly crushed. (That’s the folly of working like this: Reputation is her best record, and those voters are idiots.) Showgirl was panned for its excessive wordiness and defaulting on the promised bangers; these Encore songs largely pare back the verbiage and double down on hooks and firework-laden bridges, Swift’s metier. It’s like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer breathlessly flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love.Taylor Swift: Patient Zero – videoEvery Swift album except Reputation has a deluxe version, though just a handful of those bonus songs are keepers:Jump Then Fall(from Fearless),New Romantics(1989),Bigger Than the Whole SkyandWould’ve Could’ve Should’ve(Midnights). None of these new songs are destined to join those ranks, though Patient Zero comes closest. Hooked around a mournful and curiously processed Celtic fiddle sample, it recalls the spirit ofLover, where it felt as though Swift was trying out potential new sonic futures. Its pained chorus also evokes Tortured Poets’Fortnight: a slinky, low-key yet insidiously catchy melodic Möbius strip, with lyrics offering connection to a woman recently burned by an ex whose games Swift knows well.It’s one of two Encore songs that contain a palpable sense of humanity, unlike anything from its childish parent album.Pink Cloudingis a mature apology to a kind ex she let down – “Neither of us knew at the time / That I was a liar” – filled with the sort of regret that will never lose its shameful sting. Unlike Swift’s post-2020 turn to heavily detailed narrative writing, it’s written in a pure-pop form, braiding shades of pink and various flowers into a sweet and effective conceit without defaulting on emotional grace. Its ardent synth-pop, a nice balance of airy and punchy, also sounds a little like it could’ve lived next toCruel Summeron Lover, though truthfully it recalls Tegan and Sara’s classic 2013 album Heartthrob, which inspired Swift’s1989pop makeover.The beauty of Pink Clouding is that it sounds genuinely believable, a quality curiously missing from Swift’s songs about Kelce. Tortured Poets bonus trackSo High Schoolis as close as she’s gotten; the Showgirl songs about their romance framed it as a triumph over venal and conniving haters. It’s a very strange lens through which to write about supposed true love, and one she returns to here. The appallingCleveland!is all about how Kelce loves her despite internet commenters saying she can’t dance (a long-dead criticism) and that she’s annoying, and is sung with such oozing self-satisfaction it’s like being repeatedly poked and asked if it hurts. Spiritually, it is a cut-and-shut of two of her worst songs ever, Lover’sMe!(about being cringe but free) and Showgirl’sHoney(about other women being jealous haters). Despite her long-term collaborator Jack Antonoff not being part of the Showgirl era, it still sounds like warmed-over Bleachers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTaylor Swift: Cleveland! – videoIt is a mess of contradictions: it has an oddly sour tang for such a festive, all-bells-jangling confection, like biting into a lavishly iced cake to find the sugar swapped for salt. For a song about having found the one, its standards are barrel-scrapingly low: “You only need to find one person in this entire world / Who doesn’t find you completely insufferable!” she declares. Girl! Aim higher! Where on Honey, and other recent songs, she has proven strikingly eager to call other women bitches, here she coyly stops short of calling herself a “whore” and “bitch” in incomplete lines that make conspicuous features of those gaps.Taylor Swift’s singles – ranked!Read moreAnd for all that she laments the haters, she sure does write a lot of songs about them. The more dogshit like Cleveland! she releases, the more criticism it may garner, in turn generating inspiration for … more songs like this. It is Swiftian Groundhog Day: she seems unwilling or unable to extricate herself from the vast web of self-reference she now seems condemned to operate within, having reached the point in the corporate life cycle where novelty is all but exhausted and it’s easier to double down on core values.It’s hard to tell what any of this has to do with Showgirl (other than pushing the album back to No 1 until Christmas). Every song sounds as though it could have been appended to a different record. Closing trackBabylonis sub-Evermorein its overcomplicated narrative of a fractured family and grave, watery production. You could point to their very loose shared theme, each taking different angles on the gap between a facade and an intimately understood truth – though the greater truth affirmed by this batch of music is that the more Swift releases, the weaker her output gets. It doesn’t take any detective work to deduce that the healthiest thing for her creativity would be to let the curtain fall for a while.Explore more on these topicsTaylor SwiftPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new film | Crime films | The Guardian
description: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV
Author: David Smith
Headline: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV
Content: Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in PrimetimePhotograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenRobert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in PrimetimePhotograph: Courtesy of A24Crime films‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new filmExperts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TVDavid Smithin WashingtonFri 25 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAman from Long Beach, California, is here to have sex with someone he believes is a 13-year-old girl. When the journalistChris Hansenwalks in, the man’s stomach drops. He is caught, and it is the end of his life as he knew it. Hansen asks what his fate should be. “The electric chair?” he asks. No, replies Hansen. “Dateline NBC.”Primetime review – Robert Pattinson’s preening TV host hunts paedophiles but real drama proves harder to targetRead moreThis is the opening scene ofPrimetime, a film directed by Lance Oppenheim, released in the US this week (a UK release follows on 30 October). It explores how a network news show turned sting operations into must-see television, raising a host of ethical questions about justice, voyeurism and society’s willingness to dehumanise certain offenders for profit and entertainment.The swaggering Hansen is played byRobert Pattinson, whose recent movies includeThe Batman,The DramaandThe Odyssey. He delivers a line that captures the film’s argument about a societal turning point: “There used to be a pillory in every village. Now, there’s a television in every living room.” But the real Hansen, 67, hasbrandedthe movie an “insult” and “identity theft” without having seen it.Going head-to-head with ABC’s Lost in primetime, Dateline NBC’s To Catch a Predator was one of the defining TV hits of the US ratings wars of the mid-2000s, an era before streaming. The programme targeted men suspected of soliciting sex with minors in online chat rooms. Volunteers from the citizen watchdog groupPerverted Justiceposed as underage children, engaging adults in conversations and then arranging meetings at fake homes.There, decoy actors playing the supposed teenagers would be waiting. The men would be confronted on camera by Hansen while police officers stood outside, ready to make arrests. The formula proved hugely successful. By the 2006-07 season,To Catch a Predatorwas averaging about 7 million viewers an episode, turning Hansen into a star with his own catchphrase: “Have a seat.”David Osit, director of Predators, an acclaimed 2025 documentary about the show, says: “The show was sordid and creepy and amusing and you could find many different ways to relate to what was happening. You could identify with the parents, you could identify with Chris Hansen, you could identify with the schadenfreude of watching these men have the worst day of their lives.“You can see that even in the marketing for Primetime: a lot of it’s reposting old clips of To Catch a Predator. It’s quite clear that this still has an effect on people because it is at this nexus of discomfort and basic human instinct. In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs and we enjoy discomfort from a safe vantage point and that’s what the show was able to offer people.”View image in fullscreenTo Catch a Predator still taken from Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators.Photograph: Courtesy of DogwoofBut in 2006 the operation took a fatal turn.Bill Conradt, an assistant district attorney in Rockwall county, Texas, allegedly contacted a decoy posing as a 13-year-old boy but changed his mind. The team went ahead with the police operation at his home after he failed to appear at the sting house. Conradt killed himself as a local Swat team entered, with the television crew outside.The episode prompted a lawsuit that was eventually settled out of court, as well as a series of journalistic investigations including reports by ABC’s 20/20 and Esquire journalist Luke Dittrich, whose 2007 article,Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die, would later become a key source for Ajon Singh’s screenplay for Primetime. By 2008 To Catch a Predator had been cancelled.‘He stole the show’: do Oscars beckon for Robert Pattinson, star of four of the year’s biggest films – and Batman?Read moreBut years earlier, local law enforcement agencies across the US had already been quietly wrestling with the dawn of internet solicitation. In Kentucky, then attorney general Greg Stumbo oversaw a series of state-led sting operations aimed at snaring men suspected of soliciting sex with minors.Working alongside local officials – including Jerry “Peanuts” Gaines, the sheriff of Bowling Green – Kentucky’s bureau of investigation used a young-looking female agent to pose online as an underage teenager. The state partnered with Perverted Justice to engage men in online chat rooms and lure them to monitored locations. The stings resulted in more than 20 arrests in Kentucky.Stumbo recalls:“None of them had a criminal record. They were a firefighter, they were a university teacher – people that you just walk around and see every day on the street. It’s scary when you think about how many people like that there are out there who are predators for our children.”Only after Kentucky authorities concluded their stings did Hansen and his Dateline NBC crew arrive in Bowling Green to carry out interviews. Stumbo notes that state prosecutors kept tight control over their files, refusing to hand over criminal evidence tapes to network producers while trials were pending. But the message sent to potential offenders, Stumbo says, was immediate: “The talk was, ‘Don’t go to Kentucky. They’ll catch you if you go to Kentucky.’ That’s what we wanted the talk to be, obviously.”View image in fullscreenTo Catch a Predator still taken from Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators.Photograph: Courtesy of DogwoofAsked whether the sting setup – and the subsequent television spectacle – crossed an ethical boundary into entrapment, Stumbo is adamant. “Nobody ever came to me and said that and it wouldn’t do any good if they did. We didn’t do it for that purpose. We did it because we wanted that word that was spread through that community of people who look at those types of situations: don’t come to Kentucky.”And for the men caught on camera whose lives evaporated in an instant, Stumbo offers no quarter. “I’m a prosecutor. I probably am a little bit hard about stuff like that. I don’t find any excuse in that. Yeah, you feel sorry for anybody that stoops that low in life, but to intentionally want to go and do that type of activity with a minor, I have no sympathy for them.”Perverted Justice, founded by Xavier Von Erck, was also the engine behind Dateline NBC’s To Catch a Predator. Von Erck’s relationship with national media began in early 2004, following a series of stings with local television stations. In a single week CBS’s 60 Minutes II, ABC’s Primetime Live and NBC’s Dateline NBC asked him to replicate his model on a national network scale.Von Erck immediately knew which he would not choose. He says via email: “We had caught a national news producer for ABC News at our first sting in Milwaukee. He showed up to that very first sting house we ever did, and ABC News did not fire him despite our pressure campaign … So obviously I wasn’t going to work with Primetime Live.”Von Erck managed volunteers remotely, screening chat logs and enforcing boundaries, while operatives Frag and Del Harvey worked inside the sting houses with Dateline NBC producers. He recalls one particularly disturbing suggestion from a producer: that a target be encouraged to get into a hot tub with one of the female decoys. “We said no.”Von Erck fiercely defends Perverted Justice’s record, claiming more than 600 convictions, a 99.1% conviction rate and statutory changes in all 50 states. He dismisses accusations of entrapment, arguing that his operatives never made first contact and that convictions based on their evidence survived appeals.View image in fullscreenActors Bokeem Woodbine, Phoebe Bridgers, Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever at Venice film festival, 5 September.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageHe writes: “In fact, out of the dozens of cases in which convicted individuals desperately appealed to a higher court, convictions due to the evidence we supplied were *never* overturned. It is quite a silly notion to believe that someone can be ‘induced’ to want to sexually assault a 10-15 year old. It requires a specific predilection.”He says he spoke to Hansen only twice and regards To Catch a Predator as fundamentally dependent on his group work. “Without my organization, there was no To Catch a Predator possible at that time,” he says. “It would have been a tall reporter standing inside of a house interviewing no one.”That history is one reason Von Erck is so hostile to Oppenheim’s film. He accuses the filmmakers of inventing scenes, opinions and locations involving him. “I don’t regard ‘Primetime’ as being a movie made about the story of To Catch a Predator because from what I know from watching the trailer and reading reviews of the movie, it seems like most of the details of the movie are absurdly inaccurate when it comes to my organization in particular.“It feels like an oddly and purposely malicious portrayal, especially of myself, given that every review I’ve seen that mentions the way they have portrayed me is literally something I did not do, things I never said, and places I never was ever even physically at. Frankly, I find it bewildering that they are using my legal name and semi-likeness while completely inventing every opinion, statement, act and physical location that they portray me as in the movie.”The Guardian made repeated attempts to contact Oppenheim and Dittrich but without success. Hansen did not respond to requests for an interview. But he has used other platforms to condemn Primetime as an “insult” and complain that the actorDenis Learywould have been better casting than Pattinson.View image in fullscreenA scene from Primetime.Photograph: Courtesy of A24In aninterview with USA Today newspaperon Wednesday, Hansen said: “They wanted to exploit the brand that I’ve built over the last 45 years. You can decide whether that’s ethical or legal or identity theft or however you look at it. But it seems a little exploitive, as Hollywood often is.”Intriguingly, he has alsobought advertisingfor his true crime streaming network TruBlu to play before screenings of Primetime. The move strikes Osit, the director of Predators, as characteristically shrewd. “It does fit with the Chris Hansen I know,” he says. “That’s a savvy and intelligent thing to do for what Chris Hansen is interested in doing, which is to get people to see his investigations.”Osit argues that when commercial news networks commodified vigilante justice, they established a precedent that has only accelerated in the age of social media and streaming. In modern iterations of the format, networks and digital streamers no longer feel compelled to blur the faces of suspects or provide traditional journalistic safeguards. He argues that ethical qualms have increasingly been swept aside.“We’ve societally accepted that these men are not human beings. They’re not deserving of the same rights or protections that someone who committed a different kind of crime and has their face blown up on the internet might be. We’ve societally accepted it’s quite acceptable to shame these men and that is their punishment for this crime.”Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?Read moreOsit found Hansen to be a charismatic combination of both journalist and entertainer and does not think To Catch a Predator’s intentions were cruel. He admires Hansen’s ability to interact with people but does not agree with some of the ways that he conducts himself professionally.“If Chris was interested in ending child predation, the investigations wouldn’t still be going on,” Osit comments. “That’s not what we’re doing here. However, Chris has been told by many, many people over the years that they’re grateful for his investigations and those people exist. There are also many people who think that those investigations are problematic and then there’s a lot of people in between.”Ultimately, Osit contends, fixating on Hansen’s personal motives misses the more uncomfortable truths that To Catch a Predator exposed about its audience.“The more interesting question than who is Chris is who are we? Why do we enjoy this show? What do we get out of the show? What is this show reflecting about the society we live in where we sexualise teenage girls so much and yet create circumstances where we will ask people to show up to a house because they think it’s safe and people are playing these games on the internet where they’re pretending to be different ages?”Osit adds: “This is a world that we helped create as a society and those are more challenging questions to ask about who we are as human beings because it involves maybe interrogating how culpable we are in the culture that decides to treat young people as attractive objects for men who can’t get mental help to avoid being sucked into these issues. Those are questions that a movie is not going to deal with.”Primetime is out in the US now, in Australia on 29 October and in the UK on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsCrime filmsRobert PattinsonUS crimeThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d strip for £100!’ Dominic West and Sienna Miller on nudity, narcissism and their juicy new show War | Drama | The Guardian
description: The stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revolting
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revolting
Content: ‘I decided to be narcissistic’ … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreen‘I decided to be narcissistic’ … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesDramaInterview‘I’d strip for £100!’ Dominic West and Sienna Miller on nudity, narcissism and their juicy new show WarEmine SanerThe stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revoltingFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a London hotel room, Dominic West is weighing up how much he would accept to strip to his socks. In the new series War, West plays a social media billionaire who is supposed to be fairly decent, though there’s one excruciating scene – goading someone to strip for money – that reveals he’s definitely also a bit of a git. “That, I suppose, is the kick billionaires must get: that people would do anything for money,” he says. He wonders what his price would be. His co-starSienna Millerlaughs and says he’d do it “for the lols”, and West grins and says: “No, I’d want three figures. A hundred quid.”War is a juicy eight-part legal drama, where Miller and West are a divorcing couple – she a narcissistic film star, he said billionaire – so just about all their scenes together are suppurating with contempt, which is fun, but also a bit of a shame because they have such good chemistry. They first worked together 21 years ago in the West End production of Shakespeare’sAs You Like It. “So we had a history, which was great,” says Miller. There have been many times she’s gone into jobs where “on the first day you’re married to someone and you don’t know them. It’s helpful to have some sort of rapport.”West was cast first – he had worked with the creator George Kay previously on the classy BBC drama The Hour, and Kay had written the role of Morgan Henderson, a tech entrepreneur, with him in mind. Miller plays Carla Duval, a Hollywood star who wants half of her philandering ex’s wealth – with the help of her formidable legal team. Neither Carla nor Morgan have much to recommend them. Miller struggled, she says with a laugh, to “find the more human aspects of her, until I realised it was really fun not to. I decided to have fun leaning into the unappealing qualities of Carla, which was quite uncomfortable for somebody who errs on the side of people-pleasing. To not be invested in other people’s reactions or responses. To be narcissistic, basically.”View image in fullscreenThrowing shade … Miller with James McArdle and Phoebe Fox in War.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/Sky/HBO/New PicturesFor West, it must have been just as tricky finding his way into playing a “benign billionaire”. Do they exist? The BBC podcast Good Bad Billionaire came in useful, he says. Only a handful of the billionaires covered could be considered “good”. “Basically they’re the ones who give away all the money … It was intriguing to me, the idea of a benign billionaire.” But Morgan obviously has a ruthless side – the hardball divorce negotiations, and that strip scene. “And you go, oh,nowwe see why he’s a billionaire. But other than that, I was doing what Sienna was avoiding, and I do all the time, which is desperately try to make people like me.”Was the high-profile divorce based on real-life cases? No, says Kay when we speak. Only one scene was inspired by real events – when the actor and director Olivia Wilde wasserved custody papersat a public event on behalf of Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis. “It was one of our most emotional days [on set],” says Kay, “because it’s such a horrible thing to do.”The show was inspired by a conversation Kay overheard in a queue in an airport lounge. “This woman screamed ‘Yes!’ into her phone. I turned around, because I’m quite nosy, and said: ‘Can I ask what has made you so happy?’” She told him her husband had finally signed the papers after a four-year divorce battle. The more Kay looked into high-stakes, high-end divorces, the more he realised it was filled with drama – the prenups, the affairs, the property – and ideal for the kind of glossy legal shows he’d grown up watching. “I’m a kid of the 90s,” he says. He loved the big law shows such asAlly McBeal, and laterThe Good Wife, andThe West Wingwas inspiration as a workplace-based drama. “I loved the humour. I wanted to do something with the sort of zip and repartee of those shows.” It’s the reason the cast of War is so comedian-heavy, includingMiles JuppandNick Mohammedas solicitors at rival firms. “People [who] are just super-sharp on the cues because if anyone slows down, it dies on its feet.” (Extra fun fact: Mohammed and Celia Imrie, who plays a barrister, were also filming The Celebrity Traitors at the same time. “They were so tight-lipped!” says Kay.)View image in fullscreenLaw and disorder … West with Nina Sosanya and Pip Torrens in War.Photograph: New Pictures/Sky/HBOHe had previously worked with writer Abi Morgan on her showThe Hour; Morgan’s seriesThe Splitalso features glossy divorce lawyers, but Kay says his were “all American references”. There’s already a second series with the rival law firms taking on a defamation case. Expect more juice.A public divorce brings wild scrutiny of the private lives of the people going through it, and when it’s a celebrity couple – as Morgan and Carla discover – it’s on a different scale altogether. Miller and West both have experience of this, though not in divorces. West had a brief period of what might politely be called “marital scrutiny” (in late 2020, photographers camped outside his house after photographs were published of him with hisThe Pursuit of Loveco-star Lily James) but Miller had years of intense hounding during her relationship with the actor Jude Law. A victim of phone hacking by the News of the World, she won damages in 2011, gave evidence to the Leveson inquiry, and settled with News Group Newspapers in 2021 over alleged hacking.“They [the paparazzi] were hounding you, weren’t they?” says West, remembering scenes outside the London theatre where they worked in 2005. Yes, says Miller, “but it feels like another life and another world. It’s now almost, from a kind of sociological perspective, interesting to look back on what the culture was like then.”What is curious, though, is why Miller seems so willing to put herself through it in her work: in War, as in Netflix’sAnatomy of a Scandal, she’s harassed by paps and dealing with an unfaithful husband. Having only got the later scripts after signing on, she didn’t know what Carla would be dealing with. She laughs and says maybe directors instantly think of her for “that kind of storyline, which is something I’ll now avoid”. But does it stir up difficult memories, or is there a catharsis in playing it? “Maybe that’s it. Maybe it is kind of reframing it for myself – to pretend at it, and to then remember how crazy that was as a way of living.” Separately, Kay says his stars’ personal experiences didn’t influence the casting or writing. “One of the things we did quite quickly was we resisted any of that meta-referencing, because they are incredibly good actors, and these parts are different from their own experiences.”West has had plenty of accolades, but Miller has always been underrated; she has said that the emphasis on her personal life probably derailed her career. She puts in a wonderful performance in War, as she has in other roles such as the weighty 2018 filmAmerican Woman. “I feel less like I have to prove something, and I’m not sure whether that’s because I don’t have anything to prove, or I just don’t care about proving myself any more,” she says.There are also a few better roles now for older women. “I remember speaking to actresses who were like: ‘You’re so lucky that you’re turning 40 now, because we were obsolete when that happened.’ But I still wish I’d played Juliet.” She remembers speaking to a theatre heavyweight not so long ago and asking if he thought she could still play Juliet. She laughs as she remembers: “He said, ‘I just think people will struggle to see you as a virgin.’” West adds with a laugh, “You just need an old Romeo.”Has this show put them off ever getting divorced? “Of course!” says West (married since 2010). “I think that’s the big takeaway. I was talking to a guy who was rich and getting a divorce, and he backed up everything in the show. The interesting thing, and George anatomises it so well, is how two people who loved each other can descend into warfare. That’s where the drama is: that knife edge between love and hate. You get it in any relationship, when you’re arguing or whatever, but this is in a wildly expensive public arena. Like a battle in any commercial situation, with big lawyers, your marriage becomes that.” A commodity, says Miller (she’s engaged to the actor Oli Green), “to be bartered with, and the more acrimonious, the more money [for the lawyers]”.The stress and vitriol unleashed by this divorce, arguing over numbers so big they’re almost meaningless, seems barely worth it. I’d have settled for a lot less to avoid it (I’d be a terrible divorce lawyer). “I imagine that kind of money to be incredibly corrosive,” says Miller. “I have been in proximity to people who have a huge amount of money, and I just don’t see them as happier. I mean, it’s a revolting amount of money.” West has given billionaires more thought recently than he’d probably like to. “If you’ve got several hundred billion, and you’re not solving the climate crisis, then really something’s deeply wrong.”War is on Sky Atlantic on Friday2 Octoberat 9pm.Explore more on these topicsDramaTelevisionSienna MillerDominic WestfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: MNEK on writing smash hits, battling self-doubt and his solo struggles: ‘I’m a fat Black gay man. Try selling that’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The artist has written for Beyoncé and been nominated for two Grammys, yet individual success has eluded him. Now he’s back with a new album that puts queer joy in the spotlight – and, he says, he’s finally ready to enjoy himself
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: The artist has written for Beyoncé and been nominated for two Grammys, yet individual success has eluded him. Now he’s back with a new album that puts queer joy in the spotlight – and, he says, he’s finally ready to enjoy himself
Content: Hot and heavy … MNEK.Photograph: Lewis VornView image in fullscreenHot and heavy … MNEK.Photograph: Lewis VornMusicInterviewMNEK on writing smash hits, battling self-doubt and his solo struggles: ‘I’m a fat Black gay man. Try selling that’Alim KherajThe artist has written for Beyoncé and been nominated for two Grammys, yet individual success has eluded him. Now he’s back with a new album that puts queer joy in the spotlight – and, he says, he’s finally ready to enjoy himselfFri 25 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a south-east London warehouse, Uzoechi Osisioma Emenike, more commonly known as MNEK, is sitting on a bench in a makeshift locker room surrounded by semi-naked men. One particularly muscular individual suggestively adjusts a jockstrap, while another, taller and toned, removes his vest before eyeing MNEK with a loaded gaze. It’s a lot of sexual tension for a Tuesday morning. But such is the life of a pop star on the set of a music video.“It is very gay, you’re not wrong there,” MNEK says, while getting his makeup done for the shoot. The video being filmed is for the fittingly titled Muscle Marys.., the third single from the 31-year-old south Londoner’s second album, Bulldozer!! In one corner of the warehouse, behind a large vanity curtain, a group of dancers are being hosed down while filming a shower scene. The water, a runner has assured me, is warm.The album is MNEK’s first solo record in eight years and its title is confrontational. “As a six-foot-four Black man, I am very conscious of the space I take up,” he explains. “I am often trying to squeeze myself down. I mean look at where we are right now …” He gestures at the low-ceilinged room. “Can I stand up straight in this space? But that’s the reality of being as large as I am. Bulldozer came about because it’s one of those words that I found very triggering. But because of that, it felt like the right title.”No one can argue against MNEK’s outsized impact on pop music. He signed his first publishing deal aged just 14, and as a writer-producer has worked with the likes of Beyoncé, Kylie Minogue, Madonna, Christina Aguilera, Little Mix and Flo. His songs – Never Forget You, a duet with Zara Larsson, and Head & Heart, a 2020 collab with DJ Joel Corry – have amassed more than 1bn streams. Earlier this year he was nominated for his second Grammy for Larsson’s song Midnight Sun, which he co-wrote and produced.As a solo artist, however, things haven’t always been so big. His debut album, 2018’s underrated Language, peaked at No 81. “I lost a lot of confidence after that,” he says. “I live every day knowing that most, if not all, of my money is made from being a writer and producer. But my solo music is also something I care about. Still, a lot of the time, I will be the only person vouching for me to make my own music.”double quotation markWhile there is a very rich queer culture within the Black community, there’s also a deeper history with homophobiaThe visuals and lyrics of Language were also explicitly queer, with one reviewer at the time suggesting the muted response to the record was a result of homophobia and racism. “When it comes to going to the public with my own music, I am a fat Black gay man. Try and sell that.” Still, as an artist, he wanted to be true to who he was. “I feel like [withholding my sexuality] is something that maybe could have benefited me, but now we’ll never know. I just didn’t want to be on stage singing about girls if it wasn’t my truth.”While MNEK says he began working on his second album just after Language came out, his poor mental health, the pandemic and other work commitments left him feeling he couldn’t make a coherent record. “I needed to figure out how to get back to the pure desire of wanting to make a project,” he says. A separation from his management helped. “It took me back to being 14. I was making music and there were no expectations other than me being excited about it.”That purity of intent paid off. Bulldozer!! is MNEK at the height of his powers: an electric rush of window-rattling grime, Godzilla-sized hooks, cavernous club bangers, oily UK garage and lushly layered harmonies. Sonically, it’s his personal and musical identity unapologetically stuffed into a hulking pop beefcake.View image in fullscreenSixpac … MNEK performing at Pride In London in July.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Getty ImagesIts themes are equally big. Songs such as The Wall!! address pushing through self-doubt (“Six foot four and I still got growing pains,” he sings), while both the braggadocious, Channel U-indebted Reverse!! and Dirty Little Secret!!’s stuttering R&B explore encounters with “DL trade” (men who sleep with other men secretly, or on the “down low”).Does he have experience with that community? “I have over the years. It’s not my reality right now. But it’s complicated. While there is a very rich queer culture within the Black community, there’s also a deeper history with homophobia, which starts with colonialism, of course. There are a lot of people who believe in the ‘batty man’ ideology and that being gay is a sin. Those God-fearing environments create DL people. It’s not about shaming anyone. I’m just saying: ‘You don’t have to drag me into it.’”There is also a sonic thread MNEK is pulling at, too. “Those songs are influenced by the grime and garage and two-step I grew up listening to,” he says. “I consider it dance music, as much as house and disco and all the different things I explore on the record. I wanted to claim some ownership of that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat has proved harder than anticipated. When he tried to clear a sample of Lethal Bizzle’s Pow! for Reverse!!, his request was shut down. “They weren’t comfortable with the lyrical content,” he says with a sigh. “Even though Pow! is hardly a song about morality, [queerness] is a no-go area in a lot of these communities.” Other requests were easier: Lady!! interpolates Geri Halliwell’s Bag It Up, with MNEK subverting Ginger Spice’s turn-of-the-millennium battle of the sexes into a song that embraces gender fluidity, while Oh No!! All the Boys!! samples the piano riff from the Clash’s Rock the Casbah.‘Men explicitly loving men is so threatening to the status quo’: why are gay male pop stars being shut out of the music industry?Read moreDesirability politics, meanwhile, come to the fore on Muscle Marys.., which addresses the toxicity of male body standards in the gay community, something MNEK has experienced first-hand. “There was one instance where I had hooked up with a guy. He was a total Muscle Mary, a quintessential LA gay,” he recalls. “I found his Twitter account. It turned out that he had tweeted saying: ‘Hey, this British musician is messaging me. I don’t think he’s that attractive, but should I do it just to say I did it?’”That’s horrible, I say. “It’s vile. In those intimate settings, of course there’s an element of transaction there, but you want to feel desirable.”Body image is something MNEK has struggled with his entire life. “I’ve always been fat. It’s something that you’re dealing with or running away from or keeping a tab on,” he says. “But I’ve taken up the gym, which has become part of the fabric of my life, as far as feeling confident about my body.”Just then, someone comes in to say they’re waiting for MNEK to film. The dancers have dried off and the locker room is set up. MNEK jumps up, tugging on a vest, protecting the white fabric from his dyed yellow hair (“It stains everything!”). Despite the simple get-up, he looks ready to be a pop star again. “I wish I hadn’t been so hard on myself [before] because I’m really fab and I’ve done really great things in my life. This time I want to really, really enjoy it.”Bulldozer!! is out now.MNEKtoursthe UK and Ireland to 15 November; tour starts Bristol.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockDance musicR&BinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | Games | The Guardian
description: The game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane
Author: Patrick Lum
Headline: The game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane
Content: ‘The simple act of flying around looks astounding’ … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoView image in fullscreen‘The simple act of flying around looks astounding’ … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoGamesReviewAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasyPlayStation 5, Xbox, PC (version played); Bandai NamcoThe game generates blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through the skies, while your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy planePatrick LumFri 25 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe core appeal of any Ace Combat game lies in the moment when the beautiful clouds part, the sunlight glints off your perfectly rendered state-of-the-art fighter jet, and guitar-shredding music kicks into overdrive as your locked-on missiles speed away to obliterate an enemy plane. All of that is 100% present in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. What’s new is the way it delivers its unexpectedly compelling story.Set in the Earth-like alternative world of Strangereal, where every country is absolutely obsessed with fighter planes and giant superweapons, Ace Combat drafts you into the role of a fake ace pilot called the Wings of Theve – a propaganda invention to raise the morale of a besieged nation, similar to real-life rumours about Ukraine’sGhosts of Kyiv. You rapidly find yourself becoming an actual legendary pilot, soaring through the skies with your buddies and raining hell upon your oppressors as everybody cheers on the radio. Speaking of ghosts, you have one in your ear – your predecessor, whom nobody else can hear, a gravelly voice waxing lyrical about flying, war and whatever else is on his mind as you flit about.Despite slavish devotion to the accurate depiction of military hardware, Ace Combat has always been more concerned with making flying fun than sticking to realism. Simplified, more intuitive controls and training scenarios are available to help ease beginners into the pilot’s seat, while as a series veteran I was happier with the expert control scheme, which opens up more complex manoeuvres like missile-evading rolls and zero-G turns. Importantly, the simple act of flying around looks astounding; action replays unerringly choose the best camera angles to make you look like a true ace (instead of someone simply doing their best not to smash straight into the ground).This is a game all about dogfighting, but there’s a pleasing variety of mission types ranging from bombing runs and escorts to more convoluted scenarios such as taking out a giant, railgun-equipped “land battleship” rampaging through a city’s streets, or hunting radar-invisible supersonic planes by trying to spot their tell-tale contrails. It’s all thrilling stuff; the game is perfectly tuned to generate high-tension, blood-pumping moments as you twist, turn and weave through endless rains of missiles while an orchestra goes absolutely wild and a well-produced radio drama plays out over the open airwaves.It can all get a little confusing in the heat of battle, especially in the first-person cockpit view (which I otherwise highly recommend). Deciphering what the game is telling you to aim for next amid the visual clutter can be a trial – a button to target priority mission objectives directly wouldn’t have gone amiss. The clouds, too, can disorientate; I have never seen skies as gorgeous before, but you’ll soon learn to read the atmosphere for its tactical considerations as much as for its beauty.Gameplay innovations are more incremental than sweeping. You can issue commands to your wing-mates, as in much earlier games in the series, but new to AC8 is environmental destruction. Some buildings and vehicles crumble when damaged: falling debris or explosions can trigger devastating chain reactions and you are no longer forced to target weak points to do damage to larger vessels, though it usually remains more efficient. Your plane can also glance off surfaces, taking a bit of damage, which is a relief; in previous entries you would explode instantaneously if your wing so much as clipped a tree branch.View image in fullscreenImpactful … Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.Illustration: Bandai NamcoLarger, more impactful changes are reserved for how the game tells its story. AC7’s cut-scenes were closer to motion comics than movies, which worked fine for mission briefings but less so for anything involving human emotion. Here, fully animated first-person segments meld with more traditional cinematic cut-scenes (and some really effective smash-cutsbetweenscenes) to really bring your wing-mates and the drama to life. Enemy incursions might occur during routine landings or refuelings, too, keeping you on your toes.Ace Combat has always owed a debt to the movie Top Gun, and AC8 borrows liberally from the more recent sequel Top Gun: Maverick, with closeup pilot face-cam shots and a handful of story beats lifted straight from the film. Dialogue can be a bit clunky (again like Top Gun, or perhaps Metal Gear Solid); characters will occasionally pause midway through an otherwise natural-sounding conversation to deliver some convoluted plot exposition or an ideological clanger. But between the truly amazing shot framing and cinematography, emotive motion capture and voice acting, the series’ trademark soaring music and a story that actually sticks the landing, I ended up oddly moved. This is not something you necessarily expect from an arcade flight combat sim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnfortunately I was unable to try the game’s online multiplayer mode, Ace Combat Online, which was only available for a very short time during the review period. But even leaving that aside, AC8 is a triumph, a perfectly composed symphony of fire and steel that absolutely soars.Released on 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesAdventure gamesArcade gamesSimulation gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears | Games | The Guardian
description: I’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played together
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: I’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played together
Content: ‘We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun’ … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.Illustration: APView image in fullscreen‘We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun’ … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.Illustration: APGamesPlaying video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tearsDominik DiamondI’ve been holed up in an flat, affectionately dubbed the ‘brotel’, with my son for weeks – and we’ve revisited the first game we ever played togetherFri 25 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTShareIhave spent the last three weeks living with my 22-year-old son in a two-bedroom flat he has dubbed the ”brotel”. We cook curries and watchLanterns. We barbecue meat and analyse Tarantino movies. We get pizza and we play video games. Boy, do we play video games!The first game I ever played in co-op with him was Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 in 2009, when he was five. He wasn’t the most accomplished sidekick, notsogreat at placing a mobile gun turret while under fire from what seems like a bazillion enemy soldiers, but we had a laugh. It started the video game bond between us before his sister introduced him to Banjo-Kazooie and Rayman, and he stopped being a preschool warmonger. Probably for the best. So how would it be tackling the same game nearly two decades later?We start with the two Special Ops missions we used to play. We never completed them because, once again, he was five – and I am left-handed, which makes me rubbish at joypad-controlled first-person shooters without the help of auto targeting. Thankfully, one of those circumstances has now changed.View image in fullscreenGuard dogs in the snow … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s Evasion mission.Photograph: ActivisionThe first mission is officially called Evasion, but to us it has always been “the guard dogs in the snow”, because they got us every time we played. Our initial attempts highlight the differences between us as gamers. And men, if I’m being honest.I am paranoid. I sense calamity around every corner, so I creep forwards, mostly crouching, frequently crawling on my belly, slowly and carefully scouting for enemies using my sniper scope. Charlie is running through the level firing from the hip likeLeeroy bloody Jenkins. Which means he alerts all the dogs, who for some reason are able to smell me from miles away and nom nom nom me to oblivion.We fail. We fail again. But we are having so much fun.Teamwork eventually emerges through compromise. He holds back a bit, I grow less timid. I snipe from a distance, he finishes them off up close. And, most importantly, we take out the guard dogs first. We realise that was where we went wrong two decades ago. These dogs are superhuman. I would love a level where you got to play as them.We finally complete the mission. It has only taken us 17 years! We go straight into the other level that we never conquered: Homeland Security, AKA “defend the garage from five waves of attack”. This takes a fair few goes, but we have such great communication by this time that it’s never a chore. We leap from our twin La-Z-Boy chairs in celebration when we win.We gambol through mission after mission. Suspension, AKA “bridge with helicopters”, is a riot from start to finish. We have a great rhythm. I bazooka from afar, Charlie sprints in to mop up. In Snatch and Grab, we take a computer file then boot it from an aircraft graveyard, avoiding helmeted Juggernauts; it’s pure unadulterated gaming joy. Even when, once again, we fail.As I am writing this, thanks to whatever AI is lurking in my computer scanning everything I type or possibly even think, an article pings up about the online gaming cheat industry, which is now apparently worth $8.5bn. I’m sure there are reasons why people invest so much money in cheating – but talk about ripping the soul out of something fun.View image in fullscreenA familiar sight … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s multiplayer.Photograph: ActivisionI have loved these last few weeks gaming with my son. I feel like I have gone back to basics. After decades as an uptight stressed dad, I am finally carefree, because I have recently gone back to working for myself. And I am a very forgiving boss. Sitting there with pizza, beer and another bloke, playing games till the wee small hours without a care in the world … this is what gaming was like for me when I was my son’s age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m not sure you ever top that period in your life as a gamer – when you get that first job that allows you to leave home, get your own place, buy whatever game you want and play it to your heart’s content, before you become burdened by the responsibilities of relationships, mortgages, parenthood and, worst of all, ambition.When those things arrive, you are lucky to squeeze in an hour of play here and there. You just try to get as far through a game as you can in that time because you don’t know when the next free hour will come, and you still feel guilty because you feel you should be doing something more grownup instead. You know, something that might help pay the rent.Now, though, I am back in gaming heaven. It won’t be for ever: my son and I are due to move to different parts of the world in a few months. But he turns to me after one session and says that he will look back on this as some of the best times we ever had together.I turn my head because I am still a Scottish dad and I don’t want him to see me cry.
