Even if those tears are the most beautiful big, happy ones.Dominik Diamondis on tourwith his show Dominik Diamond Sings the Video Games from 29 September to 6 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyShooting gamesParents and parentingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Meryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues? | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators
Author: Ben Child
Headline: The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators
Content: Aslan in The Lion the Witch and the WardrobePhotograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenAslan in The Lion the Witch and the WardrobePhotograph: Disney/Sportsphoto/AllstarWeek in geekMoviesMeryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues?Ben ChildThe Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentatorsFri 25 Sep 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTShareIt is a confusing time to be alive, given how often these days Hollywood indulges in revisionism. Who knew that the Wicked Witch of the West wasthe heroineafter all, thatCruella de Vil simply had a difficult childhood, or thatMufasa was adopted? Now it turns out that Aslan, CS Lewis’s messiah with a mane, is a lioness – or at least, may sound like one in Greta Gerwig’s upcoming adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, because Meryl Streep is providing the voice.News that the Oscar-winner might be portraying Narnia’s Christ-like big catfirst surfaced in April last year, prompting a flurry of complaints from conservative Christians. This week, the naysayers were back afterEmpire published a first look at the film, along with an interview with Gerwig in which the director confirmed the casting and explained her choice of actor. Streep, it turns out, was hired not because the Barbie director desperately fancied stoking the flames of controversy, but because she needed someone over 70 who could convey both wisdom and childlike wonder.“I wanted someone who was profound but not pretentious, who had gravitas but not morose self-seriousness,” Gerwig said. She also explained she wanted one of the finest actors working today, adding: “That list is not a long one.”View image in fullscreenThe Magician’s Nephew director Greta Gerwig.Photograph: Presley Ann/Getty Images for Lucas Museum of Narrative ArtSome American evangelical commentators have already made up their minds that this new version of Narnia comes from from the seventh circle of hell. Radio host Jenna Ellis accused Gerwig of “profaning Christ with the divine feminine”, while Texas preacher David Fairchild called the casting “creative vandalism”.The Daily Wire’s Isabel Brown saidthe decision to cast Streep was offensive because “CS Lewis literally intended Aslan to be the incarnation of Christ inside the world of Narnia”. She pointed to the end of Lewis’s novel The Voyage of the Dawn Treader, in which Aslan tells Lucy and Edmund they will come to know him by another name in their own world. For Brown, casting Streep was a “deliberate mockery of Christianity”.There has been no confirmation from Gerwig that this new Aslan is in fact female. And not everyone agrees that casting Streep is a problem: Christian writer Mary Pezzulohas pointed out the ironythat some evangelicals think it’s perfectly all right for Jesus to be portrayed as an animal yet draw the line when he’s given a woman’s voice. “Very Online conservative Christians really think that portraying Christ as a lion, a carnivorous beast with notoriously smelly urine who sleeps 23 hours a day and steals meat from hyaenas, is beautiful sacred art,” she wrote. “But having Christ portrayed by a woman is sacrilege.”However you view this one, it’s weird that a film adaptation of one of the least known books in the Narnia series now feels like the subject of an emergency reconvening ofthe Council of Nicaea. Also, Gerwig has said she plans to reimagine the fantasy world through a rock opera prism: the great lion king’s eyes have been coloured like David Bowie’s mismatched peepers in publicity shots, and the creation of Narnia is apparently designed to look and sound as if Genesis is being staged by the Spiders from Mars. Daniel Craig is playing the deeply suspect sorcerer of the title, while Emma Mackey steps into Tilda Swinton’s shoes as the White Witch, Jadis. But all anyone can think about is that Aslan now sounds remarkably similar to Miranda Priestly, Julia Child and Mrs Thatcher.View image in fullscreenMeryl StreepPhotograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesThat’s actually a shame, because The Magician’s Nephew has enough going on that it shouldn’t require a culture war to make a splash. Its story sees two children discover a wood full of pools leading to other worlds; one takes them to a dead city beneath a dying sun, where they wake the queen who exterminated its entire population and accidentally bring her back to London. The book has a sense of madcap wonder about it that occasionally makes all the waiting for Aslan to turn up in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, only for him to immediately sacrifice himself, feel like a glacially paced, religiously didactic slog by way of comparison.Remember whenBarbiewent from a potentially cheesy movie about an anatomically unlikely child’s doll to the most talked about film of the year? Something similar could happen here. And then again, Streep might just be playing a lion in a children’s film. Either way, it seems remarkable that an actor whose voice nobody has yet heard in the movie has apparently displaced the White Witch herself – or perhaps even some of her famously addictive turkish delight – as Narnia’s most devious and malign influence.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekGreta GerwigMeryl StreepCS LewisFilm adaptationsChristianityReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for the Pogues | The Pogues | The Guardian
description: Ahead of a greatest hits tour, original members Spider Stacy and James Fearnley will join us to answer your questions
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Ahead of a greatest hits tour, original members Spider Stacy and James Fearnley will join us to answer your questions
Content: The Pogues in 1984: Shane MacGowan, James Fearnley, Jem Finer, Andrew Ranken, Spider Stacy and Cait O’Riordan.Photograph: Steve Rapport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Pogues in 1984: Shane MacGowan, James Fearnley, Jem Finer, Andrew Ranken, Spider Stacy and Cait O’Riordan.Photograph: Steve Rapport/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewThe PoguesPost your questions for the PoguesAhead of a greatest hits tour, original members Spider Stacy and James Fearnley will join us to answer your questionsBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 25 Sep 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenShane MacGowandied in 2023, you’d be forgiven for wondering whether the Pogues could carry on, given what a singular frontman he was – and given the band had been dormant since 2014. But grounded by original members James Fearnley, Jem Finer and Spider Stacy, the Pogues have been playing hugely acclaimed reunion gigs in recent years with various guests sitting in for MacGowan – and as they go on a greatest hits tour around the UK this autumn, Fearnley and Stacy will be joining us to answer your questions.The Pogues’ history stretches back to the late 70s when MacGowan, Stacy and Finer played together in London; Fearnley, meanwhile, was a member of MacGowan’s punk band the Nips.The Pogueseventually formed in 1982, investing the traditional music of their Irish heritage with the energy of the city’s punk scene.They released debut album Red Roses for Me in 1984, the following year’s Rum Sodomy & the Lash took them into the UK Top 20, and then 1987 brought Fairytale of New York, their eternally popular Christmas song. The brilliant but wayward MacGowan was eventually fired from the group in 1991, and Joe Strummer stepped in for a time before being replaced by Stacy; the band soldiered on for another couple of albums before splitting in 1996.But while there have been no more studio albums, the Pogues reformed in 2001 and played on and off until 2014. After MacGowan’s death, the richness of the band’s catalogue and the originality of their takes on Irish folk standards was brought into renewed relief; concerts celebrating 40 years since Red Roses for Me were warmly received, with the Guardian’s Patrick Clarke saying in afive-star reviewof a London date: “It could so easily have been a pale imitation, glorified karaoke. And yet, it’s utterly triumphant.”Their greatest hits tour promises a “superlative collection of special guest musicians and singers, among them the cream of the current generation of Irish artists”, and before it kicks off on 28 November, Fearnley and Stacy will answer your questions about the band’s history and future. Post them in the comments below before 4pm BST on Monday 28 September, and their answers will be published later in the week.Explore more on these topicsThe PoguesFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockFolk musicShane MacGowanIrelandcalloutShareReuse this content

title: Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list | Prix Goncourt | The Guardian
description: Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media
Content: The author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesPrix GoncourtNovelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listThélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social mediaPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorFri 25 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.View image in fullscreenThe novel on display inside a bookstore in Paris.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersAllegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”View image in fullscreenOrélien at Les Correspondances literature festival in Manosque this week.Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty ImagesThe author of the anonymous X account was lateridentified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaroas one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokeism” on film and TV.On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged caution over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.Libération alleged inan articlethat the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”The Canada-based publisher said it was important not tojump to conclusions, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me,” adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.Explore more on these topicsPrix GoncourtAwards and prizesPlagiarismFictionFranceAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Birdwatching is close to rapture’: Margaret Atwood on why she has given C$1m to avian research | Margaret Atwood | The Guardian
description: Award-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Award-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology
Content: Margaret Atwood‘Birdwatching is close to rapture’: Margaret Atwood on why she has given C$1m to avian researchAward-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biologyWords and photographs byLeyland Ceccoin Pelee IslandFri 25 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareView image in fullscreen‘They’re social, playful and just a very intelligent bird’… Margaret Atwood on ravens.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianIf she could be any bird,Margaret Atwoodwould transform into a raven. “They’re very smart. They’re social, playful and just a very successful bird,” she says while seated in a corner of a bird observatory in the Lake Erie Islands archipelago. “They’re quite an intelligent problem solver.”View image in fullscreenPelee Island sits at the nexus of two important migration routes, making it a destination for birds travelling thousands of kilometres each year.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianThe observatory, which she set up with her late partner, Graeme Gibson, is located on the west shore of Pelee Island – the southernmost community inCanada– and is so new that there are no lightbulbs in a handful of lamps.Pelee sits at the nexus of two important migration routes, making it a destination for birds travelling thousands of kilometres each year. Ravens are not among its regular visitors – only one was spotted in recent memory, in 2023 – butAtwood likes the old Inuit joke about them.A hunter arrives at a place he has never camped before, and asks a raven where to spend the night. “The raven says, ‘The base of that hill is a good place,’ and so he sets up his little tent there,” says Atwood.“In the middle of the night, a boulder rolls down the hill and crushes him. And the raven, as he’s enjoying the feast, says, ‘Works every time.’”View image in fullscreenThe bestselling author has blended the lines that separate humans and birds in her work.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianThe bestselling Canadian author, whose prophetic works of speculative fiction have won countless awards, has blurred the lines that separate humans and birds bothin her workand, at times, in her life.She and Gibson, also a novelist, once dressed up for a party as Odin’s ravens, Thought and Memory. They wore black gloves and fashioned beaks from black construction paper.Gibson died in 2019. In his final years, vascular dementia overtook his ability to journal about the birds. Still, he would watch them daily.View image in fullscreenPelee Island is accessible only by boat and plane and sits 20 miles off the Ontario mainland in Lake Erie.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The Guardian“Our back yard feeder and our birdbath were attracting only sparrows and robins and grackles and the occasional pigeon, but he didn’t care: every bird was worthy of attention,” Atwood wrote in a foreword to Gibson’s book, The Bedside Book ofBirds. “‘I no longer know their names,’ he told a friend of ours. ‘But then, they don’t know my name either.’”Now, Gibson’s legacy is about to help expand humanity’s understanding of birds. On Friday Western University, in London, Ontario, announced that Atwood had donated C$1m (£540,000) to celebrate her late partner’s love of birds.The gift will create the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology, with the goal of better understanding the fundamental processes that shape how birds move, adapt and behave in an environment undergoing profound transformation.Atwood has championed many causes, including Indigenous education and human rights, but environmental protection is at the forefront of them.“I have what they call a platform,” she says. “And I also had what they call extra money.”View image in fullscreenPelee Island has intact Carolinian forests.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianBehind the deadpan is a longstanding belief in the power of science to answer deceptively simple questions about the natural world. How do birds navigate thousands of kilometres? How do they sense magnetic fields? How do they know where to go?“Look at navigation,” says Chris Guglielmo, the co-director of the advanced facility for avian research at Western University, which received Atwood’s gift.“We have a lot of descriptive understanding of what happens when we manipulate the magnetic fields, for example, the bird changes its orientation. We know they have these senses. But how they actually work is still a big mystery, and very exciting for people to try to study.”The university has emerged as a global leader in avian research, developing the world’s first hypobaric climatic wind tunnel for bird flight in order to better study how they move through different types of air.Guglielmo and his team have also made significant contributions to understanding how migratory birds fuel themselves, travel and survive long-distance journeys. But even the leading minds remain stumped by many of the mysteries that still surround the lives – and minds – of birds.View image in fullscreenVincent Moreau, a researcher with the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, helps ‘band’ birds that are caught each morning in fine mesh nets. Staff log details about the bird to help study their migratory patterns.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The Guardian“Our new graduate students sometimes struggle to come up with a scientific question,” Guglielmo says. “And we tell them, there’s a million questions we don’t know the answer to. I have a whiteboard covered with potential questions. I just don’t have enough funding, people and time to even begin answering them.”That’s why when he received the call about the gift, he was told to sit down first.“It made me feel so good that we’re not only reaching and having impact in the scientific community, but that more broadly in the public sphere,” he says, adding that the gift was a “validation” of work done by the university’s scientists.View image in fullscreenPelee Island is an important migration stopover for more than 200 species of birds.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianWeeks before the gift was announced, Atwood celebrated the opening of the Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre on Pelee Island. Resembling a towel hung loosely from a clothesline, Pelee Island is a rare enclave that blends Carolinian forest, dunes and marshes. Sitting at the intersection of the Atlantic and Mississippi migration routes, each spring it welcomes more than 200 species, not to mention thousands of serious birders.At the event, she was simultaneously treated as literary royalty – attenders queued nervously for a chance to speak to her and pose for photographs – and as Peggy, the no-nonsense islander who often spends months at her cottage there and is woven into the community of 235 full-time residents.The new building expands the footprint of the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, which the couple co-founded more than two decades ago to study the transcontinental movement of birds. It is also a refuge from Atwood’s nemesis: chiggers.“You don’t know about chiggers?” she says of the six-legged larval mites hiding in the grass around the building. “Once you learn about their bite – and the itching that never stops – you never forget.”While Atwood was exposed to birds – and chiggers – during a youth spent in the Ontario hinterlands with her forest entomologist father, Gibson became a bird lover later in life, with the zeal of a born-again religious convert.“At its heightened moments, birdwatching can encourage a state of being close to rapture,” he wrote in his book. “It is an ecstasy that is said to accompany the writing of poetry; sometimes it comes when we’re listening to music.”View image in fullscreenThe red-tailed hawk, the bird that sparked Graeme Gibson’s love of birdwatching.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesHis “spark bird” – the name birders give to the particular species that triggers a lifelong love of the pursuit–was the red-tailed hawk, which is spotted frequently on the island.Others, including the blackpoll warbler, are declining rapidly. The warbler breeds in the northern boreal forest, as far north as the Arctic, before embarking on a nonstop journey of almost 1,800 miles over open water to South America. Its population has dropped more than 80% in the last five decades, making it the fastest declining songbird.Canada and the US have lost nearly 3bn birds since 1970. While certain species, including ducks and birds of prey, have surged in number, birds that travel thousands of miles each year have dropped in population by nearly 30%.The declines, expected to increase further with the climate emergency, matter profoundly for a place such as Canada, where many bird species are migratory.Atwood says the four biggest threats to birds – windows, cats, toxic pollution and environmental destruction of their habitats – are all things humans can help stop.The first two are easier to address, but the latter are more challenging.“People think: we can cut down this forest, and we’ll just make another forest over there. It’s not going to be the same. Birds have specific habitats that they need, so it’s not like spreading butter on a piece of toast.”Atwood, who has spent much of her career imagining dystopian futures, is nonetheless optimistic about a future that has not yet been decided.“Let’s say hope is a built-in human characteristic. Unless you’re deeply depressed, you wake up every morning thinking, what will this day bring? Maybe it will be a chocolate bar. Maybe there’ll be some surprises. If our ancestors didn’t have that, we probably wouldn’t be here,” she says.View image in fullscreenMargaret Atwood with Graeme Gibson at a cocktail party at the Book Lovers Ball at the Royal York hotel in Toronto.Photograph: Steve Russell/Toronto Star/Getty Images“All of us trust this possibility that the doors are not locked. Yes, you may open door A and fall down a flight of stairs, but you may open door B and there will be a chocolate bar.”She points to how young people, especially children, appear hardwired to engage deeply with nature.“The passion is built in. They’re very interested in anything that moves, anything outside, and unless some grown-up teaches them to be afraid of such things, that interest will continue,” she says. “We are part of the natural world. It’s your choice of how to be in it.”More than 11 years ago,Atwood and others signed a letter of outrageafter the Oxford Junior Dictionary dropped a number of nature-themed words – including raven – in favour of a technology-heavy vernacular.The writer Robert Macfarlane and the children’s book illustrator Jackie Morrisreleased an elegy to youthful wonderin response to Oxford’s decision. But against the odds, birding is surging in interest among young people.“If there’s no young people interested in a thing, whatever that thing is, it will die out. The fact that it’s not dying out, but it’s going in the other direction, is quite hopeful,” says Atwood. “I was talking to some booksellers recently, and I said, ‘What are young people buying?’ They said, ‘They’re buying great big fat Victorian novels.’ Who would have thought that?”Birding can nevertheless appear to be a rather niche interest. To those who do not quite grasp the appeal: “I don’t think it’s a question of what birders are seeing that you’re not. It’s a question of what they’re feeling that you’re not,” she says.“So maybe you should take some magic mushrooms. Because it all comes down to passion. Most of what we do in our lives we think it’s reason; we think it’s something that you can put into an argument. But everything begins with emotion.”View image in fullscreen‘Utopia is impossible, but if you don’t believe in the ability to attain something better, you will inevitably end up in a dystopia. Because dystopia is quite possible,’ Atwood says.Photograph: Leyland Cecco/The GuardianAtwood has spent much of her career examining the implications of societies that allow their freedoms and ecosystems to erode. But she is also a critic of those who neglect the relationship between humans and the natural world, cautioning that neglecting one can have dire consequences for the other.“It’s easy, for example, to raise money for kidneys. Because people think: ‘Everybody’s got kidneys. I’ve got kidneys. If anything happened to my kidneys, I would want there to be a kidney facility for me,” she says.“But people don’t make that immediate connection between their bodies and the natural world. There’s so much research that shows just how beneficial it is for our bodies to spend time in nature.”Indeed, Atwood’s writing has long contained a warning that societies can allow the systems that sustain them to erode, often recognising only too late what was lost.“Utopia is impossible, but if you don’t believe in the ability to attain something better, you will inevitably end up in a dystopia. Because dystopia is quite possible,” she says.“Or to put it another way, we’re much better at creating hell than we are at creating heaven. Although I also think heaven would be quite boring.”

title: Ai Weiwei unveils his epic new Australian work: ‘90% of art is just garbage. Real art questions the existing order’ | Ai Weiwei | The Guardian
description: From his farm in Portugal, the acclaimed artist speaks about war, peace, the state of the world – and his 40 metre sculpture Mushrooms, on Sydney Harbour
Author: Michael Donkor
Headline: From his farm in Portugal, the acclaimed artist speaks about war, peace, the state of the world – and his 40 metre sculpture Mushrooms, on Sydney Harbour
Content: ‘People want you to behave, want you to be a nice guy’: Ai Weiwei, whose work Mushrooms is on show outside the Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘People want you to behave, want you to be a nice guy’: Ai Weiwei, whose work Mushrooms is on show outside the Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianAi WeiweiAi Weiwei unveils his epic new Australian work: ‘90% of art is just garbage. Real art questions the existing order’From his farm in Portugal, the acclaimed artist speaks about war, peace, the state of the world – and his 40 metre sculpture Mushrooms, on Sydney HarbourMichael DonkorThu 24 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 21.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s like a film set. Like it’s not real,” the bemused Uber driver says as we pass through a succession of silent rural villages washed with milky sunlight. He’s right: signs of human life are weirdly absent during our windy journey through the Alentejo. I’m making my way to Ai Weiwei’s secluded farm, nestled deep in the Portuguese countryside, where arguably the world’s best known living artist has quietly lived for the last six years.When I arrive, I am ushered inside a vast cathedral of a building, a replica of Ai’s erstwhile, andcontroversially demolished, studio in Shanghai. The space is cavernous. It’s gridded by huge wooden columns and its dizzyingly high ceilings are webbed with beams. There is no artwork on the walls, nor are there any obvious signs of production or activity.Margaret Preston: Australia’s most beloved and contested artist?Read more“People say, what is this building for?Forwhat? Fuck that. Maybe it’sfornothing,” Ai tells me with a shrug. “It’s empty. And emptiness, people cannot accept.”Ai has been busy filling other vacant spaces: I’m visiting him to chat about the unveiling of his latest work, Mushrooms, this year’s Neil Balnaves Tallawoladah Lawn Commission outside Sydney’s Museum of Contemporary Art. Characteristically epic, elliptical and urgent, this installation is 40 metres in length, and consists of 500 identical cast iron sculptures of combat helmets on an elevated platform. The title alludes to the visual rhyme between mushroom caps and the shape of the helmets – as well as the fungal associations with decay, death and the fragility of life, brutally exposed by armed conflict.View image in fullscreenAi Weiwei’s Mushrooms, outside the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) in Sydney on the Tallawoladah Lawn.Photograph: Anna Kucera“Curiosity” and “boredom” generally shape Ai’s creativity, and the origins of this particular commission are “very simple”. In 2015, Ai began work on Human Flow,his documentary on the migrant crisis for which he and his team travelled to 23 countries. The process of producing this film led him to reflect more deeply on the causes of these perilous mass movements across the globe: war – or more specifically, the mechanics and munitions involved in contemporary warfare.“I studied for two years to understand the military, arsenals, who designs bombs, and how they are used. Then, when Russia threatened Ukraine and Ukraine asked for help from Germany, the German chancelloroffered them 5,000 helmets. I laughed,” Ai says. “I thought, wow, that’s interesting. So, at the beginning of the conflict, you can say Germany or Europe did not understand the nature of the war.”View image in fullscreenMushrooms consists of 500 identical cast iron sculptures of combat helmets, with the title alluding to fungal associations with decay, death and the fragility of life.Photograph: Anna KuceraLast year, Ai also visited Ukrainian soldiers on the frontline four times. He scrolls through his iPhone and shows me pictures and footage he took during his time there: Ai being taught how to use a rifle, the troops sporting uniforms he had embroidered with motifs of sunflowers. He plans to use these clips in an upcoming film.But he is keen that I do not simply see these experiences and this background as research for the new MCA piece. “I never prepare my life so I can make an artwork – or create artwork for my life,” he says. Mushrooms was also shaped by its future home, “a beautiful location” that he has visited several times, with a dramatic view of the Sydney Opera House. That interested him too: “That building represents rational, peaceful enjoyment … but at the same time we have to re-announce that there are wars going on and peace is essential for any civilised society.”His choice of words – “re-announce” – is striking. Throughout our conversation, over green tea, Ai seems despairing about a collective and cold amnesia about the parlous state of our geopolitics; if not amnesia, our deliberate refusal to truly engage with the doomed state of our world. “We cannot be blind, we cannot say I don’t know the situation,” he says. “You know the situation and you just pretend you don’t know it.” When speaking about the genocide in Gaza, he seems, too, deeply concerned about the lack of connectedness within modernity, our failure to understand that “if injustice happens to one person, it happens to the whole of humanity as well”. Much of his art, not least his trip to the battlefields ofKharkiv, seems an attempt to reestablish a connection and commitment to other human beings, however difficult and dangerous that might be.View image in fullscreenMushrooms was also shaped by its ‘beautiful location’ with a dramatic view of the Sydney Opera House.Photograph: Anna KuceraCan art play some role in offering him hope about the future of humanity? No, he says, typically pugnacious and plain speaking: “Art today is very corrupted – 90% of what we see in most institutions, or in so-called artistic circles, I think is just garbage. Real art questions the existing order.Artis not about representing so-called beauty, but rather to question the existing judgment about everything in politics, in life, in personal relations, in individual judgment – but this kind of art is never encouraged. People want you to behave, want you to be a nice guy, pleasant, cheerful, enjoying your life. And so most work we see in the museums is very decorative and sentimental, rather than having any relations to human struggle and our reality.”The Chinese word for mushroom is 蘑菇 or mógū, a term often associated with slowness, delay and dawdling. While our discussion regularly returned to Ai’s dissatisfaction with the tardy pace of societal and institutional progress, the conversation itself was leisurely. Despite describing himself as “the most interviewed human being” and claiming to have been interviewed “more than 1,000 times”, he is generous, fleetingly mischievous – and often startlingly wise. I’m curious, after Mushrooms, where his interests might take him next. But his existence is not so teleological: he has no “goals”.“The only thing we should try to do,” he says, “is live a life which can naturally capture the light.”Ai Weiwei’s Mushrooms is free to visit now on the Tallawoladah Lawn at the Museum of Contemporary Art in SydneyExplore more on these topicsAi WeiweiSydneyArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Channel 5’s revival of Play for Today goes wild | Television | The Guardian
description: The drama series continues with an ill-fated camping trip. Plus: Graham Norton’s chatshow returns with Tom Cruise. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The drama series continues with an ill-fated camping trip. Plus: Graham Norton’s chatshow returns with Tom Cruise. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Refreshing … Play for Today: Wild.Photograph: Andrew JohnstonView image in fullscreenRefreshing … Play for Today: Wild.Photograph: Andrew JohnstonTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Channel 5’s revival of Play for Today goes wildThe drama series continues with an ill-fated camping trip. Plus: Graham Norton’s chatshow returns with Tom Cruise. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Jack Seale,Graeme Virtue,Priya Elan,Hollie RichardsonandSimon WardellFri 25 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlay for Today: Wild9pm, Channel 5Another series of Channel 5’s revival of the famed Play for Today strand begins with this comedy drama starring Amit Shah,Joel Fry and Daniel Mays as three university mates whose annual wild camping trip is the setting for midge attacks, lost phones and festering grievances. The characters are broadly drawn and their mishaps predictable, but it’s still refreshing in these tough TV times to see a channel maintaining a platform for standalone original drama.Phil HarrisonGeorge Clarke’s Amazing Spaces: First Home8pm, Channel 4The gentle mackem continues his vaguely dystopian quest to find and celebrate British people who have had to improvise because normal houses are unaffordable. Leading the way are a young couple who plan to live in a converted bus. In Cornwall, meanwhile, could some old toilets become viable homes?Jack SealeYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaThe kooky whodunnit starring Brooke Shields as a murder-solving novelist wraps up its first season with an impulsive road trip to track down the missing mom of sidekick Andi (Amalia Williamson). The Thelma and Louise vibes are soon scuppered by an undercover assassin in hot pursuit.Graeme VirtueThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneAfter Negan and Maggie’s big conversation last week, she has upped sticks to Manhattan (inside the Statue of Liberty’s nose, to be precise) while Negan is zoning out playing Gears of War 2 (an Easter egg for The Walking Dead diehards). The wall drawings Maggie comes across suggest that this semi-peace is about to be horribly interrupted.Priya ElanLive from the Lycett Arms10pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenCheeky pint … Joe Lycett.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PAWell, no one has shut it down yet!Joe Lycettcontinues to keep the drinks, comedy and general shenanigans flowing in his newly opened pub. As is now the custom, he’ll be joined by a pair of celebrity guests – one to run the bar, the other to lean on it.Hollie RichardsonThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneGraham Nortoncontinues to snag the big guests as this evergreen chatshow returns. It begins with Tom Cruise, Florence Pugh, Lolly Adefope and John Bishop arranged awkwardly on his couch – and also features a musical performance from Emeli Sandé.PHFilm choice28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (Nia DaCosta, 2026),9pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenBizarrely moving … Ralph Fiennes as Dr Kelson in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.Photograph: Sony Pictures EntertainmentFor the second instalment of the post-pandemic horror trilogy,Nia DaCostatakes the directorial reins from Danny Boyle for a poignant yet surprisingly funny tale, which largely shuns the series’ rabid terror in favour of pathos and a tiny sliver of hope. Teenager Spike (Alfie Williams) has been captured by Jack O’Connell’s disturbed satanic cult leader, Jimmy, and his gang. Meanwhile, Dr Kelson (the inestimable Ralph Fiennes) develops a bizarrely moving relationship with an infected man, Samson (Chi Lewis-Parry).Simon WardellLive sportPremiership rugby union: Northampton v Newcastle7pm,TNT Sports 1. From Franklin’s Gardens.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightJoe LycettGraham NortonChannel 5DramaEntertainment TVTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius? | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon
Content: Kylie performing in 2000.Photograph: Paul Bergen/RedfernsView image in fullscreenKylie performing in 2000.Photograph: Paul Bergen/RedfernsBook of the dayPop and rockReviewCan’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius?The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie iconJack ParlettFri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 02.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘There’s an anxiety in declaring oneself a Kylie fan,” wrote the late San Francisco poet Kevin Killian (who nonetheless once published an entire collection devoted to the singer). Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmament has often felt more precarious than that of other artists, perhaps because of her past as a soap star, and the schmaltz of some of her early material with Stock Aitken Waterman.But she has always displayed a canny self-awareness, alongside a willingness to push the envelope. It’s evident in her knowing rendition of I Should Be So Lucky as a bad poem at the Royal Albert Hall in 1996, and her many collaborations with experimental dance producers. Then there’s her instinct for giving fans what they want: inarguable bangers, like those of her 2000s imperial phase, that also possess an offbeat, idiosyncratic quality, true of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and of her 2023 viral hit, Padam Padam.Michael Cragg’s illuminating new book explores Kylie’s multiple selves, her talent for shapeshifting, and the question of why she has been persistently underrated. He makes the case that the most easily maligned aspects of her music – frivolity without subtext, fun without an underlying seriousness – are precisely what makes it so pleasurable and available for camp reclamation, its apparent disposability capable of being recast as a virtue.double quotation markThis project is unambiguously the work of a superfan and scholar of popThe Aussie girl next door is thus a different kind of gay icon to club kid Madonna, a grittier figure who looms large here, and whose own acts of reinvention have been considered not just the work of an entertainer, but of an auteur. This comparison is also a matter of taste, of course; in a particularly juicy quote included in the chapter on Kylie’s appeal among gay audiences, singer Rufus Wainwright describes her “as the anti-Madonna. She is what she is and there is no attempt to make quasi-intellectual statements to substantiate it. She is the gay shorthand for joy.”As to what makes a gay icon, Cragg nimbly tackles the question by including a committee of different voices on the subject, just as he threads his chapters through with interviews. These generate intriguing discoveries and esoteric insights from people as diverse as textile designers, academics and film-makers, all of whose work has been informed by Kylie in some way. While this can slightly disrupt the flow of the book, it also captures the communal ethos that is key to fandom.Cragg’s prose is appealingly breezy, its register more Popjusticethan Pitchfork, but never less than earnest. This projectis unambiguously the work of a superfan and scholar of pop, for whom the question of Kylie’s legacy is a high-stakes one. His book is animated by a level of devotion that may not be unique to queer culture, but is certainly one of its hallmarks. There are many reasons we worship our icons in precisely the ways we do, and Cragg’s personal disclosures about his mental health, his early experiences of the closet, and his relationship with his husband provide a touching backdrop to this portrait of why Kylie matters. As does the section reflecting on Kylie’s breast cancer, how it humanised her in the public eye, fostering greater awareness of the disease and underlining the importance of early screening.That an artist like this has the ability to bring people together might seem like an obvious point, but Cragg urges us not to underestimate “what an amazing service that is”. I finished his book with a newfound appreciation not only of her artistry, but of what she has meant to so many people. She is a singer whose generosity and mutability has allowed her fans to feel whatever they need to feel, nowhere more so than when she performs All the Lovers at her live shows, and arms sway in unison, the song’s lyrics capacious enough for multiple readings, about the adversities of queer life and all of those we have loved and lost.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJack Parlett is the author of Flamboyance: The Art of Burning Brightly (Granta).Can’t Get You Out of My Head: In Search of Kylie by Michael Cragg is published by Faber (£25). title: ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen
Content: Catherine Corless and Liam Neeson at the Dublin gala screening of The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: GEMC/GMD/BackgridView image in fullscreenCatherine Corless and Liam Neeson at the Dublin gala screening of The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: GEMC/GMD/BackgridMovies‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave filmCatherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screenRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 25 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTFirst published on Fri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiam Neesonstill remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign byCatherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”View image in fullscreenLiam Neeson, the producer of The Lost Children of Tuam, says he felt a deep sense of obligation to expose the truth.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDbIt prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.The result, nine years later, is The LostChildrenof Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961.View image in fullscreenCatherine Corless at the site of the former mother and baby home in Tuam, County Galway, where it is believed 796 infants were buried.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianAn international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children sincestarting work last year– the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died.It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions acrossIreland. Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it.View image in fullscreenMonica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, in a scene from The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: Element PicturesIn her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.”The film, based on theNew York Times article by Dan Barry, tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished.Early reviewsof the film, which was written byRebecca Lenkiewiczand directed byFrank Berry, say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actorMonica Dolangiving a powerful central performance.View image in fullscreenDirector Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson promote The Lost Children of Tuam in Toronto.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb“She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?”Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said.Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said.View image in fullscreenMonica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, with fellow actor Lalor Roddy, who plays a character called John, in a scene from the film.Photograph: Element Pictures“We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.”Berry, the director, said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.”This article was amended on 25 September 2026. The last image in the article is of Monica Dolan with Lalor Roddy, who plays John, not with Andrew Bennett, who plays Aidan Corless, as an earlier caption said.Explore more on these topicsFilmIrelandLiam NeesonChildrenCatholicismReligionChristianityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Table 17 review – a tasty romcom served with dazzle and cheek | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Marisha Wallace and Jamael Westman play exes who reconvene over dinner in Douglas Lyons’ sparky old-school charmer
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Marisha Wallace and Jamael Westman play exes who reconvene over dinner in Douglas Lyons’ sparky old-school charmer
Content: Dinner for two … Jamael Westman as Dallas and Marisha Wallace as Jada in Table 17 at Kiln theatre.Photograph: Steve GregsonView image in fullscreenDinner for two … Jamael Westman as Dallas and Marisha Wallace as Jada in Table 17 at Kiln theatre.Photograph: Steve GregsonTheatreReviewTable 17 review – a tasty romcom served with dazzle and cheekKiln theatre, LondonMarisha Wallace and Jamael Westman play exes who reconvene over dinner in Douglas Lyons’ sparky old-school charmerArifa AkbarFri 25 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis incorrigibly likable romcom comes to the UK with a series of sold out runs in New York and Los Angeles in its wake. You can see why: it slips down as easily and pleasantly as an old-school, Saturday-night TV meet-cute. Except writer Douglas Lyons’ story is a meet-again-cute because the couple at its centre are exes.It has been several years since air steward Jada (Marisha Wallace) and aspiring music producer Dallas (Jamael Westman) felt the sting of each other’s betrayals. Now they are sitting at table 17 to hash out unfinished business – and maybe relight the fire?We first meet them moments before the nervy reunion. What plays out is sparky fun, spanning the couple’s history in a similar manner to Nick Payne’s Constellations, sliding from present to past and back.Its ambition to double up as a serious relationship drama is not always met because of the imbalance of cutesy humour. The play treads similar ground to such recently successful romantic two-handers as Benedict Lombe’sShiftersbut is not as emotionally freighted, and nor does it have the larger social framework. The point here, it seems, is to entertain with comedy and elicit sentiment from romance.It works to please the crowd and melt your heart a little by the end, the actors raising the effect of the too-soft humour to make lines sound more sparkling than they are. Unfaithful acts and insecurities generate the drama, although this couple remain a little too generic.Under the direction of Zhailon Levingston, the dazzle around the script does a good job, from the music (Chaka Khan’s I’m Every Woman and some nostalgic 90s numbers) to sharp lighting design by Matt Haskins and freeze-frames that denote movement between present and past. Amy Jane Cook’s set design is the most dazzling of all – a horseshoe-shaped banquette, jauntily positioned, that revolves through the timelines and a sultry stage lit up by neon.View image in fullscreenShow-stealer … Michael Rishawn.Photograph: Steve GregsonThere are plenty of cheeky theatrical touches as Wallace and Westman make lightning-quick work of returning to the past and changing costumes, as well as giving soul-baring asides to us, in the middle of an emotionally dissembling scene. Michael Rishawn, who takes on several ancillary parts, almost steals the show with his gay restaurant host, who has a backstory of unwelcome singledom that you want to hear more about – maybe more so than the break-up-make-up drama of the couple.Still, there is great, energetic acting from the leads: the always magnetic Wallace, in a non-singing role here, oozes charisma although you do want her to burst into song in the vein of the Kiln’s previous romantic two-hander,Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York). Westman fills Dallas with life, sensitively balancing his ridiculousness with his depth of emotional injury.It’s feelgood fare that has you rooting for the couple, and leaves you thinking that in spite of their mutual hurt, they may just be meeting up again this time next year.AtKiln theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Kiln theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Phil Wang: Uh Oh review – how to achieve an eighth of an orgasm, and other millennial myths | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The standup delivers older and wiser musings and mockery, whether it’s about taches, a passion for Gail’s or a distaste for cyclists
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: The standup delivers older and wiser musings and mockery, whether it’s about taches, a passion for Gail’s or a distaste for cyclists
Content: ‘Revelling in life’s mundanity’ … Phil Wang.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreen‘Revelling in life’s mundanity’ … Phil Wang.Photograph: Matt StrongeComedyReviewPhil Wang: Uh Oh review – how to achieve an eighth of an orgasm, and other millennial mythsSoho Theatre Walthamstow, LondonThe standup delivers older and wiser musings and mockery, whether it’s about taches, a passion for Gail’s or a distaste for cyclistsAnya RyanFri 25 Sep 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLots has changed in the world ofPhil Wangsince his last tour. He has mastered the art of growing a moustache, for one. He’s bought a house in a “cool” part of London, where he lives with his houseplants and, oh, the world has tipped considerably to the right. So what does this mean for the ever-even-tempered comedian, now officially in the territory of an ageing millennial?Largely, more of the observational routines that have made his name. We get his classic riffs on what it means to be both British and Chinese, his thoughts on gentrification – you best believe he wants a Gail’s in Peckham – and his resentment at finding his views becoming progressively less progressive. All of it is gently mocking: mainly of himself, but of others, too, to varying degrees of effect. A bit about cyclists, who are apparently asking for a death wish by venturing out on a 2D vehicle, feels more snarky than he may have intended. But his David Bowie impression could use a stage all of its own.It might not push the boundaries. But, at his heights, Wang is a king of linguistics and loopholes. Why, he asks, is being described as a person of colour perfectly acceptable, but “coloured person” deeply offensive? Of course he thinks about his girlfriend when he masturbates – it’s just that his mind wanders to whether she will walk in and catch him doing it. Revelling in life’s mundanity, he makes it bloom into material.‘Audiences no longer laugh if you call their town crap’: can Phil Wang heal divided Britain?Read moreIt is a show strung together by the nagging feeling that things have got worse. Long gone are the days of sweeping millennial myths, when we were told we could achieve one-eighth of an orgasm through a spidery hand gesture performed by our classmates. Now, he’s at the stage of mourning the loss of his once-slender neck. There’s something bleakly moving about Wang’s grownup outlook: the realisation that everything he thought those wild parties and long conversations with his parents were leading to was actually just the thing. It’s a lesson in living in the moment. And a taste of the halcyon days of youth comes at the close of a pondering show, if not a consistently revelatory one.On tour until 23 MayExplore more on these topicsComedyPhil WangSoho theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: English National Ballet: Rhythm Riot review – this triple whammy brings zing, grit and chills | Dance | The Guardian
description: A trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanship
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: A trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanship
Content: Peppy energy … Daniel McCormick and Swanice Luong in Symphony in Three Movements from Rhythm Riot.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeppy energy … Daniel McCormick and Swanice Luong in Symphony in Three Movements from Rhythm Riot.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewEnglish National Ballet: Rhythm Riot review – this triple whammy brings zing, grit and chillsSadler’s Wells, LondonA trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanshipLyndsey WinshipFri 25 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDamn, there was some amazing dance going on in mid-20th century New York. You had George Balanchine forging a new American ballet, all slick speed and striking angles, and in Harlem there was the Cotton Club and the Savoy, swinging dancefloors and entertainers like the legendaryNicholas Brothers, of whom Balanchine was a fan. There’s a taste of this world in English National Ballet’s latest triple bill, with a distinctly American flavour and a focus on propulsive rhythm.Balanchine’s Symphony in Three Movements was made in 1972 as a memorial to Stravinsky, although the eponymous music is from 1945. Balanchine and Stravinsky were an absolute dream team, architects of multiple masterpieces. Here the clarity of line and stripped-back nature of the design crossed with the depth and crunchy complexity of Stravinsky’s score is a perfect balance. There’s palpable power from the pit, with theEnglish National BalletPhilharmonic relishing the music under the baton of Maria Seletskaja.The choreography has peppy energy as Swanice Luong arrives with a zing in a bubblegum pink leotard, bouncing into a jazzy tuck jump like a Gap advert. She, Emma Hawes and Ksenia Ovsyanick are like a trio of mean girls competing to be queen bee. Sharp of gesture and brilliant of smile, Ovsyanick is particularly aloof. It’s such a specific technique and ENB aren’t a Balanchine company, but they do it justice.View image in fullscreenImmensely enjoyable … Micaela Taylor’s Bow Out.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe spirit of the Nicholas Brothers arrives in a new piece, Bow Out, by American choreographer Micaela Taylor, inspired by the showstopping tap duo’s acrobatics in the 1943 film Stormy Weather. It’s an exuberant blend of classical, jazz, hip-hop, tap and Lindy hop, in soft shoes and black tailcoats, to a soundtrack of jazz, clattering tap beats, and new music by Philip Patrick Harper Bucknor, AKA Tru. Taylor bounces off the syncopation, hooking tightly into the rhythm or squeezing out the juice between the beats while the dancers snatch movements from the air. There’s precision, virtuosity and showmanship, but also something more ominous: disillusionment, farewell, a grittier texture, and showbusiness itself almost becomes its own character. An immensely enjoyable and intriguing debut from Taylor.View image in fullscreenVibes piece … Ksenia Ovsyanick and Daniel McCormick in Auguries of Innocence by Jae Man Joo.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAnother premiere comes from a choreographer who’s been working in New York for 30 years but hails from Korea, Jae Man Joo. It’s thoroughly of the now in the sense that this is a vibes piece that harnesses lots of ritualistic mass-unison movement and creates an intense, immersive world through atmospheric visuals and score. The soundtrack is two works by Latvian composer Pēteris Vasks (plus some Korean beopgogongyang drumming), outwardly emotive, strung-out strings that signify angst and melodrama, but the whole piece is so committed to its aesthetic that somehow it works.Everything is black – costumes and artfully distressed backdrop – and Sangeun Lee is like a goth Miss Havisham in bedraggled black ballgown, a ghostly figure haunting the stage. Joo’s piece is named after theWilliam Blakepoem Auguries of Innocence, a meditation on the moral failures of man and our destruction of nature. The intricacies of Joo’s interpretation are mostly lost to a first-time viewer, but there’s plenty to get to grips with in this finale to a wildly eclectic triple bill.AtSadler’s Wells, London, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceEnglish National BalletSadler's WellsBalletGeorge BalanchineIgor StravinskyWilliam BlakereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Farmer’s Wife review – a bumper crop of tenderness, toil and female strength | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Inspired by Helen Rebanks’ bestselling memoir, Hannah Khalil’s play foregrounds the women holding everything together
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: Inspired by Helen Rebanks’ bestselling memoir, Hannah Khalil’s play foregrounds the women holding everything together
Content: Outstanding in their field … Christine Entwisle and Eireann Devlin in The Farmer's Wife.Photograph: Steve GregsonView image in fullscreenOutstanding in their field … Christine Entwisle and Eireann Devlin in The Farmer's Wife.Photograph: Steve GregsonTheatreReviewThe Farmer’s Wife review – a bumper crop of tenderness, toil and female strengthTheatre by the Lake, KeswickInspired by Helen Rebanks’ bestselling memoir, Hannah Khalil’s play foregrounds the women holding everything togetherArusa QureshiFri 25 Sep 2026 06.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile anthropologists have made links between farming and the rise of patriarchal social structures, it’s impossible to deny the role that women have historically played in the agricultural workforce. In The Farmer’s Wife,Hannah Khalil’s new play inspired byHelen Rebanks’ bestselling memoirof the same name, men are entirely absent from the narrative. The focus, instead, is squarely on the women quietly holding everything together – who are usually anonymous and often unseen.The story follows three generations of women living on a family farm, their unrelenting daily workload drawing attention to the cracks that exist in a system entrenched in tradition and routine. The trio of women, simply referred to as Young, Older and Oldest, are played tenaciously by Eireann Devlin, Christine Entwisle and Roberta Kerr respectively. They hold both the heaviness and joy of an existence rooted in the land, which can be unforgiving, particularly in the context of a rapidly changing world.View image in fullscreenRoberta Kerr as Oldest.Photograph: Steve GregsonThis in-the-round production presents one day on the farm – a day that seems to have some significance to the family, although we’re not privy to why until the very end. As Older maniacally rushes around to get everything ready, it’s hard to ignore the feeling of claustrophobia that creeps in when pieces of the family kitchen are wheeled on and placed in the corners of the stage, peppered with supplies, crockery and utensils.Louie Whitemore’s inventive set, combined with Mark Melville’s highly affecting sound design, contribute to the depiction of this rural scene as something inexplicable and otherworldly. For example, when a flurry of paperwork falls from the ceiling as Older drowns in the weight of responsibility, or when the excited bark of an imagined dog reverberates around the stage and in the wings, as the characters scramble to catch this invisible, yet completely vivid, being.View image in fullscreenThe kitchen table becomes a stage in The Farmer’s Wife.Photograph: Steve GregsonAt the centre of the action is an unassuming wooden kitchen table, which bears witness to the monotony of farm life, with never-ending bills and chores, and moments that alter the course of the characters’ lives. It becomes a battleground for the conflict between mothers and daughters, but also a literal stage, for a Shakespearean monologue and a rowdy rendition of I Will Survive.Through these contrasts, as well as emotional flashbacks, Liz Stevenson’s direction underlines the tumultuous nature of farm and family life. But in the end, community proves to be key, and in its moving finale The Farmer’s Wife emphasises the true power of perseverance and camaraderie.AtTheatre By the Lake, Keswick, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreFarmingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the defiant queer dancehall of Destin Conrad and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Every one of the Grammy-nominated Floridian’s songs reveal a different side of him. His latest album, Roadrunner, is all languid reggae basslines and come-hither lyricism
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: Every one of the Grammy-nominated Floridian’s songs reveal a different side of him. His latest album, Roadrunner, is all languid reggae basslines and come-hither lyricism
Content: ‘Celebrating his Jamaican roots and queer identity’ … Destin Conrad.Photograph: RyderView image in fullscreen‘Celebrating his Jamaican roots and queer identity’ … Destin Conrad.Photograph: RyderAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the defiant queer dancehall of Destin Conrad and the week’s best new tracksEvery one of the Grammy-nominated Floridian’s songs reveal a different side of him. His latest album, Roadrunner, is all languid reggae basslines and come-hither lyricismOlive Pometsey,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 25 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromTampa, FloridaRecommended if you likeKwn, Tyla, OdealUp nextPerforming in Dallas, Texas, 1 NovemberDestin Conrad has had a busy couple of years: three albums, one Grammy nomination and a string of collaborations with fellow R&B up-and-comers such as Bellah and Nia Smith. Pick any record and you’ll hear a different side of the 26-year-old. His spring 2025 debut Love on Digital pays its dues to the genre that raised him while swerving derivative cliches with small production quirks – a vocal glitch here, a skittering Jersey beat there. Last summer’s Whimsy is a sprawling alt-jazz album that waswritten in two weeks, inspired by his time in a high-school jazz choir. A year later, Roadrunner arrived as a celebration of his Jamaican roots and queer identity – all languid reggae basslines, gyrating dancehall rhythms, drinks-in-the-air swagger and come-hither lyricism.Roadrunner doesn’t gloss over reggae and dancehall’s history of homophobia, nor does it simply condemn it. On Chi Chi, Conrad interpolates the notorious chorus of TOK’s Chi-Chi Man, flipping its calls to burn anyone seen driving with gay men into a brag: “Yes, I know they don’t wanna see me drivin’ / So I make sure I drive off in a Benzy.” He makes defiance against bigotry seem easy – fun, even – and spends the rest of the album revelling in that freedom. “I know I make them nervous,” he winks over the throbbing sub-bass of Nervous. “You want fi control me,” he moans on Obsessed. Granted, those last two lines are about flexing on peers and teasing lovers. But what’s a turn up without a little bump and grind?Olive PometseyThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenMadonna and Charli xcx.Photograph: Ricardo GomesMadonna and Charli xcx – Danceteria Afterhours“I get off the train, Hackney Wick / I’m sweet 15 in a weird outfit”: Charli blends her origin story into the Confessions II highlight, PC Music and “flavoured cocaine” mingling with Basquiat and Haoui Montaug.LSJane Remover – Beauty SleepHeavily compressed even by her standards, the US singer-producer condenses her digicore-hyperpop style into a seething, tinny cube of sound – but graces it with one of her loveliest melodic top lines.BBTLily Konigsberg – Free ByrdIf your song centres around the word “free”, it’d better feel that way. Konigsberg fulfils the brief with a winsome, characterful indie jangler about betting on herself over a too-safe relationship.LSTegan and Sara – Our Year (ft Lights)Another song eyeing the exits, set to wistful, jewel-toned synths and balmy horizon fantasias that make the Quin twins’ notion of quitting a tired town almost viscerally alluring.LS​Catherine Elicson – FigureThe front person of estimable Philly garage rock band Empath strikes out solo, defugging her band’s haze for a plaintive ballad on lo-fi electric guitar, with Vini Reilly-ish soloing.BBTMorphine – CocoonFrom a forthcoming rarities album, Cocoon revels in the sleazy, disarmingly seductive brew of sax, idle crooning and heavy bass that made the Boston band – and late frontman Mark Sandman – so brilliant.LSSpace Afrika – Pretty Gospel (ft Kiala Ogawa)Surfacing out of the cold, slow currents of ambient, post-rock and dub on the Mancunians’ new album Quiet Storm is this jazz ballad, with Ogawa’s kindly yet melancholy vocals reminiscent of Cleo Sol.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hallé/Wong review – MacMillan’s new symphony centres a great concert hall’s birthday celebrations | Classical music | The Guardian
description: James MacMillan’s sixth symphony proved an intricate, intriguing and forward-looking work. It was well paired with Stephen Hough’s exuberant ‘Emperor’ piano concerto and a Liszt rarity
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: James MacMillan’s sixth symphony proved an intricate, intriguing and forward-looking work. It was well paired with Stephen Hough’s exuberant ‘Emperor’ piano concerto and a Liszt rarity
Content: Britain’s best acoustic? … Manchester’s Bridgewater Hall, with the Hallé orchestra.Photograph: Alex Burns/HalléView image in fullscreenBritain’s best acoustic? … Manchester’s Bridgewater Hall, with the Hallé orchestra.Photograph: Alex Burns/HalléClassical musicReviewHallé/Wong review – MacMillan’s new symphony centres a great concert hall’s birthday celebrationsBridgewater Hall, ManchesterJames MacMillan’s sixth symphony proved an intricate, intriguing and forward-looking work.  It was well paired with Stephen Hough’s exuberant ‘Emperor’ piano concerto and a Liszt rarityAlexandra CoghlanFri 25 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe complain a lot about concert halls in the UK. The acoustics of the Barbican, Royal Festival Hall and Royal Albert Hall; the practicality of Usher Hall and St George’s Bristol;thoseseats at Snape Maltings, andthatfoyer at Birmingham’s Symphony Hall. But do we really have it so bad?As Manchester’s Hallé opens its season with a celebration of 30 years of the Bridgewater Hall, it’s a good moment to remember what we’ve gained in the three decades since a car park became Britain’s best acoustic. A flagship London hall may still be a fantasy, but with Gateshead’s Foster-designed Glasshouse, Saffron Hall, Kings Place and Milton Court all opening their doors since 2000, it’s hard to feel despondent.The Hallé and principal conductorKahchun Wongcelebrated their home’s birthday with a major new commission – James MacMillan’s sixth symphony. After a cycle of symphonies that seemed to work up to the choral epic of 2019’s fifth, the sixth feels like a new beginning.There are echoes of both Elgar’s Enigma Variations and Britten’s The Young Person’s Guide in a work that looks simultaneously in and out: inward to the family members who inspired four short, expositionary movements – the key to the wild parade that follows – and outward to the composers who inspired the fifth movement’s subsequent textural and formal manipulations.View image in fullscreenClever choices … Kahchun Wong conducts the Hallé.Photograph: Alex Burns/HalléThe effect is disorienting. There’s a pastoral, folk-inspired trio of flutes, a buzzing swarm of muted brass, a peal of gongs, bells and bowed vibraphone, and a yearning solo cello. And, standing apart from the rest, a Debussyean duet for harp and piano. How are we to assemble the fragments? Optimistically, MacMillan and an incisive Wong seem to urge. Low woodwind and trombones (together with a nagging siren) may attempt to pull us under, but surging life-force in brass-gilded climaxes pushes valiantly back. Tempests rage, but the still, small voice of the alto flute gently persists.What a clever choice to frame the symphony with a rare performance of Liszt’s compact epic Les Préludes (brass resplendent in the narrative highs, strings fretting convulsively in the lows) and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No 5: battles, both, for man’s survival and supremacy. Perhaps egged on by this cumulative energy, we got a more robust “Emperor” from soloist Stephen Hough than usual, his opening cadenza flinging down a gauntlet gleefully plucked up by Wong and his players in a heroic duel that climaxed in an exuberant, close-combat finale.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicHallé OrchestraJames MacMillanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I never choose the cautious option’: Royal Opera’s Jakub Hrůša on collaboration, control and conducting Wagner | Classical music | The Guardian
description: One year into the role, the Royal Opera’s music director is taking on the challenge of Parsifal, and, next season, the Ring Cycle. I’m here, and I am courageous says the conductor
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: One year into the role, the Royal Opera’s music director is taking on the challenge of Parsifal, and, next season, the Ring Cycle. I’m here, and I am courageous says the conductor
Content: ‘Theatre is a way to get to the core of an important question about our lives’ … Jakub Hrůša.Photograph: Charlie CliftView image in fullscreen‘Theatre is a way to get to the core of an important question about our lives’ … Jakub Hrůša.Photograph: Charlie CliftClassical musicInterview‘I never choose the cautious option’: Royal Opera’s Jakub Hrůša on collaboration, control and conducting WagnerErica JealOne year into the role, the Royal Opera’s music director is taking on the challenge of Parsifal, and, next season, the Ring Cycle. I’m here, and I am courageous says the conductorFri 25 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘You can choose the cautious option – or you can take the full risk and just go and conduct. Maybe I would like the cautious option, but I never choose it.” Jakub Hrůša learned to trust his instincts at the Royal Opera House back in 2022 when he conducted his first ever Wagner opera –Lohengrin– there,describing the experienceas “one of the absolute highlights of my life”. Now he’s a year into his role as the house’s music director and about to conduct his first Parsifal, staged by Evgeny Titov. And next season there’ll be yet more Wagner firsts when he conducts complete cycles of the Ring asstaged by Barrie Kosky. For most conductors, this would be a gradual process, adding the four Ring operas to their repertoire one by one, but not for Hrůša: he’ll be conducting his first Das Rheingold, Die Walküre, Siegfried and Götterdämmerung all in the space of a week.“Is it too bold? I find it wonderful!” he says. “I could have chosen to do it in my own way, in 10 years’ time, somewhere else – but I’m here, I’m the music director, the Ring should be done and wants to be done in its entirety, and I am courageous.”double quotation markThere’s so much a conductor can influence in a show: the energy, momentum, atmosphere, detail, security, freedom...Hrůša conducted Kosky’s staging ofCarmenhere in 2018, and they worked together at the 2024 Salzburg festival on Katya Kabanova by Janáček – another son of Brno, Hrůša’s home town.
